It also included a video that showed a horizontal crossed line through the No 7 as it is commonly written in Europe, suggesting that Ronaldo’s successors will all have that cross to bear when they wear the number.

Sports.title: Raphinha sees red as Brazil stunned by Japan while Argentina’s post-Messi era starts with defeat
Sports.content:
Raphinha was sent off as Brazil crashed to a 3-2 defeat by Japan in their international friendly in Singapore. The Barcelona captain had been substituted after 71 minutes, but was shown a red card after protesting against Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s stoppage-time winner on the touchline. The Brazil head coach, Carlo Ancelotti, was also sent off in a fractious ending to the match.

Japan went 2-0 up inside 20 minutes through Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura. Vinícius Júnior reduced the deficit in the 33rd minute and scored again to drag them level on 75 minutes, before Sakamoto’s controversial late winner.

Argentina’s post-Messi era began with a 2-1 defeat at home against Uruguay in Buenos Aires. The loss marked the World Cup finalists’ first match since Lionel Messi’s international retirement in early October.

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Nico Paz is crestfallen in Buenos Aires after a 2-1 defeat against Uruguay, the hosts’ first match since Lionel Messi’s international retirement. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

Leonardo Balerdi opened the scoring with an own goal in the 48th minute, before Maximiliano Araújo doubled Uruguay’s lead in the 53rd minute under their new coach, Diego Forlán. Julián Álvarez pulled one back for the hosts in the 73rd minute.

This clásico rioplatense on Friday also kicked off a new chapter for Argentina under Lionel Scaloni, who extended his contract to 2030 this week.

Messi’s retirement remains a fresh wound for local fans; notably, the La Bombonera stadium fell short of a sellout, a rare departure from the norm. While most supporters in the stands wore the albiceleste jersey with Messi’s No 10, Scaloni chose not to assign the number for the match. The coach explained he has yet to select a successor and as it is not mandatory he prefers to leave the jersey vacant for now.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On the pitch, Argentina lacked the explosive, incisive spark Messi typically produced in the final third. Neither Nicolás Paz nor Thiago Almada was able to fill that void. Argentina will hope to bounce back against Costa Rica in Córdoba on Tuesday, while Uruguay host the Dominican Republic on the same day.

Sports.title: John McGinn double saves Scotland’s blushes against North Macedonia
Sports.content:
A special occasion for Andy Robertson saw Scotland flirt with embarrassment. Collection of his 102nd cap moves him level with Kenny Dalglish in the all-time Scottish list. Robertson will soon be a record holder. This was, however, John McGinn’s night. A double from McGinn, the second a penalty, spared Scottish blushes against a North Macedonia team who threatened to administer red faces to those in navy blue.

This proved an almighty struggle for Scotland. Questions – and plenty of them – surround whether or not Sébastien Pocognoli can build on the excellent work of his predecessor Steve Clarke. For now, Scotland are a tough watch. Pocognoli looks tactically inflexible and this is not the new dawn many predicted.

“At times it wasn’t pretty,” admitted McGinn. The 32-year-old compared this Scotland process to a club team starting a new season. The rationale is fair enough, were this a remotely forgiving environment.

It was Robertson who led the dressing room inquest in the immediate aftermath of last month’s defeat to Slovenia. It is not in the Tottenham full-back’s make-up to personalise scenarios but shortcomings in the last international window, Pocognoli’s first as the Scotland manager, added to the sense that the bigger picture was important here. North Macedonia looked favourable visitors, having not scored a goal in eight outings.

Pocognoli could call upon Kieran Tierney, Scott McTominay and Ché Adams for the first time and deployed all three from the outset. It already appears the Belgian coach will not deviate from a back three. Ben Gannon-Doak took his place at right wingback, as is feasible against such weak opposition. Scotland’s approach will inevitably change for Monday’s meeting with Switzerland.

View image in fullscreen Andy Robertson, the Scotland captain, equalled Kenny Dalglish’s record of 102 caps. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Scotland had been ponderous until McTominay came within an excellent Stole Dimitrievski save of properly announcing his international return. The midfielder swivelled and struck, with Dimitrievski equal to the Napoli man’s effort.

Robertson was denied the opportunity to mark his special night with a goal by an errant whistle. The referee hauled play back for a Scotland free kick – McTominay had been upended – when the playing of advantage would have seen Robertson collect a Billy Gilmour pass in a scoring position. The Hampden crowd mumped and moaned, which rather summed up recent attitudes around this Scotland team. It feels as if the public are not yet fully engaged with Pocognoli’s project. Adams sought to lift the mood, the striker stooping for a header that took a deflection before Dimitrievski batted away.

In backing up their statistical position, North Macedonia were providing nothing by way of attacking threat. Their enjoyment came from frustrating the Scots. McTominay, who has previous for acrobatic excellence in this arena, tried a 34th minute bicycle kick that flew over the crossbar and Scotland’s most lively player tried again with a low shot which Dimitrievski blocked with his midriff. This lack of cutting edge was a Scottish concern long before Pocognoli entered the dugout. The boos that met the half-time whistle, seconds after North Macedonia had created their first chance of the evening, depicted a supporter base who remained unconvinced.

Less than a minute of the second half had been played when Gilmour produced one of the worst misses ever witnessed at this famous old venue. Calamity in the North Macedonia defence allowed Adams to steal in. The Torino striker laid the ball back to Gilmour six yards out and, with an open goal, he blazed his shot wildly over the bar. It was a genuine, utter howler.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Billy Gilmour reacts after shooting over from six yards against North Macedonia. Photograph: Russell Cheyne/Reuters

Route one broke the deadlock for Scotland. Ryan Porteous’s looping header from the halfway line caused panic in the North Macedonia defence. Adams capitalised, his pass to the advancing McGinn setting up the Aston Villa midfielder’s 23rd goal for his country. Relief was as obvious as celebration.

Although a North Macedonia response was not in the script, the equaliser epitomised Scottish slackness. A near post run from Elmin Rastoder saw him meet a menacing Enis Bardhi corner from the left. Angus Gunn in the home goal was helpless as Rastoder flicked home.

North Macedonia clearly now sensed Scottish vulnerability. While Pocognoli’s men continued to dominate the ball, North Macedonia’s counterattacking threat had increased. Officialdom, and sharp footwork from Gannon-Doak, were soon to come to Scotland’s rescue.

Gannon-Doak was instantly convinced of the foul by Dimitrievski after the Bournemouth man tried to skip past the goalkeeper. It took the VAR to inform the referee that the incident was worthy of further inspection. Intriguingly, it was not Oli McBurnie – still awaiting his maiden Scotland goal and on in place of Adams – who took the spot-kick. Up stepped McGinn, who made no mistake. While Gannon-Doak is due credit for winning the penalty, this appearance once more raised serious questions about his decision making.

That of the Scottish FA in hiring Pocognoli would be open to question had North Macedonia delivered a shock. That they did not do so spared Scotland ignominy. “It was not always perfect,” said Pocognoli. You aren’t kidding, Sébastien.

Sports.title: Youngsters will get their chance, Bruno Fernandes can thrive and touchline energy will be vital: Key lessons for Man United from incoming boss Mauricio Pochettino's 6-0 USA masterclass
Sports.content:
Youngsters will get their chance, Bruno Fernandes can thrive and touchline energy will be vital: Key lessons for Man United from incoming boss Mauricio Pochettino's 6-0 USA masterclass

Mauricio Pochettino enjoyed a stellar penultimate game in charge of the United States, thrashing Haiti 6-0.

The newly appointed Manchester United manager has just one game left before sinking his teeth into the job at Old Trafford.

He will link up with United on Wednesday, but first must navigate the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final tie with Haiti on Tuesday.

Here, Pochettino cut a fairly reserved figure on the touchline as he was rewarded for trusting youth - and even saw his team score from a corner, something United don't do much of these days.

Without further ado, here are four things Manchester United fans learned from the win.

Mauricio Pochettino, dressed in a scarf, was fairly reserved as the United States beat Haiti 6-0

Youth will get a chance

Pochettino’s arrival spells good news for United’s proud tradition of promoting homegrown youth - it is glad tidings for the likes of Shea Lacey and Kobbie Mainoo. You wonder if, for a while, JJ Gabriel will look on forlornly from Real Madrid’s reserves.

The Argentinian handed out 13 debuts in the September-October international break, including to eight teenagers in one 4-1 victory over Peru.

His strategy was no different here as he started 18-year-old Julian Hall up front and Diego Kochen, 20, in goal - both players he has given debuts to this year. He was rewarded, with Hall scoring his fourth goal in just five games for the United States, while Kochen kept a clean sheet.

Despite his affinity for the stars of tomorrow, he is a hard schoolmaster. In a column for The Athletic in 2022, he revealed that he sat a young Harry Kane down for a brutal meeting where he showed him stats and clips to justify why he wasn’t playing him more.

Pochettino had known Kane’s potential from their first training session but wanted the ‘tough conversation’ to get the best out of him. Kane went on to score 169 goals under him for Tottenham, and now he’s the best player in the world.

His trust in fresh faces could inject some much-needed enthusiasm around the club, strengthen the squad's connection with the fanbase, and increase the energy levels in one of the Premier League's oldest, most lethargic teams.

The likes of Shea Lacey will be delighted at how Pochettino puts trust in younger players

Julian Hall, 18, struck his fourth goal in five games for the United States under Pochettino

The perfect manager for Bruno Fernandes?

Pochettino has a history of getting the most out of attacking midfielders such as Dele Alli, Christian Eriksen, and Adam Lallana. You can add Cole Palmer to that list too, though he was primarily a right winger under him at Chelsea.

Manchester United desperately need him to get a tune out of Bruno Fernandes, who has cut a frustrated figure this season and whose creative efficiency has declined - though he still has nine goal involvements.

If Christian Pulisic’s performance against Haiti is anything to go by, Fernandes will be happy. The attacking midfielder scored twice, playing a free role and being given penalty duty.

The 28-year-old was also asked to muck in defensively, and that’s something Fernandes is willing to do. Across the seasons, he has often covered more ground than any of his team-mates.

Pochettino and Pulisic have seemingly had a distant relationship, despite the latter’s insistence to the contrary. The manager branded it ‘b*******’ when the AC Milan star opted out of the Gold Cup last year, and left him out of his selection a couple of months ago, bringing in 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan.

Asked about Pochettino's upcoming final game, Pulisic said at full-time: 'We're treating it like any other game.' No emotion on display.

Depending on how you interpret Fernandes - either a die-for-the-badge club servant or a primadonna - Pochettino could draw the best or worst out of the Portuguese.

Pochettino often gets the best out of attacking midfielders - will he work well with Bruno Fernandes?

He has had a distant relationship with Christian Pulisic, but the AC Milan star scored twice here

Defenders to push up high?

Pochettino tends to push his defensive lines high up the pitch and his strategy with the United States has been no different.

They were almost caught out for trying to play the offside trap early on as a simple ball from midfield sent Danley Jean Jacques through one-on-one, forcing Kochen into a good save.

Meanwhile, full-backs Antonee Robinson and Alex Freeman were constantly pushing high and overlapping in his 4-2-3-1 system - although you’d obviously expect a strong level of intent when they’re favourites against Haiti.

Given his high-line tradition, Pochettino may well favour more mobile defenders such as Leny Yoro and Patrick Dorgu.

The battle for Harry Maguire will be to convince his new boss that his other qualities compensate for his lack of pace.

Pochettino takes inspiration from the frenetic football of Marcelo Bielsa, who managed him at Newell’s Old Boys in Argentina.

But he'll have to balance his philosophy with the reality of United's woeful defensive record this campaign. Just the 15 goals conceded in the last five games...

Pochettino showed an eagerness to intervene early in the game - a possible boost after Michael Carrick suffered from slow starts

How will his touchline work compare to Carrick?

Pochettino is typically seen as an animated character on the touchline, in contrast to Carrick's statesmanlike behaviour, but he spent lots of time in his seat here.

He has calmed down somewhat these days - though he did kick a crate of bottles in frustration at the World Cup - and didn’t even react much when his team scored.

A major criticism of Carrick is that he takes too long to change things in-game, often going late with substitutions. Pochettino has traditionally leaned that way, too, but he was eager to influence proceedings here.

Even three minutes in, at a break while Antonee Robinson was being treated, he called Pulisic over for what looked like an intense tactical chat.

United have been plagued by slow starts this season, so it was encouraging to see Pochettino so alert and full of ideas early into the game. He could have coasted, really, but wanted to eke out every advantage.

Sports.title: England 78-15 Japan PLAYER RATINGS: What stopped five-try Will Joseph earning perfect score? Who was monstrous in the pack? And which star had an off day despite huge win?
Sports.content:
England thrashed Japan 78-15 on an emphatic day in London to keep their hopes of winning the Nations Championship alive.

Will Joseph scored a record-equalling five tries on his first Test start as England crossed the line 13 times on Eddie Jones' return to Twickenham.

Steve Borthwick made 12 changes from the side who thrashed Australia 45-22 and was rewarded with a barnstorming performance in his 50th Test as England head coach.

ALEX BYWATER was on hand to bring you our player ratings.

England player ratings

Freddie Steward – 7

Kicked well for Will Jospeh who caused carnage and then crashed over himself. Good in the air as usual but like his team, was never really tested.

Will Joseph – 9

Star man, ending with a mammoth five tries – a joint Twickenham record and run which included a 19-minute hat-trick. Awful defence down his wing must be taken into account.

Henry Slade – 7

One of the easiest Tests he will ever have. Took over on kicking duties from George Ford who struggled in that area.

Will Joseph was the star man with five tries as England thrashed Japan 7-15 - but he somewhat neglected his wing!

Max Ojomoh – 8

Did well to set up Joseph with a nice pass and was excellent at creating space for those outside him. England have a big call to make next week if Seb Atkinson is back fit.

Cadan Murley – 7

Joined the long list of try scorers on what was his first cap at Twickenham. Summed up his team’s hunger and clinical nature.

George Ford – 5

Given armchair ride against truly terrible opposition. Nice 50:22 kick in the second half but wasn’t accurate from the tee. Replaced by Marcus Smith.

Jack van Poortvliet – 7

Apart from an intercept, he went very well against Australia and continued on that theme. Replaced by debutant Archie McParland.

Ellis Genge – 8

Look frustrated at his team’s penalty decision to go for goal and took that anger out on Japan with some monstrously physical carrying and a try.

Ellis Genge took his anger out with some monstrously physical carrying and a try

Luke Cowan-Dickie – 6

Pounced like a cat for an impressive second-half turnover. Strong overall display blotted by yellow card.

Asher Opoku-Fordjour – 7

Was never made to work hard at scrum time. Didn’t do anything wrong but will likely not be involved against New Zealand.

Maro Itoje (capt) – 7

Took possession from a Japanese carrier like a candy from a baby. Hopefully it warmed him for the All Blacks who will be out for revenge after their Wales shock.

George Martin – 7

Got the scoreboard moving again when the game restarted. If Ollie Chessum isn’t ready for New Zealand, England will still be in safe (and big) hands.

Alex Coles – 7

He’s had a good year as an individual, even if England have struggled collectively at times. A certain World Cup squad member if fit.

On his second Test start, Henry Pollock had plenty of open space but we didn't see him in it

Ben Earl – 6

On the flank here instead of at No 8. Replaced early in the second half with far tougher tests to come. Greg Fisilau came on and was outstanding.

Henry Pollock – 6

Just his second Test start. Plenty of open space but we didn’t see him in it. Fine second-half recovery run and tackle.

Replacements: Archie McParland 6 (for Van Poortvliet 49), Greg Fisilau 9 (for Earl 52), Emmanuel Iyogun 7 (for Genge 52), Marcus Smith 8 (for Ford 58), Ben Curry 8 (for Pollock 58), Joe Heyes 7 (for Opoku-Fordjour 58), Theo Dan 7 (for Ojomoh 58), Arthur Clark 6 (for Itoje 64)

Sports.title: England pulverise Japan 78-15: Five-try Will Joseph twists knife into old boss Eddie Jones to pass early World Cup audition with flying colours
Sports.content:
What a cruel twist of fate that one of Eddie Jones’ teenage apprentices came back to twist the knife.

Will Joseph was still living in the Harlequins academy house when Jones invited him to train with the senior England team in 2022.

Joseph felt like he had won the lottery, fast-tracked into a squad with the likes of Owen Farrell and Danny Care.

Jones rewarded his efforts in training with a two-minute cameo against Australia but he had to wait more than four years for his second cap.

It finally came this weekend, against Jones’s Japan, as the centre-cum-winger scored five tries on a ruthless night at Twickenham.

Only Douglas Lambert (1907), Rory Underwood (1989), Josh Lewsey (2003) and Henry Arundell (2023) have achieved such a feat.

‘Today was a very special day,’ said Joseph. ‘I loved every minute of it. I’m pretty speechless. It was almost a perfect day'

Cadan Murley goes over for England in a swashbuckling first half at Allianz Twickenham

The power of Ellis Genge (pictured after his try), Maro Itoje and George Martin set up this win

On the bench, England’s replacements were even plotting to put Joseph on the back of their dominant driving maul in a bid to score a record-breaking sixth.

This game was billed as an early World Cup audition.

Steve Borthwick has already pencilled down circa 26 players for his 33-man World Cup squad and this was a shot for his fringe players to stake their claim.

Without question, Joseph was the standout, although it is worth remembering that his opposite man, Riku Tokito, had not played a single game of professional rugby.

Joseph was allowed freedom to roam but not once was he blinded by the spotlight of a full house in South West London.

He showed similar composure to his older brother, Jonathan, who won 54 caps for England between 2012 and 2020.

These days, Joseph Sr is one of the stadium comperes at Twickenham. At half-time, he spoke of his pride for his younger brother and reflected on the long and challenging journey towards his second cap.

‘Today was a very special day,’ said Joseph, when interviewed by his sibling. ‘I loved every minute of it. I’m pretty speechless. It was almost a perfect day. I was very grateful to get five tries in front of my family and friends.’

In the midfield, marginalised centre Max Ojomoh did everything that was asked of him

Joseph was left without a club after London Irish went bust, unused at Harlequins before finally finding his feet in the midfield at Gloucester.

Anyone who has watched the Cherry and Whites this season knows all about Joseph’s box-office skills.

He has established a silky centre partnership with Seb Atkinson, who missed out on this Japanese demolition because of a hip injury.

Joseph has the ability to cover both wing and centre and, in the era of versatility, this was a performance that should see him moved into Borthwick’s list of World Cup probables. When George Furbank is fit and firing – and ready to provide No10 cover from full-back – then Joseph could challenge Marcus Smith for England’s No23 jersey.

There would be no complaints if Joseph is now fast-tracked into the squad to take on the All Blacks next week.

He showcased his speed, footwork and vision – with his fifth try coming from an interception inside his own half.

While it was Joseph’s name in lights, the platform for this victory was laid by the power of Ellis Genge, Maro Itoje and George Martin. They muscled up from the start, with Japan lock Harry Hockings shown a 20-minute red card in the first minute.

Japan were hoping to take inspiration from Wales’ famous victory over the All Blacks but lightning never looked like striking twice. England pulverised Japan with their size and power, subjecting their old master Jones to a night that he would rather forget.

‘It kills me, that Will Joseph,’ laughed Jones. ‘I gave him his first cap and he scores five tries against me. That’s not very loyal, is it? He’s a great kid, he was always going to be a great player. Sometime you’ve got to do something for someone else. Hopefully Steve will give me some of his muesli and yoghurt.’

England capitalised on their numerical advantage in the early exchanges. They broke the line with almost every carry. In the midfield, Max Ojomoh did everything asked of him. The marginalised centre created time and space with his slick passes and clever running lines. Borthwick wanted to see more dog and grunt from Ojomoh but midfield resistance was limited. This was a long way from the blood and thunder intensity of France’s victory over South Africa, but that was no fault of the hosts.

Freddie Steward transferred his impressive club form to the international stage. He stole restarts and dominated the aerial battle, providing field position as England romped towards 13 tries.

‘We got beaten almost everywhere in the high ball,’ conceded Jones. ‘If it was a game of Aussie Rules it would have been 12-0. Our players don’t experience that in the domestic league so we’re teaching that on the run.’

In the second half, young No8 Greg Fisilau left indents in Japanese ribs. He delivered a human wrecking ball of a cameo. England are well-stocked with Ben Earl and Henry Pollock but neither is blessed with Fisilau’s raw power.

In 2018, when England looked blunt in a 35-15 win over Japan, Jones was so unimpressed that some of those players were never seen again on the Test stage.

Alex Lozowski and Zach Mercer kissed goodbye to their international careers.

This was an altogether different story. A host of players put their hand up, leaving Borthwick facing the enviable challenge of how he squeezes everyone in.

Sports.title: England's Euro 2028 mission starts NOW! Thomas Tuchel's men must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - or risk their 'DNA' cursing them yet again, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
It is four months, almost to the day, since England shrank from the call of history and lost their World Cup semi-final to Argentina in Atlanta but Thomas Tuchel may not believe that the Nations League tie against Spain in the Metropolitano on Sunday evening represents his best shot at redemption for the way things played out that afternoon in America’s South.

That is largely because Tuchel does not appear to believe he has anything to redeem himself for. The manner of his side’s capitulation - and the substitutions he made - in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium last July enraged the nation, but Tuchel said the fault was in the damned DNA of the English, that we were underlings, and that our players found it constitutionally impossible to keep hold of the ball.

Whatever Tuchel thinks, the fact remains that the tie against Lamine Yamal, Fabian Ruiz, Pedri and Mikel Oyarzabal and the rest of the world champions at the home of Atletico Madrid offers Tuchel and his players the opportunity to encourage themselves and their fans that they are not destined to be also-rans wired to fall at the final hurdle for evermore.

Spain are formidable opposition. They are on a record-breaking run of 43 matches unbeaten and have won their last 12 in succession. They haven't drawn a game since their June 15 game against Cape Verde in the World Cup. Their last defeat was on March 22, 2024, when they lost 1-0 to Colombia in a friendly. Some ask whether they are the best international side the world has ever seen.

‘Spain seem unbeatable,’ Tuchel said, when he walked into the press room at the Metropolitano on Saturday night and heard hymns of praise being lavished upon the opponents he is about to face.

‘They have a very strong identity and a very strong mentality. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are up for the fight. We are up for a spectacular match. We can see how far we can push the limits with the world champions in Madrid. The group is full of self-belief and rightly so.’

England must beat Spain to prove they can compete with the best - even if they have flaws

Thomas Tuchel must show he can find a way around the limitations presented by the 'DNA' he has complained about

This may be the toughest game that Tuchel’s England side play until the European Championships in 2028, where the final will be contested at Wembley, and they will play all their games at home. They need to go into that tournament with the belief that they can beat the best when the pressure is at its highest.

Beating Spain away in the final game of the group phase of the Nations League is not quite the same as a critical match at a major tournament but it is as stiff a challenge as Tuchel is going to face until then. Beating Croatia 7-0 in front of gangs of schoolkids in Rijeka last month was hailed as the best England performance of the Tuchel era. Which says it all, really.

It was a great performance in a relatively meaningless match. Now it is time for him to show that he can marshal an England side to succeed against the very best, not fall apart when the prize is in sight. His protestations of powerlessness in the aftermath of the Argentina defeat were not a good look for a coach who was hired with the idea that his coaching prowess and his game management could get England over the line.

Has he learned anything from the manner of the Argentina defeat? ‘This game against Spain will be proof of concept at the highest level,’ he said, ‘but we are up for it. I think we have taken the next step after the World Cup. The best thing is to trust our process and trust ourselves. We need to be clear about how we want to impose ourselves and I think that is all visible.’

Now it is time for him to show that he can find a way past the limitations of England’s footballing DNA, find a way to compete with Spain and France when it really matters, and find a way to end the culture of near misses that has come to be England’s lot in the last decade of appearances in semi-finals and finals.

England have played six matches since that day of crushing disappointment in Atlanta and scored 22 goals. But in the only one of those matches that really mattered, they lost 3-2 to Spain at Wembley in the opening tie of their Nations League campaign at the end of September, a game in which they were largely outclassed by Luis de la Fuente’s team.

Spain are what England have to aim for. Tuchel mentioned their example and their ability and their mindset straight after the semi-final loss to Argentina. ‘Ball possession plays a crucial role,’ he said at his post-match press conference in Atlanta. ‘It’s maybe not in our DNA like it is in our Spanish DNA or in our Argentinian-Brazilian DNA, to take the ball and control the game with the ball.’

This may well be their toughest game until the final of the 2028 European Championships, if they get that far

The England coach said more recently that England need to go back to trusting a traditional style that emphasises direct, high-intensity physicality rather than trying to copy Spanish patience in ball-retention. England, though, were taught a lesson in sophistication by the Spanish in September.

And for all the attention lavished on Yamal, Spain’s defence is the best in the world. Rodri, the shield for that defence and also the world’s best in the role, is not fit for this game but even without him, Spain’s back-line inspires an awful lot more confidence than England’s.

‘They were the best in the World Cup at the back,’ Declan Rice, England’s central midfielder, said on Saturday. ‘Defence wins you titles. Everyone talks about their attacking talent but you look at their central defenders, their full backs and the way their midfielders contribute to the defence, too.’

That defence will have to stop England’s resurgent front line, led by Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane, who could be flanked by Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers and backed up by the supreme talent of Jude Bellingham just behind them.

Bellingham’s improving relationship with Tuchel, which cannot have been harmed by the inclusion of Bellingham’s brother, Jobe, in this squad, is another reason to hope that England still retain the capacity to improve after the World Cup. The elder Bellingham has become England’s most influential player.

England at their best would be one of the few teams capable of extending them. Rice said on Saturday that the game between the two sides was ‘massive’. England need to prove they can find a way to get closer to the world champions. To beat them, Rice said, would be a ‘massive statement’.

‘Playing against them is a great incentive to win. It will show where we are as a group. We are trying to attack teams full throttle and with players like Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in our attack, it feels as if it is going to take off one night and maybe tomorrow night will be the night. We can beat Spain. For sure, we can.’

Tuchel needs to prove England can win, not just be noble contenders. They need to prove that their DNA need not be a curse.

Sports.title: 'Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It's my first time in Old Trafford!' - An afternoon with my 10-year-old inside the Theatre of Screams for Carrick's last stand
Sports.content:
THE guy with the flyer was persistent.

‘Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’ he asks earnestly, handing me a leaflet that announces: ‘Enough is Enough! Empty Old Trafford! Leave the stadium in the 21st minute. 21 years of failed ownership. Glazers OUT! Ineos OUT!’

More than 70,000 spectators leaving their seat and walking out of the stadium in the 21st minute have been quite the statement, especially live on Sky Sports.

But as admirable as Saeed TV’s aim is (I discover later he is some sort of youtuber), it’s hard to see gain any traction.

‘Dad, we are not walking out of the match. It’s my first time in Old Trafford,’ I am told as we continue to meander up Matt Busby Way, a declaration from my 10-year-old that causes a fair bit of mirth among the crowd.

Mate, we are walking out in the 21st minute to protest 21 years of the Glazers. Will you join us?’

‘What’s wrong with the owners anyway?’ Dan enquires innocently, which leads to a bind.

How deep down the rabbit-hole should I go with my ten-year-old on his first visit to the Theatre of Dreams.

It’s probably not the time or place to try and explain leveraged buyouts and how much debt the Glazers have saddled the club with, £1.2 billion at the last count while taking millions out of it in dividends. Do I need to go further back and talk about Rock of Gibraltar’s unexpected success on the track and the concept of stud fees?

‘They are not putting enough money into the team and taking loads of money out of the club,’ is all I offer.

‘When Manchester City need a midfielder, they can buy Elliot Anderson and Enzo Fernandez while United have to make do with someone who was sitting on Chelsea’s bench.’

He doesn’t look convinced that’s much of a reason to walk out of a football but as the cathedral of consumerism that is the Manchester United megastore has appeared, he forgets about United’s disastrous ownership model – for now, at least.

During his doomed attempt to coax Jurgen Klopp to Old Trafford around 2014, Ed Woodward apparently told him that United was the sporting version of Disneyland.

And to be sardined inside the megastore in the couple of hours before kick-off, you have to accept that the much-maligned former CEO may have been right about one thing.

Think Arnott’s a couple of days before Christmas, just with a lot more people. You even need to pass through airport-like security before even entering and spend your dosh.

One of the common refrains among United supporters is why are the Glazers holding onto the club when they don’t even seem to care.

Thirty seconds inside the megastore on match-day and you realise why the Americans are so keen to hold onto the asset they’re bleeding dry – and they probably care a great deal.

Dan gets obligatory photo at statue of United's holy trinity, a moment he will look back on

Even with the team languishing in the relegation zone, having won a single league game all season, people are keen to spend, spend, spend.

I see people wandering around with five or six different shirts, from different eras (I did succumb and bought Dan the black shirt from 95-96 season, because it reminds me of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and better times!)

You can get a photo with a replica of a Premier League trophy. That’s just £10. Or Lego sets of Old Trafford or the Munich clock.

That will just set you back £25. For many in this shop, it seems allowing the club to empty their wallet is as much a part of the day as the actual football.

There are other parts of the ritual, which remain and have yet to be infected by the poisonous atmosphere around the club – and remind the three dads bringing their kids to Old Trafford for the first time of better days.

Such as curry chips and battered sausage from Lou Macari’s chipper. And the customary photo in front of the statue of the holy trinity of Best, Law and Charlton.

The megastore was the one place that seemed immune to the toxicity in the air. Once outside again and all that could be heard was the moans and groans, mainly because Shea Lacey wasn’t starting.

Coming here since the 1990s, we have seen the skyline of Manchester transformed as it became a sleek, modern city. It seems the one place that hasn’t changed is Old Trafford. It has remained the same.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium – and not just because of the leaking roof. It could do with a lick or two of paint.

Stuck in time. It looked sleek and modern in 1999, but now there is a tired, decrepit feel to the stadium

No wonder Big Sir Jim is determined to plough ahead with his plans to make a crudely-designed circus tent ‘the Wembley of the North.’ Not that there is anyone inside Old Trafford of the same mind.

Senne Lammens has just trotted onto the field with Tom Heaton and Karl Darlow to do their pre-match warm-up when the chants start, telling Jim Ratcliffe he can stick his new stadium up his posterior.

It is a weird atmosphere, with all the chanting against the owners – both Glazers and Ineos – and nothing being sung in support of the players.

As my friend points out it must be so difficult for the team to show the best of themselves when things are this toxic in the stadium.

Dan has been to the Jodi Stand enough times on a Friday night to know there is plenty of choice and crude language at football matches, but still I nearly felt at covering his ears at some of the stuff being sung in Old Trafford last Sunday, especially that directed at CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

We had hoped that things might have been different when the game kicked off, but within a minute, Aston Villa had scored.

And three minutes later, they had scored again when Lammens fumbled Alysson’s shot into Nicolas Jackson’s path. Maybe walking out in the 21st minute wasn’t such a bad idea.

Jackson put Aston Villa two up

The crowd’s ire had gone from the owners to the players now, with a sustained chant of ‘You are not fit to wear the shirt.’ United did rally and by half-time, it was 2-2. But the mood was still dismal as we queued for a quick beer.

The 1958 Group had asked fans not to buy booze, another protest against the owners. But it seemed nobody was paying much attention to that.

One of the issues at United is that there seem to be too many splintered fan groups – there is also ClaimBackUnited and Fan Coalition ’58 – as well as Saeed TV, who seemed to be on his own solo run.

We didn’t feel bad about ignoring the booze ban, as everyone was doing it. And within a couple of minutes of the second-half, we saw the reason why. You need to fortify yourself to watch Diogo Dalot try to defend.

For much of the second-half, it seemed like Michael Carrick’s brief tenure was going to peter out in a forgettable defeat, as Villa seemed to manage the game perfectly.

Dan and his friends were growing frustrated, pointing out the players weren’t doing what their coaches tell them to do on a weekly basis, leading me to conclude that maybe my son’s under-11 side are better-coached than United.

The last on-pitch act of Carrick's tenure

And then there was the chaotic and crazy final few minutes in stoppage-time. And a draw that came out of nowhere and was celebrated like a victory.

That was the thing. Even though the mood inside the stadium was toxic for most of the game, even though the team were two down inside four minutes and the season has been a disaster, everyone still came away from Old Trafford, happy and with a smile on their face.

Only football can do that. More than that, perhaps only Manchester United – despite everything – can do that.

Sports.title: England boss Thomas Tuchel angry at being dragged into race row after being told by Luis de la Fuente: 'There is no racism in Spain!' on eve of Nations League showdown
Sports.content:
England boss Thomas Tuchel angry at being dragged into race row after being told by Luis de la Fuente: 'There is no racism in Spain!' on eve of Nations League showdown

Thomas Tuchel was dragged into a bitter race row on the eve of England's Nations League showdown with Spain.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols in case their players suffered racist abuse at the Metropolitano Stadium on Sunday evening.

England players were notoriously subject to racial abuse at the Bernabeu in 2004 and England have not played in Madrid since.

But Spain manager Luis de la Fuente reacted angrily when he was told that Tuchel had addressed the subject.

'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente said. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'

The row then deepened when a Spanish journalist told Tuchel about De La Fuente's reaction and the England coach grew exasperated with the line of questioning.

Tuchel had been asked before England's departure for Spain about England's protocols

'Tell Tuchel that there is no racism in Spain,' de la Fuente said. 'Just like in England. We are not racist.'

'I was polite enough to answer a question from your colleagues,' Tuchel said, 'and you run and ask Spain's coach and tell them that I talked about racism in Spain.

'I never talked about racism in Spain. I answered a question politely. I never expect racism. The dressing room is the most anti-racist place in the world. This is a perfect example of how you create confusion out of nothing.'

Tuchel had earlier said: 'It's important that the players know about the protocol. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch.

'We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]. There is a protocol in place.'

England midfielder Declan Rice said that Tuchel had not yet addressed the group about racism protocols but that they were clear about what they would do if any England players were abused.

England's game against Bulgaria in Sofia in 2019 was halted after allegations of racism against England players but the game was completed.

Sports.title: Declan Rice bites back at Graeme Souness: Arsenal star claims pundit doesn't understand how the game has evolved over 'old man's football' criticism - and jokes: 'My numbers aren't bad "for a centre-back!"'
Sports.content:
Declan Rice bites back at Graeme Souness: Arsenal star claims pundit doesn't understand how the game has evolved over 'old man's football' criticism - and jokes: 'My numbers aren't bad "for a centre-back!"'

Declan Rice has laughed off criticism from Graeme Souness by claiming his numbers 'aren't bad for a centre back', after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' and 'cheating' by dropping into defence.

Souness has long believed the Arsenal and England star does not do enough for a midfielder and said recently he might as well play centre back, adding that he would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona.

Rice is aware of what Souness has said but believes his return of 22 goals and 33 assists since joining the Gunners in 2023 disproves the former Liverpool midfielder's opinion.

‘My numbers since I joined Arsenal speak for themselves,’ said Rice. ‘For a “centre back”, I think that’s not bad numbers. I’ve had a lot of assists, a lot of goals. To be a top-class centre back getting those numbers, I’m delighted with that!’

Rice, who will start as an advanced midfielder when England take on Spain here in Madrid on Sunday night, added: ‘Look, Graeme’s got his opinion. I think he’s had his opinion since my West Ham days. I’ve seen his views. I can’t change his opinion. I can only do what I do, which is go on the pitch, perform, play well and block out the noise.’

Rice also believes Souness, 73, may not understand how the game has evolved.

England and Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice has laughed off Graeme Souness' criticism after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' 'cheating' by dropping into defence

Pundit Souness believes Rice would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona

‘If you speak about the positioning, the “old man's football”, look at Harry Kane, for instance,’ began Rice. 'We played him the other week and he dropped next to the centre backs 20-30 times to pick up the ball. The game is different now. It's what the game demands, to get away from your man, to go into different areas to create overloads, to create two v ones, to progress the ball up the pitch. Football is way different. It's changed a lot, and you're always trying to look for tactical advantages.

‘In terms of me as a midfielder, I'm constantly watching clips with Mikel (Arteta). He's constantly coaching me on the pitch. How I can progress the ball from deep, drop next to the goalkeeper, go to full back to get on the ball, to take the ball up the pitch.

‘So, I feel like we're now seeing something totally different to what he would see, but in his time football was different. He was a top-class midfielder who won lots of stuff. There's no argument against him. As a pundit, as a person, his career, you have to respect what he's done.

‘I didn't get to see him play, but obviously his accolades were top, and I've never got to meet him in person. If I did, there would be no disrespect. I’d shake his hand. I’d chat with him. It’s an opinion at the end of the day. It’s football.’

Sports.title: DAN BIGGAR: I was so emotional to see the joy return to Welsh rugby on a day I'll never forget - to end 73 years of hurt against New Zealand gives our pride back
Sports.content:
DAN BIGGAR: I was so emotional to see the joy return to Welsh rugby on a day I'll never forget - to end 73 years of hurt against New Zealand gives our pride back

Wales ending 73 years of hurt against New Zealand in Cardiff was the biggest shock I’ve seen in international rugby since Japan beat South Africa at the 2015 World Cup.

No-one gave the Brave Blossoms a cat in hell’s chance 11 years ago in Brighton. And as passionate a Welshman as I am, the same was true for Wales’ latest All Blacks clash.

Anyone who tells you that they knew Steve Tandy’s side was going to win is a liar! It’s been such a tough three years for Welsh rugby, both on and off the field.

To be at Principality Stadium was to see the joy return to our national sport in front of your eyes. It was incredible. So, so emotional. It was a day I’ll never, ever forget.

Wales’ rearguard was absolutely exceptional. They’ve had to take criticism for being a poor team and at times, that has been fair. During that period, the players have been told they’ve been too soft. It's been too easy to score against Wales.

But the way they defended, albeit against a much-changed New Zealand team, showed real international class. James Botham epitomised that with a mammoth tackling and player-of-the-match display. To see Botham in tears at the final whistle summed up the mood of Wales as a nation. For most of us, including former players like me who played against New Zealand many times, it was a first.

Wales beating New Zealand after 73 years of hurt was the biggest shock in international rugby I've seen in over a decade, writes Dan Biggar

Nobody gave them a chance but their defence was absolutely exceptional and they put pride back into Welsh rugby

I will never forget this day, writes Biggar - it was so, so emotional and badly needed

The All Blacks pounded away at Wales time and again in the second half. But Tandy’s men held firm, Botham leading the way. Replacements Gareth Thomas, Dan Edwards and Taine Plumtree all produced big goal-line defensive moments when it mattered most.

The more those big moments went Wales’ way, the more you started to believe. But I didn’t fully believe the job was done until Reuben Morgan-Williams kicked the ball dead to end the game. These players have now sealed their place in Welsh rugby history and they deserve all the credit they’re going to get. I’m sure there’ll be a few well-deserved beers floating about!

As I left the stadium, my overriding feeling was one of happiness. This result put the pride back into Welsh rugby and that has been badly needed. Well done, lads.

And I can say I was there!

Sports.title: Brazil players separated from referee by security as Carlo Ancelotti sees red vs Japan
Sports.content:
Brazil players separated from referee by security as Carlo Ancelotti sees red vs Japan

Security were called upon to de-escalate matters late into Brazil's shock 3-2 loss to Japan on Saturday, when Jansen Foo Chuan Hui sent off Carlo Ancelotti and one of his key players

View 2 Images Security had to move Brazil players away from Jansen Foo Chuan Hui (Image: X)

Security had to separate Carlo Ancelotti and his Brazil players from the referee during Saturday's 3-2 loss to Japan, as a friendly match quickly turned sour. The game was all square at 2-2 headed into stoppage time thanks to strikes from Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura, as well as a Vinicius Junior brace.

‌



‌



However, the already tense atmosphere turned frosty a minute into extra time, when Tatsuhiro Sakamoto scored the winner for the Asian nation. Referee Jansen Foo Chuan Hui saw now problem in Takumi Minamino's multiple challenges of Joao Gomes, which may have been given as a foul on another day - especially considering Gomes remained on the ground as his opponent ran off with the ball at his feet.

‌



Sakamoto then dinked the ball over Pedro Morisco to give Japan a late goal, and ultimately the winner. Brazil were quick to confront the official while Japanese players wheeled off in celebration, as VAR confirmed that the goal was fine to stand.

‌



Man Utd turned me down after two interviews but I still want to work in England READ MORE :

Ancelotti and Raphinha - who had just been substituted - meanwhile, were shown red cards, leading to yet further appeals from the Brazilian national team. Security were then forced to intervene and pull Ancelotti, as well as Vini Junior and Bruno Guimaraes, away from the Singaporean official in the aftermath.

In the aftermath, Ancelotti told the media Chuan Hui's reason for sending him off in the first place. He explained: "He gave me the red card because he said I was not able to control the bench, and that all the players were on the field, that is the reason.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



"A pity the result, because we don't like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many things.

"Some players who played for the first time, who showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team was good."

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Twisting the knife further on the officiating, the Italian added: "The result, obviously, is conditioned by the attitude of the referee, who did not blow the whistle. But it's not his fault; it was a high-level match, and I think he didn't have the experience to manage this type of match."

‌



Raphinha, meanwhile, was irate over a potential handball leading up to Japan's opener, as well as having penalty claims silenced. He told Globo: "First of all, I'd like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off.

"Sometimes it's hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion.

‌



"I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable. In my view, their first goal involved a foul where the opponent took the ball off me with his hand.

View 2 Images Carlo Ancelotti was sent off against Japan (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"I think it's a foul, but I can understand why it wasn't given based on the current law. Then there was the penalty in the first half, in my opinion it was a penalty, but he said no.

"Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It's very difficult not to talk about the refereeing."

Sports.title: Portugal suffer nightmare start to life without Cristiano Ronaldo in Denmark drubbing
Sports.content:
Portugal suffer nightmare start to life without Cristiano Ronaldo in Denmark drubbing

PORTUGAL 1-4 DENMARK: Jorge Jesus' Portugal did not enjoy the best of nights in their first outing since Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement, losing heavily on home soil

View 2 Images Portugal suffered a heavy loss on home soil against Denmark (Image: Miguel Riopa/AFP)

The evening started with the unveiling of a permanent re-design for the No 7 icon as Portugal embraced a new dawn without their polarising record cap holder and goalscorer.

‌



‌



Seemingly revered and maligned in equal measure these days, it had been suggested that Portugal would be now better off without Cristiano Ronaldo, whose powers in an international shirt had waned significantly prior to an explosive early exit from last month's camp which turned out to be the catalyst to him calling time on representing his country.

‌



But life after the former Manchester United and Real Madrid attacker didn't get off to the ideal start as Jorge Jesus' side were thrashed 4-1 in their own backyard by Denmark.

‌



Goncalos Ramos once again led the line with a supporting cast of Joao Felix, Bruno Fernandes and Pedro Neto. Not exactly a shortage of star-power.

View 2 Images Portugal paid tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo before the game

‌



But it was the other end where the goals flowed with Pierre-Emile Hojberg's 43rd minute penalty well and truly opening the Portuguese floodgates.

Rasmus Hojlund, who missed out on playing with Ronaldo at Old Trafford by seven months, was then at the double netting four minutes after the break and then eight minutes after that. Joachim Anderson scored a fourth in the 75th minute to rub salt in Portuguese wounds.

‌



Bernardo Silva did find the back of the net in additional time but the damage had already been done on a desperately sobering night for the natives in Braga.

While defeat for Jesus' side means they will have to wait until the final matchday to discover if they will win their Group A4, Denmark would still need to win and hope Portugal lose in order to pip them to top spot.

Sports.title: Declan Rice says England boo boys have Ben White all wrong - 'If people knew'
Sports.content:
Declan Rice says England boo boys have Ben White all wrong - 'If people knew'

Ben White has been booed by England fans after being reintegrated into the squad by Thomas Tuchel and Declan Rice has now spoken out in defence of his Arsenal co-star

View 3 Images Ben White has been booed by England fans (Image: Molly Darlington/Getty Images)

Declan Rice says if “people knew and understood” Ben White they would no longer boo him.

‌



‌



Arsenal defender White was jeered by the Wembley crowd when he came on as a substitute against Croatia and some England fans have not forgiven him for quitting the World Cup squad back in 2022.

‌



White spoke last week about his passion for playing in an England shirt but refused to go into detail about the reasons why he flew home from Qatar.

‌



And Rice says: “Ben has moved on from what's happened in the past, he's totally focused on playing for England. When he's been fit and available he's constantly put himself forward to play for England.

“He loves being here, it's not like he doesn't like being here, he loves playing for England, loves being around the lads.

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

“If people knew and understood Ben White as a character he's not fazed by anything, he goes with the flow and he just wants to play football and for England.

‌



“Fans are entitled to their opinion, it is what it is but he doesn't feel that way with England. He wants to come out and play his best football and enjoy himself. I think that's credit to him, coming on and playing for England and being booed is not easy but the way his character is it really helps him.

“It's not been a conversation for the team. It's so long ago now, it's nearly five years and it doesn't need to keep getting brought up. We need to look forward to the future and what Ben White is going to do in an England shirt, that's the most important thing.

‌



“It's a pointless conversation, Ben has moved on, no-one talks about it around the dinner table, no-one speaks about it in the pool, we just play football and do what we need to do.”

View 3 Images Declan Rice has had his say on the jeers for his Arsenal team-mate (Image: David Price/Arsenal FC)

‌



Rice has revealed he will embrace the competition from Bournemouth’s “incredible” Alex Scott as the midfielder took his place last month. He says he has stiff competition to play in Arsenal’s midfield with Bruno Guimaraes as well as the likes of Martin Zubimendi, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Mikel Merino and Martin Odegaard.

Rice said: “To be honest, Alex Scott playing was incredible. The way he's been playing for Bournemouth the last two or three seasons has been remarkable.

‌



“The way he's being spoken about is totally right because of the levels he's set for himself and I totally understand playing for England comes with competition.

“When we signed Bruno Guimaraes, when we signed Zubimendi, when we had Myles, Merino, Odegaard, you're competing with six midfielders at your club every day so for me there's nothing different throughout my whole career there's been competition. It's normal.”

‌



Rice, 27, also says that he dreams of carrying on deep into his 30s with 33-year-old Harry Kane’s success only serving to prove that if you stay fit then anything is possible. He added: “If you look at Harry … it’s not a coincidence the season he’s had, Ballon d’Or winner, not just because of his footballing ability, just everything he does off the pitch to look after himself.

View 3 Images White is back in the England fold under Thomas Tuchel (Image: Vince Mignott/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images)

‌



“His mindset is always right. He’s always looking forward to the game. He’s always preparing himself in the right way. He’s always in a good way in his mind and I feel like for me … you need to be obsessed with football, still. Y

“ou look at the greats that have played late into their 30s, they’re obsessed and they love the game. And H is one of them. And I see myself being one of them as well. I want to maximise my career, I want to play for as long as possible.

‌



“I want to play at the highest level for as long as possible. Doing that comes with sacrifices at that age, doing different things – recovery, preparing well, like I said.

“And being ready for whatever comes. Me at 33, I don’t know where I’m going to be and what I’m going to be doing but for sure I hope I’m still at the top level, competing and playing really well.”

Sports.title: Jordan Pickford discovers where he stands as James Trafford gets Spain nod AGAIN
Sports.content:
Jordan Pickford discovers where he stands as James Trafford gets Spain nod AGAIN

Thomas Tuchel has confirmed James Trafford will start in England's crucial showdown with Spain on Sunday - but insists Jordan Pickford remains his No 1 goalkeeper

View 2 Images James Trafford will start England's game with Spain on Sunday, not Jordan Pickford (Image: Getty)

James Trafford has been told he will start against Spain - and that puts a major doubt over Jordan Pickford’s status as No1.

‌



‌



England boss Thomas Tuchel also revealed fit-again Ezri Konsa will go straight back into the starting line-up against the world champions in the Metropolitano Stadium.

‌



It is a winner-takes-all showdown in the Nations League and that is why it is a surprise that Tuchel has decided to go with Trafford over his established first choice keeper which must raise questions over Pickford’s long-term future.

‌



Tuchel said: “We want to try and see how far Traff is. That hasn't changed. So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match, so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers. And Traff gets the match tomorrow.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



“It's only a football match, so hopefully he's not too over-excited or overly nervous, because there's no need to. We trust him.

“But it is different to play for England than to play for your club. And to have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way of course to show up, and to show that you're ready, and for us also to see where he is.

‌



“We know what Jordan can do for us. Jordan is at the moment our No1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments. He played in tournaments and played for me in the World Cup. It's a good goalkeeping group that we built there and they’re pushing themselves.”

England will make changes in defence to try and defeat Spain and end their 43-game unbeaten record with Konsa coming back to steady the ship.

‌



Tuchel says Konsa’s performances this season have been “amazing” and he is set to rerun after a knee issue ruled him out of the win over Croatia. He added: “I saw him when he played his first match for Arsenal after William Saliba’s injury. It just looked like he's always been there. It was seamless.

View 2 Images Pickford has been England's long-term No 1 but his position now appears to be under serious threat

‌



“For us, it’s amazing that he plays on the highest level, competes for every title, is in an atmosphere and in a situation where it really matters that you stay focused and you show up every three days. It's only positives for us.

“He did very well and we gave him the chance to take care of his little niggle. He took it seriously and he showed that we can trust him. He showed up yesterday for individual work, he showed up today for training and he's ready to play.

‌



“I think it's in itself a big match, Spain against England. I think Spain, since years, on an incredible run. They seem impossible to beat. I think we are in a very good moment. And in the best moment also to try and make the seemingly-impossible possible.

"Because we are here to win. We wanted this match desperately. We thought we were very close to beating them in the first match with a good performance. It's an achievement in itself that we already have 12 points. I think it was a tricky group, when we saw the draw.

Article continues below

“So we have 12, and have a final. It's exactly what we want. And I think it's two powerful teams, two teams in a very good place at the moment. Two teams who like to dominate the ball and create chances. We feel in a good place. It's the moment to show up and try to win.”

Sports.title: Tenerife boss claims ban for keeper involved in fatal Jesus de Miguel clash is 'too light'
Sports.content:
Tenerife boss claims ban for keeper involved in fatal Jesus de Miguel clash is 'too light'

Jesus Owono, the goalkeeper involved in the collision which led to the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, has been banned for 12 matches by a disciplinary committee

View 2 Images Jesus Owono has been banned for 12 games (Image: Getty)

The manager of Tenerife says the 12-game ban given to goalkeeper Jesus Owono following the collision that led to Jesus de Miguel's death seems "a bit light".

‌



Owono collided heavily with De Miguel in mid-air during the Spanish Segunda Division match between Tenerife and FC Andorra at the start of this month. The forward, 30, tragically died the following day, sending Spanish football into mourning.

Owono was sent off as a result of the collision and was banned for 12 games by a disciplinary committee on Friday.

Alvaro Cervera, the head coach of Tenerife, has commented on the length of Owono's ban, which was the maximum penalty available to the disciplinary committee given they could only consider the offence on the pitch rather than the tragic consequences of the collision.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

While he feels the ban is light, he also acknowledged that the regulations do not "specifically account for what happened". "I think that, just as in other areas of life, there are rules or laws that must be followed," said Cervera, whose team will play for the first time since De Miguel's death on Sunday against Ceuta.

"Since the current regulations don't specifically account for what happened, I believe they have simply adhered to the rules and imposed the number of matches permitted by the regulations.

"Anything else I might say would just be my own personal opinion, which I'll keep to myself. It might seem a bit light when compared to other cases, but in reality, I don't think the rules allow for anything else."

View 2 Images Jesus de Miguel died aged 30 following a collision with the goalkeeper during a game earlier this month (Image: CD TENERIFE/AFP via Getty Images)

The disciplinary committee shared that the referee's report said Owono was sent off for "violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play".

The 25-year-old released a statement following De Miguel's death, which read: "These are the most difficult days of my life. I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to process what has happened.

"I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many questions to address.

"I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the ⁠pain we are experiencing. Rest in ⁠peace, Jesus."

Sports.title: BBC legend slams 'discipline' after broadcast axe and admits he tunes into rival
Sports.content:
BBC legend slams 'discipline' after broadcast axe and admits he tunes into rival

A BBC icon has explained that he listens to a rival of the broadcaster as a result of the "comprehensive service" it provides

View 2 Images The BBC cut 5 Live's classified results section in 2022 (Image: Leila Coker - WSL, WSL Football via Getty Images)

Mike Ingham has argued that BBC Radio 5 Live has surrendered much of its "discipline" following the controversial choice to scrap its classified football results segment back in 2022. The broadcasting legend has also revealed that he now listens to talkSPORT, which he considers a "comprehensive service."

‌



The 76-year-old formed a partnership with Alan Green for nearly a quarter of a century between 1990 and 2014, commentating on the most significant matches in Britain and across the globe. Ingham and Green provided coverage of FA Cup finals, World Cup tournaments and European competitions, with the former renowned for his articulate style and presentation.

In 2004, Ingham was promoted to the position of 5 Live's chief football correspondent. He stepped away from his position following the 2014 World Cup, bringing an illustrious career to a close, though he has remained an avid listener of the output from his former colleagues and those who followed.

Jesus Owono given maximum ban for tackle that resulted in Jesus de Miguel's tragic death READ MORE :

Marcus Rashford causes issue as Man Utd set to trigger his team-mate's contract clause READ MORE :

Yet the iconic commentator doesn't always support the decisions taken by the BBC, as shown by his disapproval of 5 Live axing their classified segment four years ago. Discussing the decision, Ingham told the Telegraph: "It's like building a house without the bricks.

"Those two-and-a-half minutes were like taking stock at the end of a hurly-burly afternoon. It was a great bit of broadcasting when it was done by James Alexander Gordon, like the shipping forecast.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

"I think 5 Live has lost a lot of, not professionalism, but discipline. I was reared on hitting the pips. My family gets so exasperated with me now because I'm such a stickler for time. A lot of that has been lost, it has become much more easy come, easy go."

He added: "I just think the BBC has spread itself too thinly. It's just trying to do everything, as opposed to trying to concentrate on the things it does best.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"For me, the programme should always come before the podcast. That's me though, not being able to move with the times."

A BBC statement issued when they chose to axe 5 Live's results segment said: "We appreciate the strength of feeling towards the classified football results within Sports Report. It's always difficult when a programme with a special history changes, but there are good reasons for the change.

"With the addition of the 5.30pm live Premier League match to our coverage, Sports Report has been condensed into a shorter programme - cut from 1 hour to 25 minutes. The classifieds were taking around 5-7 minutes to read, which would have taken up around a third of the programme - constraining the range of sport we could cover.

View 2 Images Mike Ingham (left) has spoken about the BBC (Image: Getty)

"We'd like to assure our listeners that results from across the football leagues will still be shared during the programme and through the afternoon. Results are also available in full on the BBC Sport website and during Final Score on BBC One. Having a live match at 5.30 is a great addition to the 5 Live schedule."

Ingham has also made the striking admission that he now tunes into BBC Sport's long-standing rival talkSPORT, owing to the network's capacity to deliver a "comprehensive service" to its audience. He said: "I think they [BBC Sport] were complacent about talkSPORT.

"When it began it was a bit blokey, now I think it's a more comprehensive service and the range of presenters they have really makes it work. Simon Jordan is brilliant, Jeff Stelling's there and they do the results at 5 o'clock on a Saturday."

Sports.title: Man Utd ready to spend big in January as Mauricio Pochettino picks his targets
Sports.content:
Man Utd ready to spend big in January as Mauricio Pochettino picks his targets

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino will need to hit the ground running with the Red Devils languishing in the Premier League relegation zone

View 2 Images New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino

Mauricio Pochettino will be backed in January with MAJOR transfer funds.

‌



‌



Manchester United are ready to dip into the market to strengthen their squad with a top defender the No1 priority. And Pochettino will get a say on targets as part of United’s vision for success with their new manager who is joining on a two-and-a-half year contract.

‌



United have been reluctant to do business in the winter window but there is an acceptance that they need reinforcements in defence. They are also likely to look at a forward - Como’s Argentina star Nico Paz has also been linked - but a big-name striker is more likely for the summer.

‌



Benjamin Sesko has been struggling with injury but it is in defence where there is a chronic problem as they failed to land a left back to provide back-up for Luke Shaw.

‌



United have spent big in the last two windows as they targeted forwards in 2025 with Sesko, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha all arriving.

They signed midfielders last summer with Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans all arriving for big money but have had mixed results.

‌



United wanted to look at next summer for major defensive reinforcements but the squad appears to have gone backwards as they find themselves languishing in the relegation zone.

That will bring forward the plan for a defender to arrive in January to bolster the squad and Pochettino will have a say on targets after previous criticism about a lack of joined up thinking on transfers.

‌



View 2 Images Pochettino was emotion during his presser ahead of USA's game with Haiti

Pochettino is certain to have his own targets and enjoys developing and working with young and homegrown players. He is also on record about his admiration for Marcus Rashford in the past so it could be an exciting time for him.

‌



Pochettino was emotional at a press conference in the United States farewell press conference ahead of their two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti.

The former Spurs and Chelsea boss will then jet across to England next week to help prepare for his first game in charge at Liverpool next Sunday.
