Admission into GCU, in those halcyon days, when merit decided the fates of individuals, instead of being the President’s son or the Governor’s daughter, was based on merit. You didn’t bring your father into the exam hall; you came with your brain to lay claim to admission to next year’s Form I set. GCU was one of the best in Nigeria then; competition was very stiff; there were no guarantees except your results. Dozens of princes, sons of Ministers, and business tycoons applied; tried their best but few were chosen. Albert Akpomudje was one of the few chosen to start Form I in GCU.

Life’s selection process is akin to climbing a mountain; the surface area gets smaller and more difficult as you climb up. If obtaining admission to GCU was tough enough, aspiring to read law was even more difficult. Young Albert made the step up more difficult for himself by applying for admission to Lagos State University Law School, widely regarded as the having the best law faculty nationwide. Again, this was an institution which had set out to achieve excellence in training legal officers. That meant the best faculty and administrators available, as well as the best students as inputs. Garbage In Garbage Out, GIGO, was stoutly rejected. Just as the finest steel pass through the hottest furnaces, graduates of LASU Law School are regarded as the best setting out on their careers in law. The record is astonishing. Prince Albert went in as a young man; and emerged as a personally well-disciplined young adult; ready to climb another mountain of life as a lawyer.

Practising law, anywhere in the world, especially in Nigeria, is like wanting to be a professional footballer in the English Premiership. To reach the top, become a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, SAN, you must be more than good; you must be exceptional. Being the coach’s son counts for nothing when the final team selection is made. At any rate, our hero has never asked for favours; all he wanted was a level-playing field to prove his mettle. He became SAN in2001. That was commendable enough. He emerged as the 54th Chairman of the Body of Benchers, Nigeria this year. In that capacity, he now heads the Nigerian Bar; after succeeding the former Chief Justice of Nigeria, CJN, Olukayode Ariwoola.

He never abandoned his roots while climbing up the ladders of success. The HRM is a firm believer in giving back to the institutions which nurtured him and prepared him for life. He is currently the President Worldwide of Government College Ughelli Old Boys Association, GCUOBA.

Happy birthday, Sir, and happy first coronation anniversary as well. The King of kings will grant Your Royal Majesty long life, more prosperity, sound health and peaceful reign over Olomu Kingdom. Olomu will experience steady positive economic and social development.

PERVERTION OF DEMOCRACY: TELL ME. WHO IS PDP PRESIDENTIAL CANDIDATE?

“Tolerance becomes a crime when applied to evil” – Thomas Mann,

It has once been said that democracy is the only form of government which allows those working to subvert it to campaign openly. Nobody in North Korea, Russia, China or even Egypt can mount a podium for five minutes, with a bull-horn, and call for democracy. It will be his last statement on Earth. When some of us courageously confronted the military during the 1980s until 1999, we laboured under what has turned out to be a serious illusion; we suffered for nothing. I went to detention seven times, three under Babangida and four under Abacha, during the period. The last under Abacha was almost my last time in the world; but for Divine intervention. I lost friends, money and jobs and almost got divorced because I strongly believed that democracy, practiced as it should, remains the best form of government.

We have seen three recent examples, Brazil, Israel and the United States of America, of what can happen when people freely express their views, through ballot boxes, regarding who should govern them. In Brazil, the incumbent was re-elected; in Israel and the US, voters swept out the ruling parties. There were no reports of the electoral bodies altering votes; no justices determined that a fourth place finisher won the election.

What has that got to do with the PDP presidential candidate? A lot, as I will soon explain.

Among the things which will destroy a democracy, according to Mahatma Gandhi, 1869-1948, the first was: “Politics without principles”. The President or Prime Minister or Chancellor is the nation’s highest political leader. It is expected that anyone aspiring to that position would hold certain principles which would constitute the foundations of government policies – if elected into office. Every presidential candidate is expected to present his own principles of governance which are distinguishable from those of other candidates when there are several candidates contesting; and to fight for his views.

The Wike-led Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, a monstrous relic of the party formed by the G-34, led by Dr Alex Ekwueme, has unleashed on the Nigerian electorate a presidential candidate who does not campaign. He is, by personal choice, so obscure, that I have not met anybody who knows his name. What is wrong with that? Again, quite a lot. Let me again quickly explain.

Given the open partisanship of INEC and the judiciary, the PDP presidential candidate on the ballot paper might be a deliberate intention to use it to divert votes from opposition parties in their strongholds. It is unthinkable that the party seriously expects him to win. That being the case, he has been planted, with the help of INEC and courts, for purposes which will soon unfold.

I am appalled that anyone, pretending to love his country, would lend himself for the promotion of such schemes which destroy our democracy.

ATTACK ON OPPONENTS IN APC STATES

“War is nothing more than the continuation by other means” – Karl von Clausewitz, 1780-1831.

Tinubu won the 2023 election without bloodshed. Irrespective of whether he wins or loses the 2027 election – if and when it is held – the winner may enter Aso Rock with violence still here and there. One political party – the All Progressives Congress, APC – is heating up the polity to the point of turning politics to warfare. To the party, I have a word of caution. Widespread post-election unrest has sometimes resulted in the unintended consequence.

Follow me on Facebook @ J Israel Biola.

World.title: Baby-hungry single women are the reason some men are having the snip!
World.content:
By Bunmi Sofoloa

A few months into a fledging relationship, divorcee Donald was in bed with attractive, much younger partner when she whispered a proposal that punctured the mood. It wasn’t so much as actual demand as a loaded question that had Donald reconsidering the future – not only with her, but about his life in general. Yes, the 52-year-old father-of-three was besotted with his flavour-of-the-moment. “I was having the time of my life,” he admits, “but one thing was entirely out of the question – more children.”

So when in the heat of the moment, his 30-something girlfriend asked whether they should use contraception or not, he found himself in a quandary that was later to result in rather drastic action. “There was such a big question mark, at the end of the sentence,” recalled Donald. “I didn’t doubt she’d make a fantastic mother, but that wasn’t what I wanted.”

While the couple did use contraception that night, things fizzled out months later. According to Donald, “It was a coincidence that I went on to have a vasectomy shortly afterwards. Luckily I was still abroad and could have it on the NHS, though it was performed at a private clinic. I was very professional – I was in and out fairly quickly one lunch time without any complication afterwards. Totally worth it for my peace of mind.”

As dramatic a reaction as that may seem, Donald still maintains it’s a prudent course of action, not just for himself, but for other divorced dads dating childless younger women. He explains: “On numerous occasions during my single life, women have casually asked about contraception. You have to be careful because these are the ones looking for a man to father their children. And they can be ruthless in their pursuit of that…”

Is this the bravado of a deluded middle-aged man? Or the uncomfortable truth about dating as a divorced, evidently fertile male? As a psychotherapist with 20 years of experience in couple counselling puts it: “I have discovered that men like Dan are far from the only middle-aged divorced father, choosing a vasectomy to safeguard their return to the dating market – to the extent that the most common age range for men undergoing the procedure is 41-45.

“There are several factors behind this – the high rate of marital breakdown, men fearful of being ‘tricked’ and single women in their 30s and now even 40s suddenly experiencing the all-encompassing desire to become mothers. In some cases, they are becoming increasingly predatory about seeking ‘father material’. Although convinced they didn’t want children while they built their careers, suddenly – bam! – their biological clock starts ticking. It really can happen over-night. They will do anything and everything to pursue this, even if it means duping a man into having unprotected sex.

“Their targets, meanwhile, fear getting trapped in the wrong relationship, but also dread the financial implications of a new baby. If you don’t have the wealth of ageing tycoons and celebrities, who have gone on to have second and even third families, then the impact on your life is going to be enormous.

After Donald’s experience with the first partner he had after his divorce from the mother of his two sons 12 years ago after 17 years of marriage, he became more forthcoming with subsequent girlfriend. “Fortunately at first, I had a serious relationship for four years with someone who didn’t want children,” he says. “I then had a one-year relationship before embarking on a couple of short-term ones. The women were typically in their 30s. If it looked as though we were going to sleep together, I always address the issue of children head on, explaining that my days of playing football every weekend with a toddler were long over. There were a number of awkward situations with those interested in more than an amorous affair, but I’m someone who’s very careful. I’ve never had unprotected sex.

“I’ve done the small children phase of my life and it isn’t something I’d want to do again. It has upset some women and I appreciate that I’m being somewhat selfish. But I remain loyal to my existing children. I have two fantastic sons who are grown up now. I have a great relationship with them. I can’t imagine how they’d react if I told them that a little brother or sister was on the way. Seven years after I had the vasectomy, I haven’t regretted it once.”

Immaculate Conception (Humour)

A mother took her daughter to the doctor’s. “She’s been having strange symptoms”, said the mother. The doctor examined the daughter carefully. Then he announced: “Madam, I believe your daughter’s pregnant”.

“That’s impossible”, the mother gasped. “Why, my little girl has nothing whatsoever to do with men, do you darling?” “No, mummy, I’ve never so much as kissed a man”. The doctor then looked from mother to daughter. Then he walked to the window and stood there, staring out. Finally, the mother asked: “Doctor, is something wrong?”

“No”, he replied. “It’s just that the last time anything like this happened, a star appeared in the East, so I was looking to see if there was another one”.

Mind Your Language (Humour)

A virile young Italian soldier is relaxing in his favourite bar in Rome, when he attracts a gorgeous, young blonde. They go back to his apartment and make love. Afterwards, the soldier says with a smile: “you finish?” She frowns and replies: “No”. Surprised, the young man reaches for the beautiful girl … and the love making resumes. She seems to enjoy herself. As the love making ends, the soldier asks smugly: “This time, you finish?”

She returns his smile and whispers contentedly: “No”. Puzzled but determined, he reached but determined, he reached for her again. They make love once again until the exhausted man falls back, gasping. Barely able to turn his head he asked|: “So you finish?” “No!” She shouts back. “Stop asking. I no Finish, I Swedish”.

World.title: Justice Lifu, Appeal Court and NJC, by Tonnie Iredia
World.content:
For the benefit of those who have not quite followed the story of Justice Peter Odo Lifu, this article begins by restating the highlights of the relevant events. In June 2026, the said Justice Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja ordered INEC to deregister five political parties namely: Africa Democratic Congress, Action Peoples Party, Accord Party, Action Alliance, and Zenith Labour Party. Unfortunately, the Court of Appeal had ordered a stay of proceedings on the matter about a month earlier, but Lifu ignored the order and went ahead to deliver judgment. On appeal, the Court of Appeal found a huge space to take the high court judge to the cleaners. It did not only set aside Lifu’s judgment, it used the harshest rebuke in recent times on the judge.

In the words of the judges of the Court of Appeal, Lifu’s conduct was ‘the highest form of judicial impertinence’, ‘judicial rascality’, ‘judicial indiscipline and gross insubordination’ and ‘a brazen violation of the hierarchy of the court and the 1999 Constitution.’ As if to establish that it was not doing anything new, the court recalled the Supreme Court’s precedent where the apex court had held that a judge who deliberately disregards the order of a superior court is ‘unfit for the bench.’ Many commentators agreed with the condemnation of Lifu because he wrongly assumed jurisdiction to act on a suit filed by a body without legal capacity. Lifu also didn’t even get the facts of the case right as he ordered the deregistration of parties which did not fail the test of registration.

At this point where everyone is up against Justice Lifu, I consider it necessary to draw attention to the fact that the anti-Lifu posture does not tell the entire story. Although I can’t clap for Lifu, I have searched in vain for what can encourage me to clap for the Court of Appeal either. Indeed, being the higher court with judges of greater professional experience, I am not persuaded that the Court of Appeal did better or was in any way right in openly castigating and publicly rebuking an erring judge. It would have been better for the entire judiciary if the Court had just overturned the verdict without abusing the person of the judge. In addition to not adding any judicial value to the reversal of the earlier verdict, the abuse only derogated from the image of the judiciary.

Instead of sending an internal report to the NJC, the Appeal Court created a problem for the entire judiciary by using strong terms on a judge thereby prompting Nigerians to expect his removal within minutes. Months after, the removal didn’t happen. Lifu is not only still there; he has since done more harm as far as many members of the public are concerned. In fact, two days after the NJC axed other erring judges, Justice Lifu delivered a second controversial judgment nullifying the ADC primary election and reinstating a factional leadership. This establishes clearly that the damaging words on Lifu were superfluous. The point to be made is that the Court of Appeal was right to set aside the Lifu judgment. It was also right to insist on hierarchy, but was wrong to communicate that insistence through personal condemnation.

Perhaps our Court of Appeal should emulate courts in other climes. In the UK for instance, the Supreme Court, in R (Miller) v. Secretary of State for Exiting the EU UKSC 5, overturned a decision of the Divisional Court on a matter of weighty constitutional importance, without a single personal adjective directed at the lower court or the judge in person. In Nigeria, the Court of Appeal which has no power to remove a judge attempted to pre-empt the National Judicial Council (NJC) that has the mandate to discipline judges. The situation now is that the said unfit Lifu is still in office; and the powerful judges of the Court of Appeal have been ignored while our sleeping NJC has continued snoring heavily leaving many people to create several theories on the NJC’s posture.

My standpoint today is supported by the fact that under the Constitution and the Code of Conduct for Judicial Officers, all judges are bound by the same rules. Two of those rules which are relevant here are i) A judge must be temperate, courteous, and restrained in language, even when criticising a lower court, ii) A judge must not make unnecessary personal attacks that bring the judiciary into disrepute. In line with these rules, one can say without any fear of contradiction that a higher court that insults lower courts but refuses to police its own tone and diction stands the risk of losing moral authority. It would appear therefore that the breach of the above rules on temperate language is responsible for why the NJC is over sleeping. Otherwise, the noise that has been made about Justice Lifu is strong enough to wake up the dead.

Surprisingly, in spite of formal protests by parties and other groups which see Lifu as a tool for judicial partisanship, the latest move by the NJC in which it disciplined 9 judicial officers, had no mention of Justice Lifu. Indeed, as of November 2026, there has been no public query, no investigation report, no timeline, no statement from NJC on Lifu’s petition. One pro-NJC advocate says the body may have learnt lessons that are making her cautious. For example, if the NJC, after due process, is unable to agree with the Court of Appeal, it would be accused of shielding Lifu. If on the other hand, it removes him, it may be seen as merely rubber-stamping the Court of Appeal. In either case, the NJC loses the advocate concludes.

At the same time, there are critics in other disciplines who are sick and tired of an unduly silent NJC. To them, the current situation is that the story has shifted from judgment and politics to communication and accountability, because a disciplinary body that cannot communicate its process clearly creates suspicion. The luck the judiciary has is that many people often forget that it is an arm of government. As a result, the few media professionals in Nigeria who have the courage to hold government accountable to the people face only the executive and the legislature. Of recent however, some of our judges are inadvertently telling us all that so much is wrong with our judiciary.

If so, the media and social activists must begin to beam their searchlight to the direction of the judiciary. The other day, a respected retired justice of the Supreme Court asserted that our judiciary now operates like market stalls. Courts of coordinate jurisdiction have continued to give conflicting decisions in breach of warnings by the Chief Justice of the federation. In addition to this situation which greatly confuses our people, it has become the norm for parties to a case; to both claim to have won the case. The fact that at the end of every case in Nigeria, each counsel has the audacity to address the media and claim victory even when his side actually lost in a particular case, points clearly to poor systemic communication.

The National Judicial Council (NJC) which is established under Section 153(1)(i) of the 1999 Constitution (as amended) has the mandate to exercise disciplinary control over judicial officers. As the sole constitutional gatekeeper for judicial discipline in the country, the NJC is not an advisory body. When a judge is accused of defying a superior court, there is no other institution the public can turn to. The Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) can petition; civil society can protest; the media can even produce sensational reports on the subject but it is only the NJC that can discipline. It is a huge monopoly which carries with it a corresponding monopoly on communication. If the NJC does not speak, no one can speak authoritatively on its behalf. In controversial cases such as those heard by Lifu, silence cannot be golden.

Public trust in the judiciary has been patently eroded. It does not speak well of our judiciary for our leading politicians to publicly declare that they will not go to court to fight the outcome of the 2027 elections. Our judiciary must immediately evolve a better model of communication to earn public trust. In Kenya, the Judicial Service Commission publishes an annual report listing the number of petitions received, the number disposed of, and the average time for disposal. No judge is named until misconduct is established thereby assuring the public that the system works. In Ghana, the Judicial Council regularly issues short statements confirming receipt of petitions and expected timelines. The public does not know the outcome in advance, but it knows the Council is functioning. Is our NJC gagged?

World.title: I don’t want to be stereotyped because of my looks – Obioma Ofoegbu
World.content:
Obioma Ofoegbu

By Ayo Onikoyi

Nollywood actress Obioma Ofoegbu has spoken about the challenges of being stereotyped because of her plus-size physique, saying she is determined to establish herself as a versatile performer capable of taking on diverse roles.

In an interview with Potpourri, Ofoegbu said she had repeatedly been offered roles that portrayed her as an older woman or confined her to characters typically associated with plus-size actresses.

“My biggest challenge when I started was not being stereotyped because of my body type. A lot of times, they tried to give me roles just because I’m a plus-size woman. They would make me older in some movies or give me the same stories that a plus-size woman is expected to tell,” she said.

The actress, who officially began her film career in 2020 after years of participating in stage plays and theatre productions during her school days, said she had rejected several roles in a bid to break away from such limitations.

“I’m young. I don’t have to play an older woman or a married woman just because I’m plus-size. I don’t want to be placed in a box because of my looks, my appearance, or where I live,” she added.

Speaking about her most challenging role, Ofoegbu identified her performance in Africa Magic’s series, The Low Priest, where she portrayed a villainous character who undergoes a transformation.

She described the experience as physically demanding, revealing that she had to learn more Igbo, chant incantations and endure challenging filming conditions.

The experience, she said, strengthened her confidence in her abilities and taught her that preparation and resilience could help her handle demanding characters.

Despite her preference for diverse roles, Ofoegbu admitted that economic realities in Nigeria could make accepting stereotypical roles necessary, particularly for emerging actors trying to establish themselves financially.

“I’m not a Funke Akindele yet. I’m not big enough to be producing as I please, so definitely I would take up those roles. I would grow as an actor, save, build and get my face out there,” she said.

She also described acting as an uncertain source of income for emerging performers, advising actors to develop alternative income streams rather than depend entirely on film roles.

On film promotion, the actress, who also has experience as an executive producer, maintained that actors should support projects they feature in but insisted that producers must have independent marketing strategies.

Her long-term ambition, she said, is to have her work recognised beyond Africa and collaborate with filmmakers across different parts of the world.

“I’m an actor, I’m not just a Nollywood actor. I like to see myself as an actor. Nollywood is a starting point for me,” she said.

World.title: RIBADU: A PROFILE IN COURAGE
World.content:
DECAN honours Nuhu Ribadu for strengthening Nigeria’s counterinsurgency campaigns, writes SAMBO YAKUBU

Leadership is often measured not only by the responsibilities entrusted to an individual but also by the confidence, recognition and institutional influence that grow around the discharge of those responsibilities. In Nigeria’s demanding national security environment, where the consequences of failure are measured in lost lives, displaced communities and destroyed livelihoods, the emergence of a credible and coordinated security leadership is particularly significant.

For National Security Adviser (NSA), Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, the steady growth of his public profile is becoming increasingly evident. His latest recognition by the Defence Correspondents Association (DECAN), which honoured him for strengthening Nigeria’s counterinsurgency campaign and recording gains in the fight against terrorism, is another indication of the attention his stewardship is attracting within the national security community.

The award, presented at the third edition of DECAN’s conference, carries significance beyond the ceremonial value of a plaque or commendation. It represents an acknowledgement by professionals who regularly report on defence and security matters of the importance of strategic coordination in confronting Nigeria’s complex security challenges.

The association described Ribadu’s contribution in unmistakable terms, recognising his “outstanding leadership, strategic coordination and dedicated service in strengthening and managing Nigeria’s national security architecture” as National Security Adviser to the President.

Although the award was received on his behalf by the Director of Legal at the Office of the National Security Adviser, Zakari Mijinyawa, the recognition reinforces Ribadu’s growing visibility as a central figure in the country’s security policy and coordination efforts.

It is a profile that has been shaped by the extraordinary demands of the office he occupies. Nigeria has battled the Boko Haram insurgency for approximately 15 years, a conflict that has exacted an enormous human and economic toll. Lives have been lost, communities devastated, properties destroyed and productive activities disrupted, with the consequences extending far beyond the immediate theatres of conflict.

The country’s security challenges have also evolved. While terrorism and insurgency remain major concerns, banditry, kidnapping, organised criminal networks, cyber threats and other emerging risks have expanded the responsibilities of the national security establishment.

In such an environment, the NSA’s office occupies a strategically important position. It must help bring together the intelligence community, military institutions, law enforcement agencies and other relevant stakeholders to ensure that national security responses are coordinated, informed and aligned with the country’s priorities.

This is where Ribadu’s leadership is attracting particular attention. The growing recognition of his role reflects an appreciation of the fact that winning the security battle requires more than individual operations by separate agencies. It requires a system in which information is shared, intelligence is properly assessed, institutional responsibilities are clearly understood and operations are guided by a common strategic direction.

The theme of the DECAN conference, “Beyond Kinetic Warfare: Harnessing Technology and Intelligence-Led Operations for Nigeria’s National Security,” is therefore especially relevant to the broader conversation about Ribadu’s growing profile.

It captures the changing character of modern security challenges and the need for Nigeria to move beyond an approach defined exclusively by the deployment of force.

Military operations remain indispensable in confronting terrorist groups and armed criminal organisations. However, lasting progress depends equally on the quality of intelligence, the ability to anticipate threats, the effective use of technology and the coordination of institutions responsible for protecting the country. A terrorist network cannot be effectively dismantled merely by confronting its armed operatives. Its sources of finance, communication channels, recruitment structures, supply chains and support networks must also be identified and disrupted. This requires intelligence cooperation, investigative capacity, technological resources and sustained institutional collaboration.

Similarly, the fight against banditry and kidnapping requires an understanding of criminal networks that operate across geographical and institutional boundaries. No single security agency possesses every capability necessary to address these threats independently.

The significance of an intelligence-led approach is that it enables security institutions to act with greater precision, anticipate emerging dangers and make better use of available resources. It also offers the prospect of reducing unnecessary risks to civilians and security personnel.

By bringing senior military and security officials, government representatives, policymakers and journalists together around these questions, the DECAN conference provided an important platform for examining the future of Nigeria’s security architecture.

Ribadu’s recognition at such a gathering is noteworthy because it places his stewardship within a conversation that goes beyond the immediate headlines of military operations. It highlights the importance of the strategic architecture that connects policy, intelligence, technology and operational responses.

His growing profile also reflects the wider responsibilities of the NSA’s office in a country where security and development are deeply interconnected. Insecurity does not merely threaten lives; it undermines agriculture, discourages investment, disrupts education, weakens local economies and places additional pressure on public finances.

A farmer unable to access his land because of terrorist or bandit activity is a victim of insecurity, but the consequences extend to food production and national economic stability. A business forced to close because of repeated attacks represents not only a private loss but also a setback to employment, investment and government revenue.

This reality makes the coordination of national security efforts an essential part of the country’s wider development ambitions. Security is not an isolated government responsibility. It is a foundation for economic transformation, social stability and national cohesion.

Consequently, the growing recognition of Ribadu’s leadership should also be understood within the context of the need to build a more integrated security system—one capable of responding to immediate threats while strengthening the institutions and partnerships required for lasting stability.

There is, however, an important distinction between recognition and results. An award, however prestigious, cannot by itself establish the success of a national security campaign. The ultimate measure of Ribadu’s stewardship must remain the safety of Nigerians, the restoration of communities affected by violence, the protection of livelihoods and the capacity of security institutions to prevent and respond effectively to threats.

This makes the DECAN honour both an acknowledgement and a challenge. It recognises the importance of the work being undertaken while reinforcing the expectations that accompany the office.

For Ribadu, the responsibility is therefore to convert growing institutional recognition into sustained and measurable security improvements. Nigerians need to see stronger intelligence coordination, more effective disruption of criminal networks, improved protection of vulnerable communities and a security architecture that earns public confidence through professionalism and accountability.

The media also has an important role in this process. Defence correspondents are uniquely positioned to interrogate security policies, examine operational outcomes, highlight institutional gaps and provide citizens with informed assessments of developments. Their recognition of strategic leadership is meaningful, but their responsibility to scrutinise the performance of the security system remains equally important.

Ultimately, Ribadu’s growing profile is a reflection of the national attention now focused on the strategic leadership of Nigeria’s security architecture. His recognition by DECAN underscores the importance of coordination, intelligence and institutional cooperation in confronting a security crisis that has endured for far too long.

Nigeria needs a security system that is not only capable of responding to attacks but also sufficiently intelligent, technologically equipped and institutionally connected to prevent them. It needs leadership that can bring different agencies together, sustain a common direction and insist that national security remains a collective priority.

The recognition of Nuhu Ribadu by the Defence Correspondents Association is an encouraging endorsement of the importance of that responsibility. But the greater honour will be earned when the gains of strategic coordination translate into safer communities, restored livelihoods and a country in which citizens can live, work and pursue their ambitions without the persistent fear of violence.

Yakubu writes from Abuja

World.title: WIKE’S PUSH FOR GLOBAL PARTNERSHIPS
World.content:
From proposed partnerships with German cities to plans for daily flights between Doha and Abuja, Nigeria’s Federal Capital Territory is making a stronger case for international investment and cooperation.

When Germany’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Stefan Rössel, visited Federal Capital Territory Minister Nyesom Wike at his official residence in Life Camp, the Minister put forward a practical proposition: Abuja should work directly with German cities to develop its agricultural sector, expand its digital capabilities and equip more young people with skills for employment and enterprise.

In a separate engagement, Qatar’s Ambassador, Al-Hail, outlined plans for more frequent flights between Doha and Abuja and proposed that the two capitals share expertise in urban transport and smart-city development. Taken together, the engagements show how Wike is using diplomacy to open Abuja to partnerships that can help the city grow and serve its residents better.

“Our vision is to see Abuja become one of the best cities in the world,” Wike said during the German envoy’s visit. His references to Berlin, Munich and Washington, D.C., placed Abuja’s ambition in a global context.

The proposed German partnerships give that ambition a practical focus.

For farmers and agribusinesses in the FCT, cooperation could bring access to expertise that improves productivity and helps them reach new markets.

For young people, technical and vocational training could open routes into employment or help them start businesses.

Rössel commended the visible changes in Abuja and indicated interest from Germany and other European partners in urban planning, infrastructure and city governance. That creates room for direct exchanges between the people who run cities: planners, engineers, transport officials and public service managers. They can compare what works in their cities and adapt those lessons to Abuja’s needs.

Qatar brings another opportunity. Ambassador Al-Hail announced plans for Qatar Airways to increase its Doha–Abuja service from four flights a week to daily operations from November 2026.

A daily connection would give conference organisers, investors and business travellers more flexibility. It would also make it easier for Abuja-based businesses to meet partners and explore markets abroad.

The envoy’s proposal for cooperation on integrated transport raises a question that matters to residents and visitors alike: how easily can someone travel from the airport into the city and onward to surrounding communities? Qatar’s experience connecting airports, cities and regional routes offers a useful starting point for that conversation.

Abuja already has a place on the world’s diplomatic map. Wike’s push is to turn that standing into a development advantage. The next step is to give these opportunities a clear shape: training linked to jobs, technical exchanges that improve city services, and transport connections that make Abuja easier to reach and do business in.

The promise of opening Abuja to the world is that the benefits reach the people who call it home.

Dr. Jumai Ahmadu, Director, Reform Coordination and Service Improvement Department, FCTA

World.title: AMUPITAN: REFLECTIONS ON THAT “CHATHAM HOUSE” HECKLING
World.content:
Amupitan should be criticised on evidence, in the proper forum, and with the aim of improving the election, argues TUNDE OLUSUNLE

Thursday, November 12, 2026, Joash Amupitan, SAN, the law professor who is Chairman of INEC went to Chatham House in London to speak on a panel discussion titled “Nigeria’s 2027 Elections: Democratic Trajectory and Regional Stability Beyond the Ballot.” He went to explain, to answer, to be questioned. What met him outside was not questioning. It was ambush. Protesters surrounded his vehicle, blocked its path, hurled insults at him, and demanded his resignation. He was called a fraud, an agent of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), a man procured to return President Bola Tinubu in January 2027, willy-nilly.

Whatever one thinks of INEC, that scene should trouble every democrat. I hope insinuations that a few INEC officials who accompanied Amupitan to the engagement had APC campaign adornments on them are untrue. That would have been daft, insensitive, reckless, irresponsible, and unacceptable. But a man who had come to submit himself to public scrutiny was denied the dignity of being heard. The protest mistook the messenger for the malady. It revealed a deeper Nigerian habit: we personalise institutional failure until the person becomes the institution, and then we destroy the person in the hope that the institution will somehow heal itself. It never does.

Let us be clear, and let us be fair. The anger is not invented. It has a history, and it has a cause. Nigerians have watched elections disappoint them too often. They watched 2023 damage confidence in INEC in a way from which, by Amupitan’s own admission at Chatham House, the Commission has not yet fully recovered. They have now watched the discovery of suspected artificial intelligence-generated photographs and duplicate entries in the preliminary voters’ register. When citizens who went to verify their own names found strange faces staring back at them, it was not paranoia to ask questions. It was citizenship. On November 9, 2026, Amupitan himself gave the country the scale of the problem. After a review of the 2025/2026 Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise, which harvested 11,088,238 records, INEC removed 1,608,660 invalid registrations. It removed a further 873 records belonging to verified deceased voters. It identified 54 persons across 10 states for alleged involvement in registration irregularities for disciplinary action and possible prosecution.

It admitted that some registration officers had abused their authorised access and that historical rot dating back to 2011 still clings to the register. That is a damning admission. But notice what it is and what it is not. It is not a cover-up. A Commission intent on rigging does not publish its own shame. It does not invite the public to display and object to its preliminary register from October 9 to 15. It does not announce that 268,000 cases were re-examined after public complaints, that 217,722 were found invalid and removed, while 50,278 were cleared and retained. It does not ban ordinary webcams for registration, approve an Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, and promise a final register on December 15. A Commission intent on fraud conceals its fraud. This one, under Amupitan, exposed its own wound and began to clean it in public. This is the first test of objectivity: to distinguish between a problem discovered and a problem created.

The 1.6 million invalid entries, almost enough to have decided the vote difference between the presidential candidates of the APC and the Peoples Democratic Party, (PDP), in the 2023 election, are not Amupitan’s creation. Let’s be clear. They are the inheritance of a system that has been porous for years, exploited by low-level operators, distorted by new technology, and neglected by successive managements. To blame the man who found the rot for the existence of the rot is to punish the doctor for diagnosing the disease. The second test is performance. Amupitan has not merely talked about reform. He has run elections. Since his appointment in October 2025, he has delivered three off-cycle governorship elections in Anambra, Ekiti and Osun, alongside Federal Capital Territory Area Council elections and 16 legislative by-elections. In each governorship contest, the result reflected the popular will, and the outcomes cut across party lines: APGA in Anambra, APC in Ekiti, Accord in Osun.

A captured umpire does not produce results that embarrass the ruling party’s expectations in one state and confirm them in another. He produces a pattern. There has been no pattern here, except the pattern of results being declared promptly, in Anambra and Osun a day after voting, where such elections once dragged for days and ended in inconclusive agonies. Even more telling, as Amupitan promised the Senate when he was screened, losers congratulated winners. In a country where every election used to end in a tribunal, that is not a small thing. It is the beginning of a culture. That is how trust is rebuilt: not by grand speeches but by small, repeatable acts of competence. The third test is character. Amupitan did not seek this job as a politician seeks office. He lived and worked all his life in academia. He was a contented teacher wholly committed to instruction, research, and the unglamorous work of managing students, a department, and a faculty. He was sought out for the INEC hot seat. He did not climb to it.

He brings to the Commission the habits of the lecture room: evidence before assertion, procedure before passion, correction before concealment. At Chatham House, he remained in his vehicle and made no audible response to the invective. Some read that as arrogance. It was, in truth, restraint. And at that same session, he did something no recent INEC chairman has done so plainly. He pledged that he would not accept any appointment from anybody after his tenure because coming to serve is based on trust. In a country still smarting from the sight of his predecessor accepting a diplomatic posting after leaving office, that pledge was not rhetoric. It was a deliberate severing of the suspicion that INEC is a stepping stone to reward.

None of this means Amupitan is above criticism. He must be criticised and criticised relentlessly but criticised on evidence, in the proper forum, and with the aim of improving the election, not destroying the umpire. Opposition parties have every right to demand a clean register, to interrogate the 54 officials, to ask how historical duplicates will be purged, to monitor the nationwide mock accreditation on November 28, and to test the new safeguard that prevents an inaccurate polling-unit result from reaching IReV at all. That is oversight. That is democracy. What they do not have a right to do is to make the conduct of the election impossible by turning every controversy into a personal war against the chairman. If Amupitan spends his days answering one court injunction per day, responding to one manufactured scandal per day, defending his person against one mob per day, who will run the election? Distraction is not accountability. Harassment is not oversight.

A country that harasses its umpire into paralysis should not be surprised when the match is abandoned. Amupitan is, in many ways, a victim of our political imperfections. The anger that boiled over in London was not really about Amupitan. It was about 2023. Maybe also about 2019 when an opposition candidate was reportedly leading the presidential poll comfortably, and the INEC server developed a sudden “glitch,” which torpedoed popular expectations. It was about years of broken promises. It was about a feeling, shared by millions, that the vote does not count. Amupitan happened to be the man standing in front of the car when that anger needed a face. But if we allow that anger to consume the one man who is actually trying to fix the register, who is actually removing invalid names rather than defending them, then we will have committed a peculiarly Nigerian self-harm: we will have punished reform because it was not perfect, and in doing so, we will have made perfect reform impossible.

Let us, therefore, make a distinction our politics too often refuses to make: between INEC as an institution with a troubled history and Amupitan as a man with a short, verifiable record. Judge the institution by its history and demand that it change. Judge the man by his record and allow him to change it. To the opposition, I say this with respect: your strongest weapon in January 2027 will not be a protest in London. It will be a clean register, a vigilant polling agent, a credible result sheet, and a chairman who knows that the whole country is watching him. Give him the space to deliver that. Hold him to his own promises. Demand the final register on December 15 and audit it line by line. But let him work.

To the ruling party, I say this with equal candour: do not mistake an alibi on Amupitan’s behalf for a defence of yourselves. The best service you can render him is to leave him alone. Do not make his independence suspect by claiming him as yours.

Nigeria does not need a perfect INEC chairman. It does not have one, and it never will. It needs an honest one, given the room to be honest, and held firmly to account for the honesty he promises. Amupitan has earned, by his short record, the right to be given that room. Let us stop heckling the man and start helping the process. The election is not his. It is ours. And if we break the umpire before the match, we will have no one to blame but ourselves when the game is lost.

Olusunle, PhD, Fellow of the Association of Nigerian Authors (FANA), is also a Fellow of the Nigerian Guild of Editors, (FNGE)

World.title: ECHOES OF SUN TZU
World.content:
O. JASON OSAI writes that Nigeria’s future should not be sacrificed on the altar of individual ambition or partisan loyalty

Sun Tzu was an ancient Chinese military strategist, philosopher and reputed general who lived during China’s Spring and Autumn period, around the 6th century BC. He is best remembered as the author of The Art of War, one of the most influential treatises on military strategy, leadership and the management of conflict ever written. But he was more than a student of warfare. He was an astute observer of human nature, political power, leadership, deception and the consequences of poor judgement. His central philosophy is that the highest form of victory is not the destruction of an adversary, but the achievement of one’s objective without unnecessary bloodshed or devastation.

Sun Tzu understood that war is an expensive undertaking, that internal division weakens nations, and that a leader who fails to understand the consequences of his ambitions could ultimately destroy the very state he sought to defend or control. One of his most enduring propositions is that a nation must be governed with wisdom, discipline, strategic foresight and an appreciation of steadfast focus on the common good. In his philosophy, power is not an end in itself; it is an instrument that demands responsibility and restraint.

Although the popular saying that “an evil man would burn his own nation to the ground merely to rule over its ashes” is frequently attributed to Sun Tzu, there is no reliable evidence that he actually said or wrote it. Yet the sentiment of the statement raises a profound question that resonates far beyond ancient China: What happens when the personal ambition of those who seek power becomes more important than the survival and prosperity of the nation? It is against this philosophical backdrop that the Nigerian experience invites reflection, and this is the objective of this piece.

Moving forward, we ask: What does the saying mean? Simply answered: It describes a leader whose hunger for power is greater than his love for his country. Such a person would: One, offhandedly destroy national institutions than allow someone else to lead. Two, create division and conflict to maintain control. Three, sacrifice the people’s welfare to protect personal ambition and four, leave the country devastated, provided he remains in power.

More than two millennia after Sun Tzu, Nigeria presents us with a compelling study in the relationship between power and ambition on the one hand and national destiny and good governance on the other hand. One is compelled to ask whether those currently entrusted with the responsibility of preserving the Nigerian state fully appreciate the difference between winning political battles and securing the future of a nation. For what value is political victory if the institutions of government are weakened, the economy battered, the people impoverished and the national spirit diminished? A country is not a trophy to be won, nor is its population collateral damage in the contest for political supremacy. The ultimate measure of leadership is not how long one holds power, but the legacies that are bequeathed the nation when one eventually leaves office.

The peculiar tragedy of the Nigerian situation is that it is at war with itself and so cannot identify the enemy. Drawing from Sun Tzu’s metaphor, Nigeria is being burnt down by those entrusted with the power of the state, and the most worrisome and frightening aspect of this unfolding national catastrophe is that the fire is not coming from a single direction. It is being fuelled by political recklessness, institutional decay, economic mismanagement, brazen kleptomania, insecurity and an alarming disregard for the welfare of ordinary citizens.

Experience over the years shows that a nation does not collapse in one dramatic moment. Sometimes, it dies gradually, one compromised institution of governance at a time, one abandoned responsibility after another, until the very foundations upon which its existence rests begin to crumble. Currently, the National Assembly has become an extension of the executive and the judiciary has lost its bite. Any person with a modicum of sense of reasoning will recognize and accept that Nigeria is speedily slipping down a very slippery socioeconomic slope. Nigeria is heading towards disaster; the nation is at the edge of a yawning canyon.

The economy is suffocating millions. The cost of living has become an unbearable burden for families and the middle class has been obliterated. Confronted by diminishing opportunities and an uncertain future, the youth now look beyond their homeland for hope. Japa, the phenomenon of traveling overseas in search for greener pastures, has made its way into the Nigerian lexicon and its relevance is no more limited to traveling to Europe and America, Asian countries and some less endowed African countries have become desired destinations. Farmers cannot confidently return to their fields in some parts of the country. Communities are ravaged by insecurity, while citizens struggle to reconcile the paradox of enormous resources of their country with the poverty that defines their daily existence.

Sadly, in the face of this national distress, the political class is unapologetically preoccupied with the acquisition, retention and consolidation of power and the brazen display of ill-gotten wealth through ostentatious lifestyle . Political survival seems to command greater attention and urgency than national recovery. The contest for political advantage frequently overshadows the imperative of governance.

Tzu’s metaphor of burning the nation to the ground simply to rule over its ashes, finds appropriateness here when taken against the backdrop of a country where political ambition is cold-heartedly indifferent to the consequences of its pursuit. Nigeria is not the private estate of its political leaders.

It belongs to its people. Therefore, its future should not be sacrificed on the altar of individual ambition, partisan loyalty or the desperate struggle for political relevance. The tragedy of a burning nation is not actually the destruction of its physical structures; rather, it is the erosion of public trust, the death of collective aspiration and the gradual loss of faith in the possibility of a better tomorrow.

What Nigerians need now is leadership that understands that power is a responsibility, not a personal inheritance; that governance is about people, not political trophies; and that patriotism must be demonstrated through service, sacrifice and accountability more than political slogans, elaborate ceremonies and endless promises of illusive transformation.

At no time in the history of this nation have despondency, desperation and dejection been boldly inscribed on the faces of Nigerians from Sokoto to Oyorokoto and from Badagri to Bakassi. A house on fire does not need occupants arguing over who owns the furniture. It needs people willing to put out the fire. Nigeria is aflame. The question is whether those entrusted with saving it recognise the flames, or are simply waiting to inherit the ashes. Another question is: have the victims of the current socioeconomic inferno realized that the dividing line in the society is socioeconomic, not religious, ethnicity and the other social malaises that are exploited by politicians so they would continue to exploit the nation and the masses?

Two parting questions: Are those currently competing and jostling for public office and political power in Nigeria seeking to rescue the nation from those bent on sinking the ship of the Nigerian State or are they merely hustling to preside over it and further the ruins? Does Nigeria need people with capabilities, competence and character at the helm of affairs or bleeders who masquerade as leaders? These are the questions that should agitate the mind of every voter.

Prof Osai writes from Port Harcourt

World.title: Senator Paulker Declares Loyalty to PDP, as Party Prioritises Tinubu’s Re-election in Bayelsa
World.content:
Olusegun Samuel in Yenagoa

The former Deputy Minority Whip of the 8th Senate and three-time Senator representing Bayelsa Central, Senator Emmanuel Paulker, has declared his unwavering loyalty to the Peoples Democratic Party PDP).

Speaking when he received members of the State Working Committee and other party leaders, led by the state chairman, Hon. Chief Alabh George Turnah, during a courtesy visit at his residence in Yenagoa, he reaffirmed his unbroken loyalty to the PDP and declared that he does not intend to leave the party.

Paulker, who represented Bayelsa Central between 2007 and 2019, assured members of the party of his commitment to the resurgence of the party.

“Since 1998, I have not left the PDP for even a second. I will not leave this party.”

Paulker, while commending Turnah for his courageous and dynamic leadership of the party, assured him of his total commitment and support.

He also urged the leadership to remain united, focused, carry all stakeholders along and pursue reconciliation despite internal challenges.

“My doors are open to you at all times. Hold firm; the party is in safe hands under your leadership, and I am with you all the way.”

Paulker expressed confidence that the PDP would emerge stronger and bounce back to power in the state.

He enjoined leaders and members to remain committed to the party’s success, stressing that all the big names in Bayelsa politics started their politics from the PDP.

Turnah, in his remarks, described Paulker as a founding pillar of the PDP in Bayelsa, acknowledging his contributions to the party and the state’s political development.

He noted that Paulker’s experience, wisdom and guidance have remained a source of inspiration and strength to the current leadership of the Party in the State.

Meanwhile, the leadership of the party has resolved to transfer full responsibility for the campaigns of its National Assembly candidates to the candidates themselves.

A statement by the party’s publicity secretary, Ikaebimo Mark, stated that the leadership of the party will now concentrate its efforts on the statewide campaign for the re-election of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu under the National Rainbow Coalition arrangement.

Mark, who disclosed that the decision was taken at the regular meeting of the State Working Committee held on Thursday, 12th November 2026, added that it is in accordance with the directive of the party’s national leader, Nyesom Ezenwo Wike, issued in consultation with the National Working Committee of the Peoples Democratic Party.

According to Mark, consequently, all National Assembly candidates are directed to take complete charge of their respective campaigns and to intensify community-to-community engagements across the state.

He stated that the candidates are advised to proceed independently with their campaigns, as most have already been doing.

Mark however noted that the party will, however, remain available to offer guidance and support whenever any National Assembly candidate seeks such assistance.

World.title: Deputy Speaker Kalu Charges Abia APC Presidential Campaign Council To Deliver Votes For Tinubu, Shettima
World.content:
Ahead of the presidential campaign flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Abia State on Monday, the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Rt. Hon. Benjamin Kalu, has charged the members of the campaign council to work hard to ensure victory for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and all APC candidates in Abia State in the coming election.

Addressing the campaign council members made up of the party’s governorship candidate, Chief Eric Opah, party Chairman, Hon. Chijioke Chukwu, all the candidates of the APC in the elections, Directors and Secretaries of the campaign council directorates, stakeholders and indeed, members of the party in Abia State who converged on his country home, Bende on Friday, Kalu said that the party must ensure that President Tinubu and Vice President Kashim Shettima win in the State.

He said: “We are working hard for ourselves. APC is a moving train. We are progressing. The party belongs to you and I. We are not doing one man show. We will work to make everyone proud and happy. We are working hard against all odds”.

The Deputy Speaker who is also the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign (South) 11 emphasized that a vote for the President is a vote for the reconstruction of Igbo land and for a seat in his government.

“A vote for Mr. President is a vote for the reconstruction of Ala Igbo. When we vote for him, we are voting for our seat in his government. So, we must ensure our votes count in this coming election. We must ensure Mr. President Tinubu and all our candidates in Abia win,” he said.

Kalu further announced that after the flag-off on Monday, the campaign will move into the nooks and crannies of the 17 local government areas with the Renewed Hope message, with rallies planned in all the local government areas.

“After the flag off on Monday, we will begin to enter the nooks and crannies of the local government areas with the renewed hope message. We will do rallies in all the local government areas. We are working hard for our vote. Everyone should get ready,” he said.

The Deputy Speaker stressed that every member of the council has work to do, assuring them of support.

“I want you to know we have work to do, each of us. We are here to support and stand by you. Why we need to flag-off is that without it, we cannot go to the trenches,” he said.

Kalu also directed members to secure buildings in their various local government areas and wards to serve as campaign headquarters for the Presidential campaign.

“I also encourage you to look for buildings in your various local government areas as campaign headquarters of the Presidential campaign for Mr. President. The same in your various Wards. We will do local government tours to campaign for Mr. President,” Kalu said.

The highpoints of the meeting included the distribution of APC branded T-shirts and other campaign materials to the stakeholders and members across the 17 local government areas of Abia State.

World.title: At APC Presidential Campaign Rally In Jos, Tinubu Orders Decisive Security Action Against Plateau Attackers
World.content:
.Pledges to rebuild all displaced communities

.Warns against political violence, assuring Nigerians of peaceful 2027 polls

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu at the weekend revisited the age-long communal attacks in Plateau State with a declaration that his government is taking stern security measures against those carrying out the dastardly acts in the state.

Speaking at the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Rally in Jos, the Plateau State capital on Saturday, the President outlined fresh measures to address the prolonged insecurity in Plateau State, where recurring attacks have resulted in killings, destruction of homes and displacement of several communities.

Tinubu disclosed that he had directed security agencies to intensify operations against those responsible for violent attacks and ensure restoration of lasting peace across the state.

His words: “I have directed all the security agencies to take decisive action and sustain peace and stability on the Plateau.

“What we should be getting is prosperity, not havoc, not crisis. Our government is not elected to inflict wounds on one another or to bury people. We have to lift people up from adversity to prosperity”.

He stressed that the security arrangements would particularly target threats confronting rural communities, where farmers and other residents have been forced to abandon their homes and livelihoods.

According to him, 1,000 forest guards were undergoing training for deployment, while surveillance cameras earlier promised by his government had already been procured to enhance intelligence gathering, early warning systems and rapid response to security threats.

“We are reinforcing security deployment and strengthening coordination and rapid response.

“One thousand forest guards are undergoing training right now. You will feel them. You will see them. You will feel secure in your villages and communities.

“The surveillance cameras are already procured, as I promised. They will further strengthen early detection and early warning security operations”.

The President also pledged to rebuild communities destroyed by attacks and facilitate the return of internally displaced persons to their ancestral homes.

He said the Federal Government would work closely with Governor Caleb Mutfwang and other relevant stakeholders to rehabilitate affected settlements and restore normal economic and social activities.

Said he: “I assure those displaced that we will rebuild your communities. We will rebuild your communities, and we will bring you back to your communities.

“To our displaced families, I say once again, government is working to see you return, to bring you back, to rebuild your communities.

“We will work with Caleb Mutfwang and other leaders to rebuild those communities and take you back to settle in the comfort of where you belong”.

Tinubu offered condolences to families who lost loved ones in the attacks and residents whose homes and livelihoods had been destroyed.

“Crises and attacks have inflicted deep wounds on Plateau. Too many lives have been lost, homes destroyed, communities displaced.

“To every bereaved family, every survivor and everyone unable to return home, I offer my heartfelt condolences for your loss and pray that only God will console you”, he said.

The President urged Plateau residents to live peaceful together and resist attempts to exploit their ethnic, religious or political differences.

According to him, the state’s recovery from years of conflict would depend on the willingness of its diverse communities to live together in mutual respect and work towards common development objectives.

“We are one single family created by the same God Almighty. We are just living in different rooms, speaking different languages and behaving in different ways, but living in different rooms and speaking different languages does not make us enemies of one another.

“We have to live together. We have to farm together. We have to build this Plateau and this country together. It is our responsibility to behave as brothers and sisters”, Tinubu further said.

The President also while assuring Nigerians that the 2027 polls will be peaceful, warned individuals and groups plotting to unleash violence or intimidate voters that his government will not tolerate any attempt to undermine the democratic process.

Government, he explained, will ensure adequate security for citizens to exercise their constitutional rights without fear, urging voters to disregard those seeking to provoke violence and turn out peacefully to cast their ballots.

He had, in an earlier statement on Friday, condemned violence accompanying political activities, directing security agencies to act firmly against individuals attempting to disrupt public order.

At the rally, Tinubu reiterated his determination to ensure a peaceful electoral atmosphere, urging the electorate not to allow threats of violence to discourage their participation in the democratic process.

He also canvassed for votes for APC candidates at all levels, encouraging voters to support the party in the presidential, governorship, National Assembly and state House of Assembly elections.

“APC, from top to bottom. APC, progress”, he stated.

Also speaking, Vice-President Kashim Shettima credited the progress in Plateau and nationwide to Tinubu’s “transformational and courageous leadership,” calling the president a unique leader.

Shettima praised Plateau residents for their contributions to Nigeria in education, agriculture, the military, trade, culture and sport. He described the people of the state as “a gift to the nation” and said the APC has returned to seek a renewed mandate.

He urged voters to support Tinubu, Plateau Governor Caleb Mutfwang and other APC candidates in the 2027 elections.

On his part, Senate President, Senator Godswill Akpabio said the creation of state police is in the pipeline as part of efforts to improve security across the country.

APC National Chairman, Nentawe Yilwatda, also cited the provision of surveillance cameras and forest guards among the federal government’s commitments to Plateau.

According to him, the state has benefited from the Federal Government in terms of roads, two army battalions, a brigade and four security command centres.

Yilwatda described Tinubu as a “promise keeper” and urged Plateau residents to support the president at the ballot box. He said federal projects and security measures showed that the administration had acted on commitments made to the state.

Governor Mutfwang welcomed Tinubu to Jos, describing Plateau as a home of peace and tourism and a state with a significant place in Nigeria’s political history.

He said Jos had hosted major political events and welcomed the president’s presence at the rally.

He thanked President Tinubu for federal support, particularly in road infrastructure, education and healthcare. He said his administration has been explaining the impact of federal initiatives to residents and expressed confidence that continued cooperation would benefit Plateau State.

Mutfwang also outlined state programmes designed to address employment, transport and security needs. He added that an initiative would create opportunities for about 2,000 young people to work remotely for organisations in the United States and Europe. He also referred to a tech-driven command centre to support crime detection and other security operations.

The governor said new CNG buses were being added to reduce transport difficulties for residents.

He acknowledged that security challenges remain and expressed hope that displaced people would be able to return to their ancestral homes with continued government intervention.

𝐃𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 Pre𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 Cam𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐠𝐧 Cou𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐥, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, urged Plateau residents to vote for Tinubu, saying the president deserved another term.

He praised the administration’s economic management and said increased federal revenues would give governments more resources to deliver public goods.

Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon. Tajudeen Abbas also urged voters to re-elect Tinubu and Mutfwang. He said residents should compare and contrast the projects done by previous governments with what the current administration is doing today.

Former Plateau State governors Joshua Dariye and Simon Lalong, former Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives Ahmed Wase, and former deputy governor, Pauline Tallen separately pledged support for Tinubu.

They cited federal projects in the state and the appointment of Plateau indigenes to national positions, including Yilwatda’s election as APC national chairman.

World.title: Makinde: We Won’t Allow Religion to Divide Us Over 2027 Polls
World.content:
Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan

Oyo State Governor and presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), ‘Seyi Makinde, on Saturday, said his administration will not allow religious differences to divide the people of the state, insisting that the people share a common ancestry and must remain united irrespective of their faith.

This is just as the League of Imams and Alfas in Yorubaland said it will not declare support for any politician or political party ahead of the 2027 general election.

Makinde, who made the declaration in Ibadan at the opening of a three-day conference for Imams, Alfas/Ulama, political office holders and traditional rulers, tagged, ‘Rabitah 2026,’ organised by the League of Imams and Alfas in Yorubaland (Rabitah tul Aimma wal Hulammai fii Biladi Yoruba), also appealed to Muslim leaders across the state to use their influence to promote unity, peace and political stability ahead of the elections.

The conference, with the theme, ‘The Responsibilities of Politicians and Electorate During and After Electoral Process,’ had in attendance prominent Islamic clerics, scholars, traditional rulers and political stakeholders from across the South-west.

Makinde noted that discussions surrounding the choice of the next governor of the state had intensified ahead of the elections, urging political and religious stakeholders not to allow such developments to create divisions along religious lines.

He said: “We won’t allow religion to divide us. Let us pray for our state and country because this is the period leading to the next election, when a new set of leaders will emerge.There is a lot of discussion going on right now about the choice of who will become the next governor.

“What matters most is that we must stay united. The progress of Oyo State is what is important to us, and I believe God will answer our prayers. For us in Oyo State, religion is not an issue.We have all religions in our various families, and we have always coexisted peacefully.”

Makinde further illustrated the historical and familial connections between Muslims and Christians in Oyo State, disclosing that his own family background reflected the religious diversity he was advocating.

“I, standing before you, am Oluseyi Makinde.

Makinde was my grandfather on my father’s side. My father’s name is Olatunbosun, and my grandfather, Makinde, lived and died as a Muslim. Those who are familiar with Oyo know this history.

“If I were to convene an extended family meeting this evening, about 65 per cent of those who would attend would be Muslims. I want to appeal to us that we must not allow ourselves to be divided along religious lines because we share the same ancestry and the same blood flows through our veins,” he said.

In support of the conference, the governor announced a donation of N50 million to the organisers, describing the gathering as an important platform for religious engagement and collective prayers for the state and the country.

He also called on Muslim clerics and traditional religious leaders to play a constructive role in the 2027 electoral process, noting that they would have a significant opportunity to engage voters before they make their choices at the polls.

The Chairman of the League’s Board of Trustees, Sheikh Muhammad Habibullah Adam Abdullahi El-Ilory, in his remarks at the event, said the organisation could not announce any preferred candidate or political platform ahead of the forthcoming elections, stressing that Islamic clerics were not politicians and that their responsibility was not to campaign for political office-seekers or parties but to pray for the emergence of credible leaders.

“We are religious leaders; we are not politicians, but we are the fathers of politicians. We will not declare support for any political party or politicians.We, the League of Imams and Alfas in Yorubaland, cannot declare support or announce our support for any politician or political party. We can only pray to God for Him to give us credible leaders,” he said.

The conference was attended by the APM governorship candidate in Oyo State, Hon. Bimbo Adekanmbi; his running mate, Mufutau Open Salawu; and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate, Alhaji Hazeem Gbolarumi.

Also present were the League’s President, Sheikh Jamiu Kewulere; Chief Imam of Ibadanland, Sheikh Abdulganiy Abubakar Agbotomokekere; Alfa Agba of Ibadanland, Sheikh Abdulbari Adetunji; Grand Mufti of Yoruba Land, Sheikh AbdulRasaq AbdulAzeez Ishola; Secretary-General of the League, Sheikh Mustapha Oseni Adewale Hamzat; Chairman, Oyo State Pilgrim Welfare Board (Muslim Wing), Sheikh Hashim Atere; and Prof. Kamil Olosho.

Others included the Aare Musulumi of Yorubaland, Alhaji Daud Akinola; the Soun of Ogbomosoland, Oba Afolabi Olaoye; the Onigbeti of Igbeti, Oba Bashir Abioye; and the Iyalode Adini of Yorubaland, Alhaja Sedeekat Aderibigbe, alongside other prominent Islamic clerics, scholars and Muslim faithful from Oyo, Osun, Ogun, Ekiti, Lagos and Ondo States.

World.title: ‘Zoalize was robbed’ – Miss SA pageant fans
World.content:
Zoalize Janse van Rensburg failed to make the Miss South Africa Top 5. Images via IG

Not for the first time, pageant fans are crying foul that a favourite – Zoalize Janse van Rensburg – was knocked out of the running to become Miss South Africa.

The beauty queen failed to make the Top 5, despite being a top contender and having international pageant experience.

Tiyani Makamu was crowned the winner at a glittering finale at the Sandton Convention Centre.



‘ZOALIZE WAS ROBBED’

On social media, pageant fans have expressed their shock and disappointment that Zoalize Janse van Rensburg did not make it to the Miss South Africa Top 5. Some have even accused the pageant organisers of “robbing” the 20-year-old law student of the crown.

“Zoalize… she embodies and represents the Miss SA brand so well. She IS the definition of Miss SA. This is robbery!”, commented one fan under the official pageant account.

Another wrote: “Zoalize deserved soooo much more! I can’t believe y’all robbed our girl”



You robbed Zoalize😭💔 — Goonerette (@Goonerrett) November 14, 2026

Zoalize was robbed I’m so mad on her behalf — Lú. 🇨🇩🇵🇸 (@_uluyanda) November 14, 2026

Ultimately, the Top 5 was named – Tiyani Makamu, Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo, Lesego Khumo Nyathela, Makhosazana Azana Masango and Simoné Nonhlanhla Tshituka.

Tiyani was named Miss South Africa 2026 whilst Cwenga and Lesego were crowned first and second princesses, respectively.



PAGEANT HISTORY

Zoalize van Rensburg was tipped as a favourite to win the Miss South Africa crown as she was a familiar face in the pageant world.

In 2023, she placed as first princess at the Miss World South Africa finale, and a year later re-entered and won the crown.

Last year, she represented South Africa at Miss World in India. Although she failed to make the Top 40, she won the Best Designer Dress award for Africa.



This year, Zoalize – a law student and published children’s book author – entered Miss South Africa for the first time. At just 20 years old, she had a strong fan base and an even stronger advocacy campaign – Her Never Too Young to Advocate initiative focuses on youth empowerment, education and giving young people a voice.

She has also used her platform to speak at the 2024 United Nations International Social Justice Conference.

World.title: Miss South Africa 2026 – meet your new queen!
World.content:
Miss South Africa 2026 has been crowned, and she is Tiyani Makamu.

The 27-year-old communications professional and entrepreneur succeeds 2025 title-winner Qhawekazi Mazaleni.

MEET THE MISS SOUTH AFRICA WINNER

Tiyani Makamu was crowned Miss South Africa at a glittering finale at the Sandton Convention Centre, hosted by former pageant queen Jo-Ann Strauss and Lawrence Maleka.



Her first and second princesses are Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo and Lesego Khumo Nyathela, respectively.

Tiyani is a 27-year-old Group Digital Lead and Client Success Executive who has a degree in PR and Corporate Communications.

Her advocacy is centred on entrepreneurship and skills development, youth unemployment, and expanding access to education and knowledge.

The Top 5 also included rugby WAG Simone Tshituka and singer and model Makhosazana Azana Masango.

PRIZES

The 2026 Miss South Africa winner not only receives a crown and title, but also a R1 million cash prize and R500 000 in dedicated funding for her social-impact projects.

The First Princess receives a R250 000 cash award and a dedicated R150 000 Impact Fund, whilst the Second Princess gets a R150 000 cash award and a dedicated R100 000 Impact Fund.

The top three contestants will also receive executive development opportunities, mentorship, wellness support, access to regional and international leadership networks, and the opportunity to lead initiatives focused on education, entrepreneurship, health, and youth development.

World.title: Curro commits R500k to get SA swimmers to Beijing World Aquatics Championships
World.content:
Curro commits R500k for 21 swimmers to travel to Beijing to attend the World Aquatics Championships. Image via Facebook

Curro, South Africa’s largest network of independent, private schools, has pledged half a million to help 21 swimmers – including Olympian Chad le Clos – travel to the World Aquatics Championships in Beijing.

This comes after the sporting federation, Swimming South Africa (SSA), issued a notice calling for each swimmer to contribute R55,000 each towards their trip – or risk losing their places on the team. It also comes in the wake of gold medallist Tatjana Smith announcing her decision to switch sporting nationalities to the Netherlands, citing her grievances with SSA.

The sporting tournament takes place between 1 and 6 November.



CURRO PLEDGES R500K TO GET SWIMMERS TO BEIJING WORLD AQUATICS CHAMPIONSHIPS

In a statement, Curro announced it would commit R500 000 to send the 21 South African national swimmers to the World Aquatics Championships in Beijing next month.
