Additionally, the independent schools network would host a national training camp in 2027 for the South African team and Swimming South Africa (SSA) to work with their top swimmers at Curro clinics, assisting school coaches and learners.

Curro CEO Cobus Loubser said: “We are patriotic South Africans, and we feel compelled to assist the team.

“This sponsorship helps dreams come true for swimmers who have worked their whole lives for this opportunity. It speaks to what Curro does: we create opportunities and help prepare learners for a hopeful future. Next year should be an exciting year for Curro’s thousands of young swimmers when they meet and train with their heroes.”

CONTROVERSIAL TRAVEL ARRANGEMENT COSTS

This week, news broke that SSA had issued 21 South African swimmers with a notice to pay up to R55 000 for travel and accommodation to attend the World Aquatics Championships in Beijing next month.



Swimmers were required to fork out a R40,000 deposit by 10 November and pay the remaining R15,000 by 25 November.

Those who chose to arrange their own international flights are required to pay R37,000 towards accommodation and management costs.

Additionally, swimmers are required to pay for their Chinese visas, International travel and domestic flights to Johannesburg.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs new signing reportedly goes AWOL
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs winger Faiz Abrahams has reportedly gone AWOL after failing to report for duty ahead of the club’s Carling Knockout Cup clash against Mamelodi Sundowns.

Amakhosi players regrouped on Thursday before travelling to Polokwane for a mini-camp as they prepare for the upcoming encounter. The squad is expected to return to Johannesburg on Sunday.

The 21-year-old winger, who joined Chiefs this season, was reportedly absent from the travelling squad.



Kaizer Chiefs star refuses to return to training?

According to FARPost, Abrahams has yet to report for duty following the team’s short break.

“FARPost also understands from reliable sources that the 21-year-old is yet to report for duty following the squad’s short break. Amakhosi regrouped on Thursday before travelling to Polokwane for a mini-camp, with the team expected to return to Johannesburg on Sunday. However, Abrahams was notably absent from the travelling squad,” the publication reported.

His absence comes amid reports that he has refused to return to the Chiefs camp. Sources reportedly told FARPost that the youngster has made it clear that he no longer wants to play football.

Abrahams joined Kaizer Chiefs on loan from Stellenbosch FC in August. However, he has struggled to secure regular playing time, making only a handful of appearances and scoring just once this season.

His reported absence is another concern for Amakhosi as they prepare for their cup assignment against Sundowns.

Kaizer Chiefs are yet to release an official statement or comment on the reports surrounding the winger’s alleged absence.



Should Abrahams get released?

World.title: From stress to illness: Factors driving men in Eswatini to suicide
World.content:
Speaking in parliament during discussions on the second-quarter performance reports, Mbabane East MP Welcome Dlamini outlined the key factors driving men in Eswatini to commit suicide.

With gender-based violence (GBV) at an all-time high in the country, Dlamini urged the government to also give equal attention and support to men who feel overwhelmed by their challenges, since most existing programmes do not fully cater to men.

MEN LEAD SUICIDE STATS IN ESWATINI

According to Swazi Daily News, the MP revealed that 42 men committed suicide over the last three months. He said the concerning pattern calls for practical solutions and meaningful engagement with men.



Dlamini said men grapple with a range of challenges, including unemployment, illness, domestic and social isolation.

He added that stress remains a dominant factor, as many men may feel emasculated when they are unable to provide for their loved ones due to debt, unemployment or the cost of living.

PROPOSED SOLUTIONS

The MP not only raised concerns around GBV and men’s mental health but also proposed practical solutions.

He suggested an “on-the-ground” approach that engages directly with men, including in communities, churches, social spaces and workplaces.

His proposals also included counselling, creating support groups, as well as a partnership between the health sector and the police.

He said this collaboration would ensure that men in distress receive the professional care they need and that their cases are treated with dignity and compassion.

World.title: Is Jägermeister leaving South African shelves?
World.content:
Is Jägermeister being discontinued in South Africa? Image via Facebook

A circular claiming that Jägermeister, a German liqueur, is being withdrawn from South African shelves has gone viral on social media.

But is it true?

JÄGERMEISTER NOTICE GOES VIRAL ON SOCIAL MEDIA

On the X app, an image of a notice about Jägermeister being discontinued, or at least withdrawn from South Africa, has gone viral.



The notice reads: “Jägermeister wishes to inform our valued consumers, retail partners and distributors that, following an internal review of our South African market operations, a decision has been made to discontinue the distribution of Jägermeister products in South Africa.

“Effective 31 January 2027, Jägermeister will no longer be supplied to liquor retailers, wholesalers or distributors across the country.

The notice added that “existing stock will remain available while supplies last”. It added that “once depleted, no further stock will be distributed”



In the fine print under the notice read the following: “This is a prank and is not an official statement from Jägermeister.

“No product discontinuation has been confirmed”.

Jagermeister is leaving SOUTH AFRICA@casspernyovest Don Billiato is about to double it’s profit



Get ready for the Ferarri bro bro pic.twitter.com/iPsHEgsV34  November 14, 2026

‘NOT GOING ANYWHERE’

According to Jägermeister South Africa’s Facebook and Instagram page, the circular is fake news.

A post referenced the notice, stating: “Still here, not going anywhere. Discontinued? Never that. Always read the fine print”.

The liqueur is manufactured by Mast-Jägermeister in Germany, with a South African office in Sandton that is responsible for local marketing and sales.



It is imported by Nu-World Industries.

World.title: From heatwave to thunderstorm: Heavy downpours expected in these areas
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The South African Weather Service has issued a warning for severe thunderstorms and heavy downpours across parts of the country this weekend.

The warning, valid from this afternoon, is expected over Free State, North West, Gauteng, Mpumalanga, KwaZulu-Natal, and Limpopo.

For the Western Cape, a Yellow Level 1 warning of damaging winds for Saturday has been issued.

It comes after a week of heatwaves in various areas.

READ | Joburg residents urged to take precautions as heatwave continues

The City’s Emergency Management Services has urged residents, particularly those in low-lying areas, to avoid crossing flooded roads, rivers and streams.

Emergency Services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi extended the same caution to motorists.

“We are pleading with our residents, especially those in our low-lying areas, to avoid crossing rivers and streams while conducting their daily activities. “We encourage our motorists to exercise caution while driving, extend a safe following distance and try to avoid crossing flooded roads and low-lying bridges.”

Mulaudzi said emergency service authorities will remain on high alert, monitoring all seven regions of the city for any emergencies which might occur.

World.title: No major incidents reported as matric exams near end
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Department of Basic Education is gearing up for the marking phase as the 2026 National Senior Certificate examinations near their end.

To date, the department's spokesperson, Terence Khala, said they have noted a few minor incidents reported, but none are serious enough to affect the integrity of the examinations.

READ | Senior teachers opt for early retirement as government trims wage bill

This is as he points to taxi violence in the Western Cape and scholar transport challenges in Gauteng as some of the issues experienced during the examination period.

But upon being notified of this, the department acted.

“The sector kicked in and was able to make sure that the requisite protocols were put in place. Learners in Gauteng were able to write adequately and equally in the Western Cape. “And I think it's only for us to commend the system and commend every individual that forms part of the system that assists us to make sure that we can really take this massive undertaking and make it a seamless one,” Khala said.

Markers, according to the department, will get to work on 1 December.

World.title: Six people killed in head-on collision on Eastern Cape N2
World.content:
At least six people have died in a horror crash on the N2 in the Eastern Cape.

The victims were travelling in a minibus taxi when it collided head-on with a truck on Saturday morning.

Provincial transport spokesperson Unathi Binqose said the minibus taxi was travelling from Alice towards Bizana while the truck was travelling from Kokstad towards Mzamba when the accident happened.

"Preliminary information suggests that the Toyota Quantum crossed into the path of the oncoming truck, resulting in a head-on collision. "There is also a suspicion that driver fatigue may have contributed to the crash. However, the exact circumstances surrounding the collision remain subject to police investigation," he said.

Three others were seriously injured, while three others sustained slight injuries.

"The injured were attended to by emergency services and transported for medical treatment".

The victims are believed to be university students travelling home to Bizana.

This comes just a day after seven people died in another crash on the N2 near Ndabakazi.

World.title: Madlanga Commission hears ex-JMPD top cop allegedly forced officers to take bribe
World.content:
PRETORIA - A major drug bust operation in Johannesburg has led to explosive testimony at the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry.

The commission heard on Friday how former JMPD superintendent Phineas Manyama allegedly instructed officers to release suspects and accept whatever money was offered in return.

READ | LIVE | JMPD corruption under the spotlight at Madlanga

Testifying at the commission Tactical Response Unit officer Michael Potsane said refusing the instruction came with threats of dismissal, arrest or even death.

He testified that he regarded the instruction as unlawful and did not comply with it.

World.title: Hot weather, dry taps, fuming Joburg residents
World.content:
SOWETO - Water shortages are worsening across various parts of Johannesburg, with residents reporting days without water supply amid the heatwave.

In Soweto, one resident detailed how the community has been without water since Tuesday, with supply returning briefly during the early hours of the morning.

“We've been having challenges with water in this community whereby each and every weekend we don't have water at all. It is becoming a new normal now,” the resident said.

The resident adds that the situation becomes more concerning during the current heatwave when residents need water the most.

“We are encouraged to drink more water because people are going to suffer because of dehydration, but at this particular moment, Joburg Water is not doing justice to us."

He said adding to the frustration is the lack of communication between Joburg Water and residents.

READ | Joburg residents urged to take precautions as heatwave continues

In a statement on Saturday, Joburg Water said bulk supply meters in the Roodepoort and Soweto regions, which were closed on Thursday to rescue and boost bulk supply levels, commenced reopening on Friday afternoon.

The water utility said it is worth noting that systems were not fully opened but taken back to their original curtailment before being fully closed on Thursday.

“While some bulk supplier systems have stabilised and recovered, there are still several systems which will take time to recover over the next few days. The recovery is also impacted by the demand for the system as they are integrated. “The affected Johannesburg Water reservoirs will first need to fill to acceptable levels before the system stabilises. Customers may experience low pressure or intermittent supply and, in some cases, no water until the system recovers,” the statement read.

In the meantime, Joburg Water said alternative water arrangements are being made and deployed through the central and regional coordination groups.

World.title: A grave clash: One family's search, many families' pain
World.content:
LICHTENBURG - A quest for closure for one family has thrown Boikhutso’s cemetery in Lichtenburg, North West and countless other families into chaos and heartache.

The families claim graves were disturbed and their dignity upended during an exhumation process conducted by the North West Department of Health after it got a court order in June 2023 to dig up graves, searching for a man missing from the old Thusong Hospital.

It was suspected that he had died and received a pauper’s burial at this cemetery.

However, families say the process has left the cemetery in disarray, with some unable to identify the graves of their relatives.

Mmakhumo Moja’s family is among those affected.

READ | Fort Jackson SAPS building turns into haven for criminals

She says both her parents’ graves have since vanished, lost in the shuffle. They found the graves disturbed, soil scattered and headstones missing.

"We want our graves, and we want to know exactly where they are located. After the exhumation, we were supposed to come and clean up, but we didn't know whose graves we were cleaning. When we're supposed to do some of our cultural rites at the grave, it's a problem. “When you carry out traditional rituals, you have to come to the ancestors and engage them. But the place is a mess; it's dug up, and there are holes everywhere,” Moja said.

The North West Health Department spokesperson Tebogo Lekgethwane insists it consulted some families ahead of the dig, and flat-out denies leaving the cemetery in shambles.

But three years on, the cemetery is still in a mess, and the family’s still waiting.

They’re holding out for answers, longing for restoration, and just a little respect for their dear departed.

eNCA Bafedile Moerane filed this report.

World.title: Fort Jackson SAPS building turns into haven for criminals
World.content:
MDANTSANE - Once a well-resourced police station where officers carried out their duties but today the Fort Jackson SAPS building in Mdantsane in the Eastern Cape has become a haven for criminal activity.

Criminals have taken over the building, vandalising offices that were meant to benefit the people of Mdantsane and surrounding areas.

This has left Mdantsane residents questioning how a government-owned building intended to strengthen policing could be allowed to deteriorate while crime escalates.

READ | Vandals savage Eastern Cape school

According to the community crime organisation, the Buffalo City Special Team Task Force, criminals have had easy access to the building since a taxi crashed into the perimeter fence earlier this year.

The full extend of the damage remains unclear, however police suspect opportunists trashed the premises after hours.

Eastern Cape police spokesperson Siphokazi Mawisa said following the incidents, cases were opened, and arrests were made.

"The cases are currently before court, and the suspects are out on bail,”she said.

Measures are being put in place to deploy police units that will utilise the building on a 24-hour basis to safeguard it.

eNCA's Ronald Masinda filed this report.

World.title: What 'sober' Kenyans say about Ruto's record after Uhuru spat
World.content: The Standard Group Plc is a multi-media organization with investments in media platforms spanning newspaper print operations, television, radio broadcasting, digital and online services. The Standard Group is recognized as a leading multi-media house in Kenya with a key influence in matters of national and international interest.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”

The report shows how widespread the abuse is. “Twenty-six percent of women age 15–49 have ever experienced technology-facilitated violence from any perpetrator,” the report says, and 21 per cent experienced it often or sometimes in the 12 months before the survey. Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced it at the hands of a current, most recent or previous partner.

The burden is not spread evenly, the report states that Nairobi City records the highest lifetime experience from any perpetrator at 33 per cent, followed by Murang’a and Baringo at 32 per cent each.

“For abuse by an intimate partner, Homa Bay 36 per cent and Baringo 35 per cent lead, while in the 12 months before the survey Trans Nzoia topped the list at 31 per cent. At the other end, Mandera and Wajir report just 3 per cent, a figure that may say as much about silence as about safety,” the report says

The picture is similar among young people. A 2024 rapid study by the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, working with the UNFPA and Women Economic Empowerment, found that nearly 90 per cent of young adults enrolled in three Nairobi tertiary institutions had witnessed TFGBV, and 39 per cent had experienced it personally.

Among women who have ever had a husband or intimate partner, 27 per cent have experienced gender violence committed by a current, most recent or previous partner, and 22 per cent did so in the past year. When women were asked who was responsible, the answer was blunt. Current husbands or intimate partners accounted for 61 per cent of perpetrators, former partners for 22 per cent and strangers for just 13 per cent.

Women who have never been married or had a partner face a different threat. For them, the most common perpetrators are strangers at 45 per cent, online attackers at 23 per cent and friends or acquaintances at 20 per cent.

Warning signs

Control is the common thread. The report describes such behaviours by a male partner as “important early warning signs that may escalate into violence within a relationship.”

Sixty-one per cent of ever-partnered women say their current or most recent partner has shown at least one controlling behaviour, and 27 per cent report three or more. Half say he has been jealous or angry when they spoke to other men, and 36 per cent say he insists on knowing where they are at all times. Others describe partners who demand passwords or read messages without consent.

Age and marital status matter. Technology-based gender violence is lowest among girls aged 15–19 at 10 per cent and highest among women aged 20–24 at 37 per cent. Forty-one per cent of divorced, separated or widowed women have experienced it, compared with 27 per cent of married women and 19 per cent of the never married.

Yet the digital rights advocate Cherie Oyier, a programmes officer at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), says the low figures in some places should not be read as safety. Much of the abuse happens where nobody can see it.

“Closed applications, meaning like WhatsApp, those are the ones that most people, intimate partners will usually use,” she says. “Even as you are scrolling the internet to look for these instances, we may not be able to catch it. But it does not mean that it is not happening or that it is at a lower level.”

Culture also silences women. “Most women are told just endure, this is what marriage is about,” Oyier says. “Sometimes they don’t know, it’s so overt, like it doesn’t come out clearly that this is abuse. So most of the times, it is not reported.”

Online, abuse has been turned into entertainment. “It has become banter,” she says. “Even the people who are experiencing it have trivialised it. It’s now ingrained to you, like this is something that happens, you should expect it actually. If you post a picture, one of the things that you are thinking about is what kind of comments am I going to get.”

A 2023 report by KICTANet found that more than 30 per cent of Kenyans have experienced some form of TFGBV, while 90 per cent have witnessed it. In 2025, KICTANet and Equality Now released survivor testimonies showing how deceptive online job offers, grooming and image-based abuse leave women exposed, and how many had never received counselling despite years of trauma.

The stakes are not only digital. The 2025 Report of the Technical Working Group on GBV Including Femicide, cited in the KMDHS, indicated that many cases of homicide of women and girls, and of sexual and physical harm directed towards them, “are preceded by online and offline harassment using digital tools.”

For survivors, the law offers little comfort. “The technology is moving at a very fast pace compared to the laws,” Oyier says. In an attempt to bolster the gaps, Kenya has many fragmented laws. “You’ll have the Data Protection Act, the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, the Children’s Act, that to some extent touch on online issues, but they don’t really cohesively cover the different instances of TFGBV.”

The police, she says, often do not know either. “Just imagine you’re a woman who is in a village, for example, a village in Siaya, and you encounter violence. For you to even understand which law apply is very stressful.”

“You’re going through psychological stress and depression, and you’re also supposed to figure out which law applies in your situation. It causes even more problems for victims and survivors.”

Flagging abusive language

Artificial intelligence is adding a new layer. Even so, Oyier cautions against writing it off. “We should not vilify AI completely,” she says. KICTANet has built a lexicon to help flag abusive language and runs a tracker for online gender-based violence. “One person cannot sit down and look at everything on social media. When AI is able to pull every post that has this word, a human content moderator is able to look through it with local context and see is this TFGBV or not.”

The KMDHS findings further show that exposure to TFGBV varies across age groups and digital platforms.

“Younger women are particularly exposed on social media, with 77 per cent of women aged 15–19 and 72 per cent of those aged 20–24 who experienced TFGBV reporting abuse on social media platforms, compared with 50 per cent of women aged 40–49.”

However, messaging applications tell a different story. Women aged 40–49 reported the highest exposure through these platforms at 54 per cent, compared with 30 per cent among teenagers aged 15–19.

Wealth also influences where women encounter online abuse. Exposure on social media increases from 45 per cent among women in the lowest wealth quintile to 74 per cent among those in the highest. Conversely, women in the lowest wealth quintile report greater exposure through messaging applications, at 62 per cent, compared with 39 per cent among those in the highest wealth quintile.

These differences suggest that TFGBV cuts across age and economic backgrounds, although the platforms through which women experience it vary.

World.title: Not so fast: Court slams brake on ARA over wealth forfeiture
World.content:
Felix Mecha Nyakundi could not provide a plausible explanation for how he amassed his wealth.

The Court of Appeal has ruled that the government cannot go after a person’s wealth without prior investigations to establish reasonable grounds for suspecting that the property constitutes proceeds of crime.

In a landmark judgment, Justices Patrick Kiage, Jamila Mohammed and Nduma Nderi said that although it does not require a person to be charged for a crime for the Asset Recovery Agency (ARA) to come knocking, it bears the responsibility to link the wealth or cash to a crime.

World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Middle East aims to targets 100 million tourists by 2030 – Egypt leads the growth
World.content:
As the Arab region prepares for an exceptional winter season, the latest ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 revealed that 77 percent of travelers considering a visit to the Middle East prioritize “luxury” when making booking – a figure significantly higher than the 51 percent of travelers looking at other destinations.

The report, released on November 9, notes that “luxury” is no longer confined to five-star hotels – it now encompasses a desire for authentic cultural experiences, interactions with local residents, and attendance at heritage and religious events—a clear shift that is reshaping the landscape of regional demand.

The report arrives at a highly significant moment: the global market is recovering faster than anticipated, and the Middle East is transitioning from a mere transit hub into a primary, standalone destination.

According to the report, 55 percent of visitors to the region seek to attend cultural events, compared to 42 percent for other destinations, placing Egypt in a strong competitive position within the region, bolstered by its unique civilizational heritage and the state-of-the-art Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM).

Egypt amongst fastest-growing tourism destinations

Amidst these shifts, Egypt has emerged as one of the fastest-growing tourism destinations in the world.

In statements made on Monday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy announced that Egypt had welcomed approximately 16.2 million tourists by the end of October.

He projected that the total would reach 20 million by the end of this year- with a further increase to 22 million next year.

These figures are bolstered by a record 20 percent growth in visitor numbers, the highest tourism growth rate in the Middle East, according to a regional report by the United Nations World Tourism Organization.

The surge is not limited to visitor numbers alone; the sector generated US$ 18.4 billion in revenue during the 2025–2026 fiscal year, a 10.3 percent year-on-year increase, according to data from the Central Bank of Egypt.

The government aims to reach 30 million tourists annually by 2030, with projected revenues ranging between $ 36 billion and $40 billion.

Hitting this target requires the addition of 240,000 to 250,000 new hotel rooms, an expansion of airport capacity, and the development of tourism-related transport systems and logistics services.

While these figures reflect a tangible improvement in the sector’s indicators, they also reveal a gap between current ambitions and existing infrastructure.

Although Egypt possesses immense competitive advantages, accommodating 30 million tourists necessitates substantial investments in accommodation, transportation, and services, an area the government is currently addressing by offering incentives to investors and streamlining licensing procedures.

The new ATM report reflects a deeper shift in traveler behavior: with 55 percent of visitors to the region seeking to attend cultural events, Egypt has emerged as an ideal destination for this type of experience, thanks to its unique cultural heritage and a modern, world-class museum.

Optimistic outlook

Data from the World Tourism Organization indicates that Egypt recorded a 16 percent increase in tourist numbers during the first quarter of 2026, surpassing both regional and global averages, even as tourism slowed in some neighboring countries.

Globally, the outlook is even more optimistic; a joint report by World Travel Market (WTM) and Tourism Economics, released on November 3, reveals that international tourism is on track to reach 1.57 billion tourist arrivals and $1.8 trillion in spending by 2026, with a clear transition from mass tourism toward experience-based and sustainable travel.

The report’s projections indicate that the Middle East aims to welcome approximately 100 million tourists by 2030, an ambitious goal that requires doubling hotel capacity, as well as developing airports and air connectivity.

Egypt lies at the heart of this figure, due to its population size, geographical diversity, and its strategic location serving as a gateway between Europe, Asia, and Africa.

World.title: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity over UK airbase
World.content:
Reuters — US Air Force personnel at the RAF Lakenheath base in Britain responded to “suspected unauthorized drone activity” on Friday evening, although no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a US Air Force spokesperson said.

“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the spokesperson said by email.

Britain’s Ministry of Defence said US Air Force Security Forces personnel had responded to reports of unauthorized drone activity and that the situation had been resolved.

“We are working closely with them to establish the facts. We will provide updates in due course,” a ministry spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

The US has in recent weeks moved bombers that had been used to strike Iran out of Britain, and relocated huge refueling aircraft from Britain to Germany. A news report later said there had been a threat from Iran.

The bombers left RAF Fairford on security grounds after a group of men approached ​the base in white vans in the middle of the night on September 27.

Two men ​were charged last month in relation to ⁠that incident, with prosecutors alleging one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain. The US Justice Department said this week that a member of an Iran-backed militia had plotted to attack the Fairford air base while detained in the US on criminal charges.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that the refueling aircraft were moved due to a threat from Iran.

Britain’s domestic spy ‌chief said in October that Iran had stepped up attempts to hit ​harder targets such as military sites in Britain.

Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of malign activity in Britain, where the authorities have ​for a number of years accused it of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets.

Germany has blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August after airport workers found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.

World.title: The Trump administration is diverting billions in health funding away from low-income countries, defying Congress’ plans
World.content:
The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $605 million – according to an internal US State Department budget report and a memo to lawmakers that were obtained by CNN.

The budget plans also involve an effort to move nearly a billion dollars into a global health innovation fund benefiting US corporations, while sharply cutting global health funding for low- and middle-income countries.

The actions have drawn criticism from nonprofit organizations and lawmakers who argue it represents overreach by the administration, given that Congress holds the power to decide how money is spent.

A copy of the budget report – called the preliminary Fiscal Year 2026 allocation – reveals plans to divert or repurpose almost all of the $607.5 million in funding that Congress had allocated to supply contraception and other reproductive health services to women overseas.

Tens of millions of that funding will be diverted to support the “energy security needs” of US partners facing market disruptions amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, according to a separate memo signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in September. The memo offered few additional details on how that money would be spent.

For decades, US family planning aid has provided millions of women overseas with modern contraceptives to give them the ability to prevent or space out pregnancies, which research shows improves maternal mortality rates, family incomes and babies’ health.

In fiscal year 2024 – before Trump came back to office – US investment in global family planning is estimated to have prevented 34,000 maternal deaths, according to the Guttmacher Institute.

The budget plans also reveal steep reductions in US health assistance for most countries when compared to 2024 funding levels, according to an analysis of the leaked budget document conducted by Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization. Their analysis, which was shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication Saturday, was conducted in conjunction with the nonprofit organizations Partners In Health (PIH) and PAI, a reproductive rights advocacy organization.

The countries with the largest funding decreases for health programs are South Africa, Tanzania and Zimbabwe, which have all been hit with more than $100 million in cuts. Eight countries – Afghanistan, Central African Republic, Gambia, South Africa, Somalia, Sudan, Timor-Leste and Yemen – have had their health funding cut to zero since 2024.

Asked about the funding diversions, a State Department spokesman told CNN that “the administration is consistently evaluating the use of foreign assistance to ensure it is used to meet critical needs, including unanticipated contingencies such as the current global energy crisis, within the context of its annual appropriated budget and the authorities available to the president and the secretary.”

Asked about the department’s diversions of family planning funding, the spokesman said: “Our focus is on implementing life-saving care, including in HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and maternal and child health, through new, landmark bilateral global health MOUs (memoranda of understanding).”

A mother holds her child while waiting for treatment in February 2025 at Hossainpur Upazila Health Complex in Bangladesh, as information about contraception services backed by USAID can be seen in the background. Piyas Biswas/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

Vincent Lin, associate director of health policy and advocacy at PIH, told CNN that the latest budget moves are “counter to what Congress has put in the appropriations bills.”

“To see dollars that have been fought for and written into the law by Congress moved away or siphoned away to energy security needs, or to US private companies with a profit margin, or out of really important public health programs … I think it is devastating to see that happen,” Lin said.

“The executive branch is flagrantly not spending the money that Congress has written into law for a very specific purpose,” Lin told CNN. “On the family planning side … this is the clearest situation of the executive branch ignoring and or violating the Congressional will.”

In the last two years, the State Department has made several efforts to assume more control over US global health funding and make spending reductions, including by not transferring certain funds to the Centers for Disease Control. CNN has also previously reported on the administration’s redirection of $1.35 billion in funding intended for global health programs to cover the cost of closing the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

Many of those changes have lacked public announcements or transparency.

Public Citizen has sued the State Department in an effort to force the release of records surrounding those bilateral global health agreements, which the administration has largely kept confidential. That lawsuit is ongoing in federal court, but some of the documents have been released following Freedom of Information Act requests by watchdog groups.

Congresswoman Lois Frankel (D-FL), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, said: “The Trump administration’s refusal to spend Congressionally-appropriated funds for international family planning, as required by law, is shameful and dangerous.”

“These decisions have real, life-changing consequences for women’s health, economic security, and opportunities, as well as the well-being of their families and communities,” Frankel said in a statement to CNN.

Family planning aid diverted for ‘energy security needs’

In a memo to Congress signed by Secretary of State Rubio – which was obtained by CNN and first reported on by The New York Times – he said he authorized the redirection of up to $125 million in foreign aid to support “energy security needs.”

More than $48 million of that would be taken from family planning aid, according to the memo.

The memo also spelled out multi-million-dollar diversions away from other US programs, including peacebuilding initiatives between Palestinians and Israelis and overseas assistance for civilian victims of war.

In the memo, Rubio invoked a law that allows the government to use existing foreign assistance funds to address unanticipated crises, saying that funding would be used to “support exigent energy security needs for partners facing coercive supply cutoffs, market disruptions, and inflated costs – particularly due to the deliberate, extortionary actions of Russia, China, and Iran.”

It comes as the war in Iran has disrupted energy markets and led to a huge increase in global oil prices.

The State Department memo didn’t give further details on how the money diverted for energy security would be spent.

A Democratic Congressional aide told CNN the funding diversion is “an authority that they do have, but it is unlike it’s ever been used before.”

Separately, the State Department budget document shows that another $32 million originally allocated for the United Nations Population Fund is also being diverted into other health programs.

And a further $524 million in family planning aid is being withheld without a justification given, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI. That funding is listed in the State Department budget document as “To Be Programmed.” Other publicly available budget documents list that sum as “unallocated,” which analysts said suggests the funds have not been made available for spending.

“This decision is not consistent with the congressional history of bipartisan support for family planning and reproductive health care,” said Nabeeha Kazi Hutchins, president and chief executive of PAI. “It is Congress that holds the power of the purse, and the actions of this administration and the statements of this administration raise very serious concerns about whether the executive branch is exceeding its constitutional authority.”

“For us, this is not just an isolated budgetary decision,” she told CNN. “This is part of a much broader policy direction that’s increasingly restricting women’s health and wellbeing.”

It’s not the first time the Trump administration has indicated it does not plan to spend money on family planning or reproductive health aid, despite the bipartisan allocations made by Congress. Last year, Rubio said in his testimony before the House Committee on Appropriations that with regards to family planning programs, “we’re not going to be in that business globally.”

The Trump administration has also previously conflated certain kinds of contraception with abortion – something that medical professionals have refuted.

Shifting money into ‘innovation fund’ as foreign countries hit with aid cuts

The 2026 budget document also showed plans to move $888 million of global health funding into an “innovation fund” that backs US companies working in science, technology and medicine.

At the same time, more than $1.6 billion is being cut from global health funding for foreign countries, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI.

The move comes after the Trump administration last year launched an overhaul of the way the United States provides health assistance throughout the world, called the “America First Global Health Strategy.” The stated goal of the strategy is to have aid recipient countries further develop their own health systems – and the US decrease its assistance spending.

But Public Citizen, PIH and PAI argue that in reality, the funding cuts and diversions are making it more difficult for countries to bolster their own health systems.

“The administration’s cuts to country level programming takes away resources that support local health systems and services that deliver care and stop diseases from spreading. The simultaneous increase in resources for the innovation fund prioritizes commercial interests over these fundamental global health objectives,” the three organizations said in their analysis.

The administration’s justification of the new “America first” strategy was that NGOs were wasting money and it should go directly to foreign governments instead, according to Peter Maybarduk, who directs Public Citizen’s initiative on access to medicines. “But the reality is, we’re going to take money from the governments and the NGOs and give it to big corporations,” he said.

Public Citizen’s report also raised concerns about a lack of transparency regarding how government contracts will be awarded through the “innovation fund” of $888 million, which is far more money than when the fund was first created in 2025.

The administration originally set aside $60 million for the innovation fund, according to FY 2025 budget documents.

“The State Department has not clarified how it will solicit and review awards under the (innovation) fund,” wrote Public Citizen, PIH and PAI in their report, which also criticized the department for “increasingly relying on non-competitive sole-source awards.”

The State Department spokesman told CNN: “The Trump administration is continuing to explore ways to identify and leverage American innovations to save lives, and to do so more cost-effectively while working with Congress.”

The department did not respond to CNN’s question regarding the specific process for awarding contracts through the innovation fund.

CNN has previously reported on the Trump administration’s use of no-bid contracts in other areas of government, particularly surrounding the renovation and construction projects in Washington, DC.

There has been little public information about the specific projects and companies that the global health innovation fund will go towards. However, the State Department has recently announced some partnerships that it says promote American innovation, including contracts with the drone delivery company Zipline, the pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences and SC Johnson.

“Without a transparent and accountable process for new awards, funding could flow not to those with the best proposals for public health impact, but to those with direct, private access to the administration,” the Public Citizen report said. “Moreover, new technologies are not a substitute for direct support to countries.”

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis hold mass funeral as they call for action to protect civilians
World.content:
A mass funeral procession was held in the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Wednesday for at least 43 people allegedly killed in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition, according to Saba news agency, which is run by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The victims were killed in a strike Saturday on six homes in Al-Shariya, a Yemeni village east of Sanaa, Saba said. Among the dead are 21 children and 10 women, the agency reported.

Footage aired on the Houthi-run Masirah TV showed large crowds gathered at a graveyard. Men carrying rifles were seen digging graves.

Ahead of the funeral, Masirah TV published graphic images showing children lying motionless, whom Houthi authorities said had been killed in the strike. The attack involved three consecutive raids that also hit ambulance crews and rescue workers, it said.

CNN has reached out to the Saudi government as well as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen for comment.

Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had brought years of relative calm, after Saudi-backed forces struck Sanaa Airport in an attempt to block a Houthi plane arriving from Iran.

Houthi forces retaliated by launching an offensive and captured territory along Yemen’s western coast and near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key trade route.

Saturday’s attack comes as casualties surge in Yemen, where the years long conflict has dragged the country into a severe humanitarian crisis.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported on Tuesday that at least 2,025 people were killed or wounded between Oct. 31 and Nov. 8, including 163 deaths in the strategic northern city of Marib alone.

In response to the worsening conflict, the UN Security Council on Thursday voted unanimously to renew its Yemen sanctions regime for another year, extending targeted asset freezes and travel bans until November 2027 amid the escalating violence.

The UK-drafted resolution — which strongly condemns the Houthis’ military offensive as well as their missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping — also expands a UN monitoring panel to include maritime security experts and affirms that arbitrarily detaining UN and humanitarian workers is grounds for sanctions.

An administrative building belonging to Aramco that was damaged in a Houthi attack, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

On Wednesday, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled parliament appealed to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to intervene amid the intensifying fighting. The parliament claimed that hundreds of Saudi airstrikes over the previous five days had killed or wounded more than 300 people, most of them children, women and elderly people. CNN hasn’t independently verified the figure.

The Houthi-run Health Ministry also said Wednesday that at least 359 civilians had been killed and 780 wounded in what it described as the latest Saudi escalation. The ministry said most were women and children.

The Houthi armed forces said Tuesday that Saudi Arabia had carried out 93 airstrikes and missile attacks over the previous 24 hours, targeting sites including civilian and energy infrastructure across Houthi-controlled areas.

The rebel group, in turn, continues to target Saudi infrastructure, including the King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh, and oil facilities. In October, back-to-back attacks on the airport killed at least 20 people and wounded hundreds of others.

On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones over Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. On Thursday, it intercepted another over Riyadh.

The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, calling the coalition’s claim “another lie.”

Over the weekend, a building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district of Riyadh was damaged in a missile attack.

Correction: This story has been corrected to say 2,025 people were killed or wounded in Yemen between Oct. 31 and Nov. 8, according to the World Health Organization.

World.title: Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, schools and governments around the world
World.content:
A massive Microsoft outage that has left people around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life is nearly fixed, according to the latest word from the company.

Microsoft has apologized for the outage, which could end up costing billions in lost productivity. Microsoft said the outage was caused by a “technical issue” rather than any cybersecurity breach. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

The company reported that queues of emails waiting to be delivered are “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.”

Problems started midday Thursday on the US East Coast, and quickly spread around the globe. As many as 430 million users were reportedly affected at some point.

In the United States, some companies’ frustrated workers went home early on Thursday. In Australia, businesses couldn’t print invoices and some schools couldn’t hold online classes on Friday.

And there was no quick fix. As of 10:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, the outage was still widespread, affecting untold millions of people.

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft said in a post on X around 1 p.m. ET on Friday. “We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.”

“We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” the company added. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

The disruption has caused a wide range of reactions. Some US office workers celebrated the email blackout and joked that they could start the weekend early. Others barely missed a beat, connecting with colleagues via Slack, phone and even the old-fashioned way: in-person.

But small businesses scrambled for Microsoft alternatives to communicate. Local governments alerted constituents to call instead of email.

The outage could cost $7 billion in lost productivity, according to an estimate by Anderson Economic Group, a Michigan-based think tank. Patrick Anderson, the firm’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate.

In Australia, Friday began with a realization that the Microsoft cloud was unresponsive. The outage took out live feeds from courts, and schools texted parents to phone in any absences until email systems were restored.

Australia’s national broadcaster, ABC, reported people missing job interviews because they couldn’t connect to virtual meetings, and even some supply issues with distribution centers stocking supermarkets due to the outage.

At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening “in the Americas,” but over time, it became clear the troubles were global.

Downdetector showed a peak of 130,000 reports about Outlook outages, but that figure understated the scope of the problem, since most people do not report their experiences.

World.title: Expert explains Finance Ministry allocating state-owned land on the Red Sea to reduce public debt
World.content:
Economist Fakhri al-Fiqi explained that the decision to allocate 112 million square meters of state-owned land in the Red Sea governorate to Finance Ministry for investment purposes does not entail selling the land or transferring its ownership.

During a phone interview with the “Modern MTI” television channel on Friday, Fiqi noted that this allocation is not a new development – it was enacted via a presidential decree as part of the state’s broader strategy to leverage its assets for economic gain.

The decision authorizes the Finance Ministry to grant usufruct rights to the land or to utilize it as an in-kind asset for economic development, he explained.

The proceeds generated would then be directed toward servicing the public debt and reducing its burden, while the state retains the underlying ownership.

Usufruct rights

The economic expert emphasized the necessity of distinguishing between allocating land under a “usufruct” (right-of-use) arrangement and selling land to transfer its ownership.

Fiqi’s remarks came in response to questions regarding whether the government intends to sell state-owned land to generate financial resources to help repay public debt.

He clarified that the announced measure concerns the management and economic utilization of assets through usufruct rights, rather than the relinquishment of ownership.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi had issued a presidential decree allocating over 112 million square meters of state-owned land in the Red Sea Governorate to Finance Ministry.

The decree was published in the Egyptian Gazette on Wednesday.

This land is to be used for the purpose of reducing public debt and issuing sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic financial certificates)—a move aimed at leveraging state assets to lower the national debt burden.

World.title: Egypt, UN showcase results of EU-Funded Joint Program Supporting Refugees
World.content:
Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Migration, Ambassador Neveen Elhussein, United Nations (UN) Resident Coordinator in Egypt Gianluca Rampolla del Tindaro and representatives from the European Union (EU) led a high-level field visit Thursday, 11 November 2026.

The visit brought together senior Government officials, representatives of United Nations agencies and heads of Cooperation from partner missions to observe firsthand the results of the EU-funded UN Joint Program on Refugees, Migrants and Host Communities. It demonstrated how coordinated and institutionalized international cooperation can translate into meaningful improvements in the lives of refugees, asylum seekers, migrants and members of host communities.

The delegation visited education and health facilities in 6th of October City and Omraneya rehabilitated through the Program, reflecting that supporting refugees and migrants must go hand in hand with strengthening national systems and public services. The delegation reaffirmed its support for the Joint Program and commended the results achieved through the close partnership with the Ministry of Health and Population and the Ministry of Education and Technical Education.

Egypt has consistently shouldered its responsibilities in hosting refugees and asylum-seekers. Today, it hosts 1.1 million registered refugees and asylum seekers alongside several million migrants, including millions of migrants in vulnerable situations.
