World.title: Millions of Americans use marijuana to sleep, but new study raises troubling questions
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Marijuana may be making sleep quality worse, despite its widespread use as a sleep aid, a recent Northwestern Medicine study found.

The findings of the study, which included 1,266 participants, showed that both lifetime and recent cannabis users objectively had worse sleep quality, although they did not report their sleep to be worse.

Participants were monitored for almost 35 years, from young adulthood into middle age, with scientists tracking their use of cannabis over time.

AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

In middle age, participants wore a sleep monitor on their wrist for a week and filled out surveys about their sleep quality.

This allowed researchers to compare objective and subjective reports of participants’ sleep.

"Our data do not support the belief that cannabis is helpful as a sleep aid," said senior study author Mercedes R. Carnethon, Ph.D., as Northwestern Now reported.

"As cannabis becomes increasingly available and accepted, it's important to better understand its long-term associations with health behaviors such as sleep," Carnethon added.

CLICK HERE TO 

Among all participants, a greater lifetime exposure to marijuana was linked to worse objective sleep quality.

Those who had a higher cannabis usage over time were generally asleep for a lower percentage of the night and experienced more sleep disruption.

Similarly, recent cannabis users were more likely to have more sleep fragmentation and lower sleep efficiency, compared to people who never used the substance.

The study also found there was a much higher chance that recent cannabis users would sleep longer than eight hours per night.

The study discusses the differences between objective and subjective reports of sleep quality.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"What makes this study particularly interesting is that participants who used cannabis demonstrated objectively poorer sleep, yet their own assessments of sleep quality did not reflect those differences," Alfred Joshua, M.D., a board-certified emergency medicine physician based in California, told Fox News Digital. (He was not involved with the new study.)

"In other words, someone may believe marijuana is helping them sleep, while objective measurements suggest otherwise."

Researchers considered multiple outside factors including age, race, sex, smoking frequency, alcohol consumption, physical activity and more.

Even with these factors taken into account, the study found a consistent correlation between cannabis use and poorer objectively measured sleep.

The mode of cannabis consumption, such as smoking versus taking edibles, was not considered.

"These findings raise important questions."

"It is not surprising that the actual quality of sleep of these subjects, after chronic marijuana use, is poor compared to those who do not smoke marijuana because people who claim that they need to smoke marijuana before they go to sleep, in order to relax, are only kidding themselves," board-certified psychiatrist Carole Lieberman, M.D., of California told Fox News Digital. (She, too, was not affiliated with the new study.)

"It is more a psychological addiction than a physical one," she added. "They enjoy the high that they get right away, but the marijuana doesn't help them to sleep better."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The researchers found that greater cumulative cannabis exposure was associated with reduced sleep efficiency, increased sleep fragmentation and more time spent awake after initially falling asleep," said Joshua, the board-certified emergency medicine physician.

"These findings raise important questions about whether habitual marijuana use is a sustainable strategy for managing sleep problems," he added.

Fox News Digital recently reported on other cannabis findings.

A study of nearly 450,000 American adults, for instance, linked cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings were scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9. They showed that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.

Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

World.title: Private planes and roadtrips: AEW goes above and beyond to get to Phoenix for Full Gear despite travel chaos

All Elite Wrestling (AEW) dropkicked a nationwide nightmare to make sure its talent and personnel made it to Phoenix for Full Gear on Saturday despite travel chaos that plagued millions across the U.S.

AEW owner Tony Khan brought in some wrestlers and other workers on private planes just to make sure they were going to show up for the fans, who were expected to pack the Mortgage Matchup Center for one of the company’s top pay-per-views on the calendar.

"I know it’s been an incredibly challenging few days for a lot of people," Khan said in a video posted to his social media. "My sympathies to everybody affected by all of the flight cancelations and delays. Yesterday, as you can imagine, was a hectic day as it was for a lot of people with the flights grounded and that applied to all flights yesterday – private and public flights. For AEW, we’re the same as everyone else, we’re not trying to break any rules. Everybody was grounded and we started formulating a plan that has come together really, really well."

Khan said everyone on the Full Gear pay-per-view card arrived in Phoenix. Khan sent private planes at three "hub locations" to bring the wrestlers and other personnel to the Mortgage Matchup Center. The only thing that changed was the Tailgate Brawl – which will occur on the Full Gear pre-show.

Khan said he believed everyone probably would have made it on their scheduled flights.

"I think it was virtually impossible given how many flights of people who work in AEW have been canceled had I not dispatched the private planes to the three hub locations, I think it’s very unlikely everybody would have made it here. I think there probably would have been some changes to the main card."

Adam Copeland, who battles Kazuchika Okada for the AEW International Championship, said it was "challenging" to get from the East Coast all the way to Phoenix.

"I was going down the runway about to take off for Denver and the pilot came on and said there’s a ground stoppage nationwide. I was like, ‘OK.’ I called Beth (Phoenix) and she came and got me and I went home," he said. "No idea if I was going to make it today. All of my flights started getting canceled one after the other after the other. Everyone else’s flights were starting to take off but mine weren’t.

"Even still, my flight to get out here is tomorrow at 5:37. So, Tony Khan sent a plane to come get us. Poor (Tony) Schiavone got there early so he was sitting there at 9 o’clock. I don’t think we were taking off until 11 so I was like, come have a coffee, come pet my dogs. We had a big dog cuddle-fest this morning and my girls got to meet Tony and we had some coffee – we made the best of it."

Tony Schiavone, one-third of the AEW broadcast team, was set to fly out of Atlanta when he made the last-minute decision to take a smaller plane out of Asheville, North Carolina, because of the uncertainty that he may have been delayed or canceled. He told his wife he wasn’t going to drive all the way to Phoenix, but he would have if he had the time to make the 27-hour trip.

"But that was OK because I waited, got to hang out with Adam Copeland, which was pretty cool," he said. "It was a pretty cool day but it was a very challenging day. I guess I got here around 2 o’clock local time here in the afternoon. My car is still in Asheville. I have no idea how I’m gonna get it but it doesn’t matter. I’m glad I’m here. I would do anything to make it to Full Gear. … I would have driven to Phoenix! I would have, but I didn’t have the time."

Mark Davis and Jake Doyle, the duo known as Davis and Doyle, will challenge for the AEW World Tag Team Championship against The Young Bucks. But it was far from easy for them to get to the arena.

"Tumultuous last 24 hours leading up to Full Gear," Davis said. "For me, I had to run across the great state of Florida. I went from Tampa to Orlando, trying to get a flight – didn’t happen. Thankfully, the big guy had our back and I think he’s pretty excited to see Davis and Doyle take down some Young Bucks here this evening at Full Gear."

Doyle made it clear, "It’s a bad day to be a Buck."

"It was already a bad day to be a Buck but then I had to drive to Detroit, then drive to Chicago, then sit on a private jet, which is pretty awesome, but I had to sit on that jet for eight hours, waiting to get here to tear up these Young Bucks.

"So, Tony Khan, thank you for that jet. Young Bucks, I don’t feel sorry for you."

Matt and Nick Jackson – The Young Bucks – were only in California. They had to make the drive to Phoenix.

"We told each other, we’re blessed, we’re in California. A lot of these guys are coming further than us, but we will do anything – planes, trains and automobiles – we will be here at Full Gear," Matt Jackson said. "We have a big match tonight – Davis and Doyle. Two intimidating meatheads that actually had our number the last couple times when we’ve been in the ring. We talked about it on the drive. We had six hours to really think about it and strategize. Yeah, the travel sucked but we’re ready and we’re gonna rock the house tonight at Full Gear."

Excalibur, Schiavone’s broadcast teammate, said he was at the gym when he got a text about the travel chaos. He said he planned to jump in a car to go from Southern California to Phoenix. He drove five hours to get to the arena but took solace in the fact he got a chance to stop in the desert he doesn’t normally stop in.

"I made it. I wouldn’t miss this for the world. I know people have much tougher travel days than I did. I mean a five-hour drive, it’s doable, but in wrestling terms, it’s nothing," he said. "I wasn’t going to miss this for the world. I know a lot of people in AEW, everybody in AEW, has the same idea, same feeling, if there’s any way possible for them to be here today, they’re gonna be here at Full Gear. … There’s nothing that can keep me from Full Gear today."

Nigel McGuinness, the third person on the broadcast team, got to Phoenix from Los Angeles. He jumped in his car when he learned about the travel woes.

"There was no way I was gonna miss Full Gear," he said. "There’s something about being in professional wrestling where you make the show no matter what. I’ve never missed a show and there was no way I was going to miss Full Gear."

World.title: Thousands of flights canceled or delayed Saturday after FAA’s nationwide ground stop
World.content:
Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.

By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.

A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.

What caused the ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.

“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.

Why disruptions continued Saturday

Airlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.

But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.

Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.

Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.

In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.

Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.

Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.

Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.

Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.

Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers. Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty

“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”

With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare

Ground stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.

In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.

Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

World.title: FAA ground stop throws college football into chaos, while the NFL is safe
World.content:
A Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that lasted more than four hours and canceled over 7,000 flights Friday affected the travel plans for several teams across multiple sports.

Follow along for live coverage.

Multiple games in college football had to be rescheduled to accommodate new travel plans, while a handful of NBA teams changed their flights as a result of the ground stop. Every NFL game, meanwhile, will be played as scheduled, as all road teams were scheduled to travel Saturday.

A few backup referees for the NFL

Every NFL game will stick to its original start time, a league spokesman confirmed to NBC News. Teams playing Sunday typically do not travel until Saturday, meaning the league was largely unaffected by the Friday ground stop.

The New England Patriots and the Detroit Lions, who are playing in Munich, Germany, both traveled overseas well ahead of the stop.

While the league’s teams and players will arrive as scheduled, the NFL did have to modify officiating crews for Sunday’s games.

NFL referee Duane Heydt in Seattle on Oct. 25. Alika Jenner / Getty

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” a league spokesman said.

Three backup referees — Duane Heydt, Barry Anderson and Don Willard — will be used Sunday. Heydt was assigned to a game in New Orleans and Anderson to one in Tennessee, while Willard will be the side judge for games in both Indianapolis and Cincinnati. (The kickoffs in those two games are more than seven hours apart, and the stadiums are separated by less than 120 miles.)

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise,” the league spokesman said.

Many college football games have been pushed back

Travel plans for more than a dozen teams were affected by the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

Some schools opted to fly out on Saturday morning for games scheduled the same day, while others — including the Alabama Crimson Tide playing at Vanderbilt — took a bus to their destination.

Several kickoffs were pushed back to later Saturday to accommodate new travel plans, including the games between Baylor and BYU, Arizona State and UCF, and Utah and Arizona.

The game between Oklahoma and Ole Miss, however, was pushed back to Sunday after Ole Miss couldn’t figure out its travel in time — and it drew a strong response from the Sooners.

“We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned. But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution,” Oklahoma Athletic Director Roger Denny said in a statement. “After multiple conversations with the league office, [SEC] Commissioner [Greg] Sankey informed us of his decision to move our game to Sunday, over our strong objection. After continued discussions, he further informed us that our failure to play on Sunday at the directed time would result in a forfeit.”

Denny’s statement added: “Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans. Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations, and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference’s decision tonight.”

No major issues for the NBA and NHL

A few NBA teams — such as the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Chicago Bulls — had to reschedule flights from Friday night to Saturday morning, but otherwise it’s largely business as usual for the league.

An NBA source confirmed to NBC News all games would take place as scheduled as of Saturday morning, though noted there were a lot of moving parts.

“Flights are late, get stuck on the runway, just like it does in the normal commercial world of flight, so it’s just part of it,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said before the team’s game Friday. “We’ve all been part of it. You just adapt.”

Atkinson’s star guard Donovan Mitchell was not enthused about the new plan, as Cleveland has a quick turnaround to another game Saturday.

“This is unprecedented,” Mitchell said Friday, per Cleveland.com’s Chris Fedor. “Back-to-back. Three-hour flight. It was already going to be a tough one. But if they say we have to play then we have to play.”

Mitchell added he would have liked for the game to be canceled.

The NHL, meanwhile, has not announced any changes to its schedule. The league had only two games on Friday night, allowing most teams to travel for their road games prior to the stoppage, according to The Athletic.

World.title: Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, as vote counting continues
World.content:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis, as vote-counting continues in the state.

Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with each new batch of votes reported this week. A “likely” characterization indicates that the NBC News Decision Desk has at least 95% confidence that Peltola will win the race.

See live results here.

Alaska’s is the only remaining 2026 Senate race in which the NBC News Decision Desk has not yet made a projection.

If Peltola wins, Democrats will have a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year.

The race remains uncalled a week after polls close as votes continue to be counted. Alaskans vote heavily by mail and ballots postmarked by Election Day are counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 13 — and a few days later than that for valid overseas voters.

In a race with such a narrow margin, these final votes are important, especially given Alaska’s ranked-choice rules.

If no candidate wins a majority of the vote on the first ballot, the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated and second-choice votes from that candidate’s supporters are counted. The process then repeats until someone gets a majority.

World.title: He was drafted as an NFL team’s future. It arrives now.
World.content:
When Heisman Trophy-winning quarterback Fernando Mendoza was selected first overall by the Las Vegas Raiders in April’s NFL draft, he updated his biography on LinkedIn to say that he was “focused on preparation, growth and discipline.”

Emphasis on the first part.

It is a quirk of the NFL that teams historically race to draft a quarterback early, then play them as little as possible for much of their first season. Teams view the position as so demanding and the pro game so fast that they want their prized picks to prepare as much as possible before inheriting the pressure of an entire franchise.

Mendoza’s time to prepare ended Tuesday, nine games into his rookie season.

Now, the Raiders need him to produce.

Mendoza won the Heisman after leading the Indiana Hoosiers to the 2025 national championship. Adam Hunger / Getty

Before Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline, Las Vegas (4-5) traded veteran starting quarterback Kirk Cousins and elevated Mendoza to starter ahead of Sunday’s Week 10 matchup against the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks (5-4). Cousins had thrown 20 touchdowns, the most by any quarterback to change teams midseason in NFL history, per NBC Sports research.

After starting 3-0, the Raiders have lost five of their last six games but still have what one playoff tracker pegged this week as a 15% chance to make what would be only the franchise’s third playoff appearance since 2003. Trading Cousins and elevating Mendoza “is no way to signify that we are punting on the season or looking forward to 2027,” Raiders general manager John Spytek said.

“It’s something that [Mendoza] worked very hard for since the moment he walked into this building,” Spytek told reporters this week. “He passed every test. I want to stop short of saying he’s earned it, but he put us in a position where we had to make a really hard decision today with his growth as a person, as a teammate, as a leader, as a quarterback.”

Mendoza is known as a quick study. While attending Cal, he spent his summers away from Berkeley interning at investment firms. In his first and only season at Indiana last fall, Mendoza picked up the Hoosiers’ offensive playbook so quickly that he led the perennial Big Ten doormat to a stunning national championship by using his arms and his feet.

Raiders coach Klint Kubiak, who as an offensive playcaller mentored Sam Darnold during last season’s Super Bowl run with the Seahawks, said that Cousins was “the right role model” for Mendoza to learn from and accelerate his acclimation to the NFL.

“It’s time to rally around Fernando,” center Tyler Linderbaum said. “Everyone has to step up and play for him. Obviously, it’s never easy being a rookie in that first game, but there’s 10 other guys on the field with him, there’s a whole defense, special teams unit, and just be there for him. Let him play with confidence. We’ve seen it every day in practice, the plays he can make.”

Mendoza’s only snaps to this point came Oct. 11 when he played late in a blowout loss to the New England Patriots and completed 6 of his 8 passes. Rookie debuts are inherently difficult; quarterbacks taken No. 1 overall are 5-23-1 in their first start since 1970, per NBC Sports research. Facing the Seahawks will make Mendoza’s big day even more challenging. Seattle leads the NFL in total defense, allowing just 244 yards per game.

Mendoza might not be under the most pressure of any Raiders player on Sunday, however. The team’s defense has allowed 30 or more points in each of its last six games, tied for the longest streak by a team in a season in NFL history.

“Fernando has done everything we’ve asked him to do in practice,” Kubiak said. “I think he’s exceeded those expectations, and we all know that live bullets Sunday is far different from practice. However, he showed us that he’s ready, not only physically, but mentally.”

World.title: Why Mary Peltola is on track to win in Alaska, even if ranked choice ballots come into play
World.content:
As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan will hang on to his job.

His Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is on track to win the still-unresolved Senate race under either possible scenario — with an outright majority, or if the race goes to ranked choice ballots, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of outstanding and tabulated votes.

Peltola currently leads Sullivan by 3.7 percentage points, or just over 10,000 votes. With 96% of the expected vote in, NBC News’ Decision Desk now believes Peltola is likely to win this race, though we may need to wait until Wednesday, Nov. 18, to know the final result.

If no candidate receives over 50% of the vote, Alaska determines a winner using ranked choice voting, in which the lowest-ranked candidates are eliminated one by one and their votes are redistributed according to each voter’s ranked preferences. If a voter did not rank the remaining candidates, their ballots are considered “exhausted” and are excluded from the final vote count.

Wednesday is Alaska’s deadline for final mail absentee ballots to be received by election officials, one reason why this close race has lingered for so long. Alaska reports its votes unevenly, and NBC News expects to see the remainder of these votes early next week.

Nov. 18 is also the day the state Division of Elections would run the ranked choice tabulation, if needed.

If Peltola receives over 50% of the vote, she will win the election without needing to go through the ranked choice tabulation process. She needs to win just 53.8% of the remaining ballots to clear this mark — a real possibility given her strength in recent vote reports. On Friday night, she received 58% of the newly reported votes.

Sullivan, the incumbent, has two separate paths to gain ground and win the election: making up the gap with first-choice rankings, or making up the gap via the ranked choice process. An NBC News Decision Desk analysis of the ballots already tabulated shows that the first route is highly improbable and that the second route is likely impossible.

The first route that Sullivan could use to come back would be passing Peltola in first-choice rankings. With approximately 12,000 votes outstanding, Sullivan would need to win around 92% of those in order to tie with Peltola. That would amount to about 46 points better than he has performed in the vote counted so far, and far above the percentage either candidate has achieved in any batch of ballots received up to this point. On Friday night, he received just 38% of newly reported votes.

The second route for Sullivan to retake the lead is through the ranked choice process, but an analysis of the ballots shows why this route is effectively closed to him.

There are currently 11,300 tallied ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan. Those ballots may be redistributed in the ranked choice process. With 4% of the total vote outstanding, the number of ballots with first-choice votes for candidates other than Peltola and Sullivan could rise to around 12,000. For Sullivan to net 10,400 ballots out of a pool of 12,000 and close the gap with Peltola, he would need to win around 93% of redistributed votes.

However, even that steep figure is misleadingly optimistic for Sullivan because of what we already know about how people are ranking the candidates.

The Alaska Division of Elections posts a “Cast Vote Record” for the over-270,000 ballots currently tabulated. These records show exactly how each candidate is ranked on each ballot.

Our analysis of those ballots shows that Sullivan does gain some votes from the ranked choice process, receiving a large transfer of votes from voters who backed Republican Gerald Heikes, who is in third place. But the most important thing about these votes is that a large percentage of ballots from those who backed other candidates are “exhausted” in the ranked choice tabulation process.

Over 45% of voters who ranked Heikes, Dan J. Sullivan Jr. or a write-in candidate did not rank Peltola or Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a later choice, which means that these ballots will play no role in the ranked choice tabulation.

This ballot exhaustion means that there are far fewer than 12,000 ballots available for Sullivan to make up the gap of about 10,000 votes between him and Peltola in the ranked choice process.

If current rates are maintained, only about 6,600 ballots will actually be redistributed to the top two finishers in the ranked choice tabulation. If Sullivan is more than 6,600 votes behind Peltola’s first-choice margin after all ballots have been counted, it is mathematically impossible for the Republican incumbent to catch up to Peltola in the ranked choice tabulation.

The NBC News Decision Desk will need to assess the remaining ballots as they are received to determine if our standards are met to officially project the race, or whether the outcome will be determined by the ranked choice process carried out by the Alaska Division of Elections.

World.title: Costco-brand whipped cream recalled over potential presence of cleaning chemical
World.content:
Costco members who love a whipped topping may consider going à la mode with their favorite dessert instead after the retailer’s Kirkland-brand whipped cream was recalled.

Cans of Kirkland Signature Real Heavy Whipped Cream sold between Oct. 11 and Oct. 31 are subject to a voluntary recall after some customers reported a chemical taste and smell. Alamance Foods, the manufacturer, said it has received no reports of serious effects requiring medical care.

“We have learned that one batch of Kirkland Signature Whipped Cream may contain a small amount of a cleaning chemical,” the company said.

The product was sold in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee and Wisconsin.

Customers can return the cream to Costco for a full refund, according to Alamance Foods.

World.title: Device deemed ‘credible threat’ triggers evacuation around ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois
World.content:
A suspicious device at an ethanol plant in Peoria, Illinois, triggered a temporary evacuation request for those within a 1-mile radius, with events cancelled Friday.

An evacuation recommendation for those within that 1-mile radius after Friday afternoon’s discovery at the BioUrja Renewables facility was lifted Saturday, according to Peoria police.

Police and federal authorities said early Saturday that they had found a device deemed a “credible threat” and rendered it safe, without giving details as to its nature.

A search by federal, state and local authorities turned up no other devices, but an investigation into Friday’s discovery was ongoing, police said in a statement on Saturday.

“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said separately.

Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told NBC affiliate WEEK there was an “all hands on deck” response, saying: “A device has been identified. We know it’s a credible threat. We know it’s a bomb.”

​Presley told media that FBI personnel, along with local and state police, had determined a “suspicious package was a threat and rendered it safe.”

Rep. Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., met with evacuees at Peoria Manual High School on Friday night.

“This is the designated shelter area for those that are impacted by the evacuation that’s going on just south of downtown Peoria,” he said in an update. “What we do need to make sure is that everybody’s making good decisions.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker had urged locals to “follow directions from law enforcement and stay clear of the area.”

Country music singer Jon Pardi was forced to cancel his show scheduled for Friday evening at the Peoria Civic Center.

“At the direction of the Chief of Police, tonight’s concert has been canceled due to an active local safety concern,” he posted on Instagram, adding that tickets would be refunded.

The weekend’s Illinois Comic Con at Peoria Civic Center canceled its Saturday events but said after the evacuation all-clear was issued that its Sunday plans were still scheduled.

Peoria’s Caterpillar Visitors Center, Riverfront Museum, Rhythm Kitchen Music Cafe, and Main Library and Lincoln Branch library were also closed on Saturday, those venues each said on Facebook.

Dozer Park, home of the minor league baseball team the Peoria Chiefs, also canceled a holiday event at the venue.

The nearby OSF HealthCare St. Francis Medical Center said it was “taking all appropriate precautions in response to the situation in downtown Peoria.” A statement said: “We will continue to monitor the situation and take any additional steps necessary to maintain a safe environment for those we serve and those who work at our facilities.”

In 2021, Houston-based BioUrja, which has described itself as an energy, agricultural and metals commodity trading company, purchased the former ADM (Archer-Daniels-Midland) ethanol production complex in Peoria. BioUrja CEO Amit Bhandari said at the time the facility would help it expand its presence in beverage-grade and highly-distilled industrial alcohol markets.

The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Evacuation lifted after bomb threat near industrial plant in Illinois
World.content:
An evacuation order was lifted Saturday and residents were allowed to return to their homes after a bomb threat near an industrial building in Peoria, Illinois.

The city of East Peoria said in a statement that, as of 1:00 p.m. local time, residents in the 1-mile radius evacuation zone "can return to their homes and all businesses can resume normal operations."

Peoria police said a suspicious package was found near a BioUrja ethanol plant at approximately 2 p.m. on Friday, and that hours later it was determined to be a "credible threat."

Police Chief Brad Dixon said Saturday at a press conference that there was still "no explanation on what the device was." He said the investigation is still ongoing.

"Law Enforcement will continue their investigation into this incident, and updates will be provided," the police department said in a statement.

Dixon added the package was "rendered safe" at 9:12 p.m., but searches continued for other possible devices throughout the wider area.

"The area of BioUrja has not been rendered safe, just the package that was on site. It's a large facility; there's going to be an exhaustive search," he said at a press conference.

FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley told reporters his office deployed personnel to work alongside the Peoria Police Department, Peoria Fire Department, Peoria County Sheriff's Department, the Illinois Secretary of State's Office and Illinois State Police.

"We are currently investigating this incident with all of our partners. While it is early in the investigation, know this: we will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," Presley said.

Gov. Pritzker said on social media, "I am actively monitoring the bomb threat in Peoria, and I have directed the Illinois State Police to coordinate with local authorities."

The mayor of Peoria, Rita Ali, said in an interview with WMBD News late Friday that the facility is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."

Country music singer Jon Pardi had to cancel his concert because it was in the area, saying, "Peoria we're disappointed we won't get to spend tonight with you..."

In a post on Facebook, the Peoria Police Department advised those needing shelter to go to the nearby Manual Academy.

Peoria is located in central Illinois, about 75 miles north of Springfield and 150 miles southwest of Chicago. The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River in the southern part of the city.

World.title: 3 killed when SUV crashes into North Hollywood food stand
World.content:
Police say three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night.

The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Police Department.

Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.

On Wednesday, the LA County Medical Examiner identified two of the victims as 57-year-old Teodora Villalobos and 73-year-old Maria Peck. The third victim was identified as 39-year-old Francesca Krystine Esker on Friday.

Witnesses told CBS LA the three women were street vendors in the area, and one had worked there for more than 15 years.

The critically injured individuals are also women between 50 and 55 years old.

Crews extricated one person, the driver, from the wreckage, according to LAFD.

"I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."

The scene of a crash in North Hollywood that left three people dead and several others hospitalized on Nov. 10, 2026. CBS LA

LAPD officers said the driver of the white SUV was in serious condition and was determined to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol at the time of the crash. Police identified him as Ihor Demianenko, a 61-year-old Valley Village resident. He was arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder.

Demianenko is currently being held on more than $6 million bail.

The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that Demianenko was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued.

"It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."

Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up.

Friends and loved ones remember street vendors killed

Mourners identified two of the women as Teodora, a 57-year-old woman known fondly as Doris, and Maria, 73.

On Tuesday night, some of Doris' family members of one of the three women killed stopped by a growing memorial.

"There are no words to express the absence that she's gonna have over my life," Doris' daughter, Melissa Villalobos, said. "Every goal, everything that I do is gonna be for her. Everything that I achieve will be for her, because of every sacrifice that she has done for me."

She said she hopes that her mother is remembered as a selfless, independent and hardworking woman.

"She never neglected to give someone food, never neglected to give a bottle of water," Melissa Villalobos said. "I am grateful of that time that I had her for."

Los Angeles City Councilman Adrin Nazarian, who represents the area, has partnered with nonprofit organization ICON CDC to create a GoFundMe fundraiser to assist the families of the three victims. It can be found by searching for the keywords: "NoHo Metro Station Street Vendor Support Fund."

"We sat there and talked all day, two days ago," said Laduke Warwick. "Today, she's in heaven. I guarantee they're all in heaven."

He said their relationship began years ago when he was homeless. Though he's now housed, he'll never forget the day that Doris handed him a bacon-wrapped hot dog, a soda, and struck up a conversation with him.

"They're just such amazing people. I can't believe they left like that," Warwick said. "If I could say anything to them, I'd say thank you so much for all the amazing blessings that you have shared with me in a short moment of my life, that I can't even repay with words, money or kindness.

Local street photographer Jeff Wilson snapped some photos of Doris just four months ago, calling her an "anchor" of the community after more than a decade of serving food.

"Pre-COVID to COVID, past COVID to all the ICE crazy stuff, she was here," Wilson said. "She was always doing something, helping people."

The memorial continued to grow at the spot of the crash throughout the day Wednesday, with dozens of community members stopping by to pay their respects. Of the dozens who stopped, many remembered the trio of women who were always there to lend a helping hand to those who needed it the most.

"They're mothers, grandmothers. They're somebody's somebody," said Mike Sandoval, a regular customer. "They were out here every day. I had good days, I had bad days coming through this area, and every time I needed something they were always there."

World.title: Travelers stranded, flights canceled after ground stop. Here's what we know
World.content:
Airspace across the United States slowly began returning to normal on Saturday after a rare national ground stop canceled thousands of flights and stranded travelers.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference Saturday, "We are back at full operations."

He thanked the pilots, airline staff, air traffic controllers and the FAA for their professionalism during the ground stop.

"They safely landed all of our aircraft," he said, also thanking the passengers for their patience during the significant disruption.

"Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Duffy said earlier in a social media post on Saturday. He's scheduled to appear on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday.

"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."

More than 5,000 flights were canceled Saturday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, while around 5,300 others were delayed.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, arrives for a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

How did the FAA ground stop happen?

The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. EST Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.

"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.

It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. EST Friday.

This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks.

Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.

Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said.

Duffy said Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that an L3Harris contractor was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

Visitors watch an airplane as it prepares to land at Washington Dulles International Airport after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted nationwide ground stops in Chantilly, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Cliff Owen/ AP Photo

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service." He also said that L3Harris, a technology and defense company, owned the system.

L3Harris said Saturday the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the company said in a statement, adding they take the nationwide ground stop and "its impact" seriously.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.

"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.

Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.

Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."

Request for more FAA funding

Duffy said in a post that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH."

"I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money. I've asked for a lot of money," he said Saturday. "Now, the Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me 12 and a half billion dollars. And one of the problems that we had was they weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money."

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $30 billion late Friday.

Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and Rep. Andre Carson, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a joint statement Saturday that FAA and DOT staff will brief the committees on Monday about the additional $30 billion requested by the Trump administration.

"This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share," the two Democrats said. "The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."

The pair said the Trump administration has only used $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress.

"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money," they said.

Can Americans still travel safely?

Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.

"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said Friday.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.

Bedford said there will possibly be 5,000 flight cancellations on Saturday, but airlines should be fully back on schedule by the end of the day Sunday.

"We do anticipate somewhere between four and 5000 of the 41,000 flights that are scheduled today likely will cancel, so we will still have delays and cancellations today, but that will set us up for a full recovery tomorrow," he said.

Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

An American Airlines flight takes off from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Tom Brenner/ AP Photo

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.

"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.

American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."

Southwest said Saturday the airline instituted a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty.

"We are working to get our Customers to their destinations as quickly as possible," Southwest said.

World.title: 5th Canadian soldier dies weeks after fire on military base
World.content:
A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.

Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.

About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton. It occurred on a grenade launcher range, officials said last month.

The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized.

"Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. "With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service."

The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents.

Maj. Gen. Wade Rutland said that military officials knew about the fire for hours but believed it was contained and allowed training to continue before winds suddenly shifted.

Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on Canadian soil.

"We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy, as expeditiously and transparently as necessary," Carney told reporters last month.

World.title: SpaceX pulls off first Starship recovery from orbit in spectacular fashion
World.content:
After a 22-hour stay in space, a SpaceX Starship rocket plunged back to Earth Saturday, enduring the blazing heat of reentry while homing in on its Texas Gulf Coast launch site, flipping vertical at the last moment and settling into the grasp of two huge mechanical arms on its launch gantry.

Throngs of SpaceX employees gathered nearby cheered and applauded as the rocket restarted three of its six methane-fueled Raptor engines to flip upright, rapidly slowing to a near hover as the robot arms moved in for a mechanical embrace, catching the rocket a moment before engine shutdown.

Your browser does not support the video tag. SpaceX’s Starship is back on Earth, captured in midair by giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch pad. SpaceX

"This is so incredible to see!" said SpaceX commentator Jessie Anderson. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes. Congratulations to our teammates at SpaceX, and to everyone who supported the Starship program."

A camera mounted on one of the Starship's steering fins captures a view of the Texas Gulf Coast as the rocket descended toward a dramatic launch pad capture (left), while SpaceX employees (right) gathered at the company's Starbase facility cheered it on. SpaceX

It was the first such recovery of a Starship from orbit — previous test flights ended with planned ocean splashdowns — marking a major milestone in SpaceX's drive to develop the first fully reusable orbit-class rocket, a vehicle company founder Elon Musk says will dramatically lower the cost of launching payloads to Earth orbit, the moon and, eventually, Mars.

The Starship was launched atop a Super Heavy booster Friday using the same pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility on the Texas coast. Standing 407 feet tall, the two-stage rocket is the most powerful launcher ever built, generating some 16 million pounds of thrust at liftoff from 33 first-stage Raptor engines.

Almost home. SpaceX

After propelling the Starship upper stage out of the lower atmosphere, the Super Heavy first stage attempted its own return to the launch site for capture by the gantry's mechanical arms.

Going into the giant rocket's 15th test flight, SpaceX had successfully recovered the first-stage boosters used in three previous launches. But the Super Heavy launched Friday was diverted to an offshore splashdown because of a guidance problem. The vehicle ran out of fuel and exploded moments before hitting the water.

Safely captured. SpaceX

While a disappointment to the SpaceX team, Musk said in a posting on the social media platform X the problem was a "slight underperformance of engines," adding that "these early ships and boosters are already outdated by improved designs in production or on the test stand."

"This booster loss does not change our timeline to reach high volume, fully reusable Starship flights," he said.

The Starship upper stage did not disappoint.

Beaming down crystal-clear views from cameras mounted on its steering fins, the spacecraft's belly, covered in heat-shield tiles, glowed red as the ship heated up in a fireball of atmospheric friction.

Crossing the Baja Peninsula and then northern Mexico, the big rocket rapidly descended before flying just north of the launch site, banking and dropping belly first out of low clouds, restarting its engines to flip upright and then falling at an angle toward the gantry, slowing to a near standstill as the arms closed around it.

Approaching the Baja Peninsula, the returning Starship puts on a spectacular light show as atmospheric friction creates a fiery plasma sheath around the spacecraft. SpaceX

"The room behind me going absolutely insane," SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said from the mission control center. "These people have done so much to earn this. ... I mean, that was the missing link. That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

But SpaceX will need to successfully launch and recover a large number of Super Heavy-Starships to demonstrate the statistical reliability needed for crewed flights. And the company will need to demonstrate its ability to autonomously refuel Starships in Earth orbit and keep their propellants from boiling away in the space environment.

While the system is designed to be fully reusable, the Starship upper stage uses most of its propellant getting into Earth orbit. NASA wants to use a variant of the Starship to carry astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and multiple Super Heavy-tanker flights will be needed to refuel the lander in Earth orbit before it can head for the moon.

SpaceX plans to begin orbital fueling tests in the next several Super Heavy-Starship flights. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready in time.

World.title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
World.content:
A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water.

Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.

The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said in a news briefing late Friday afternoon that 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.

Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday afternoon, with two in serious condition, Moreno said at a news conference.

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by a tanker ship in the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Gerald Herbert

There were 191 passengers and crew members aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the mayor.

Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.

Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Moreno said at a news conference Saturday that rescuers pulled approximately 100 people from the water. Nearby boats had reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water.

Emergency responders, including Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, conducted rescue and response operations, Port NOLA said. Moreno said that along with local and federal agencies, private vessels that happened to be on the river at the time responded "as volunteers to try and get people out of the water."

Moreno described the successful rescue operation as a "miracle on the Mississippi."

One witness, Jamie Holford, told CBS News he saw the American Heritage hit the dock after the collision. He described seeing people hurrying off the boat. Then, as it rolled over, some were climbing over the railings of the boat, he said.

"It looked like something off the Titanic," he said.

Asked what the collision sounded like, Holford said, "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like."

U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Coast Guard investigators were on scene working to determine what caused the tanker to lose control.

"The investigation is still ongoing, there seems to be some kind of a loss of steering," Burnham told reporters. "The exact reason why, we don't know that."

The National Transportation Safety Board sent a "Go Team" to the scene Saturday to begin its own investigation into the cause. The agency said at a news conference that investigators have recovered a Voyage Data Recorder (VDR) from the Atlantic Asphalt and asked the public for video and information. A VDR captures the vessel's speed through the water, direction, course and audio from the bridge of the vessel, according to the NTSB.

Burnham said at a news conference Saturday that approximately 16,000 gallons of fuel remain on board and that officials are assessing how to address the potential pollution. She told reporters it is too early to give a timeline on salvaging the wreckage, saying, "We're talking weeks."

Burnham noted Friday that she was working to reopen the river, which the Coast Guard had closed when the collision occurred.

"We're going to start evaluating how to reopen it as soon as possible," Burnham said.

In a Truth Social post, President Trump praised the response of the Coast Guard and other law enforcement agencies for "doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana."

The American Heritage was built in 2015 and is operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The Associated Press reports that the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. The tanker specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semisolid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

CBS News has reached out to the tanker's owner for comment.

World.title: FAA ground stop disrupts college football
World.content:
FAA ground stop disrupts college football

toggle caption i Justin Ford/Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.

Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.

"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."

Sponsor Message

Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.

While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.

Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.

In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

World.title: Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
World.content:
Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

Sponsor Message

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

Sponsor Message

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

World.title: US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
World.content:
US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.

Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.

PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.

In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.

"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.

Sponsor Message

"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.

Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.

In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.

States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.

Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.

Sponsor Message

But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.

For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.

After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."

Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."

Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.

Past administrations sounded alarms

For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.

That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.

Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.

Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.

Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.

Sponsor Message

When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.

When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.

Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.

"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.

People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.

"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"

National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.

In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.

"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.

Sponsor Message

Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."

And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response.
