"The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."

'The dog didn't bark'

Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.

Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."

Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.

"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."

Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.

"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.

Sponsor Message

"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.

Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.

More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.

toggle caption i Amy Maxmen/KFF Health News



The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.

CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.

"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."

The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.

Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.

Sponsor Message

The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."

The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.

Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.

Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.

When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.

Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.

At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.

To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.

Sponsor Message

"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. Learn more about KFF.

World.title: SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history
World.content:
SpaceX successfully catches Starship and makes history

toggle caption i Eric Gay/AP

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss.

"Can you believe it?" shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot.

SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, intended for moon and Mars travel. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

Sponsor Message

The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.

It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

World.title: Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations
World.content:
Bomb found near ethanol plant in central Illinois forces evacuations

A bomb was found near an ethanol plant in central Illinois, sparking evacuations of those who live near the industrial site as law enforcement officials investigate, authorities said Saturday.

The bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. While officials say the device has since been "rendered safe," as of Saturday morning, all residents within a 1-mile radius remained under an evacuation notice as officials continued to scour the facility for any other bombs and evidence.

Meanwhile, shelters have been set up for those displaced by the threat, authorities said.

"This is a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters just after midnight Saturday. "We need to take the blast radius seriously."

FBI Special Agent Ryan Pressley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.

"We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," he said.

No arrests have been made at this time and no injuries have been reported.

Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday that BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that's what alarms us."

It's not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don't result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.

Sponsor Message

Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after a series of bomb threats that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.

"We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests," said Dixon. "We're asking for the public's patience while we work to make this area safe."

Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago.

The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.

World.title: 'We can't let them down' -- After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead
World.content:
'We can't let them down' — After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead

toggle caption i David Zalubowski/AP

DENVER — Democrats descended on Denver for a two-day conference that was half victory party, half sober look at the road ahead on delivering for the voters who elected them.

The "What's Next" conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, was scheduled long before Democrats outperformed expectations with their best electoral performance since Watergate. It brought together rising stars — like incoming Gov. Rob Sand in Iowa and Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas — along with strategists, organizers, state and federal lawmakers and potential presidential contenders.

Held at a concert hall, with colorful artwork of party heavy hitters dotting the venue, Democrats attended sessions like "What Voters Want" and "What Needs To Change." The overwhelming emphasis from speakers was that Democrats have to earn back trust.

toggle caption i

"We won races in places where we haven't won in a long time, even in some places where we've never won. And the message shouldn't be that [voters] are fully embracing the Democratic Party," said Colorado Rep. Jason Crow in an interview.

Sponsor Message

"It took us decades to dig ourselves in a hole and to push people away from us, and it's going to take us more than one cycle to earn that trust," said Crow, who is one of the party's recruitment co-chairs.

toggle caption i Mark Makela/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

A party on probation

Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, took the party to task for not investing more in the South and in Black voters.

"When we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night just proved everybody wrong of what is possible," said Clayton to much applause. "Rural America deserves the investment from the Democratic Party and we must run towards communities that our party has run away from."

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said Democrats shouldn't rest on their laurels.

"I think we are adequately politically traumatized by the last few cycles, so that we will not draw the wrong lessons from all of this," Buttigieg said. "Because here's the thing: it is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back, or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics."

Sponsor Message

He said Democrats can learn from the current White House on two fronts, by having: "a bias towards action and a readiness to get things done coming out of the gate and at the very same time a readiness to plan for the long-term," adding Democrats should come out of the gate strong, with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.

Presumptive next Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries told the audience he has plans to do just that, with a robust agenda that includes reversing Medicaid cuts, banning congressional stock trading and mid-decade redistricting, establishing a statutory right to abortion, and overturning the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that did away with limits on political spending by corporations and unions.

The conference itself was peppered with potential presidential contenders, including Buttigieg, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, and California Rep. Ro Khanna, one of the few progressive speakers.

No one announced an official run, but many gave previews of their theory of the case.

"I do think it's important that whoever we hire to be the chief executive of this country knows how to run something, knows how to get stuff done, knows how to not just have a vision but knows how to deliver on it," Shapiro told reporters.

Someone who was previously kicking the tires for a possible White House bid — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen — told reporters he's no longer considering it, as he instead pursues the top leadership post in the Senate.

toggle caption i Mark Makela/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Should Democrats work with Trump?

Throughout the conference, Democrats debated whether and how to work with the Trump administration in order to deliver meaningful change for voters.

"If slapping Trump's name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through — hell yes, I would do that," said Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

Sponsor Message

Talarico agrees.

"The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any American presidency."

But New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill added a note of caution, describing the president as a bad faith actor.

"The art of the deal to Trump is he figures out what you want, he leverages the you know what out of you, and keeps taking, taking, taking, and never delivers," Sherrill said. "My advice to Sen. Talarico is if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it."

World.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
World.content:
FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

WASHINGTON— Friday's nationwide ground stop started when a contractor updated old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication lines, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after the rare ground stop. Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator who joined Duffy at Saturday's media briefing, said schedule problems should be resolved by Sunday evening.

Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded, which is 18% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Sponsor Message

L3Harris, a long time contractor for the FAA, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location changing copper wire to fiber optics, Duffy said. "When I tell you that we're using old equipment, we're using old equipment," he said.

He said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system, and if L3Harris was at all responsible.

"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"

In a statement on their website, L3Harris said they have been working with the FAA to modernize communication infrastructure, including converting copper wires to a fiber optic system. The contractor said they have completed more than 70% of those conversions.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.

Sponsor Message

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."

Bedford said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or any AI-related issues.

Since his time in office, Duffy said he's been asking Congress for money to make more upgrades. In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion to modernize the nation's aging air traffic control system.

On Saturday, Duffy said again that the FAA needed more money for improvements.

"This is the moment, if we don't start to switch out our systems, when, how long are we going to wait, America, and Congress?" Duffy asked.

Thousands of passengers miss flights

toggle caption i Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images

For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue, Duffy said. Bedford said all passengers will be put on new flights or they'll get a full refund, but that people should reach out to their airlines directly.

Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.

On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.

Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.

Sponsor Message

"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8 p.m. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"

She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.

The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.

For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.

"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"

"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. They even thought about driving to Florida. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."

And it did— eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.

Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.

"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.

Sponsor Message

Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.

This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

Ava Pukatch contributed to reporting.

World.title: 5th soldier injured in CFB Wainwright fire has died, officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A fifth soldier has died as a result of the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the Department of National Defence says.

Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco, of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry (3 PPCLI), died in an Ontario hospital Friday from injuries he sustained in the fire on Oct. 17, the department said in a news release Saturday.

Some of the country’s top politicians and military officials, including Prime Minister Mark Carney and Gen. Jennie Carignan — the country's top soldier — have offered condolences to loved ones and troops who knew him.

"We will honour his dedicated service and continue to stand with all those affected by this tragedy along the difficult road ahead," Carignan said.

Dal Bianco and other service members at CFB Wainwright that day were training to defend the country, choosing to put the futures of other Canadians before their own, Carney said in a statement posted on social media.

“That is service. Now, we serve them,” he said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media she was heartbroken by the news of Dal Bianco’s death.

“Our thoughts are with the family, friends, and Canadian Armed Forces community mourning this profound loss,” Smith said.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre echoed that sentiment.

"He put on the uniform to serve Canada, and Canada will not forget him. We pray for his family mourning this terrible loss, and for the 24 soldiers still fighting to recover in hospital," he wrote on social media Saturday.

The tragedy occurred during afternoon live-fire training at CFB Wainwright, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Military officials have previously said a grass fire was burning in a permanent danger area, so base firefighters couldn’t access it. Sudden strong winds in the region — Environment and Climate Change Canada issued weather warnings that day for various parts of Alberta — rapidly spread the flames.

In the initial aftermath, the fire killed four service members and injured 39 others.

The DND's news release from Saturday says 24 soldiers are still in hospital nationwide.

The military said four soldiers were moved to health-care facilities in B.C. and Ontario last week to continue treatment closer to home. Three of them were being cared for at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Hospital: two soldiers receiving around-the-clock care, a third was an outpatient — meaning they don’t have to stay overnight in hospital.

As of earlier this week, 21 soldiers are still in Alberta facilities: 15 were on ventilators and nine were in critical condition, according to Acute Care Alberta.

World.title: Copper wire replacement caused air traffic control issue that grounded flights across U.S.: White House
World.content:
Transportation secretary says investigation will look at what went wrong with 'straightforward' maintenance

Copper wire replacement caused air traffic control issue that grounded flights across U.S.: White House

Routine maintenance to replace telecom line led to air traffic control outage: U.S. transportation secretary | Duration closed caption 3:40

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told a news conference that a contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration was working at a remote location to replace a copper line when an unknown issue overloaded the aging air traffic control system, forcing the FAA to keep planes on the ground nationwide.

World.title: We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share. Here’s what we found
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether you are buying a coffee, groceries, checking the weather or unwinding with an online video, there’s a free mobile app for just about everything.

But a Marketplace investigation shows the cost of this convenience is your privacy – and the data you’re sharing goes far beyond what you might realize.

Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it goes.

To do so, Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science, and his team at the University of Calgary scanned the network traffic of the apps on an Android device. Privo, an organization that evaluates apps to ensure they comply with U.S. child privacy laws, also did a scan of the apps on iOS, Apple’s operating system.

While doing scans to see the network traffic of mobile apps on Android, some apps appeared to be sending information to outside companies around the world. The network scan above shows the activity from all the apps on someone’s phone, not necessarily the apps Marketplace tested. (CBC)

In their user policies, the apps we tested explicitly disclose that they collect or share certain data and that when you use the app, you accept their terms.

But Reardon and Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst who used to work with Privo, are concerned some apps collect more than they need and are sharing what they learn with others around the world.

That data ranges from your name and email address to your exact whereabouts.

“To me, this is not the internet we wanted. This is not the internet we deserve. It's turned into a monstrous data collection surveillance system,” Reardon said.

Here’s what we learned about each app we tested, and what you can do to protect your data.

Tim Hortons

(CBC)

The scan showed that the Tim Hortons app appeared to be sending data to third-party companies as soon as you launch it.

Reardon said one overseas third-party company built into the app appeared to be receiving enough information to create the equivalent of a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.

“This was beyond the pale,” he said.

Some of those details include:

The name given to the device (for example, Bob’s iPhone).

An identifier unique to the device.

A list of many of the sensors on the device.

The details of the device’s camera (for example, the size of your lens).

The names of the ringtones and alarm sounds used.

The names of Wi-Fi routers near you, which Reardon said can be used to determine your location.

Rollason said the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service. She noted the amount of data collected “seems quite excessive” to validate the purchase of a cup of coffee.

Marketplace isn’t identifying any of the third-party companies or their locations because accountability rests with the app developer.

In a statement, Tim Hortons’ director of communications Michael Oliveira said this third party only collects this information for “fraud prevention, account protection, and payment abuse prevention, not for marketing or advertising … or to work around guests’ choices regarding those activities.”

Oliveira said the information collected can help detect if a never-before-seen device is being used on a customer’s account or if a “threat actor” is pretending to be a customer.

He also said the third party is not allowed to sell the data and that Tim Hortons does not sell users’ personal information to third-party companies or data brokers.

PC Optimum

(CBC)

The test showed the PC Optimum app appeared to be sending 10 outside companies information about which products users are searching for — even if the product was sensitive like a search for prenatal vitamins.

One third-party company appeared to be receiving a user’s latitude and longitude and an identifier unique to the device.

The scan also showed the app sending different details to an overseas third-party including:

The first name of the user.

Their unredacted email address.

Their PC Optimum member number.

An identifier unique to the device.

How the user interacts with the app, like when they open the app and what they do in the app.

Reardon and Rollason said the data collection seemed to be more than what was necessary for the app to work properly. Based on their experience, they say they didn’t understand why the app needed 10 outside companies to know what users were searching for.

In a statement, Loblaw, the company behind PC Optimum, said the company has never sold personal information and continually reviews and strengthens its systems to protect people.

It said the information collected through Loblaw apps supports everyday features for customers such as shopping online and finding nearby stores.

The Weather Network

(CBC)

The scan showed that when users allowed the Weather Network app access to their location, it appeared to be sending a third-party company those details for targeted advertising, including:

A user's precise latitude and longitude.

The user’s local weather conditions.

The device’s advertising ID (unique to each device).

Reardon said it could allow the app to send you s based on where you are or “so you could get ads for a rainy day.”

He also noted it creates a “location history, because all of [the data sent] are bridged by this one thing that doesn't change — this device identifier.”

Rollason said understanding a user’s behaviours is key to advertisers.

“Are you using your phone more when it's raining or you're in the house, perhaps, versus going out on a nice day?” she said.

Pelmorex, the parent company of the Weather Network, said in a statement that the Weather Network does not sell any user data to third parties and data brokers. It said the app only uses location data when a user allows it and uses that data to provide the local weather and show relevant ads. It also said users can access the weather without giving the app their location.

Facebook

(CBC)

The scan showed when users give the Facebook app access to their camera roll to post one image, the app appeared to collect the metadata of other images and videos on the device that were not uploaded.

Metadata contains details like the name of the file, the date and time it was taken and the camera settings.

For whatever image or video is actually posted to Facebook, the scan appeared to show the app also collected the latitude and longitude of where the image was taken.

The app also tracked what users do while using Facebook, including every scroll and how long you linger on something.

Reardon and Rollason noted Facebook didn’t appear to share any data with third-party companies during the scan.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook, had no comment on Marketplace’s findings; however, its privacy policy does state it collects this data. The policy also says “we don't sell any of your information to anyone.”

Amazon

(CBC)

The scan showed Amazon appeared to be collecting what users searched for, even if the product was sensitive, along with the device’s advertising ID.

It didn’t show Amazon sending data to any third-party companies during the scan.

“This is to be expected with these very large companies because they have the resources to have their own ad network,” Reardon said.

Amazon said in a statement it never sells customers’ personal data. It also said it designs products and services to “protect their privacy and to put them in control of their experience."

YouTube

(CBC)

The scan didn’t show YouTube sending data to any third-party companies at the time of the test. The data appeared to only be going to the U.S.

Marketplace also tested if YouTube would follow the rules of its parent company, Google, and not play targeted advertising while a user was watching children’s content.

The test found no targeted ads while watching a children’s video.

Google said in a statement it doesn’t sell personal information.

‘You lack total control’

Ann Cavoukian, the former privacy commissioner of Ontario, said Canada’s current privacy laws aren’t strong enough, and the country's privacy commissioners also need to step up.

Speaking generally, she also said companies should be prioritizing people’s privacy by only collecting what they need and deleting data when they don’t need it anymore.

“You lack total control,” Cavoukian said. “It can be used in a variety of unorganized ways. It can come back to haunt you.”

Ann Cavoukian served as the privacy commissioner of Ontario from 1997 to 2014. (CBC)

The Office of the Federal Privacy Commissioner of Canada declined an interview, but a spokesperson said Marketplace’s findings raise “a number of concerns.”

Speaking generally, the office of Canada’s AI Minister Evan Solomon said in a statement that Canadians need privacy protections that “keep pace with changing technology and the ways companies collect, use and share their data.”

His office also noted the government introduced Bill C-36 to give people more control over their information and to force companies to be more transparent and accountable about how they handle people's data. The bill is still before the House of Commons and has received praise and criticism from privacy experts.

How can you protect your data?

Cavoukian said people should ask companies what data is being collected, why it’s being collected and ask that it be deleted as soon as the company doesn’t need it anymore.

Reardon and Rollason said there’s little you can do to stop the transmission of data because apps on your device, and the third parties in those apps, may be sending or collecting information even when your device is out of reach.

They said deleting apps if you’re not using them and only keeping what you need is the best protection.

World.title: New Orleans port sues for control of China-linked tanker that crashed into cruise ship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city's port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.

All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday, as well as the crew on the tanker.

Officials said 32 people were taken to hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. None of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said the tanker's voyage data recorder has been recovered. The device — the maritime equivalent of a flight data recorder — records information such as the vessel's speed and audio from the bridge.

NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18-24 months. A 16-member team will spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident.

$1M worth of damage alleged

The lawsuit filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million US in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.

It could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River. (Matthew Hinton/The Associated Press)

The first step is to make sure the 60,500 litres of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.

The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.

'I thought I was drowning'

The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told local news outlet WDSU-TV.

The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 19 C.

Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

People are helped out of the water by responders on Friday. Dozens were hospitalized but none of the injuries were deemed critical. (Devon Flanagan/The Associated Press)

"It's fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn't taste very good," Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.

Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the navy likely helped him.

"They taught us not to drown," Knab said.

WATCH | The moment of the crash and its aftermath: Tanker ship collides with riverboat carrying 129 people in New Orleans | Duration closed caption 1:42 A tanker ship collided with a docked river cruise boat carrying 129 passengers on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday. Rescuers scrambled to get people off the riverboat after it capsized and started sinking.

Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday's nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.

Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.

"Whether it's 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success," Montroll said.

The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.

Tanker owner a subsidiary of Chinese company

The Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-metre-long vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.

The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.

Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.

China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn't respond to an emailed request for comment.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

World.title: SpaceX Starship re-enters Earth, lands at same spot from which it launched a day ago
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Crowds cheered as SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned on Saturday from its longest flight in orbit yet to the tower it was launched from in Texas a day prior. The flight demonstrated the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decade-long effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft on Saturday returned from its longest flight in orbit yet to the Texas launch tower it was launched from a day prior, demonstrating the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decade-long effort to ‌develop a fully reusable rocket.

The towering two-stage rocket's Super ‌Heavy booster — the rocket's bottom half — carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX's Starbase, Texas, facilities. That booster had failed to return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after liftoff because of an onboard navigation issue, ⁠nixing SpaceX's plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.

But the Starship upper stage's successful return after orbiting Earth 14 times for over 22 hours marked a key engineering milestone ​in the whirlwind, multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees as ⁠the future workhorse for SpaceX's ⁠satellite business and ambitions to put humans on ‌the moon and eventually Mars.

After deploying 26 Starlink satellites in orbit Friday night while cruising some 260 kilometres in altitude, Starship on Saturday fired one of its engines to begin an atmospheric plunge. It faced blistering heat as its orbital speed of some 27,000 kilometres per hour slowed to a supersonic free-fall in the skies above SpaceX's Starbase facilities on the Gulf coast of south Texas.

The spacecraft then reignited three engines to flip itself in a vertical position and ‌steer itself toward the launch tower, where two mechanical "chopstick" arms clasped onto the spacecraft as it hovered in place.

Starship is executing a banking maneuver and final approach as it returns to Starbase for a catch https://t.co/E1WpGrlfaz —SpaceX

SpaceX's dominance in the ⁠global launch industry has been centred on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which has ⁠launched more than ⁠700 times since 2010. That ​rocket's first stage is reusable, but its second stage — the part that delivers payloads into orbit — is ​discarded into the ocean ⁠after each flight.

With Starship, ⁠Musk wants a rocket system that can fly to space and back in a manner and tempo ⁠akin to commercial airplanes.

Though Saturday's Starship recovery is a key milestone in that effort, SpaceX has ⁠yet ⁠to recover both Starship stages in ​a single mission. And Starship's heat-shield, composed of black hexagonal tiles that protect it from the blazing heat ​of atmospheric re-entry, is itself not ⁠yet fully reusable.

SpaceX is trying to engineer new tile designs that will require little to no refurbishment after each mission.

NASA's Space Shuttle system that ferried astronauts to the International Space Station before its 2011 retirement was partially reusable; its booster stages that got it off Earth were discarded after each flight. The reusable ⁠spacecraft itself had to go through ‌extensive refurbishment before re-flying.

World.title: Mike Morrice — the only candidate on the ballot — wins Green Party leadership with 96.6% of vote
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mike Morrice, the only candidate in the running, has secured 96.6 per cent of the vote to become Green Party leader, the federal party has announced.

The Greens released the results of their five-month leadership race on Saturday evening. Party members had the option of voting for Morrice or selecting none of the above.

The total number of votes cast was 3,435.

On stage Morrice told supporters that Greens will remain "laser focused" on the creating a clean economy and a just society through affordable housing and universal public health care.

"We will advocate for a government that meets the needs of every day Canadians ... ensures the ultra rich pay their fair share and takes decisive action on the climate emergency," Morrice said.

The party's search for a new leader began in June. The second candidate in the race, Nira Dookeran, dropped out in September.

Morrice was elected to Parliament in 2021. The one-term MP for the Ontario riding of Kitchener Centre lost his seat last year to a Conservative by a margin of 358 votes.

Soon after the defeat, Morrice was named deputy leader of the party and declared the next Green candidate for Kitchener Centre.

In a news release, the Green Party of Canada said Morrice's campaign brought "renewed energy" to the party.

"Young Greens membership more than doubled, accounting for over 25 per cent of all new members. Overall party membership grew by nearly 20 per cent," the release said.

His campaign also raised more than $113,302.04, which the party said is seven times the required amount.

Elizabeth May announced she would be stepping down as party leader after the 2025 federal election, while staying on as the party's sole member of Parliament.

The 2025 election saw the party's national vote share drop below two per cent for the first time in 25 years. Co-leader Jonathan Pedneault failed to secure a seat and resigned.

May was first elected Green Party leader in 2006 and stepped down in 2019. She returned to lead the party in 2022, following the resignation of Annamie Paul.

World.title: Stranded B.C. flyers out thousands amid flight cancellations due to Friday's ground stop
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Some frustrated Air Canada passengers say spotty communication and a lack of rebooking help have left them paying out of pocket amid widespread flight cancellations.

British Columbians Patricia Arndt, Corey Shack, Nancy Kristoff and Lisa Dolinski were in Cancun, Mexico, celebrating a 50th birthday but had to spend thousands of dollars to stay in Mexico after their return flight was cancelled.

"You just feel lost," said Arndt. "You’re going to have to figure it out yourself."

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop on Friday afternoon due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centres, stemming from a maintenance issue , according to officials.

Air Canada says it cancelled roughly 250 flights Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers following the FAA's order.

In an email, a spokesperson for Vancouver International Airport (YVR) said there were 54 flight cancellations Friday and another 23 related cancellations Saturday morning.

Unclear updates

Arndt said Air Canada didn’t communicate updated information in a timely manner. The airline told them they would receive an update about rebooking within 30 minutes, Arndt said, but no update came.

The four travellers said their return flight faced a two-hour delay and gate change before they received a text message saying it had been cancelled. They were forced to split up to find accommodations.

WATCH | Passengers search for alternatives: Rental cars, trains or Ubers? Airline passengers search for alternatives during U.S. ground stop | Duration closed caption 1:26

Between booking resorts and paying for trips to and from the airport, they estimated each of them spent roughly $2,000 to $3,000, with some families paying even more.

"That was the most frustrating part, because other airlines were communicating with their customers and we were getting zero communication," said Kristoff.

Dolinski woke up first thing Saturday to seek help at the Cancun International Airport, since she said Air Canada’s online platforms weren’t allowing them to book alternate flights home.

Dolinski said the Air Canada line only had one agent tending to it, and they waited three hours before eventually booking an alternate flight home on Wednesday.

Rerouting issues

She said some of her group members booked through Air Canada without extra charge but had to spend money on accommodations, while others paid out of pocket for their flights home but were able to secure a seat on Sunday flights.

McKenzie McMillan, managing partner at Travel Group in Vancouver, said Friday's mass cancellations were unlike anything seen in decades.

"This was a dramatic situation that unfolded yesterday for tens of thousands of passengers," he said.

McMillan says because these cancellations stem from an issue outside airlines’ control, airlines won’t be on the hook to cover those additional costs.

According to the Canadian Transportation Agency, if an airline delays or cancels a flight for reasons outside its control , it's not obligated to compensate affected passengers and the requirement to provide minimum assistance, like paying for food, drink or accommodation, does not apply.

McMillan said even though the FAA lifted its ground-stop order, it will likely take more than a week for airlines to get back to a normal schedule.

Air Canada says it has added flights where possible to help affected passengers, but further disruptions are expected as aircraft and crews remain out of position across its network.

World.title: AFC Toronto beats Montreal Roses to win 1st NSL title
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Olivia Chisholm's first-half goal allowed AFC Toronto to capture its first Diana B. Matheson Cup with a 1-0 victory over the Montreal Roses Saturday afternoon at TD Place in Ottawa.

The 17-year-old scored what proved to be the winner, and her first professional goal, in the 39th minute.

Sabrina D'Angelo had a clean sheet holding off the Roses, who had led the league with 48 goals.

AFC Toronto was looking for redemption after dropping last year's final to the Vancouver Rise.

WATCH | Chisholm lifts AFC Toronto over Roses in NSL final: AFC Toronto wins 1st NSL Championship with a 1-0 win over Montreal Roses | Duration closed caption 2:38 Olivia Chisholm scored the game's only goal to lead AFC Toronto to the Diana B. Matheson Cup over the Montreal Roses.

Toronto, who finished third in the regular-season standings, beat Ottawa 8-2 on aggregate in the semifinals and rode the momentum into the final.

Montreal, who finished first overall to win their first Supporters Shield, beat Vancouver 5-2 on aggregate in the semis to advance to their first championship final.

Trailing 1-0, Montreal came out hard and fast in the second half and generated a couple chances early on. Lisa Pechersky challenged D'Angelo and moments later D'Angelo had to handle an Elyse Bennett header. Pechersky had another chance in the 73rd minute trying to go back post but D'Angelo anticipated it and made the save.

Montreal pushed hard for the equalizer, generating 14 shots but just couldn't find a way to beat D'Angelo.

Montreal goalkeeper Gabrielle Lambert made a couple big saves in the 54th minute. First on Toronto's Kaylee Hunter and then managed to get her fingertips on a great chance by Shelina Zadorsky.

WATCH | Full replay of NSL final: CBC Sports: Northern Super League Championship Final - Montréal Roses vs AFC Toronto | Duration 2:44:00 The Diana B. Matheson Cup is on the line in the 2026 Northern Super League final between Montreal Roses FC and AFC Toronto.

In the opening half, the Roses had the better chances but Toronto capitalized with Chisholm's goal.

Lauren Rowe beat her defender in the box and sent a pass from near the endline to Chisholm, who had some space near the top of the box, and she side-footed a shot past the outstretched arms of Lambert.

Toronto dominated the first five minutes but Montreal's Evelyn Badu provided the Roses with their first chance in the ninth minute with a toe poke that just went over the crossbar.

The Roses entered the final riding a 12-game unbeaten streak since Maryse Bard-Montreal took over as interim head coach in August. Montreal won the Supporters' Shield with a 12-4-9 record and 45 points and was looking for the double.

Toronto was 1-2-2 in the regular season against Montreal and neither team had scored more than two goals in any of the five games.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Why Brazil?
World.content:
A sky that doesn`t charge to dream.

By Dany Cesario

HAVANA TIMES – Ever since I arrived in Brazil, there is one question I get asked repeatedly: “Why do so many Cubans come here?”

And every time I hear it, I think the question should be different: What is happening in Cuba that makes so many people decide to seek a different life?

The island is deteriorating, hardships are mounting, and people are wearing themselves out trying to get ahead. Yet the leaders’ worn-out rhetoric never changes, as if repeating the same slogans could feed a family, rebuild a country in ruins, or restore hope to those who have spent far too long waiting for change.

It outrages me that people are expected to make sacrifices without seeing them translate into a decent life. That expressing a different opinion becomes a problem, and that deciding one’s own future comes up against so many barriers.

Despite everything, there are still those who continue to justify this reality, as if defending a political narrative were more important than acknowledging the suffering of those who live it.

All of this makes me think of my mother and so many Cubans like her.

I wonder how many more years they will have to wait to live with the peace of mind they deserve. How many more promises will they have to hear before they can simply live, without worrying every day about what they will put on the table?

I’m not talking about privileges. I’m talking about rights: the right to live with dignity, to express what we think, and to make decisions about our own lives.

No government should take ownership of a people’s future or demand gratitude for what it is obligated to provide.

That is why Brazil, like any other country, does not have to be perfect for us Cubans to find what we have lacked for years: freedom, opportunities to grow, and the possibility of forging our own path without arbitrary restrictions.

It is not enough to talk about the homeland when the present is suffocating us and forcing us to pack our bags.

If we must emigrate to prosper, and if we have to seek new horizons to live with dignity, then the failure is not that of the people. It is the failure of a political system that has forced them to leave.

El destino comienza donde aprendemos a seguir..
