World.title: Advent Zagreb 2026: Festive Cheer, Cultural Highlights, and a Packed Calendar
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – It’s that time of year again! Advent Zagreb 2026 is just around the corner, promising a programme packed with festive cheer and a very full calendar.

The most wonderful time of the year is knocking at the door. Advent in Zagreb, which is considered one of the best in Europe, starts on the 28th of November and lasts until the 7th of January.

The multi-award-winning Advent Zagreb once again brings a rich cultural, entertainment and food programme, which, along with New Year’s events, will take place from the 28th of November 2026 to the 7th of January 2027. Organised by the City of Zagreb, the Zagreb Tourist Board (TZGZ) and numerous institutional and private partners, the programme will officially kick off with the traditional lighting of the first Advent candle on Ban Jelačić Square, after which the other locations will open.

zagreb’s progression as a festive city delight

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

Director of TZGZ, Martina Bienenfeld, stated that “Advent Zagreb has grown into one of the most recognisable Advent events in Europe, and this year’s edition brings new cultural content and more strongly connects city locations into a unique holiday experience. We pay special attention to culture and programmes for children and families. Among this year’s novelties intended for the youngest, I’d highlight LumiLicious on Mažuranac, which starts on the 6th of December, the feast of St Nicholas. Novelties are also The Magic Within on Marulić Square and the festive decoration of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts, whose ceremonial openings are planned for the 18th of December. Together with the new arrangement of the space in front of the Croatian National Theatre, these contents will connect the locations of the Green Horseshoe into a unique Advent promenade. In this way we enrich the Advent offer and open new possibilities for exploring the city, while at the same time putting Zagreb’s historical spaces, architecture and cultural heritage in the foreground.

The international recognisability of Advent Zagreb is also confirmed by this year’s awards and recommendations from world media. We are particularly pleased that Zagreb has been declared the best European destination for a Christmas city break in the selection of the European Best Destinations organisation, while the prestigious Time Out ranked it first on its list of the best European destinations for a winter city break in 2026, highlighting its attractiveness for family travel. Such recognitions have significant promotional value because they strengthen Zagreb’s international visibility, encourage interest in coming and contribute to its positioning on key source markets. In this context we continue with intensive promotional activities on 17 international markets, including targeted campaigns at stations of the London Underground and the Milan metro, as well as long-standing cooperation with Croatia Airlines and HŽ Passenger Transport.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

I believe that Advent Zagreb will once again achieve good tourist results this year and further strengthen Zagreb’s position as an attractive year-round destination. At the same time, we do not measure its success exclusively by tourist indicators, but also by the quality of the experience it provides to visitors and our fellow citizens. Precisely in this balance between tourist attractiveness and value for the local community we see the foundation of its long-term development and sustainability.”

The entire programme, detailed schedules of all events and current information can be found here, and we’ll also bring you descriptions of each below.

what’s on this festive season for europe’s best advent?

Julien Duval/TZGZ

What we’ve been waiting for all year finally starts on the last weekend of November. Zagreb has won a new title – it is the best Christmas city-break destination 2026 according to European Best Destinations. Along with well-known attractions such as the Ice Park, Advent on Zrinjevac, Fuliranje and numerous other events, there are also novelties for the youngest on Mažuranac, and the entire Upper Town, as well as the Green Horseshoe of the Lower Town, become a unique Advent promenade. Run with Santa Claus, dance or skate in the parks, sing on the tram or just stop and enjoy.

if you’re the musical type…

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Soloists

Museum of the City of Zagreb, on the 3rd, 6th, 10th and 13th of December at 18:00

The Zagreb Soloists continue the tradition of Advent concerts at the Museum of the City of Zagreb. At each of the four concerts the Zagreb Soloists will be joined by a young musician.

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra

Church of St Joseph, Journalists’ House

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra in the city’s historical spaces. The Church of St Joseph is the location of the first concert on the 29th of November, followed by three more at the Journalists’ House on the 5th 13th and 19th of December with performances by renowned Croatian and international soloists.

Advent concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices

Church of St John the Baptist 29 Nov, Basilica of St Anthony of Padua on the 13th of December, the Church of St Francis of Assisi on the 29th of December

Concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices bring a combination of classical music, choral compositions and Croatian traditional Advent and Christmas songs. Contemporary choral arrangements of Croatian musical heritage are performed for the first time.

Music in St Mark’s Church

St Mark’s Church, on the 13th 20th and 24th of December (Midnight Mass)

Advent tradition, performances of classical and sacred music that echo within the historical walls of the Church of St Mark. Admission is free.

Advent with the Opera of the Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb

Republic of Croatia Square, balcony of the CNT, the 5th of December at 17:30 and the 7th of December at 19:00

From the balcony of the Zagreb CNT, young soloists accompanied by piano perform opera and Advent compositions. Two half-hour concerts for residents and guests alike will fill the space in front of the theatre with holiday melodies.

seasonal music

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

From Christmas balconies to Zagreb

Balcony at the Stone Gate, balcony at Tkalčićeva 33, balcony of the CNT



Christmas melodies from Zagreb balconies performed by the six-member brass ensemble Ad gloriam brass. A unique musical experience of European flair and classical music, film themes and Christmas songs.

Festival of Advent and Christmas songs

Society of University Teachers and Other Scientists, Greek Catholic Co-Cathedral of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Church of St Peter the Apostle, Church of St Mark, Church of St Blaise, Stone Gate, terrace of Cravaticum – the Tie Museum



The Festival of Advent and Christmas songs brings festive concerts of Advent-Christmas music of different genres and eras. From classical to klapa and holiday pop songs at the 11th edition of the festival at six city locations. A children’s concert will also be held as part of the festival.

Zagreb Advent postcards

Oktogon, Neboder, Baković Sisters Passage



The vocal quartet Vox in the heart of Zagreb performs Advent compositions from Croatian and world musical heritage. With pop-up concerts, short performances without prior announcement, they will surprise random passers-by with the musical magic of Advent.

Advent under the lantern

Lotrščak Tower

World.title: New Croatian Tourism Law: Different Deadlines for Landlords to Re-Categorise Apartments
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – A new Croatian tourism law could mean that private landlords end up having different deadlines to re-categorise their apartments. Some will get five years, others will be given ten.

The mandatory re-categorisation of apartments every ten years, registration numbers for advertising accommodation via online platforms, stricter inspection supervision and higher penalties for illegal operations are some of the changes envisaged by the final proposal of the new Hospitality Activity Act, which the Croatian Parliament discussed on Thursday. Poslovni reports that although the government is announcing more order on the tourist market and an increase in the quality of service, small landlords are warning of additional obligations and uncertainty about future operating conditions.

State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport Monika Udovičić, president of the association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače (SMOi) Vedran Tomić, and president of the Guild of Hospitality and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts Hrvoje Margan all spoke about the new rules.

different deadlines for different landlords

According to the final proposal of the law, rooms, apartments and holiday homes will in future have to undergo re-categorisation every ten years. However, different transitional deadlines are envisaged for existing landlords, depending on when their approval decision was issued. According to Article 80 of the final proposal of the law, landlords whose decision was issued by the 31st of December 2015 will have to align their operations and obtain a new decision within five years of the entry into force of the relevant ordinance.

For those whose decision was issued as of the 1st of January 2016, a deadline of ten years from the entry into force of the ordinance is envisaged. This means that the deadlines do not automatically start running from the beginning of 2027, but from the day the new ordinance defining the conditions enters into force. After alignment, periodic checks will follow every ten years, which the competent administrative bodies will carry out ex officio. If it is established that the facility no longer meets the prescribed conditions, its type or category may be changed, and in certain cases the decision may be revoked.

the new rules aren’t “anti-landlord”, the powers that be claim

It was explained that hotels and campsites have so far undergone re-categorisation every four years, while the new law extends that period to five years. For small landlords, re-categorisation every ten years is envisaged. The reason for introducing the new checks, according to her, is the fact that there are facilities on the market that were categorised more than 20 years ago and whose compliance with standards has not been re-checked since then.

“This new rule isn’t directed against landlords,” the State Secretary said. She added that those who meet the prescribed conditions need not fear losing their decision. She also emphasised that the goal of the new ordinances is not to prevent existing landlords from operating, but to align standards with modern requirements.

possible consequences…

SMOi president Vedran Tomić questions the need for new categorisation, considering that online platforms and guest reviews have already become an important indicator of accommodation quality. He referred to an analysis of more than 1.6 million reviews according to which, he claims, Croatian private accommodation was rated better than hotel accommodation. Tomić believes that the entire reform is aimed at reducing the share of private accommodation and increasing hotel capacities.

Udovičić rejects such claims and stresses that the Ministry wants to protect family accommodation, but also to distinguish landlords for whom this is a traditional activity from pure rentierism, especially in residential buildings. According to her, Croatia has been receiving approximately ten thousand new beds in private accommodation year after year, while demand has not grown at the same pace, which has also affected occupancy rates.

The Ministry is therefore seeking to further encourage the quality and recognisability of family accommodation. Tomić, however, believes that the market, and not the state, should decide on the further growth of accommodation capacities.

a new rule from may the 1st, 2027

Another important change concerns all landlords who advertise their accommodation units via online platforms for short-term rental. Each such unit will have to have a unique registration number that will be submitted to the platform and displayed in the . Udovičić announced that the issuance of this number will be free of charge, and the procedure digital, via a system available through e-Citizens. According to the final proposal of the law, the provisions on registration numbers and data exchange with platforms should start to apply on the 1st of May 2027. The goal is to link accommodation data with the competent authorities and more effectively suppress unregistered renting. Unlike the registration numbers, most of the other provisions of the new law, if adopted in the proposed form, should enter into force on the 1st of January 2027.

support for more transparency and digitalisation

Hrvoje Margan, president of the Guild of Hospitality and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts, welcomed the adoption of the new law and the announced digitalisation of administrative procedures. Nevertheless, he warned that it is necessary to carefully regulate the minimum technical conditions so that the new ordinances do not become an additional administrative burden for hospitality operators. “We don’t want the ordinances to become a cleansing mechanism for hospitality operators,” he said. Udovičić replied that neither the law nor the future ordinances are conceived as a way of abolishing existing decisions, but as an instrument for modernising the system and raising quality.

The final proposal of the new Hospitality Activity Act has passed parliamentary debate, but still has to be voted on. Until its adoption and the entry into force of the new ordinances, landlords continue to operate according to the current regulations.

World.title: Continental Croatian Tourism up 60%, Million-Euro Incentives in 2027
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – Continental Croatian tourism is up by 60%, with new million-euro incentives coming in 2027 aimed at less developed inland regions.

The Croatian National Tourist Board recently launched a new cycle of public tenders for 2027, focused on the development of continental and less developed tourist regions and the promotion of events. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that the decision to announce the tenders was made by the HTZ Tourism Council at its 9th session, and funding is secured through dedicated resources from the Fund for Touristically Underdeveloped Areas and the Mainland and the Fund for Associated Tourist Boards.

big increases for continental croatia

The adopted Open Call for Expressions of Interest aims at cooperation with organisers of “TOP events” of national significance and other events in the segments of eno-gastronomy, nautical tourism, culture, sport, entertainment, MICE and health tourism. In addition, tenders have been announced for regional tourist boards in underdeveloped areas and for projects of associated tourist boards.

“By announcing new tenders for 2027 through the HTZ funds, we are continuing with concrete measures by which we encourage more balanced development of Croatian tourism, while at the same time continuing cooperation with organisers of events and top events that contribute to the attractiveness of our destinations and the attraction of guests throughout the year,” said Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina. He emphasised that since 2021, 51.6 million euros have been secured from these funds for more than 2,000 projects.

“The results are also visible in tourist traffic, which in the continental counties has increased by 60 percent in arrivals and 58 percent in overnight stays over the past ten years, while according to the latest TOMAS research, the average daily expenditure of tourists in continental Croatia has increased by 21 percent compared to 2022.

These are indicators of the growing importance of continental tourism in the overall development of Croatian tourism, and our goal is to continue this positive trend, further strengthen the tourist offer and enable local communities across Croatia to feel the benefits of tourism even more strongly,” Glavina emphasised.

encouraging cooperation

HTZ director Kristjan Staničić stressed that with these calls they want to further encourage the development of quality events that have the potential to become a reason for the arrival of domestic and foreign guests.

“We place special emphasis on touristically underdeveloped areas and the mainland, where events can play an exceptionally important role in creating the recognisability of destinations, activating local potentials and a more even distribution of tourist traffic,” Staničić said, adding that their goal is to support events that, through quality, content and organisation, can position themselves at the national level, create additional value for the destination and encourage cooperation between tourist boards, local stakeholders and the economy.

World.title: Zagreb is Finally Getting A New Tram Line
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – The City of Zagreb will finally get a brand new tram line, after over six months of “combing through” all of the submitted bids.

The powers that be in the City of Zagreb have once again selected GIP Pionir as the winner of the tender issued back at the beginning of July. Over two whole years after it was announced, the tender for works on the tram line along Heinzelova and Radnička streets can now proceed. Poslovni reports that the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures (DKOM) rejected the appeals of two companies that participated in the public procurement procedure estimated at 48 million euros, so the selection of the contractor can finally be completed and preparations for the start of works can begin soon.

This finally brings to an end the long-running complication surrounding one of the capital projects that the City of Zagreb announced back in 2023 and officially launched in November 2024. The first tender for the contractor of works on 3.7 kilometres of new tram track was announced at the end of 2024, but as the bids received significantly exceeded the estimated amount of 48 million euros (excluding VAT, as with other amounts in the text), the City cancelled the tender and announced a new one in May 2025. The value of the project remained the same, and by July four bids had been received.

After a two-month evaluation, the job was awarded to GIP Pionir, and then the problems began. A consortium of bidders led by the company Texo Molior, which also participated in the tender, decided to lodge an appeal, and the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures (DKOM) upheld that appeal in January this year. The Commission ordered the City of Zagreb, as the contracting authority, to go through all the bids again and decide on the best one, which they did this summer. This brings us to the new problem.

As can be seen on the Electronic Public Procurement Noticeboard (EOJN), the company had to send several explanations and supplements to its bid over the past six months. A few days later, however, another appeal against the selection decision arrived at DKOM. The procedure was initiated by the same consortium of bidders as the previous time, namely the companies Texo Molior from Cavtat and Zagreb’s Tigra. The City waited three months for the Commission’s decision in the first appeal procedure, the re-selection of the contractor lasted more than six months, and it has now waited almost another four months for the new DKOM decision. The appeal was rejected and the procedure can now continue.

The project, incidentally, in addition to laying new kilometres of track, also includes the reconstruction and protection of 1.4 kilometres of water supply infrastructure along Heinzelova Street and Radnička Road, as well as the reconstruction of sewer collectors built between 1920 and 1950. Only after these works are completed will it be possible, as the City of Zagreb previously explained, to start work on the new line with a total of nine tram stops.

World.title: Tallinn's Reaalkool opens €32.7 million building, €10 million over budget
World.content:
Tallinn Secondary School of Science's (Tallinna Reaalkool) new teaching building has been in use since the start of the current academic year, but the ceremony to confirm that took place today. The municipal school building cost about €32.7 million — around €10 million more than planned.

The interior is light and calm: plenty of oak veneer, walls and furniture in pale tones or terracotta, a color that also appears on floor tiles in the 142-year-old main building, tying old and new together. Teachers helped the architects with the design.

"For me the most important thing about the interior was functionality," said head of studies and physics teacher Daniel Kaasik. Physics teachers at the school, he added, had had a say in what they wanted in their classrooms.

The school now has room for its pupils for the first time, too. "The older school building was built for 300 pupils. Now there are 950–1000," Kaasik noted.

There are three physics classrooms and four laboratories in the new building, as well as sound-absorbing ceilings, a separate floor for younger pupils, terraces and a courtyard, and a new underground gym. The school canteen is housed there too, and has been designated smartphone-free.

The City of Tallinn's property department said the original 2024 estimate of €22.3 million covered only the new extension, and that restoring the historic main building and archaeological excavations — budgeted at €300,000 but costing about €1.4 million — had been responsible for pushing the total up.

The work to build the new facility was also preceded by a major archaeological dig, rich in findings.

World.title: Prime minister: We have nothing to discuss with Russia on European security
World.content:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants to distract Europe with a sort of "bucket list" of his wants, rather than a lasting peace in Ukraine, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said.

Europe's security architecture is not open for negotiation, the prime minister noted, speaking at Friday's informal European Council in Dublin, Ireland.

Michal noted Estonia is providing Ukraine with an additional €6.5 million, including €4.5 million of locomotives and €2 million for recovery.

"Putin wants us to discuss his wish list instead of focusing on achieving peace in Ukraine," Michal said. "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about the European security architecture; it is working just fine. If we wanted to make any changes to it, they would only be that Ukraine becomes a member of the EU and NATO and that Russia stops killing people," he continued, via a press release.

The prime minister said his message to other leaders was to focus on what matters — peace in Ukraine — and not be distracted by Putin's attempts to divert attention.

At #EPC in Dublin, I called for stronger support for Ukraine through another harsh winter and more pressure on the Kremlin. Russia could stop the killing today and open the way to peace. Instead, it continues targeting civilians and essential services. On AI, Europe must catch up. We need more investment and better opportunities to test advanced models and assess their risks. AI will shape both our economies and our defence. My full remarks below. — Kristen Michal (@KristenMichalPM) November 12, 2026

Michal noted the EU institutions and the E5 — France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the U.K.— are representing Europe in the Ukraine peace talks, while EU leaders, European Council President António Costa and the European Commission have a responsibility to coordinate and represent positions jointly agreed by member states.

"While active discussions on peace are taking place in various capitals, Russia continues to attack Ukraine," he said. "Ukraine faces a very difficult winter. The European Union must find the resources to help Ukraine get through it and ensure that it has everything it needs to defend itself."

Michal also addressed the topic of Artificial Intelligence (AI) while in Dublin. He said Europe must not replace one dependence with another. "We must not replace our dependence on imported fossil fuels with dependence on foreign artificial intelligence," he said.

The prime minister added the EU has two major advantages here — its single market and its data — and must use them better. "We cannot remain merely users of artificial intelligence developed by others. We must also have strong companies and technologies of our own," he continued.

Leaders also discussed AI with French firm Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch and Professor Geoffrey Hinton, one of AI's pioneers; the Estonian prime minister said Europe needs capital, computing power and the ability to grow across the single market, with investment directed at robotics, autonomous vehicles and smart healthcare.

World.title: Retired general: Without women, Estonia may run out of conscripts, reservists
World.content:
Estonia will not find enough conscripts in future because of demographics, meaning conscription should be extended to women, a retired general said.

Speaking at a public lecture by Defense Minister Martin Herem at the University of Tartu, Maj. Gen. (retd) Veiko-Vello Palm said Estonia cannot meet its target of over 4,100 conscripts a year by 2040, adding women will help address that issue as well as bringing a degree of rational behavior to proceedings.

The issue of women conscripts has already been addressed in recent months; in general conscription has an effect long beyond the terms, around a year, personnel serve – as conscripts remain on reservist lists and are liable to attend annual exercises thereafter.

Palm said the challenge is renewing that reserve. "We could state that a 55-year-old today is the same as a 35-year-old in the old days, but at the end of the day that isn't really the case."" he said. "

"It seems we have no other option for renewing the reserves than a completely total conscription," Palm went on. Even now, with compulsory conscription, Estonia takes only a little over 50 percent of each male cohort for all sorts of reasons, he added. "Inevitably the drop-out rate before conscription is relatively high — whether because of mortality, which is fortunately low, or mainly health problems."

Veiko-Vello Palm speaking at the University of Tartu lecture. Source: University of Tartu.

Palm said despite this Estonia's picture is not that bad compared with Finland's. "Finland, too, has universal conscription, but about 60 percent of each cohort reaches military training." Even matching that, he said, would not get Estonia to the required number.

As to the supposed physical standards objection sometimes raised by opponents of women conscripts, Palm said a young woman in good shape already meets every physical requirement as set out for men. "The first counter-argument is that men also have different physical standards" — the defense forces already accepts that a 50-year-old and a 22-year-old machine gunner are in different condition, despite carrying the same work on the battlefield.

Palm said a clear problem is physical dimensions, and that the state should therefore develop equipment suited to women. "This is especially important for personal protective equipment such as flak jackets, body armor and helmets," Palm continued.

Palm also argued that a larger share of women would bring more rational and logical behavior and thinking to the Estonian Defense Forces. "A share of women in the defense forces would undoubtedly be positive for defense leadership, but also for military decisions."

Former Supreme Court chief justice Rait Maruste argued in May that national defense obligations should apply to women as well, calling the male-only system discriminatory and saying modern defense includes many functions that do not require physical strength. Anu Rannaveski, director general of the Defense Resources Agency (KRA), said at around the same time that female conscription is "rather a question of when, not if," and by October that around 250 women serve on active duty and women "can handle any unit," including special operations, engineers and military intelligence. This year's intake was cut to about 700 from the usual 4,000 as a "gap year," with all 32 women who opted in accepted while two-thirds of male applicants were not — and both Defense Minister Martin Herem and current EDF commander Andrus Merilo, who succeeded Herem as commander-in-chief, believe female conscription should be encouraged yet remain voluntary.

Women in any case serve in the EDF as regular soldiers and in the volunteer Defense League and its women's counterpart, Naiskodukaitse.

World.title: Mari-Liis Jakobson: Will AI turn voters into livestock?
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is a native of bureaucracy, but humans must retain control over political decision-making and the ability to conduct reality checks, writes Mari-Liis Jakobson.

In recent weeks, Estonia has been shaken by several announcements of layoffs driven by companies' efforts to reorganize operations and use artificial intelligence to automate work previously performed by people. AI is already transforming the private-sector labor market, but how will it reshape government and democracy?

Israeli historian Yuval Noah Harari has pointed out that artificial intelligence is a far better bureaucrat than a human being. Humans are not evolutionarily designed for bureaucracy. Our ancestors developed in environments without legal codes, bank accounts, reports or administrative procedures. Bureaucracy is a relatively recent invention in human history, one to which we have never fully adapted.

According to Harari, AI, by contrast, is a native inhabitant of bureaucracy. Databases, regulations and endless procedures are its natural environment. Unlike humans, it can process enormous amounts of information simultaneously and do so without becoming tired.

For that reason, it is easy to imagine election promises promoting an AI-powered state. Why should a person spend weeks processing an application if AI can do it in minutes? Why could AI not draft legislation, analyze its impacts or even run entire government agencies?

It sounds tempting: less bureaucracy, faster services and lower costs.

Yet Harari also paints a much darker picture of the future. He compares the potential relationship between humans and AI to the relationship between cattle and humans. A cow can observe people and understand some aspects of human behavior, but it knows nothing about financial markets or legal systems through which humans determine its fate.

Similarly, Harari argues, we may one day discover that AI has created administrative, legal and economic systems so complex that humans can no longer grasp how they function. We may remain part of the system while losing the ability to truly control it. We could become comparable to livestock.

Now to democracy.

AI fits very naturally into the logic of technocratic governance and would probably make a fairly effective authoritarian ruler. Democracy, however, is not merely about transmitting commands or finding the most efficient solution.

Democracy is based on people's right to decide what kind of society they want to live in, what values matter to them and who should hold power. These decisions are not always rational or efficient. They are often contradictory, slow and inconvenient. And although modern democracy is not something evolution directly equipped us with, the skills of cooperation and negotiation that lie at the heart of self-government have been among humanity's key evolutionary advantages.

A human-centered constitutional order is also the primary safeguard against AI dominance. How much authority we allow AI to have in that sphere remains our own choice.

Of course, AI can still play a valuable supporting role. It can help organize and process information, translate and analyze. The larger question is how much we should allow AI to construct reality itself.

"How much authority we allow AI to have in that sphere remains our own choice."

Concerns that people increasingly live in simulations rather than reality were expressed by French thinker Jean Baudrillard more than 45 years ago. Earlier technologies also made it possible to create distorted perceptions of reality, from rumors to Photoshop. But the speed and realism with which AI can produce deepfakes and reshape the ways we seek information have elevated simulated realities to an entirely new level.

Examples of AI distorting reality are already plentiful.

Before this year's elections in Hungary, an AI-generated video was published on the official Facebook account of Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. In the video, opposition leader Péter Magyar appeared to receive a fictional phone call from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. To be fair, the video did include a disclaimer stating that it had been created using AI.

Before Slovakia's 2023 election, a fabricated audio recording circulated in which opposition leader Michal Šimečka appeared to discuss manipulating election results with a journalist. The recording was released just before voting, leaving very little time to debunk the misinformation.

Ahead of Germany's parliamentary elections last year, the Alternative for Germany party used AI-generated imagery contrasting an idealized Germany with a threatening picture of immigration. These were not photographs of actual society but synthetic images designed to reinforce a political message.

Estonia has not been immune to these developments, although incidents of comparable severity have not yet been reported. It is high time to discuss whether political parties are willing to agree on transparent principles governing the use of AI in election campaigns and what forms of use should perhaps be ruled out altogether.

Such agreements would not eliminate the risk of influence operations originating outside the parliamentary system, but they would make it easier to condemn them when they occur.

It is also worth considering whether journalists and voters are prepared for a situation in which a highly convincing but completely fabricated political scandal emerges just before an election.

Estonian politicians may disagree on many things, but presumably none of them wants to be turned into livestock.

World.title: Estonia's Saatse 'boot' bypass opens, ending drive through Russia
World.content:
The Saatse boot bypasses have opened, ending the need for drivers in southeastern Estonia to pass through a roughly 400-meter stretch of Russian territory.

A 400-meter bypass around the boot's "heel" along with a longer 4.7-kilometer bypass around its "sole," which skirted the border, have been opened, with the work costing €2.5 million plus VAT over six months.

The Transport Board also laid 2 km of dust-free surfacing on the nearby Matsuri–Sesniki road and built bus turning points at the villages of Lutepää and Sesniki.

"As of today Estonian law applies at every point on this road, and the PPA can assist Estonian people anywhere along it," said Meelis Saarepuu, head of the Police and Border Guard Board's (PPA) southern prefecture border bureau.

One local resident, Meelike Kruusmäe-Veinberg, who lives on a nearby farm, said the difference was practical. "In winter the Poogandi road was in very poor condition; every day someone went into the ditch." Now, she said, the road is wide and gentle, with the edges visible from everywhere.

Local government elder Raul Kudre said the new road makes travel easier for many in Setomaa, a historic cultural region.Around 300 or more people would regularly XXX use the route in summer, and it provides access to local features such as a 50-place care home whose relatives visit constantly, and a museum.

Janar Taal, the Transport Board's southern region head, noted the road runs through a nature protection area and the terrain surprised even the builders. "The water table is very high in places here and had to be battled with," he said.

Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said via a press release Seto people should now be able to travel by road without going through Russia — and that the closure of the boot last autumn had meant longer journeys for ambulances, rescue services and police.

The Saatse boot consisted of anomalous stretches of road that passed through Russian territory, meaning drivers on the Värska–Ulitina road had to cross into Russia to stay in Estonia. Guidelines were in place on minimum speeds and how to act while driving through the "sole," as well as on what to do if the vehicle broke down at some point while on the Russian side.

Its removal followed an incident in October 2025 in which armed Russian uniformed personnel were seen on the boot's road. The stretch of road was blocked to traffic soon after.

World.title: SDE prime minister candidate: Don't despair over Russia's demands — act instead
World.content:
While Russia has dominated the Abu Dhabi talks and shaped the agenda, there is no need to despair, Social Democratic Party (SDE) prime ministerial candidate Jonatan Vseviov said.

Nothing in Russia's demands is new or surprising, the answer "no" must continue to be given them, while slogans are no longer enough — Europe needs real deeds and its own decisions, Vseviov went on.

There is absolutely nothing new or surprising in these demands." Russia has been talking about them since the start of the war, or even before it, and they are exactly what Russia has always sought: not just Ukraine, but turning Europe's security on its head," said Vseviov, who recently stepped down as Foreign Ministry Secretary General to run for SDE at the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.

"As firmly as we have said no to all of this so far, as firmly we must keep saying it," Vseviov went on, adding the right actions are needed too. "The trouble is that a 'no' is no longer enough as an empty slogan; real deeds are needed."

Europe, the SDE candidate said, must finally understand that its security and future depend on no one else but itself, even as the U.S. remains significant. "Europe's security and its future do not depend on anyone else, but require our own decisions and our own real steps."

To that end a serious discussion about Europe's security architecture is under way with American participation, Vseviov noted. "I wouldn't want to and cannot speak on behalf of the United States" — adding that media reports show how the talks have been proceeding under Russia's tactical lead, with the range of topics on the table lining up exactly what Russia has always desired them to be, and the Russians dominating both the framing and the order of topics.

Ultimately, none of this was any reason to throw in the towel, but rather a teachable moment on how to proceed.

"There is no need to draw any final and fundamental depressing conclusions from this alone, but it is worth drawing the lesson that if we want the future to be ours, then it is worth taking action ourselves," Vseviov concluded.

German outlet Bild reported on Friday that Russia's proposals for a new European security order, which it wants discussed alongside a Ukraine peace agreement, include demands directly concerning the Baltic states, Finland and Moldova in addition to questions of Ukraine's status.

Reform MP Marko Mihkelson, chair of the Riigikogu foreign affairs committee, called the Abu Dhabi meeting a "diplomatic special operation" aimed at imposing Russia's terms, noting that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said outright Russia has no interest in a ceasefire because it does not want to give Europe time to regroup. Diplomat Jüri Luik said European representatives were present in Abu Dhabi but not allowed into the main meeting room, meeting separately instead, and argued it is in the EU's interest to find a way for Europe to take a seat at the table while keeping member states informed and seeking their approval for any commitments. On the military side, Colonel Aron Kalmus of the Estonian Defense Forces said the only concrete outcome of the talks so far is a prisoner exchange, with the number exceeding 1,000 on each side for the first time.

World.title: Two Estonian journalists ran the New York City Marathon on two continents
World.content:
Thousands of miles apart, two Estonian journalists ran the New York City Marathon together — one through all five boroughs, the other on a 42.2-kilometer route around Tallinn.

The New York City Marathon is one of the world's biggest mass-participation races, drawing so many professional and amateur runners from around the globe that entry is largely determined by a lottery.

For many runners, simply making it to the starting line of one of the "World Majors" is a milestone; crossing the finish line is a dream come true.

For 32-year-old investigative journalist Märt Belkin, running was once anything but. A longtime reporter on politics and business for some of Estonia's largest newspapers, he had spent much of his life feeling that sports simply weren't for him.

"I was a bit of a bookworm as a kid, and a chubby boy, as they say," Belkin said. Even when he wanted to take part in gym class, he couldn't imagine himself being any good at sports.

Belkin's gym teachers generally let him off the hook, giving him a passing grade and telling him not to worry about participating.

"I never thought I would ever actually enjoy sports," he acknowledged.

Hit the ground running

In February 2025, Belkin and his Eesti Ekspress colleagues Holger Roonemaa and Oliver Kund won the Bonnier Prize, one of Estonia's most prestigious journalism awards, for a series of articles on a fraud case involving former minister Kalle Laanet.

But this career high point was followed by a difficult period in Belkin's professional and personal life, culminating in the loss of his job and mental health struggles.

"I realized that, in addition to ADHD, which I've known about for several years, I was probably also dealing with fairly severe depression," he said.

Belkin started taking antidepressants in May. The initial adjustment was rough, but then one morning he woke up with an unexpected urge: he wanted to go for a run.

Running quickly became a new hobby for Belkin, also serving as a form of meditation and a way to cope with everyday worries. As he lost weight, his runs grew longer — perhaps even a little too quickly.

"It started out reasonably, but then got out of hand," he admitted. He ran nearly 200 kilometers in June, more than 300 in July and over 600 in August.

Märt Belkin running the New York City Marathon remotely in Tallinn. Source: Pealtnägija/ERR

After signing up for a 10K race in Tallinn early this summer, Belkin ended up running both the 10K and half-marathon at the event this fall, with only a couple of hours between them.

The burst of enthusiasm eventually led to an overuse injury, which still affects his gait. But even that didn't put him off taking on an even bigger challenge: the New York City Marathon.

American highlights in Tallinn

With little hope of snagging a lottery spot in New York, Belkin found a workaround through the event's official virtual race, which allows participants to complete the same distance on their own route within a designated week and log their results in an app. Runners can even register to receive a medal.

While the actual marathon course winds through all five New York City boroughs, Belkin mapped out his own 42.2-kilometer route around Tallinn. He chose a landmark for each kilometer along the way, many with some connection to the U.S. or to prominent Americans who have visited Estonia.

Among the stops were the striking monument by the water on Pirita tee honoring American parachutist, balloonist and inventor Charles Leroux, who died during a balloon jump over the water in 1896, and Kalev Sports Hall, where American saxophonist Charles Lloyd and his quartet performed in 1967, causing a stir in the Soviet Union.

"They initially couldn't even get permission from the Soviet Union's Ministry of Culture, but they performed here in the end, on the very last day," Belkin explained, adding that the symbolic "bridge" between East and West made headlines around the world.

Another stop was Gloria Restaurant in Tallinn's Old Town, where Hillary Clinton and John McCain reportedly held an informal dinner in 2004.

According to the story Belkin recounted, the two visiting American senators had a vodka-drinking contest at the restaurant. Clinton, who allegedly suggested the challenge, won after four shots, drinking McCain under the table.

'A party on every corner'

Meanwhile, on the morning of November 1, fellow Estonian journalist Kristjan Pihl headed to Staten Island, where tens of thousands of runners were preparing for the official race near the start of the course.

"There are people here wrapped in blankets, eating the last of the breakfasts they'd packed along from home and waiting for the signal to head to their starting corral," he said as he joined them.

Kristjan Pihl crossing the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from Staten Island to Brooklyn at the start of the New York City Marathon. November 1, 2026. Source: Pealtnägija/ERR

As the race began, runners crossed the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge into Brooklyn, kicking off a course that weaves its way through all five New York City boroughs: Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan.

The crowds and the energy never let up along the 26.2-mile route.

"There are so many people everywhere," Pihl said as he ran. "There's a party on every corner, DJs are playing, people are dancing. And kids and old people alike — everyone's out cheering on their own."

Personal achievements

Back in Tallinn, Belkin's route took him through the city center and Kalamaja before heading toward Stroomi Beach, which he joked is Estonia's answer to Brooklyn's famous Brighton Beach.

He felt good at first, but at some point his old injury began to hurt, and the mental strain of the long distance — decidedly quieter and more solitary than Pihl's in New York — started to set in.

"Everything is starting to get on my nerves a little," he said. His carefully curated marathon playlist wasn't working, and neither were the audiobooks he'd tried. Eventually he'd turned to making up anagrams in his head.

"I'm trying to come up with ways to entertain myself," he explained.

In New York, Pihl reached the finish line in Central Park with a time of 3:59:58, setting a new personal best.

"Now it's over with, and I can be proud of myself," he said. "I think this is one of the biggest athletic achievements of my life — and will stay that way for some time."

In the Estonian capital, Belkin crossed his own finish line in an almost deserted Kadriorg Park shortly before midnight, with a time of seven hours and 58 minutes.

"I can't believe it," he said as he slowed to a stop. "I'm still not quite sure how to feel."

Belkin admitted the final 1.5 kilometers had been unexpectedly brutal. "All these fears and doubts just kept welling up," he said. "All I could do was just keep running, keep running," he added.

The experience, he added, was unreal. "But honestly, I'm actually really glad I did it."

World.title: Saaremaa residents could lose beachfront property development exemptions
World.content:
Saaremaa Municipality has spent years developing a comprehensive plan for the island but fears some previously approved reductions to coastal construction restrictions may not carry over.

Most of the former municipalities in Saare County had previously negotiated exceptions allowing construction in certain coastal areas closer to the shoreline than the 200 meters generally required on islands. Saaremaa has more than 110 such areas, covering nearly 1,000 hectares.

The Environmental Board now says these existing exemptions from coastal construction restrictions may not be carried over into Saaremaa's new comprehensive plan.

"Under the Planning Act, when a new comprehensive plan is adopted, the previous one becomes invalid and the reductions to construction exclusion zones approved under it no longer apply. The municipality must then review whether those reductions are justified and resubmit the applications," said Kaili Viilma, head of the Environmental Board's nature use department.

"If highly valuable species or habitats have emerged in these areas or the coastline has changed, the Environmental Board may determine that the previous justification is no longer valid and that granting building rights at the expense of these natural habitats is no longer warranted," Viilma added.

The municipality has found itself in a difficult position and wants to defend its residents' interests.

"People either historically owned or purchased properties where the construction exclusion zone had been reduced by 100 meters. How can we now tell them that the 100-meter limit no longer applies and that the new plan will restore it to 200 meters? That hardly seems fair. We will still apply to the Environmental Board for these exemptions. And if the board rejects them for some reason, we believe the Environmental Board should bear responsibility," said Saaremaa Deputy Mayor Priit Riim.

The Environmental Board confirmed that all reductions to construction exclusion zones approved under existing detailed plans must also be reviewed. However, the board emphasized an important distinction: If construction has already begun within a reduced exclusion zone, the restrictions will not be reinstated.

"If implementation of a plan has already begun, we will take that into account when making our decision. In practice, the construction exclusion zone will remain as originally planned," Viilma said.

The municipality wants all existing exemptions to remain in effect and intends to seek their inclusion in the comprehensive plan.

"At least as I see it, no one has the right to take that away. That would amount to interfering with people's property rights," Deputy Mayor Riim said.
