NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-metre) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometres) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but also Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

World.title: Maritime security in focus at India-Belgium naval talks
World.content:
Commander of the Belgian Navy, Rear Admiral Tanguy Botman, held talks with Indian Navy Chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan on a range of issues, including maritime security, operational engagements, and collaboration in naval technology, officials said on Saturday (November 15, 2026).

The bilateral talk was aimed at strengthening maritime cooperation and further deepening navy-to-navy engagements between the two countries.

On arrival, he paid homage to fallen soldiers by laying a wreath at the National War Memorial. Thereafter, he was accorded a ceremonial guard of honour at the South Block lawns.

He also interacted with other senior officials to explore avenues for enhancing bilateral cooperation. India and Belgium share longstanding maritime linkages.

The visit marks an important milestone in bilateral navy-to-navy relations and is expected to provide impetus to maritime cooperation through strengthening existing engagements and exploration of new avenues for collaboration, the official said.

World.title: In Jharkhand, even jails are not safe: Babulal Marandi
World.content:
The Leader of the Opposition in the Jharkhand Legislative Assembly Babulal Marandi on Saturday (November 14, 2026), cornered the State Government over a series of criminal incidents.

He cited the incidents of including the sexual assault of a youth in Hotwar Jail, the alleged rape of a minor girl by a Congress MLA from Simdega, and the alleged rape of a woman who had gone to the Gamharia police station seeking justice.

Fifteen police officers were suspended in connection with the alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman on the premises of the Gamharia police station in Jharkhand, Saraikela-Kharsawan district, on November 1, 2026.

Launching a sharp attack on Sorens’ government, Mr. Marandi said law and order in Jharkhand has collapsed and it raises serious questions on the functioning of the government.

Addressing a press conference at the state Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) office in Ranchi, Mr. Marandi said that such incidents are continuously coming to light, and they are deeply disturbing.

“Today, in Jharkhand, neither jails nor police stations nor the residences of legislators are safe. What has happened to Jharkhand? How have conditions in the state deteriorated to such an extent that ordinary citizens no longer feel safe anywhere?” Mr. Marandi said.

‘Prisoners are not safe even in jail’

Expressing concern over the incident at Hotwar Jail, Mr. Marandi asserted that while a jail is considered the most secure place, even there, prisoners are not safe.

A man has recently filed a police complaint against 19 people, including Birsa Munda Central Jail officials, alleging severe abuse of his 20-year-old son inside the jail.

The father had accused jail inmates and staff of sexual assault of his son and forced him to consume narcotics while he stayed there as an undertrial prisoner.

“A 20-year-old youth was allegedly subjected to gang sexual assault. This incident is truly chilling. When the victim filed a written complaint, it was torn, and he was not even provided with proper medical treatment,” Mr. Marandi said.

He added that he had previously written to the government regarding incidents involving women at Hotwar Jail as well. Mr. Marandi further mentioned that even the court took cognisance of the matter, but instead of taking action and ensuring accountability, the government attempted to cover it up.

Senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader demanded the immediate removal of all responsible jail officials and the transfer of the accused inmates to another prison.

Reacting to the allegations against a Congress MLA, Bhushan Bara from Simdega, Mr. Marandi said that since the case involves an MLA from the Congress party, which is part of the ruling coalition, the government is under pressure.

Mr. Marandi mentioned that he had met with the victim, who shared her ordeal with him. He alleged that the MLA’s wife and sister also physically assaulted the girl. Mr. Marandi demanded an impartial investigation and strict action against those found guilty.

Hours after an FIR was registered against Mr. Bara on the charge of raping his minor domestic help, police said on Saturday (November 14, 2026) that they booked two persons for allegedly abducting and coercing the girl into making a “false” statement against the legislator.

427 deaths in police custody

Raising the issue of deaths occurring in police and judicial custody, Mr. Marandi said that, according to a report submitted by the state government to the Jharkhand High Court, 427 individuals died in police or judicial custody by 2026.

“Notably, 262 of these cases were not subjected to a judicial inquiry; instead, they were investigated by an executive magistrate. On May 14, 2026, the High Court had expressed deep displeasure and had directed that 262 cases be investigated afresh within six months,” Mr. Marandi said.

He added that despite the expiry of the deadline, no clear information regarding the progress of these investigations has emerged.

World.title: Villagers in 25 districts cast votes for panchayat elections’ final phase in Rajasthan
World.content:
Villagers in 25 districts of Rajasthan cast their votes for the fourth and final phase of polling on Saturday to elect the Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti members at a total of 2,524 seats. An estimated 72% turnout of voters at 11,905 polling stations was recorded by the end of the day.

The polling for first, second and third phases of Panchayati Raj elections was held on October 22, October 28 and November 3, respectively. Counting of votes for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti elections across all four phases will be held on November 20, followed by elections for Zila Pramukhs and Panchayat Samiti Pradhans.

There were delays in polling at several places due to glitches in electronic voting machines (EVMs), while the voters at some villages in Baran and Jaisalmer districts boycotted the polling to press for their demands.

The villagers at Mundakya and Mundki in Baran boycotted the voting in protest against an irrigation project adversely affecting their lands. They have been demanding fair compensation for land acquisition for the project. The villagers at Bhojraj Ki Dhani in Jaisalmer did not cast their votes in protest against alleged anomalies in the reservation for Other Backward Classes.

Police took two persons into custody at a polling station in Sikar district’s Hapas village when they created a commotion while insisting on carrying their mobile phones inside the booth. The situation escalated when they began arguing with the polling officials and the policemen, leading to their detention on charges of disturbing peace.

The highest polling at 77% was reported at Baseri in Dholpur district. A total of 8,843 candidates are contesting 2,524 seats in the fourth phase, including 382 Zila Parishad wards and 2,142 Panchayat Samiti wards. There are 1,322 contestants for Zila Parishad seats and 7,521 for Panchayat Samiti wards.

Bharatiya Janata Party leader and former Minister Rajendra Rathore’s son Parakram Singh and daughter-in-law, Kanika, are among the prominent candidates contesting for Zila Parishad seats from Churu district.

The final phase of polling covered Balotra, Baran, Banswara, Beawar, Bharatpur, Bikaner, Bundi, Chittorgarh, Churu, Deeg, Didwana-Kuchaman, Dholpur, Hanumangarh, Jalore, Jaipur, Jhunjhunu, Jaisalmer, Karauli, Khairthal-Tijara, Pratapgarh, Sawai Madhopur, Salumber, Sikar, Sriganganagar and Tonk districts.

World.title: Major among 4 troops martyred, 24 terrorists killed during operations in KP and Balochistan: ISPR
World.content:
Four troops, including a major, were martyred while 24 terrorists were killed in multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s North Waziristan, the military’s media wing said on Saturday.

In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said that since Nov 13, armed forces have been conducting multiple IBOs “around Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki, including area domination and patrolling of the Quetta-Taftan National Highway (N-40) to keep it secure for local traffic and sustain operations”.

On the night of Nov 13/14 in Kolpur, security forces “successfully neutralised eight Indian-sponsored terrorists of Fitna al Hindustan (FAH), including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition”, ISPR said.

The state has designated Balochistan-based terrorist groups as Fitna al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.

It added that on Nov 14, FAH terrorists “targeted military vehicles on patrol with armed quadcopters”, resulting in the martyrdom of Major Omer Minhas Nasir, resident of Chakwal district, and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan from Kotli Sattian.

“This cowardly act has not shaken the resolve of the security forces. The tempo of operations will be maintained and IBOs will continue with the same vigour to secure the local population and eliminate the menace of terrorism,” ISPR affirmed.

It added that clearance operations in these areas will continue “until the threat is completely neutralised”.

This photo, shared by ISPR on Nov 14, shows ammunition and equipment recovered from terrorists in Balochistan.

It further said: “Backed by India and other hostile intelligence agencies, FAH is actively trying to use drones and other technical means, including IEDs (improvised explosive devices), to target innocent civilians and security forces, so as to undermine the efforts of the government and security forces to maintain peace and normalcy in the area.”

Accusing India of providing terrorists full financial support and supplying it with the “latest gadgetry”, the ISPR asserted, “The security forces are fully alive to this evolving threat and will deny the terrorists any space, whatever means they employ.”

ISPR affirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign under vision ‘ Azm-i- Istehkam ’, as approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan , will continue at full pace”.

The military’s media wing warned that security forces and law enforcement agencies “will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”.

In an earlier statement, ISPR said two soldiers were martyred and 16 terrorists were killed as security forces continued a series of IBOs in North Waziristan.

According to the military’s media wing, multiple khwarij locations were engaged in the general areas of Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas in North Waziristan.

“Following fierce fire exchanges, in last twelve hours, 12 khwarij, including two Afghan nationals belonging to Indian-sponsored Fitna al Khwarij were sent to hell in Ali Khel, while two khwarij each were neutralised in Mir Ali and Datta Khel, thereby causing a significant blow to the khwarijs’ network operating in the area,” ISPR said.

Fitna al Khawarij is a term used by the state for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

ISPR said that during the operations, 43-year-old Havildar Asmat Ali and 32-year-old Naik Aftab Ali embraced martyrdom.

“Weapons and ammunition were also recovered from the killed Indian-sponsored khwarij, who remained actively involved in numerous terrorist activities, including the killing of innocent civilians,” it said.

The statement said that sanitisation operations would continue to eliminate “remaining holed-up khwarij from these areas”, adding that the counterterrorism campaign would continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored terrorism from the country.

‘Step forward in war against terrorism’

President Asif Ali Zardari, in separate statements, paid tribute to the security forces for their successful operations and expressed condolences over the martyrdom of the troops.

He expressed his condolences to the bereaved families of the martyrs, terming the sacrifices by officers and soldiers a “source of pride for the entire nation”.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also appreciated the professional competence, bravery and prompt action of the security forces in the operations, state-run APP reported.

He prayed for the martyrs’ ranks and for patience for their families.

“The enemy is making nefarious attempts to sabotage regional peace by targeting innocent civilians and security personnel. However, our armed forces are fully capable of thwarting every nefarious design of the enemy,” he was quoted as saying.

The premier affirmed that operations “against externally sponsored terrorism will continue with full force until its complete elimination”.

“The supreme sacrifices of our brave soldiers further strengthen our national resolve to completely eradicate terrorism,” he said in an earlier statement.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said he was deeply saddened by the martyrdom of “brave military personnel in a drone attack on a military convoy in Kirdgap, Mastung”.

Strongly condemning the “cowardly attack”, Dar affirmed that the nation “stands united with our armed forces and resolute in its determination to eliminate terrorism”.

In his statement, Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti termed the killing of eight terrorists a “significant step forward in the war against terrorism”.

In a post on X, he declared that “every attempt to spread unrest in Balochistan and block the path to development will be thwarted”.

Paying tribute to the martyred major and havildar, CM Bugti wrote, “The state is committed to completely eradicating terrorism and protecting the lives and property of the people. There will be no compromise on peace and stability in Balochistan.”

Rise in terrorism

The operations come a day after ISPR said 74 terrorists were killed in IBOs in KP and Balochistan.

On Friday, it said 43 terrorists were killed during operations conducted over 48 hours in KP, including 35 in North Waziristan’s Mir Ali and eight in Orakzai district. Another 31 terrorists were killed in Balochistan during an operation launched on Nov 3.

Pakistan has seen a surge in terrorism, especially in KP and Balochistan, since the banned TTP ended its ceasefire deal with the government in November 2022, vowing to increase attacks.

According to Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , the country’s security environment continued to show considerable volatility from Oct 30 to Nov 5, 2026, with renewed terrorist activity in parts of KP and the former tribal districts, alongside intensified counterterrorism operations and changing patterns of militant violence.

While attacks rose from 8 to 20 in former tribal districts, Balochistan presented a different pattern; it recorded 11 attacks, down from 15 the previous week, although fatalities increased from five to seven.

The weekly increase came against the backdrop of a substantial month-on-month reduction in terrorist violence recorded during October.

Earlier this month, a soldier was martyred and 17 terrorists were killed in two IBOs conducted in Balochistan’s Kachhi and Kharan districts on Nov 1, ISPR said.

Correction: An earlier version of this story said 14 terrorists were killed in North Waziristan. The error is regretted.

World.title: India stun Pakistan by one wicket in last-ball U-19 Asia Cup final thriller
World.content:
Mohit Ulva and Chigurupati Venkata held their nerve to guide India to a dramatic one-wicket victory over Pakistan in the ACC Men’s U-19 Asia Cup final, chasing down a target of 338 on the final ball at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Muscat on Saturday.

India were staring at defeat at 252 for eight in the 42nd over before Ulva and Manal Chauhan revived their hopes with a 57-run partnership for the ninth wicket.

Chauhan struck three fours and three sixes in his 32-ball 47 before falling at 309 in the 48th over, leaving India needing 29 from the final 16 deliveries.

Ulva and Venkata then added an unbeaten 30 runs for the last wicket to take India home. With eight runs required in the final over, Ulva, who finished unbeaten on 49 off 26 balls, including five fours and three sixes, struck the winning boundary off Ahmed Hussain’s final delivery. Venkata remained not out on 11 off eight balls as India finished at 339 for nine in 50 overs.

Captain Lakshya Raichandani had earlier top-scored with 80 off 101 balls, while Aaryavir Sehwag contributed 58 from 61 deliveries.

The pair provided India with a strong start, putting on 95 for the opening wicket before Sehwag was dismissed in the 18th over.

Pakistan, however, kept striking at regular intervals to regain control. Raichandani departed at 217 in the 37th over, and India lost their eighth wicket just one run later, with the scoreboard reading 252.

Rizwanullah was Pakistan’s most successful bowler with three for 53 in his 10 overs, while Niqab Shafiq claimed two for 57.

The defeat denied defending champions Pakistan a successful title defence after they had entered the final unbeaten, winning all three group matches, including an earlier victory over India, before overcoming Bangladesh in the semi-final.

Earlier, Pakistan posted 337 for nine after opting to bat, with Usman Khan scoring a century and Abdul Qadir and captain Farhan Yousaf making valuable half-centuries.

Usman and Hayam Khan provided Pakistan with a steady start, putting on 62 for the opening wicket. Hayam struck four boundaries in his 23-ball 21 before falling in the ninth over.

Usman then combined with Qadir in a commanding 135-run partnership for the second wicket.

Qadir provided the acceleration with an attacking 80 off just 54 balls, hitting three fours and eight sixes before being dismissed on the last ball of the 27th over with Pakistan at 197 for two.

Usman continued to anchor the innings, reaching his second century of the tournament. The left-hander struck 107 off 111 deliveries, including 11 fours and three sixes, before falling in the 37th over with Pakistan at 240 for three.

Farhan maintained the momentum with a 60-ball 63, including four fours and three sixes. He added 59 runs for the fourth wicket with Ahmed Hussain, who contributed 17 off 20 balls.

Pakistan had looked set for a total in excess of 350 after reaching 204 for two at the halfway stage. However, India’s bowlers pulled things back in the closing overs, restricting Pakistan to 337 for nine.

Kavya Paresh Patel led the Indian attack with four for 68 in his 10 overs, while Venkata, who came into the side in place of the injured Ishan Sood, claimed three for 40 from five overs. Arjun Rajput took one wicket for 43.

Ulva was named player of the match for his decisive contribution in the chase, while Sehwag received the player of the tournament award.

World.title: FO says Climate Minister Musadik Malik nominated to represent Pakistan at SCO moot in New Delhi
World.content:
The Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday that Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik had been nominated to represent Pakistan at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi from Nov 20-22.

In a statement, the FO said the gathering would bring representatives from SCO member states to discuss issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding.

“The government of Pakistan remains committed to promoting dialogue among civilisations and fostering people-to-people contacts within the SCO framework in a spirit of mutual respect,” the statement said.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on X: “Pakistan who is chairing the SCO Council of Heads of State (CHS) in 2026-27, will participate in SCO Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi this month.”

According to Indian news outlet ANI, 10 SCO members — including Pakistan — have been invited to participate in the inaugural Civilisational Dialogue. It added that the gathering was proposed by New Delhi.

In a press briefing on Friday, Indian foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that India has invited several SCO member states to take part in the dialogue, adding that New Delhi looks forward to hosting the gathering.

Islamabad has a long history of engagement with the SCO through hosting meetings and chairing bodies within the group. It also holds the permanent chairmanship of an SCO working group on poverty alleviation, which focuses on improving living standards across the region.

In October 2024, Islamabad hosted the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting , which India’s Minister for External Affairs Dr S. Jaishan­kar attended on behalf of his prime minister.

Jaishankar’s trip, months before the May 2025 military conflict between the neighbours escalated tensions, marked the first such visit by an Indian foreign minister in nearly a decade.

Last month, India sent its SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri to Islamabad for a preparatory meeting for the next SCO CHS meeting in August 2027, which Pakistan is set to host.

“This is my first time on Pakistani soil; these SCO-related programmes will continue throughout the year and culminate in the Islamabad summit,” the Indian official had told PTV News.

Pakistan’s chairmanship of SCO CHS marks another step in the country’s growing engagement with the regional organisation, which has expanded its focus from security cooperation to economic development and regional connectivity.

DPM Dar has noted that Pakistan’s membership has evolved from observer status to proactive full membership since 2017, reflecting its commitment to multilateralism and regional cooperation.

Earlier this month, Pakistan also assumed the chairmanship of the SCO Interbank Consortium (SCO-IBC) for 2026-27, the Ministry of Finance said, with HBL Chairman Sultan Ai Allana taking charge for the period.

“The development coincides with Pakistan’s chairmanship of the SCO for the same period, reflecting the country’s role in promoting regional trade, investment, financial connectivity and economic cooperation”, the ministry said.

World.title: Thousands rally in Antalya to demand climate justice as COP31 talks hit midpoint
World.content:
Thousands of protesters on Saturday took to the streets in the Turkish city hosting COP31 to accuse the climate summit of failing those bearing the brunt of environmental destruction.

The show of dissent comes as negotiators approach the crunch final week of global climate talks in Antalya, with nearly 200 nations scrambling to strike a deal by Friday.

The summit is not expected to produce a major breakthrough, frustrating activists demanding tougher curbs on planet-warming fossil fuels and fresh pledges to help poorer countries adapt to climate impacts.

In downtown Antalya, under rainy skies, thousands of protesters dressed in costumes and shouting slogans marched under close police supervision in the largest demonstration since COP31 began on Monday.

“We are suffering the consequences of climate injustice, yet our voices are never heard at the COP,” said Halime Saman from the People’s Climate Summit platform, one of the groups behind the rally.

“Turkiye is the co-chair of COP31 but still has no roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels. New power stations and coal mines are being opened,” she told AFP.

Yasar Gokoglu, a 78-year-old demonstrator, travelled nearly 600 kilometres from Adana in southern Turkiye to denounce what he called “a masquerade sponsored by monopolies”.

Protesters hold bird effigies during a demonstration organised by climate activists on the sidelines of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya on Nov 14, 2026. — AFP

Police estimated that more than 7,000 people attended the protest, which was organised by environmental groups, trade unions and rights organisations, and proceeded without any major incident.

Civil society activists had raised safety concerns ahead of COP31 after Turkiye embarked on a crackdown on the LGBT community in September. Some LGBT protesters waving rainbow flags participated in the march.

Demonstrators were only allowed to join the rally after being searched by police.

‘No quick fix’

Much smaller demonstrations inside the COP31 venue this week, including one attended by Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, have been mounting pressure on political leaders to act faster on the climate crisis.

The negotiations hit the halfway point Saturday, but countries remain far apart on contentious issues including financing adaptation measures in developing nations, defending climate science, and shifting from fossil fuels to clean energy.

Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, who is chairing the formal negotiations, said there had been “really good and positive conversations” but some issues required more time.

Outside the negotiations, Turkiye is urging countries to join a voluntary pledge to raise the share of global final energy demand met by electricity.

The summit, which closes on Nov 20, takes place against a difficult backdrop, with a conflict-driven energy crisis and geopolitical tensions tempering expectations.

“There’s no climate quick fix. No single COP can magic this crisis away, but each must drive progress,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell told reporters on Saturday.

MNA presents five parliamentary recommendations

At the Pakistan Pavilion at COP31, Parliamentary Secretary for Information and Broadcasting Barrister Danyal Chaudhry addressed a high-level dialogue and stressed that the world needs to acknowledge the economic cost of climate inaction, according to a press release.

At the dialogue, titled ‘Adapting Under Austerity: Delivering Paris Commitments in Debt-Stressed, Climate-Vulnerable Economies’, he stated that Pakistan’s core needs to ensure that the pursuit of fiscal sustainability does not compromise Islamabad’s capacity to protect people from severe climate impacts.

“He noted that past policies introduced in the name of fiscal consolidation increased taxation and discouraged climate-resilient development — an approach the Government of Pakistan believes directly undermined its climate objectives,” the press release said.

Chaudhry emphasised that the world must “function as one global village and one global family”. The secretary further noted that addressing the climate crisis requires collective action on a shared planet and there cannot be separate standards for wealthy and developing nations.

He presented five key parliamentary recommendations for climate-vulnerable and debt-stressed nations.

“First, he called for climate-proofing fiscal and taxation policies by mandating climate impact assessments for major financial decisions so they do not drive up the cost of sustainable development,” the statement said.

Second, he stressed the need to safeguard the transition to renewable energy through stable, predictable policies that do not penalise households or businesses investing in clean energy.

Chaudhry also called on governments and lenders to treat adaptation as an investment rather than an expense, stressing that investing in climate-resilient agriculture, water management, early warning systems, and disaster-resistant infrastructure reduces future recovery costs.

Next, he advocated for reforming global debt architecture through debt-for-climate swaps, climate-contingent clauses, concessional financing and extended repayment schedules, so disaster-prone countries are not forced to “sacrifice essential development”.

Chaudhry went on to call for strengthening parliamentary oversight of climate financing by requiring annual reports on climate-related taxes, subsidies, budget allocations and measurable adaptation outcomes, the press release said. He added that national fiscal frameworks must remain fully aligned with Pakistan’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plan.

World.title: 'Check, one two': Technical glitch hits US presser on air travel chaos
World.content:
Trump administration officials were left red-faced on Saturday when their public effort to address the massive tech disruption that grounded thousands of US flights was itself hit with embarrassing technical glitches.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy took the podium and began addressing a much-anticipated and televised press conference a day after a disastrous nationwide ground stop across US airspace — one blamed on ageing technology — when a deep, echoing hum began to emanate from the microphones and speakers.

“Check one two, three four, five six seven?” Duffy said into the mic.

As cameras rolled, he paused, looked around, and stepped away.

“[I] apologise for that,” he said, as technicians scrambled to replace microphones and adjust cables.

Duffy soon resumed, but brittle feedback hit the room seconds later and his demeanour shifted, presumably all-too-aware that the symbolism of an on-camera tech meltdown after such a major flight disruption was not going unnoticed.

“This is not operational? OK,” said Duffy, appearing deeply irritated.

“This is our kind of, uh, day.”

Duffy was speaking to reporters with the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, and, ironically, with the FAA’s chief technology officer Rebecca Guy, who he said was doing a press conference with him for the first time.

Duffy and Bedford repeatedly pointed to ongoing systemic issues with transitioning from ageing air traffic control technology from the 1970s and 1980s to more modern equipment.

As technicians scrambled, US networks carried the awkward pause — lasting an excruciating three minutes — live on the air.

World.title: Abdul Samad’s late strike sends Pakistan into historic SAFF Championship final
World.content:
Abdul Samad Arshad struck a sensational late winner to guide Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final, as Nolberto Solano’s side held off sustained pressure from hosts Bangladesh to secure a dramatic 1-0 semi-final victory at the National Stadium on Saturday.

With Bangladesh dominating possession and looking the more likely side to break the deadlock, Samad produced a moment of individual brilliance in the closing stages to silence the home crowd and make history for Pakistan football.

The Denmark-based forward collected the ball on the right, skilfully shifted it between his feet to create space before unleashing a powerful left-footed drive that beat goalkeeper Mehedi Hasan Srabon with around five minutes of regulation time remaining.

The victory marks another significant milestone in a remarkable year for Pakistan football, with the national side now just one win away from claiming its first regional title.

Bangladesh enjoyed around 62-64 per cent possession and looked to make the most of home advantage, but Pakistan remained disciplined and organised defensively, frustrating the hosts while posing a threat on the counter-attack. Despite having considerably less of the ball, the visitors registered more shots and efforts on target.

Bangladesh, who had topped Group ‘A’ unbeaten with victories over Bhutan and Sri Lanka, pressed for an equaliser in the closing minutes.

Frustrated home supporters even threw a flare onto the pitch, briefly interrupting play, but Pakistan held firm to secure a famous victory.

The result also ends a long history of semi-final disappointment for the Shaheens, who had reached the last four on four previous occasions without managing to progress to the final.

Solano’s men had reached the semi-finals as Group ‘B’ runners-up after opening their campaign with a 3-2 defeat to India, despite a spirited late fightback, before responding with a convincing 3-0 victory over the Maldives.

The arrival of several overseas-based players, including Samad, for the knockout rounds provided a timely boost, with the group-stage fixtures having fallen outside the FIFA international window.

Pakistan will now face arch-rivals and defending champions India in Tuesday’s final after the latter defeated Bhutan 2-1 in the other semi-final.

Solano’s side will be aiming to cap their historic campaign by overcoming India and securing Pakistan’s first-ever SAFF Championship title.

World.title: Musk says Nvidia will lose 'critical' deals without Jensen Huang
World.content:
Elon Musk said on Saturday that chipmaker Nvidia would lose “critical” deals without its now-ousted chief executive officer (CEO) Jensen Huang.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.

In a post on X, Musk said that while Huang drove the supply chain “brilliantly” at Nvidia, many such deals were “a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract”.

“Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

The SpaceX boss went on to praise the former Nvidia CEO: “If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through.

“Sure, we’d put together a purchase order at some point later, but I never for a second thought it wouldn’t happen.”

The billionaire has separately said on X that a petition was underway to reinstate Huang and that he would sign it. It was not immediately clear whether Musk was referring to the internal effort reported by Wired.

Nvidia declined to comment on the Wired report as well as Musk’s post. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.

Pressure had mounted on Huang after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities had been investigating.

Nvidia then said its board was probing whether its then-CEO “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

On Thursday, CNN reported that the US intelligence community was still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing.

The report said there was “disagreement among US officials about the strength of the evidence that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS)” to spy on Jensen Huang.

Insiders and tech titans in the running

Huang’s exit plunges the $4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia’s swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry’s biggest labs.

Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.

Haas’s name has been making the rounds among analysts since Huang’s exit. He spent seven formative years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013.

Nvidia’s finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO.

Nvidia’s board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the CEO role and had not formally engaged any potential candidates.

Some analysts expect the next CEO to break from Huang’s three-decade reign as the hands-on “chief conductor” who personally steered engineering roadmaps, geopolitical negotiations over exports to China and massive investments across the AI ecosystem.

A potential shift toward a more institutional leadership structure would come as Nvidia faces heightened regulatory scrutiny and a growing consensus among US lawmakers to further restrict the company’s chip exports to China.

Analysts view Kress as a steady financial authority, while veteran engineer Ian Buck is seen as a top candidate after leading development of CUDA, the software platform that powers Nvidia’s AI chips.

Apart from Haas, external names discussed by analysts include AMD chief Lisa Su, who has navigated the key China market, and Micron chief Sanjay Mehrotra, whose memory chips power Nvidia servers.

Other candidates cited by industry watchers include Marvell head Matt Murphy and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who oversaw the iPhone maker’s in-house silicon development.

Former Apple chief Tim Cook was floated by US President Donald Trump, as Nvidia’s board evaluates whether to prioritise financial continuity, deep technical expertise, or experience running a global tech heavyweight.

World.title: President Zardari, PM Shehbaz discuss country's political, economic and security situation
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday discussed the country’s political, economic and security situation in detail, the premier’s office said.

PM Shehbaz warmly welcomed the president upon his arrival at the former’s residence in Lahore’s Model Town, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) and the Presidency said in identical statements.

The premier briefed the president on his recent visit to Turkiye, where he participated in the 31st Conference of Parties to highlight Pakistan’s efforts in climate action.

Both leaders exchanged views on “cooperation among allied parties, continuation of consultation and progress on public welfare projects”, the statement said.

It added that the two leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to working together to accelerate economic stability and development in the country.

National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq Khan, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, PM’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, ex-PM Raja Pervez Ashraf, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla and MNA Hamza Shehbaz were also present during the meeting.

President Zardari’s meeting with the premier comes just two days after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi called on the president.

After media reports emerged claiming that Naqvi and the president had discussed the possible formation of new provinces during their meeting in Nawabshah, the President House clarified that “no such discussion” took place.

The Presidency explained that “matters concerning national security and the regional situation” were discussed during the meeting.

The last publicly reported meeting between President Zardari and PM Shehbaz was on Oct 10, where the two discussed the country’s security situation just a day before the federal government imposed emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

In August, the prime minister had called on the president and briefed him on the Makkah defence pact signed days earlier between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
