World.title: [Tambay] Tiis-ganda muna tayo para sa mga bisita ng ASEAN Summit
World.content:
Masusubok ang pinagmamalaki nating Filipino hospitality ngayong linggong ito. Sabi ng Tito feels ng inyong friendly neighborhood tambay “best foot forward” tayo, tiis-ganda muna ika nga, dahil ang daming bigating bisita na mga world leader ngayong ginaganap dito sa atin ang ASEAN Summit.

Dahil sa extra-long holiday na idineklara para mabawasan magkaaberya habang ginaganap ang taunang pulong ng mga pinuno sa Timog-Silangang Asya at iba pang bigating lider, maraming taga-Maynila ang “lumayas” muna para magbakasyon. Mga tulad kong kapos sa badyet o panggastos ang naiwan sa siyudad. Kaya kami ang balagoong humarap sa mga bisita at iparamdam sa kanila ang Pinoy-style ng magiliw na pagtanggap.

Asahan ang trapik sa mga lugar na malapit sa pagdarausan. Isantabi muna ang road rage. Huwag mang-trigger. Kung kukulo ang dugo at feeling maninigaw o magmumura, hingang malalim muna at magbilang kahit hanggang isang daan.

Sa madaling salita, maging mahinahon sa mga aksyon. Magpaka-banayad sa mga kilos, huwag padalos-dalos. Ipakita natin ang tunay na mukha ng Pinoy.

Bukod sa 10 líder ng mga bansang kapwa-kasapi ng Pilipinas sa ASEAN, papasyal din dito sina US President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Brazilian President Lula da Silva, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japan Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Korean President Lee Jae-myung, at United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres.

Narinig ko sa radyo na may nagrali na mga estudyánte. Naalala ko tuloy yung panahong aktibista pa ang tambay na ito. Ganyang ganyan din ang pinagkaka-abalahan ko noong araw. Pero ngayong lolo feels na — kayong mga bata ang bahala diyan. Taas energy lang, pero huwag mananakit. Respeto sa kapwa pa rin ang paiiralin.

* * *

Sa isang banda, nagkaroon ako ng patikim ng Asian engagement noong nakaraang linggo.

Pinalad ang inyong friendly neighborhood tambay na makadalo sa isang conference ng mga journalist mula sa iba’t ibang bansa sa Asya. Ang ika-30 anibersaryo ng Konrad Adenauer Stiftung’s Media Programme Asia (KASMPA) ay ginanap sa Chiang Mai, Thailand. Dating fellow ang tambay na ito ng KASMPA sa Asian Center for Journalism at Ateneo (ACFJ). May 150 na mga journalist sa 18 bansa ang nagtípon sa Thailand mula November 4-8.

Naroon din ang mga kinatawan ng grupong Asia News Network. Noong panahon ko sa Inquirer, nakailang beses din akong naatasang dumalo sa mga pulong ng ANN.

Kasama sa matutunog na paksa sa KASMPA ay hagupit ng tinatawag nating sa Pinas sa Super El Niño.

Kapansín-pansín ang pagkabagábag ng mga diyarista sa India sa El Niño phenomenon. Maraming dumalong peryodísta mula sa India at idagdag mo pa ang mga kalapit bansa nito. Ilang beses kong narinig sa mga usapan ang El Niño. Bilang Pinoy mapapansin mo ang pagbigkas nila dahil hindi nila masabi ang letrang “ñ” kaya ang tawag nila dito ay El Nino.

Tanong ko sa aking sarili: Bakit labis ang pagkabahalà ng Asian superpower na India, na isang rice-exporting nation, sa maaaring salpok ng tinatawag nating Super El Niño? Isa ang India sa mga bansang pinag-aangkatan ng Pilipinas ng bigas.

Habang mainítan ang usapan sa forum sa Thailand, lumipad ang isip ko at bumalik sa Pilipinas. Bukod sa payo na magkanya-kanyang bili ng balde, may iba pa bang ginagawang paghahanda ang gobyerno ng Pinas? Sapát na kaya ang mga plano nila? Ilang timba ba ang kailangan ko sa bahay?

Food security ng Asya ay maaapektuhan. Kung dahil sa El Niño sasadsad ang ani ng palay sa India, apektado din tayo dito sa Pilipinas. Nakasandal tayo sa produksiyon ng bigas ng ibang bansa. At lahat, as in LAHAT, ng bansang nag-aangkat ng bigas ay makadadanas ng parusa ng El Niño. Kasama na diyan ang mga kapwa kasapi natin sa ASEAN na mga rice exporters na Thailand, Vietnam, at Laos. Umaangkat din tayo sa kanila ng bigas.

* * *

Tulad ng inaasahan, napadpad din ang mga napag-usapan sa conference ng mga journalist ng Asya sa sitwasyon sa South China Sea.

Maraming peryodistang Filipino sa conference na iyon, naka lalamang ang bilang ng mga kababayan natin higít sa mga taga-Tsina. At maiintindihan mo yan, dahil ang media program ng KAS ay nakabaon sa prinsipyo ng malayang pamamahayag.

Nakahulma sa isipan ng mga nakapagtapos sa media program ng KAS na tungkulin ng bawat mamamahayag ang magbigay makabuluhang impormasyon na makatutulong sa pagpapasiya ng mga mamamayan.

Iyan ang dahilan kung bakit maraming talakayan sa conference ang umikot sa pakikialam ng kani-kanilang gobyerno sa malayang pamamahayag.

(Maisingit lang: Nandoon din sa Thailand sa sesyon ng mga journalist ang kasapi ng editorial board ng China Daily, ang state media ng Tsina na naglarawan sa isang animation na unggoy ang mga Filipino.)

Bumalik sa alaala ko ang paksa ukol sa Tsina habang nanonood nung Huwebes ng Day 43 ng impeachment trial ni Vice President Sara Duterte. Nagtanong kasi si Senador Robin Padilla: “Bakit po issue yung pagpunta sa China… Kasi po nakailang beses na po ako nakapunta sa China.” Tanong ni Padilla ang prosekusyon.

Sabi nga ni Representative Terry Ridon, wala namang problema sa biyáhe papuntang Tsina. Pero kung talagang nakikinig si Padilla, mapapansin niya ang pag-iwas sumagot ng mga witness. Wala namang mali sa China trip, pero bakit tila pinagtatakpan at ayaw maaalala ng witness?

Nagtataka din ang tambay na ito, bakit tila “destination of choice” ng mga kawaní ng Davao City ang China. May promo ba para sa kanila? Aaminin ng tambay na ito na totoo namang magandang pasyalan ang Tsina.

Saka alam naman nating lahat ang pagkíling ng pamilya Duterte sa Tsina. Nagsimula iyan nung pumihit si dating Pangulong Rodrigo Duterte pabor sa Tsina sa mga isyu nito kontra sa Estados Unidos. Mula noon, kung susundan natin ang mga statement at maging ang pananahimik ni VP Sara sa West Philippine Sea, lumalabas na kontrabída pa ang Pilipinas.

Noong minsan naisulat ko na “close” at bilib na bilib si Sen Robin sa pagiging gentleman ng Chinese ambassador. Ngayon, naintindihan ko na kung bakit. Sabi nga ng senador, nakailang beses na siya nakapunta sa Tsina.

To be fair, nakadalaw na rin si Sen Robin sa Pag-asa Islands sa West Philippine Sea. Pero, baka naman hindi ako nakababasa o nakapapanood, ang pagkampi niya sa mga taga-Philippine Coast Guard na nasasampolan ng katapat nila sa China coast guard at mga barkong para-military.

Di ba dapat, Sen Robin, ang mga bata natin sa Philippine Coast Guard ang bida sa bangayan nila sa Tsina sa West Philippine Sea? Iba po yata ang script na sinusundan ninyo? – Rappler.com

Si Chito de la Vega ay Tambay ng Rappler dalawang beses kada buwan. Kasama rin siya sa mga anchor-host ng programang Balita Kwento Serbisyo ng DZME 1530.

World.title: What are the government’s Super El Niño measures?
World.content:
Several government agencies have begun their preparations for the effects of Super El Niño

A “very strong” Super El Niño is underway, and government agencies and the public should be on the lookout, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) warned.

According to the weather agency, several parts of the country will experience below-normal rainfall and drought starting this November.

Ahead of PAGASA’s announcement, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. directed concerned government agencies to take necessary measures to prepare for the impacts of the weather phenomenon. Task Force El Niño also said the country has allocated P7.7 billion for its El Niño response.

So what measures has the Marcos administration put in place against Super El Niño?

Irrigation, water management

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has established water impounding structures and rainwater harvesting systems to boost water supply and prepare for potential forest and grass fires, which have a higher probability during El Niño.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is also helping with community-based interventions by rehabilitating water sources, such as reservoirs, multipurpose water infrastructure, and water harvesting facilities, through Project LAWA (Local Adaptation to Water Access).

For its part, the Department of Agriculture (DA) is assessing irrigation systems and helping farmers adjust planting schedules based on local weather and water conditions.

The National Irrigation Administration will strengthen and rehabilitate some of its solar-powered pumps. NIA will also deploy mobile solar pumps in drought-prone, water-stressed areas and vulnerable farming communities to provide immediate irrigation support.

It will also remove sand and debris from irrigation canals to improve water flow. The NIA will also utilize groundwater maps from the DENR’s Mines and Geosciences Bureau to identify water sources for solar-powered pump irrigation systems.

The Department of Science and Technology (DOST) also has Project SARAI (Smarter Approaches to Reinvigorate Agriculture as an Industry in the Philippines), which will provide localized crop advisories.

Food security, potable water

The DA will provide high-quality and drought-tolerant seeds, fertilizer, farm mechanization, irrigation support, and water-saving technologies. It has also entered into a rice supply agreement with Vietnam. This allows Vietnam to deliver 1.5 million metric tons of DT8 rice to the Philippines through April 2027 at a fixed price of $450 per metric ton.

The DSWD’s flagship initiative, BINHI (Breaking Insufficiency through Nutritious Harvest for the Impoverished), will promote food production through household and community vegetable gardens and the adoption of appropriate agricultural practices.

Last September 28, DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian also introduced the very first Atmospheric Water Generator system. This technology extracts moisture from humid air and converts it into potable drinking water. It is currently being implemented in Barangay Gilotongan, Cawayan, Masbate, to address the water shortage there.

Gatchalian also introduced the portable water filtration kits to the public at a Malacañang press briefing on October 14. This kit can be attached to any water bucket. He said the Food and Drug Administration has certified the safety of the filtration system, saying that the water it produces meets Philippine drinking water standards for the analyzed parameters.

Energy supply

With electricity demand surging, the Department of Energy (DOE) has standby generator sets and is looking into battery systems, ship-integrated power plants, and diesel power plants as alternatives, especially for the already vulnerable Visayas grid.

The DOE is also expecting over 2,700-megawatt projects across the country to be completed this year. These are solar, wind, and hydroelectric power plants. An additional 4,758 projects are expected to be completed in 2027, boosting power generation.

Health

The Department of Health (DOH) is ramping up its education campaign and preparing for the potential influx of El Niño-related patients in government-run hospitals. It has temporarily assigned hospital personnel from other departments to treat patients with heat-related illnesses, including heat exhaustion, heat stroke, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The DOH also has a surge plan that allows hospitals to deploy additional staff and monitor other heat-triggered illnesses.

Though not yet concrete, the health department plans to have dedicated fast lanes in hospital emergency rooms for patients with heat-related illnesses, and increase emergency room consultations.

Guidelines for class suspension

The Department of Education (DepEd) issued guidelines on October 26 to help schools prepare for the weather phenomenon.

School heads will also account for localized decision-making tools based on daily indoor classroom temperature and humidity readings taken in the morning, noon, and afternoon. The guidelines will be integrated into the four-level framework: Hayo, Hinay, Hinga, Hinto.

Hayo (go ahead) – schools will maintain face-to-face classes if the heat index remains below 27°C

Hinay (be careful) – in-person classes may be shortened or shift to a hybrid, home-based setup if the heat index falls between 27°C and 32°C

Hinga (rest) – physical classes are suspended, and learners will have lighter home-based tasks if the heat index reaches this extreme caution stage between 33°C and 41°C

Hinto (stop) – all physical and home-based activities are suspended if the heat index reaches 42°C and above

However, this must be vetted by the schools division office or the local government unit to avoid the abuse of class suspensions.

Cloud seeding

In the Visayas, cloud seeding has started. This technique enhances the chances of light and moderate rainfall by introducing sodium chloride into cloud moisture. As of October 22, the Philippine Air Force has completed 38 cloud seeding activities. P30 million was also allocated to aid sugar farms, where operations will begin this November.

The DA has also requested an additional P270 million to enhance rainfall and assist in crop production.

Food, cash aid

Through DSWD’s Project LAWA and BINHI, the department will provide temporary employment to low-income families, farmers, fisherfolk, and disaster-affected households. Beneficiaries will receive cash aid while working for the two flagship initiatives in their communities.

The DSWD also said it has family food packs on standby, with measures in place to prevent spoilage.

The DA already has funds intended to assist farmers and fisherfolk. Palace press officer Claire Castro said the Department of Budget Management is coordinating with Malacañang to determine whether additional funding for the government’s El Niño response will be needed. – Rappler.com

World.title: The mountain took her family. Now she is fighting to save the hospital that saved her.
World.content:
MISSION. The present-day Good News Clinic and Hospital in Banaue, Ifugao. Nearly 70 years after its founding, the nonprofit Christian mission hospital remains the municipality’s only hospital, providing essential medical services despite staffing and financial challenges.

At 12, Carol Abayao survived a landslide that killed four members of her family. Twenty-eight years later, she is the only full-time doctor at the mission hospital that first treated her injuries, carrying the weight of keeping medical care within reach of Banaue's mountain communities.

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – On the morning of October 15, 1998, in the mountain town of Banaue, Ifugao, 12-year-old Carol Abayao was asleep when the mountain came crashing into her family’s home.

A landslide triggered by heavy rains buried the house in mud and earth. Her mother, two brothers, and maternal grandmother were killed.

Carol survived.

Another brother, who happened to be outside, escaped the disaster. Carol, trapped inside, has little memory of how long she remained beneath the debris before rescuers found her.

She remembers the mud, the confusion, and the strange sensation of waking from what seemed like a dream.

She was taken to Good News Clinic and Hospital, a small Christian mission hospital in Banaue, where surgeon Dr. Antonio Ligot attended to her injuries. She was later transferred to another facility for further treatment.

Her recovery was long. She needed assistance moving around and spent time in a wheelchair before she could walk again.

But there was something far more difficult than learning to walk.

For some time, Carol believed that the rest of her family might also have survived. The adults caring for her struggled to tell her otherwise.

When the truth finally came, she had to confront a loss no child should have to bear.

She was in her second year of high school. Her teachers allowed her time to recover, and eventually she returned to her studies.

Life went on, although much of the life she had known was gone.

What she could not have imagined then was that the hospital where she had first received treatment would one day be entrusted to her care.

Today, at 41, Dr. Carol Abayao is the medical director of Good News Clinic and Hospital, the only hospital in Banaue.

She is also its only full-time resident physician.

And keeping the hospital running may be the greatest challenge of her medical career.

“It’s hard. It’s hard,” she told Rappler during a lengthy interview.

Her responsibilities extend well beyond treating patients. She must also help keep the institution financially afloat, recruit medical personnel, improve services, and make decisions that affect the lives of people who have few alternatives when serious illness strikes.

“I only have 24 hours in a day,” she said.

Most of those hours, she is also on call.

Dr. Carol Abayao speaks with an elderly patient at Good News Clinic and Hospital. All photos courtesy of Good News Clinic and Hospital

The hospital stands in a municipality celebrated around the world for the Banaue Rice Terraces, where generations of Ifugao farmers have carved astonishing agricultural landscapes into the mountains.

The terraces have drawn visitors for decades. But beyond the postcard views is the less romantic reality of living in a place where geography can turn medical emergencies into dangerous journeys.

Good News has been serving Banaue since 1956, when Dr. James Irvine, an American physician and former military medical officer, established the mission hospital under the Far East Gospel Crusade.

The institution later came under Filipino management and continues to operate as a non-stock, nonprofit Christian hospital.

Its mission combines medical care with spiritual ministry, a commitment reflected in the prayers, Bible readings, and personal support offered by its staff.

For residents needing hospital care, however, its importance is also practical.

Good News handles medical and pediatric cases, normal deliveries, and some emergencies. It provides laboratory, X-ray, and ultrasound services, although complicated cases must be referred elsewhere.

The nearest higher-level hospital, Ifugao General Hospital in Lagawe, is approximately an hour away by road. Patients requiring more advanced treatment may need to travel farther, including to hospitals in Region 2.

In the Cordillera, an hour’s journey is not always an hour. Heavy rains, landslides, and road conditions can complicate travel, particularly when a patient needs urgent care.

An undated archival photograph shows Good News Clinic and Hospital nestled in the mountains of Banaue, Ifugao.

Carol knows this geography intimately. She grew up here, lost her family to it, and eventually chose to return to practice medicine.

But hers was hardly a straight path to becoming a doctor.

After high school, Carol enrolled in veterinary medicine at Benguet State University. She spent three years studying before changing direction and pursuing nursing in Manila, graduating in 2007.

Her childhood experience had influenced that decision, although she had not yet imagined herself becoming a physician.

Like many Filipino nurses of her generation, she struggled to find stable employment. She volunteered in Mayoyao, Ifugao, and later returned to Manila for intensive care training at the Philippine Heart Center.

She considered working abroad. Australia was among her options, and she had begun preparing her application.

Then her father became ill.

Carol returned home to help care for him. When he died in 2012, she found herself grieving once again.

This time, she withdrew to the family farm. She grew vegetables and rice, leaving behind, at least temporarily, her plans for a nursing career.

It was during a visit to Good News that she encountered Ligot again.

The surgeon who had cared for her after the landslide was still serving at the hospital, where he and his wife, Sylvia, had worked since 1988.He encouraged Carol to return to nursing.

She joined Good News in 2013, working at the institution that had been part of her life since childhood.

There, she saw how the shortage of doctors affected patients. The hospital could provide basic care, but its limited resources meant that people sometimes had to travel elsewhere for treatment.

She began considering medicine.

Ligot encouraged her, but there was a problem. She did not have the money.

Medical school required years of tuition, books, living expenses, and other costs. She had already lost both parents, and her siblings had responsibilities of their own.

Still, she decided to try.

In 2015, Carol entered medical school, supported by relatives, friends, and people who believed in what she wanted to accomplish. Some helped with tuition, while others contributed toward everyday expenses.

She remembers assistance coming even from people she barely knew.

Dr. Carol Abayao, born and raised in Banaue, wears traditional Ifugao-inspired attire.

She completed medical school in 2019, finished her internship in 2020, and passed the physician licensure examination in 2021.

Afterward, she entered government service at Conner District Hospital in Apayao. She also attempted neurology residency training at East Avenue Medical Center in Metro Manila, but health difficulties and the demands of training eventually led her to leave the program.

She continued practicing as a general physician.

Through those years, Good News remained part of her life. Whenever possible, she returned to Banaue to serve as a reliever.

Then, as the hospital faced another leadership transition, she was asked to come back permanently.

The decision was difficult.

A government position offered greater employment security. Good News was a small private mission hospital still recovering from financial losses during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Patient visits had fallen sharply in 2020 and 2021 as people feared contracting the virus in medical facilities. The hospital’s revenue suffered, adding to longstanding difficulties in maintaining staff and equipment.

Leaving government service meant exchanging relative stability for a hospital that needed more resources than it could comfortably afford.

Yet Carol could not entirely separate the institution’s future from her own history.

The people at Good News had cared for her when she was a child. Ligot had encouraged her to become a doctor. And the community she had grown up in still needed physicians willing to stay.

In January 2025, she formally assumed the position of medical director.

She now carries two responsibilities that would ordinarily demand separate people: treating patients and helping manage the hospital.

Dr. Carol Abayao, medical director of Good News Clinic and Hospital in Banaue, Ifugao, examines a patient.

Three other doctors serve as relievers when their schedules permit, but they work elsewhere and are not permanently stationed at Good News.

An interim hospital administrator assists with management. Even so, much of the clinical responsibility remains with Carol.

Her ambitions for the hospital are substantial, though hardly extravagant.

She wants more doctors, better equipment, additional diagnostic services, and the ability to treat more patients without sending them to facilities hours away.

She says the Department of Health has approved an increase in bed capacity from 18 to 25 just this year. More beds, however, mean little without the personnel to attend to the patients who occupy them.

“We need more doctors,” Carol said.

Finding them is another matter.

Rural hospitals struggle to attract physicians who may have better-paying opportunities, more advanced equipment, and easier access to professional development elsewhere.

Good News must also maintain affordable charges while meeting operating expenses.

As a nonprofit mission hospital, it relies on income from medical services, PhilHealth reimbursements, donations, and support from churches and other benefactors.

Carol wants to keep fees manageable for patients, many of whom have limited financial resources.

But affordability has a cost, too. Salaries must be paid, supplies replenished, and equipment maintained.

Faith sustains the hospital’s mission, but faith alone cannot pay every bill.

Carol makes no attempt to romanticize the workload.

She admits that exhaustion sometimes catches up with her. When it does, she withdraws for a while, finding time to pray, reflect, and seek advice from people she trusts.

She has learned that caring for others requires recognizing her own limits.

Despite the difficulties, she sees reasons to keep going.

The present-day Good News Clinic and Hospital in Banaue, Ifugao.

Patient numbers have increased since she returned, she said. She is careful not to assume that the increase means more people are becoming ill.

Perhaps residents are regaining confidence in the hospital. Perhaps improvements in its services have encouraged more people to seek care.

She does not claim to know.

What she does know is that the hospital has begun expanding its services, and she wants that progress to continue.

“I am hopeful,” she said.

Her faith remains central to how she understands the unexpected course of her life. Looking back, she sees a series of detours that eventually brought her to the place where she now serves.

There was veterinary medicine, nursing, the possibility of working overseas, the years of grief, and the time spent farming. Then medical school, government service, and the decision to return to Banaue.

She believes God led her here.

But she also knows that the future of Good News cannot rest on one physician’s determination.

The hospital needs doctors willing to serve, supporters prepared to help sustain its operations, and resources that would allow more patients to receive treatment without leaving their community.

For almost seven decades, it has provided medical care in a place where distance can determine how quickly help arrives.

Carol wants to make sure it continues.

On October 15, 1998, rescuers pulled a young girl from the wreckage of her family home and brought her to Good News Clinic and Hospital.

Twenty-eight years later, she is the doctor responsible for caring for people who come through its doors.

The hospital was there when she needed it.

Now she is doing everything she can to make sure it will be there when someone else does. – Rappler.com

World.title: What to expect as 49th ASEAN Summit begins in Manila
World.content:
LIVE

The South China Sea Code of Conduct, Myanmar's political standing in ASEAN, and the Middle East crisis' impact on oil and food security will likely top the agenda

MANILA, Philippines – Leaders from Southeast Asia and beyond are gathering in the Philippines for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17, with United States President Donald Trump, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, and other world leaders expected to attend.

Among the biggest issues on the agenda are continued negotiations over a South China Sea Code of Conduct, Myanmar’s unresolved political crisis, and how ASEAN can mitigate the impact of the Middle East conflict on the region’s oil and food supplies.

Leaders will also discuss closer economic cooperation, including the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, as the Philippines prepares to hand over the chairmanship to Singapore. – Rappler.com

World.title: Carmelle bags first-ever Eurovision Asia crown
World.content:
FILIPINA WINNER. Carmelle is the first-ever winner of Eurovision Asia.

With her high-energy performance of 'Sobra-Sobra,' Filipina singer Carmelle Collado tops the jury and fan votes to win the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia

MANILA, Philippines – Carmelle Collado of the Philippines emerged as the first-ever winner of Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

The Bicolana singer received 211 points — topping both the jury and fan votes — to win over artists from 10 other countries on Saturday, November 14, in Bangkok Thailand.

Carmelle performed the high-energy, dance-pop track “Sobra-Sobra,” which was composed by Nica del Rosario and Mat Olavides.

Play Video

The Filipina teen received a jury vote of 93 points, and then received 118 points from the fan vote to emerge as the overall winner.

Carmelle beat Thailand’s representatives Mang and Daou, who sang “Aroma.” The duo received 170 points to finish in second place.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, performing “EM TIÊN,” rounded out the top three with 164 points.

Carmelle, a 19-year-old Tawag ng Tanghalan singing champion, was chosen to be the Philippines’ representative during the country’s selection night on August 30.

This is the first-ever Asian edition of the Eurovision Song Contest. The annual singing competition was first organized in 1956 by the European Broadcasting Union.

Notably, in 2025, Filipino-Austrian singer JJ won Eurovision with the song “Wasted Love.”

Eleven countries competed in the inaugural Eurovision Asia: Bangladesh, Nepal, Cambodia, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam, South Korea, Laos, Bhutan, and Mongolia. – Rappler.com

World.title: From micro to massive, ASEAN’s entrepreneurs face regulatory hurdles
World.content:
BIG BUSINESS. Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala speaks during a panel at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on November 14, 2026.

‘It's incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,’ former CIMB chairman Nazir Razak says, criticizing ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration

MANILA, Philippines – A food vendor at a weekend bazaar might have little in common with a conglomerate investing across Southeast Asia, yet both can find themselves grappling with regulations that make growing their business harder than it should be.

For Go Negosyo founder Joey Concepcion, governments should give microentrepreneurs some wiggle room, particularly when they are just starting out.

Speaking on the sidelines of the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Saturday, November 14, Concepcion recalled how he began his own entrepreneurial journey.

“When I started as an entrepreneur, I didn’t apply for any permit,” he said, also pointing out that many successful food vendors at bazaars sometimes sell products without certificates of product registration.

Play Video

Concepcion knows a thing or two about building a business. He heads RFM Corporation, which is behind the Selecta ice cream Filipinos love, while his family’s other business, Concepcion Industrial, makes the Condura refrigerators that keep it cold. Through Go Negosyo, he has also spent years helping fledgling entrepreneurs get their businesses off the ground.

“If I were the government, I’d just let it go for now and allow them to continue. And eventually, they will gradually follow the rules,” he said. “It cannot be too strict in the process though.”

Beyond permits, Concepcion said small entrepreneurs also struggle with financing and developing better products. This is where mentorship becomes important, particularly in helping businesses become viable enough to qualify for bank loans.

Larger businesses also have a stake in their success. After all, Concepcion noted, sari-sari stores are important outlets for products sold by major manufacturers.

“Because if they close shop, then our sales obviously will also go down,” he said.

Different barriers for bigger businesses

The difficulty of navigating regulations does not disappear as businesses grow; it only changes. Across ASEAN, even its most successful businessmen still grapple with differing national standards, investment approvals, and employment requirements.

Ayala Corporation chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala said these differences complicate efforts to expand across the region, despite the complementary strengths of Southeast Asian economies.

“There’s still a lot that needs to be done,” he said during a separate panel. “How we would like as a company to be able to move within these different countries in a much easier way, but the standards that we have, the approval standards, the way to get your investment filed, it’s different in each of these countries.”

Play Video

Malaysian banker Nazir Razak, former CIMB Group chairman, had stronger words for ASEAN’s slow progress toward economic integration.

“It’s incredibly frustrating that even the simplest of ideas seem to have a lot of difficulty getting implemented,” he said.

Nazir recalled how CIMB expanded across Southeast Asia in anticipation of the ASEAN Economic Community, launched in 2015 to great fanfare and with the ambition of establishing a single market and production base.

“I felt we were all dressed up with nowhere to go,” he said.

ASEAN has nevertheless continued attracting investment. Foreign direct investment rose 10% to a record $246 billion in 2025, according to the ASEAN Investment Report 2026. Investment originating within the regional bloc also grew 34% to $40 billion, accounting for 16% of total inflows.

Still, Nazir feels that ASEAN has plenty more unlocked economic potential, but its leadership structure could be holding it back. He criticized how much of the authority rests with the chair, which changes every year, rather than the secretary-general, who serves a five-year term. He argued that the arrangement needed reform to help the bloc move faster.

“So you imagine a company where all power is with the chairman, but the chairman changes every year. That would be completely dysfunctional,” he said.

The Philippines is set to hand over ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship to Singapore for 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands of students protest vs Pax Silica, Trump’s arrival in Manila
World.content:
PROTEST. Students of the Polytechnic University in Sta. Mesa, Manila stage a walkout on November 13, 2026, to protest the Pax Silica initiative and the arrival of US President Donald Trump for the 49th ASEAN Summit.

More groups are expected to stage protests across the country in the coming days, coinciding with the ASEAN Summit

MANILA, Philippines – Thousands of students from different parts of the Philippines staged protests on Friday, November 13, against the US-led Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s expected arrival in the country for the ASEAN Summit.

Filipinos have raised concerns about the initiative’s potential environmental impact and the possible displacement of indigenous peoples and farming communities.

In Manila, students from the University of Santo Tomas (UST), Asia’s oldest Catholic university, walked out of their classrooms to join the protest.

“Pax Silica is reported to generate hundreds of thousands of indirect and induced jobs. However, projections are not promises and promises are not guarantees, especially when dealing with a global power like the United States,” the UST Central Student Council Executive Board said.

“It is not enough to ask what development Pax Silica can offer; we must also ask who stands to benefit from it, and more importantly, who will bear its costs,” it added.

At De La Salle University, at least 1,500 students also walked out of their classrooms to protest against the initiative.

STUDENT PROTEST. Students from De La Salle University’s Manila Campus walk out of their classes on November 13, 2026, in protest of Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s visit for the upcoming ASEAN Summit. Photo by Zara Pineda/Rappler

Students from different campuses of the University of the Philippines, Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Miriam College, and Ateneo de Manila University also joined the demonstrations.

RALLY. University of the Philippines Manila students stage a snake rally at the College of Arts and Sciences in accordance with the UP system-wide walkout on November 13, 2026. Photo by Axel Cainglet/Rappler

In Benguet, around 9,000 students from various schools, including UP Baguio, Saint Louis University, and the University of the Cordilleras took to the streets to express their opposition to Pax Silica.

Play Video

Students from Central Luzon State University also staged a protest on Thursday, November 12.

The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.

However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.

Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.

“’Kung ano man ang panawagan ito ay sana hindi dinadaan sa pagprotesta although ito ay kanilang karapatan. Pero sa panahon ngayon mas magandang nagkakaroon ng mas masinsinang paguusapan kung ano man ang concerns ng mga estudyante,” Castro said during a press briefing on Saturday, November 14.

(Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right. In these times, however, it would be better to have more in-depth discussions about whatever concerns the students may have.)

Different groups are also expected to stage protests in different parts of the country in succeeding days, coinciding with the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com

World.title: Taal Volcano records spike in quakes after days of low activity
World.content:
File photo. Time-lapse footage of a minor phreatomagmatic eruption at the Taal Main Crater at 1:45 p.m. on April 10, 2026. The event generated a short 200-meter plume, as captured by the Main Crater (VTMC) and Daang Kastila (VTDK) observation stations on the western and northern rims of the Main Crater, respectively. Alert Level 1 remains in effect over Taal Volcano. Screengrab from Phivolcs’ Facebook page.

LUCENA CITY — Taal Volcano in Batangas recorded a spike in volcanic earthquakes over the past 24 hours, ending several days of relatively low seismic activity, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) reported Sunday, Nov. 15.

In its latest morning bulletin, Phivolcs said the volcano registered 17 volcanic earthquakes during the 24-hour monitoring period.

From Nov. 10 to 14, Taal recorded only single-digit numbers of volcanic earthquakes daily, with a combined total of 27.

Article continues after this 

Data from Phivolcs showed that from Nov. 1 to 15, the volcano logged 198 volcanic earthquakes and one episode of volcanic tremor.

Phivolcs explained that volcanic earthquakes are generated by processes occurring within an active volcano and are classified according to their arrival patterns, amplitudes, and wave periods.

READ: Taal Volcano logs minor phreatic eruption on Tuesday

Volcanic tremors, meanwhile, are continuous, low-frequency seismic signals that may exhibit regular or irregular waveforms.

During the latest observation period, no upwelling of hot volcanic fluids was observed in the main crater lake on Taal Volcano Island, which is situated at the center of Taal Lake.

Article continues after this 

Phivolcs also reported that no volcanic smog, or vog, was detected.

Despite the increase in seismic activity, Taal Volcano remains under Alert Level 1, indicating abnormal conditions and continued volcanic unrest. /mcm

World.title: Police bust P7.8M smuggled cigarettes in Lanao del Sur
World.content:
Police operatives conduct a post operation inventory of confiscated suspected smuggled cigarettes in Barangay Mapantao ,Picong, Lanao del Sur, on Friday night, Nov. 13, 2026. Photo by PRO-BAR

COTABATO CITY—Acting on a tip from concerned citizens, police confiscated P7.8 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes in Picong, Lanao del Sur, on Friday night, Nov. 13, police confirmed Sunday.

Brig. Gen. Christopher Abecia, Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR) regional director, said joint police operatives from the Picong Municipal Police Station and regional and provincial police mobile force units conducted the anti-smuggling operation in Barangay Mapantao, seizing 195 cases of suspected smuggled cigarettes.

Earlier, police received intelligence information about unidentified men loading suspected smuggled cigarettes onto a cargo truck inside a warehouse in Barangay Mapantao.

Article continues after this 

READ: Lanao del Sur police recover P3M smuggled cigarettes on residents’ tip

As police personnel approached the warehouse, several men were seen fleeing in different directions, leaving behind the cigarettes and abandoning their loading activity.

Police found boxes of imported Cannon, San Marino Gold, Fortune, Platinum Seven, Fort, and Commando cigarettes.

Abecia commended the operating personnel for their prompt response, effective coordination, and successful conduct of the intelligence-driven operation.

“I commend our personnel for their vigilance and dedication in carrying out this operation. This accomplishment demonstrates the importance of intelligence-driven policing, timely action, and strong coordination among our operating units,” Abecia said.

Following the operation, Abecia said PRO-BAR would continue to intensify efforts against smuggling and other illegal activities to protect communities and prevent illicit trade in the Bangsamoro region. /mcm

World.title: High-value drug suspect arrested in Marawi; P6.8M shabu seized
World.content:
The suspected drug peddler (seated) with anti-narcotics agents and police officers following a buy-bust operation that led to his arrest in Marawi City on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Photo by PDEA-BAR

COTABATO CITY — A high-value drug suspect was arrested in a buy-bust operation in Marawi City on Saturday, Nov. 14, yielding approximately one kilogram of suspected shabu worth P6.8 million, according to the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency–Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PDEA-BAR).

George Paul Alcovindas, PDEA-BAR regional director, identified the suspect as alias “Ali,” 42, married, and a resident of Barangay Proper, Maguing, Lanao del Sur.

Alcovindas said the seized drugs were concealed inside a green Chinese tea bag labeled “Guanyinwang (AOE).” The suspected shabu (methamphetamine hydrochloride) weighed approximately 1,006 grams and was valued at P6,840,000.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cops arrest 5, seize P6.8-M shabu in Marawi drug bust

He said police and PDEA agents recovered the buy-bust money and seized a mobile phone, a Toyota Hilux, and identification cards from the suspect.

Alcovindas said PDEA Maguindanao del Sur spearheaded the operation, with support from the PDEA Lanao del Sur Provincial Office, Marawi City Police Station, the Philippine Army’s 4th Mechanized Battalion, and the 1403rd Maneuver Company of the Regional Mobile Force Battalion 14-A.

The arrested suspect will face charges for alleged violation of Section 5 (Sale of Dangerous Drugs) of Republic Act No. 9165, or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. /mcm

World.content:
Pagasa weather update

MANILA, Philippines — The easterlies will bring cloudy skies and rain to parts of Mindanao on Sunday, while other parts of the country may experience rainshowers and thunderstorms, according to the state weather bureau.

In its 5 a.m. weather forecast, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the easterlies, or warm winds coming from the Pacific Ocean, would prevail over Mindanao in the coming days.

READ: 9 areas under danger-level heat indices on Sunday – Pagasa

Article continues after this 

“In Mindanao, expect cloudy skies with scattered rainshowers, especially over Surigao del Sur, Agusan del Sur, and Davao Region due to easterlies,” weather specialist Obet Badrina said.

Badrina said a large part of Luzon, including Palawan, would experience fair weather, with chances of rainshowers and thunderstorms.

The Visayas would have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers and thunderstorms. The rest of Mindanao would experience hot and humid weather, with possible localized rainshowers and thunderstorms in the afternoon and evening.

Badrina said no low-pressure area or tropical cyclone was being monitored inside or outside the Philippine area of responsibility. He added that no tropical cyclones were expected in the coming days.

World.title: Palace: Gov’t saves P260M on Asean Summit vehicles
World.content:
VIPRIDES Some of the Lexus luxury vehicles loaned to the government for the top-levelAsean Summitdelegates. —LEXUS PHILIPPINES/FB

The government saved an estimated P260.4 million in transportation costs for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit and Related Summits through vehicles and logistical support provided by three private companies, Malacañang said Saturday.

Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Claire Castro said Hyundai Motor Philippines, Lexus Philippines through Toyota Motor Philippines, and Grab Philippines provided transportation support for the regional gathering.

READ: LIVE UPDATES: Asean Summit 2026 and related meetings – Nov. 14, 2026

Article continues after this 

“We were able to have savings of about P260.4 million,” she said.

According to Castro, Hyundai provided 50 vehicles valued at P146.6 million, while Lexus contributed vehicles valued at P93.8 million.

Drivers, fuel included

Grab, meanwhile, deployed vehicles with drivers and covered fuel and toll expenses, with its contribution valued at P20 million.

“Hyundai and Lexus lent vehicles and also covered their insurance and maintenance),” Castro said.

All loaned vehicles will be returned to the companies after the Philippines’ Asean 2026 hosting period, she added.

Article continues after this 

Lexus Philippines earlier announced it would provide an electrified fleet of LS 500h sedans and LM 350h luxury vans to transport official delegates and dialogue partner representatives across Metro Manila during the summit.

The company, an official mobility partner for the Philippines’ Asean 2026 chairship, said its Manila teams would provide operational support throughout the regional gathering.

Article continues after this 

Toyota Motor Philippines, through Lexus, had also provided transportation support for earlier Asean meetings in Cebu as part of its partnership with the country’s organizing committee.

The Palace official said technical personnel, emergency roadside assistance and towing services would also be available to ensure the safety and reliability of transportation operations.

World.title: Marcos EO sets up national council on AI development
World.content:
Artificial intelligence stock image.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed an executive order setting broad parameters and directions for the government as artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly becomes part of daily life, giving rise to both opportunities and concerns in the business sector, the job market, the education system, the media, and other tech-driven fields.

Signed by the President on Nov. 12, Executive Order No. 131 primarily creates the National AI Council (Naic), an interagency body responsible for coordinating, facilitating and monitoring the implementation of the national Al framework, Palace press officer Claire Castro announced on Saturday.

READ: Marcos signs EO adopting AI governance framework, creating nat’l council

Article continues after this 

“Through this executive order, the President recognizes the importance of AI in improving the lives of Filipinos, not just in advancing technology,” Castro said at a briefing at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) Summit’s International Media Center in Pasay City.

“Its goal is to ensure that AI is implemented responsibly, safely, and ethically, with adequate safeguards to maintain public trust,” she added.

Castro also said the order seeks to ensure that AI development delivers concrete benefits to workers, businesses, communities, and the entire country.

Important elements

“There is a need to establish a mechanism for coordinated action that will accelerate the implementation of the Al Governance Framework and strengthen collaboration, operationalization, and monitoring of efforts among government agencies, together with the private sector, academe, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, to ensure the timely and accountable execution of its key strategies,” the order stated.

EO 131, as published in The Official Gazette, outlines four frameworks of “interconnected elements”:

Article continues after this 

Ethics and principles, which ensures that any AI development and deployment is guided by transparency and “human centricity,” empowering and protecting human beings rather than undermining them.

Standards and assurance, which requires that appropriate technical standards, testing and evaluation and other mechanisms support the responsible, safe, secure, and trustworthy development and use of Al.

Risk-based policy toolkit, which provides that government measures must be “proportionate to the nature, context, and level of risk and may include general and sector-specific guidelines”.

Enabling resources, which mandates the government to strengthen institutions, data research and development, capabilities, infrastructure, and demand generation to support responsible Al development, deployment and use.

The executive order directs the NAIC to review the framework at least once every two years, or earlier “when warranted by significant technological, regulatory, or market developments […].”

Upskilling, reskilling

Since 2024, the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) has been pushing for the National AI Strategy for the Philippines (NAIS-PH) to guide AI’s development and deployment through 2028.

Article continues after this 

The government approved NAIS-PH in May 2025 to serve as the strategic direction for the development and adoption of Al in the country.

In August, Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. noted that, “For years, AI projects across the government were energetic but scattered.”

Solidum had said that at the center of the national framework were five core strategies: infrastructure, workforce, innovation, ethics and policy, and deployment.

He has emphasized the importance of upskilling and reskilling the country’s workforce through expanding AI programs with the help of higher education institutions.

A research brief by the International Labor Organization (ILO) published in February noted that, based on a global index of occupation-based exposure, “more than one-quarter of employment, or 12.7 million [workers], are exposed to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in the Philippines.”

It said that this exposure rate was the highest among member-states of the Asean.

“However, exposure does not equate necessarily to full job replacement but rather the automation of tasks within occupations,” the ILO said. It estimated that only 3.6 percent of jobs fall into the highest GenAI exposure category with “elevated risk of job displacement.”

“Rather than outright automation, the most significant impact of GenAI on the Philippine labor market is likely to be the transformation of jobs, potential gains in productivity and enhanced employment quality,” it said.

Affordable, accessible AI

In a video message delivered earlier at the Asean Business and Investment Summit 2026, Mr. Marcos called on businesses across Southeast Asia to make AI tools more affordable and accessible to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).

He said MSMEs must be equipped with technology to compete in an increasingly technology-driven economy.

READ: LIVE UPDATES: Asean Summit 2026 and related meetings – Nov. 14, 2026

“For MSMEs, we are advancing an approach that brings AI adoption together with training and practical support,” the President said. “Our aim is to help entrepreneurs spend less time on repetitive tasks, make better use of their resources, and reach more customers.”

He said the Philippines was making the responsible use of AI a priority in its development agenda. —LUISA CABATO

World.title: Rizal Memorial Football Stadium to get P1.3-B facelift care of Fifa
World.content:
Rizal Memorial Football Stadium —CONTRIBUTED PHOTOS

For nearly a century, the Rizal Memorial Football Stadium has stood at the heart of Philippine sport, its Art Deco façade bearing witness to the triumphs, heartbreaks, and aspirations of generations of Filipino athletes.

Opened in 1934 and built as the centerpiece of the Rizal Memorial Sports Complex, the stadium is more than concrete, steel, and turf.

It is a living monument to Philippine football history, a venue where the nation’s sporting identity has unfolded before packed grandstands and international audiences.

Article continues after this 

READ: Thousands of LSIs crammed inside Rizal Memorial stadium amid COVID-19 risks

On Sunday, that history is opening a new chapter.

Following the country’s successful hosting of the inaugural Fifa Women’s Futsal World Cup in 2025, International Football Federation (Fifa) president Gianni Infantino will channel nearly US$20 million (roughly P1.275 billion) into the redevelopment of the Rizal Memorial Football Stadium and the construction of three regional football training centers across the country—all at no cost to the Philippine government.

Infantino will sign a landmark agreement on the development grant with Philippine Sports Commission Chairman Patrick Gregorio and Philippine Football Federation President John Anthony Gutierrez on Sunday at the PSC House in Manila.

READ: PBA to host games at Rizal Memorial Coliseum on Saturday

Article continues after this 

“Fifa is successful around the world, and the Philippines was a big part of that because we hosted the first-ever Fifa Women’s Futsal World Cup. And because of that success, this donation from Fifa will help us rebuild the Rizal Memorial Stadium,” Gutierrez told the Inquirer.

“We are able to reap the success of the nation’s hosting of the Fifa Women’s Futsal World Cup,” Gregorio also told the Inquirer.

Article continues after this 

Art Deco meets athleticism

Gianni Infantino

The stadium opened in 1934 for the 10th Far Eastern Championship Games, then Asia’s premier sporting competition and a precursor to the Asian Games.

Designed by renowned architect Juan Arellano, whose masterpieces include other Art Deco structures like the Manila Metropolitan Theater and the Old Legislative Building, the stadium immediately became one of Southeast Asia’s most impressive sporting venues.

Its first football matches featured the leading national teams of the era: China, Japan, Indonesia (then known as the Dutch East Indies) and the Philippines. Historical records show crowds of up to 40,000 spectators attending matches during the 1934 Far Eastern Games, underscoring football’s popularity in prewar Manila.

The venue survived war, reconstruction, and political change. Damaged during the Battle of Manila in 1945, it was rebuilt and restored into the centerpiece of Philippine sports once again.

The stadium hosted football competitions during multiple Southeast Asian Games editions and became the regular home field of the Philippine national men’s and women’s teams. It served as the country’s primary venue for Fifa World Cup qualifiers, AFC Asian Cup qualifiers, AFF Championship matches and major regional club competitions.

‘Azkals’ era

Patrick Gregorio

During the prewar years, Chinese legend Lee Wai Tong, regarded as one of Asia’s greatest footballers, dazzled crowds at Rizal Memorial while representing China in the Far Eastern Championship Games. Japanese star Taizo Kawamoto, one of Japan’s football pioneers, also played on the stadium’s turf in 1934.

In later decades, the stadium welcomed many of Asia’s strongest national teams, including Japan, South Korea, China, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and regional club powers competing in AFC tournaments.

For Filipino fans, however, the most beloved figures to grace the venue were the heroes of the “Azkals” era.

Players such as Phil Younghusband, the country’s all-time leading scorer, his brother James Younghusband, Neil Etheridge, Chieffy Caligdong, Stephan Schrock, Misagh Bahadoran and Angel Guirado helped transform Rizal Memorial into a fortress during the Philippine football renaissance of the 2010s.

Enter Filipinas

The women’s national team also created memorable moments here, with generations of Filipinas using the historic ground as a platform for the country’s rise in women’s football.

While various improvements have taken place over the years, the stadium’s most significant modernization before the new Fifa-funded project came in preparation for the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.

The venue received extensive upgrades, including improvements to the playing surface, grandstand facilities, athlete areas, lighting and spectator amenities to bring it closer to international standards.

Those renovations allowed the stadium to continue serving as the national football team’s primary home while preserving its historic architectural character.

Yet football leaders knew more was needed if the Philippines hoped to compete with the region’s elite football nations.

That opportunity arrived after the Philippines successfully hosted the first Fifa Women’s Futsal World Cup in 2025.

Recognizing the country’s contribution to Fifa’s growth and the tournament’s success, Infantino approved the mammoth funding that will dramatically reshape Philippine football infrastructure.

Under the agreement signed by Fifa, the PSC and the PFF, Rizal Memorial Football Stadium will undergo its most ambitious redevelopment since its opening in 1934.

“We will now have a beautiful football stadium that we can really be proud of with no cost to the government and can host big international competitions,” Gregorio said.

When completed, the full-scale upgrade of the venue will feature a 25,000-seat state-of-the-art football facilities, modern spectator amenities, a permanent home for the Philippine Football Federation and infrastructure capable of hosting major international competitions.

The project forms part of a broader master plan for the Rizal Memorial Sports Complex, including improved pedestrian access, a jog path and integrated public spaces.

John Anthony Gutierrez

For the grassroots

The funding package also includes three regional football training centers in Luzon, Bacolod City, and Cagayan de Oro. Each center will feature three full-sized pitches and athlete dormitories, giving young players access to world-class facilities without needing to relocate to Metro Manila.

For Gutierrez, the investment ensures that the legacy of the Fifa Women’s Futsal World Cup extends well beyond the tournament itself.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.
