During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Kazakhstan-China rail freight transportation rises 8% in January-October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. Rail freight transportation between Kazakhstan and China totalled 31.8 million tonnes in January-October 2026, up 8% compared with 29.4 million tonnes in the same period of 2025, according to the Ministry of Transport of Kazakhstan.

Growth was recorded in both directions. From China to Kazakhstan, rail freight transportation reached 12.1 million tonnes during the first ten months of 2026, an increase of 9% compared with the same period last year.

Of this volume, 5 million tonnes were transported through the Dostyk border station, up 13%, while shipments through the Altynkol station totalled 7.1 million tonnes, representing a 6% increase.

In the opposite direction, from Kazakhstan to China, rail freight transportation amounted to 19.7 million tonnes, up 8% year-on-year. By border crossing, 13.1 million tonnes of cargo were transported through Dostyk, an increase of 12%. Freight volume through Altynkol reached 6.6 million tonnes, up 1%.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan, the country's total freight transportation volume reached 796.2 million tonnes in January-October 2026, up 0.9% compared with the same period of 2025. Total freight turnover amounted to 430.3 billion tonne-kilometres, an increase of 0.3% year-on-year.

Rail freight transportation across Kazakhstan amounted to 279.2 million tonnes, down 1.1% year-on-year. Meanwhile, rail freight turnover increased by 0.8% to 245.4 billion tonne-kilometres.

Trend's calculations show that rail freight transportation between Kazakhstan and China accounted for approximately 11.4% of the country's total rail freight volume during the reporting period.

World.title: Vučić heads parliamentary faction in Serbia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. Aleksandar Vučić, leader of the "United Serbia" electoral list, has been elected head of a parliamentary faction in Serbia's parliament.

According to Vučić, a decision on the name under which the faction will operate — "United Serbia," "Serbia Against Terrorism," or another name — will be made on Monday or Tuesday morning.

He noted that he would personally lead the faction at the initial stage. However, Vučić expressed doubts about whether he would be able to remain in the position for an extended period.

World.title: Turkmenistan's cashless payment transactions decline 5.3% in 9 months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. The number of cashless payment transactions in Turkmenistan decreased by 5.3% year-on-year in January-September 2026.

The data was calculated by Trend based on information published by the Central Bank of Turkmenistan.

According to the calculations, only two banks recorded an increase in the number of cashless payment transactions during the reporting period. Halkbank posted a 4.4% rise, while Senagat JSCB recorded an increase of 3.3%.

The remaining banks reported declines, although the scale of the decrease varied. The Central Bank of Turkmenistan saw the number of transactions fall by 4.2%, followed by the State Bank for Foreign Economic Affairs, down 6.4%, and Turkmenistan State Commercial Bank (SCBT), down 7.7%.

According to Trend’s calculations, the decline reached 10% or more at several other banks. Rysgal JSCB recorded a 10% decrease, while Turkmenbashi JSCB reported a 10.3% drop.

The sharpest contractions were registered by Turkmen-Turkish JSCB and Dayhanbank SCBT, where the number of cashless payment transactions decreased by 12.1% and 12.7%, respectively.

Overall, the number of such transactions fell from 91.3 million in January-September 2025 to 86.5 million in the same period of 2026.

For reference, the Central Bank of Turkmenistan launched cashless payments in 2001 with the introduction of the domestic Altyn Asyr card scheme. While the initial infrastructure was developed in the 2000s, broader adoption gained momentum in the mid-2010s as part of government efforts to digitize the economy.

In August 2020, the government announced the launch of the Halkbank Terminal mobile application, developed by JSCB Halkbank to allow merchants to accept cashless payments directly through NFC-enabled smartphones, replacing traditional POS terminals. The initiative was presented as a step toward expanding cashless payments and introducing contactless payment technologies across the country.

Alongside payment terminals, Turkmen banks have expanded digital banking services, including Internet Banking, Mobile Banking, e-commerce payment platforms and specialized applications such as Senagat Töleg, while continuing to develop the national Altyn Asyr bank card payment system. These services enable customers to pay for utilities, telecommunications, transport, taxes, and other public services electronically.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva holds series of meetings at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. On November 14, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, met with Salim bin Mohammed AlMalik, Director-General of the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO), on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

During the meeting, the sides discussed opportunities for expanding cooperation between the IDEA Public Union and ICESCO. In this regard, the sides touched upon creating new opportunities for Azerbaijani youth to gain international experience in environmental protection and sustainable development.

The parties exchanged views on implementing joint initiatives aimed at promoting environmental education in schools, greening, waste sorting, water conservation, and energy efficiency.

Discussions also focused on opportunities for organizing international environmental summer camps in Azerbaijan with the participation of youth and implementing joint awareness-raising projects in the field of biodiversity conservation.

The sides discussed the prospects for supporting youth activities in environmental innovations and carrying out joint efforts aimed at developing innovative solutions for air pollution, waste management, water resource protection, and climate change adaptation.

X X X

On November 14, Leyla Aliyeva also met with Max Bello, Global Ocean Expert at the Blue Marine Foundation, and Michael Fishbach, Co-Founder and Executive Director of the Great Whale Conservancy.

The meeting featured discussions on the impacts of the declining water level of the Caspian Sea on the marine ecosystem, biodiversity, and coastal areas, as well as enhancing international cooperation to address existing environmental challenges.

They also exchanged views on expanding marine protected areas in Azerbaijan, conserving Caspian seals and other rare marine species, protecting their natural habitats, and exploring opportunities for international experience exchange and cooperation in this field.

X X X

The same day, Prime Minister of Tonga Lord Fatafehi Fakafānua visited the Azerbaijan pavilion at COP31. The Prime Minister of Tonga was briefed on the stands set up and the projects presented there.

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Foundation VP Leyla Aliyeva attends event on "Women and Climate Investments: Empowering Women Leaders in the Turkic World to Contribute to Climate Action" (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, attended a panel session on the theme "Women and Climate Investments: Empowering Women Leaders in the Turkic World to Contribute to Climate Action", held at the Azerbaijan pavilion at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Addressing the event, Leyla Aliyeva highlighted the vital role women play in the life of society and the importance of their empowerment. She also emphasized the necessity of expanding cooperation among Turkic states in this area.

Noting women’s active participation in the projects of the IDEA Public Union, Leyla Aliyeva said that initiatives implemented particularly in the regions create new opportunities for women.

Speakers at the panel included Bahar Muradova, Chairperson of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs of Azerbaijan; Mahinur Özdemir Göktaş, Minister of Family and Social Services of Türkiye; Umayra Taghiyeva, Deputy Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources of Azerbaijan; and Sakina Babayeva, Chairperson of the Board of the Association for Women's Entrepreneurship Development in Azerbaijan.

Discussions focused on increasing women's economic activity in combating climate change, expanding access to climate investments, and ensuring their participation in decision-making processes as key priorities.

The speakers stressed the importance of expanding cooperation, experience exchange, and joint innovative initiatives among women entrepreneurs across the Turkic world.

World.title: Azerbaijan faces risk of failing to secure $411.8M foreign loan in 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Azerbaijan is facing the risk of failing to secure 700 million manat ($411.8 million) in foreign loan next year.

The the opinion issued by the Chamber of Accounts on the draft law "On the state budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027" noted that, given the low execution rate of foreign loans in the current year, the allocation of a significant share of foreign borrowing to finance the state budget deficit for the coming year, combined with the fact that the projects intended to be financed through these funds aren't substantiated within the "Budget package", increases the risk that the planned borrowing won’t be fully realized.

According to the opinion, 2.73 billion manat $1.6 billion) is expected to be raised through government borrowing in 2027 to finance the state budget deficit. This is projected to account for 86.8% of total financing.

"According to information provided with the 2027 state budget draft, 700 million manat is expected to be raised through foreign loans. However, the 'Budget package' doesn't provide information on the projects to be financed through these funds or the amounts allocated to them.

Although more than 1.71 billion manat ($1.01 billion) was projected to be received through domestic and external borrowing in 2026, no funds had been received during the first nine months of the reporting year. Meanwhile, 125 million manat ($73.5 million) was received through externally borrowed loans, equivalent to 14.7% of the annual forecast of 850 million manat ($500 million) for 2026," the opinion pointed out.

World.title: Carers of people with disability left exhausted navigating NDIS
World.content:
Caregivers of people with disabilities say navigating the NDIS to try to get more support for their loved ones is leaving them feeling exhausted and taking a toll on their mental health.

It comes as accessing the NDIS becomes increasingly difficult, after cuts in funding for some sectors began to be rolled out on October 1.

Amanda Solarino, who lives in Romsey just outside Melbourne, is the full-time carer for her 21-year-old son Alex, who is autistic, non‑verbal and has an intellectual disability.

Ms Solarino said she was continuously replacing furniture and fixing walls as a result of her son's escalating aggression, and she struggled to get the help she needed from the NDIS.

Some of the damage caused by Alex at home. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"Alex's aggression isn't just directed at us or the furniture anymore — he's now turning it on Erica, his 19‑year‑old sister," she said.

"She's so anxious she won't walk down the hallway unless she knows exactly where he is."

Her son's disability also comes at a steep financial cost.

Amanda Solarino lives with several health conditions herself. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

"No one's paying to fix the furniture he breaks ... the $2,000 couch he breaks with his head or the two beds he's broken in the last 18 months," she said.

" The NDIS doesn't pay for ... all the iPads he breaks over his head. "

Ms Solarino said Alex had been kicked out of programmes providing day care in their area, and in a neighbouring town, leaving the family with one support worker who can only come for six hours every Monday.

Ms Solarino has had to plaster the walls after Alex damaged them. (Supplied: Amanda Solarino)

The stress is affecting Ms Solarino. She has chronic migraine disorder and requires injections every 12 weeks, and her arthritis has worsened.

"They're suspecting autoimmune problems, probably brought on by all the stress," she said.

After Alex's aggression worsened, the NDIS escalated his housing request to crisis level and eventually approved his specialist disability accommodation.

Ms Solarino said the new plan did not fulfil the provisions she had asked for, but she was too exhausted by the process to fight it.

She said all she wanted for Alex was for him to live with some dignity.

"And it's the hardest thing to keep standing up every time you get knocked back," she said.

'Real-world' consequences

On the Sunshine Coast, the family of Breanna Medcalfe, a 24-year-old law student with a spinal injury and quadriplegia, has also faced challenges getting the NDIS help she needs.

Ms Medcalfe is completely paralysed from the neck down and relies on assistance for all activities, including driving and showering.

Breanna Medcalfe now relies on her parents for care. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

Ms Medcalfe has one support worker, but mainly relies on her 60-year-old parents to take care of her daily care responsibilities.

She would like more NDIS-funded support hours, but her requests have been declined.

"Because I have mum and dad and I live at home with them, they are like my informal supports, and they therefore can provide the main support, which is incorrect," she said.

" It's taking a toll on their bodies and their mental health because they have to always be around for me. "

Ms Medcalfe is lodging an appeal against a review of her NDIS plan.

"We haven't yet come to the point where we've run out of support hours, but we've been very restricted as to what we can do," she said.

"Why do we have to justify that we're disabled enough to need this funding?"

Ms Medcalfe says its not right that her parents have to care for her all the time. (ABC News: Josh Dye)

The NDIS refused to answer specific questions about supports provided by family members and the lack of resources in regional areas, referring the ABC to its website.

A spokesperson defended the agency's role in providing "critical, essential services" and confirmed that funding resets for social, economic and community participation and improved daily living supports had gradually rolled out from October 1.

The spokesperson said supports vital to the health, safety, and wellbeing of participants would be excluded from the changes, and added that new safeguards will protect participants with 24-hour care needs.

Ms Medcalfe and her support worker Katy-Lea Holmes. (ABC News: Josh Dye )

Ms Medcalfe says she wants the NDIS to understand the real‑world consequences of its decisions.

"We're not asking for, you know, over the top things," she said.

World.title: US investigators say too soon to know what caused tanker-cruise ship collision
World.content:
The US National Transport Safety Board (NTSB) says it is on a "fact finding" mission to figure out how a tanker collided with a cruise ship that had more than 100 passengers.

More than 100 rescued after tanker crashes into cruise ship in US A tanker has collided with a river cruise boat docked near the port of New Orleans with more than 100 passengers onboard.

All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship and tanker survived the collision in New Orleans on Friday, local time.

Officials said 32 people were taken to hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled, but none of the injuries were critical.

Eight remained hospitalised on Saturday.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the tanker's voyage data recorder had been recovered, and a 16-member team would spend a week in New Orleans investigating the incident.

Loading...

NTSB member John DeLeeuw said the agency expected to release a preliminary report within 24 to 30 days, with the final investigation report expected in 18 to 24 months.

“We are still in the fact-finding stage. We look at the maintenance record, the history of the ship. We actually look at a number of things, but it is way too soon [to know what happened]," Mr DeLeeuw said.

Survivor recalls harrowing minutes in river

The first warning Joe Knab, a passenger on the American Heritage cruise ship, had of the imminent collision was the tanker blasting its horn several times.

The hit was hard, and the cruise ship immediately started leaning. The crew quickly gathered everyone on the third deck, got them in life vests and started getting them off the boat.

But the vessel suddenly rolled and sent Mr Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River.

Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

"It's fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time," Mr Knab told WDSU-TV, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.

" I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn't taste very good. "

Emergency services help people out of the water after a tanker crashed into a cruise ship in New Orleans. (AP: Devon Flanagan )

Mr Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered after the incident. The rest of his belongings were in the river but somehow his phone still worked.

He said he was in the water for about 15 minutes, and joked that his 20 years in the navy likely helped him.

"They taught us not to drown," he said.

Lawsuit leads to warrant to get control of tanker

A lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $US1 million ($1.47 million) in damage to its terminal.

A judge issued a warrant on Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.

The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham told reporters on Saturday.

Emergency crews work at the scene of the collision. (The Advocate via AP: Enan Chediak)

She said the first step was to make sure the 60,500 litres of fuel on the boat were removed safely.

Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Captain Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.

ABC/wires

World.title: Lambie suggests change to childcare subsidies to cut spending
World.content:
Independent senator Jacqui Lambie says the government should means test several subsidies, including child care, as it looks at ways to tighten its budget.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers is facing growing pressure to rein in government expenditure ahead of December's budget update due to cost-of-living pressures including persistent inflation and a fifth interest rate hike this year.

The Tasmanian senator has suggested one possible lever for the government is to better target assistance at those who need it most.

"We've got to target better in this country," she told Insiders on Sunday.

She proposed different levels of subsidy for child care depending on income, using a couple with $500,000 income between them as an example.

The ministers who have managed to save money As the government pursues savings "across the board" ahead of the mid-year budget update, an ABC analysis shows only a handful of ministers have managed net savings so far this year.

"Why aren't we means testing you? Why aren't we doing what we used to do and say, you can have 10 per cent rebate. Not this much rebate," she said.

Asked whether that principle would apply to other subsidies like those on electric vehicles, Senator Lambie said, "Means test it all, why not? That's where you'll get some money from."

Senator Lambie stressed that she had not seen her constituents under such financial strain since the COVID-19 pandemic, with some turning to putting meat "down their pants and walking out" of supermarkets to feed their children.

"I don't see this financial situation turning around overnight. And I think we've got a couple of more years of it," she said, pointing to uncertainty across several issues like the war in the Middle East.

Gas reservation to face parliament

As politicians return for the final sitting fortnight of the year, the government hopes that it can pass its nationwide gas reservation scheme which it says will put downward pressure on prices.

The scheme would force liquefied natural gas exporters to keep up to 20 per cent of their product for Australia's domestic market and address consistent threats of shortfalls on the east coast.

Senator Lambie says she will support the legislation when it is debated in the Senate but has called on the government to have "enough courage" to put a 20 per cent tax on export gas.

"Start taking our resources back into our own hands, but we're actually making money off out of them," she said.

The idea is supported by members of the crossbench including the Greens and independent senator David Pocock, who state a 25 per cent tax on gas exports could raise billions of dollars in annual revenue.

The proposal has been repeatedly rejected by the government who argue it needs to protect trade relationships with Asian partners and points to the existing petroleum resources rent tax, which has upwards revisions in forecast revenue.

Shadow Minister for Defence James Paterson said the opposition was concerned about the future of gas investment in Australia as it works constructively with the government, not revealing where it has landed on the gas reservation bill.

"We do want to have more gas here for Australians to access, particularly for industry whose prices have been driven through the roof on Labor's watch," he told Sunday Agenda.

"And we want to see more gas extracted here in Australia. But the government has not done anything to make that easier."

World.title: Police investigate suspected fatal stabbing of man in Melbourne's south-east
World.content:
Police are investigating the suspected stabbing death of a man in Melbourne's south-east.

Emergency services were called after a man with suspected stab wounds was found on the corner of Leonard and Beach streets in Frankston at about 1:20am today.

After efforts to revive him, including CPR, the man, who is yet to be formally identified, was declared dead at the scene.

Homicide detectives are probing a potential connection between the man's death and an earlier incident at a property in Lucerne Crescent.

They have set up crime scenes at both locations.

A woman was arrested at the scene of the man's death in relation to another matter.

Police allege the people involved were known to each other.

Anyone with information that may assist the investigation is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online.

World.title: Journalist urges federal government to intervene in NT 'social catastrophe'
World.content:
A veteran ABC journalist has delivered a searing analysis of Northern Territory politics in a new book that chronicles how government policies have worsened life outcomes for Aboriginal people in the NT.

Murray McLaughlin's new book is out now. (Supplied)

In his new book The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure, Murray McLaughlin — who worked as an ABC TV current affairs journalist and later as an adviser to the Northern Land Council (NLC) — argues the federal government has been mostly passively complicit in the welfare of the Territory's Aboriginal citizens declining over five decades.

As well as a critique of failure, the book serves as an appeal to the federal government to intervene in a territory McLaughlin describes as a "beguiling and bewitching place, a unique wonderland".

He writes:

"While Canberra's reluctance to dictate prevails, one certainty remains: the Territory will never right itself. "A mendicant jurisdiction beholden to the Commonwealth is allowed to bring embarrassment and shame upon the whole country with policy agendas that disproportionately impact on Aboriginal people while it lavishes benefits on the non-Aboriginal population."

He says the Albanese government "has done little to avert the social catastrophe unravelling before its eyes".

"As Canberra pours billions of dollars into the Territory to shore up northern defence systems and the petrochemical industry prepares to prosper from the bountiful gas fields to be fracked in the immense Beetaloo Basin south-east of Darwin, housing, health and education markers continue to deteriorate for the Territory's Aboriginal population, especially those living in remote communities."

Patrick Dodson wrote the foreword to The Northern Territory: A Litany of Failure. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

In the book's foreword, former Labor senator Patrick Dodson, for whom McLaughlin worked as an adviser, reinforces its central message: That the NT's self-government in place since 1978 has been "a failed experiment" which has hastened "a collapse of social order".

But Mr Dodson writes that he and McLaughlin share hope that the Commonwealth will use "a rare political window … to show leadership and imagination in rebuilding the Territory and redirecting its troubled course".

Land rights under attack, Intervention 'cataclysmic'

Much of the book's conversational, accessible political history of the Territory is told from McLaughlin's firsthand reporting experience, and then from the sidelines of fights between the NLC and NT governments on policies affecting the rights of Aboriginal people.

He takes readers on an evocative journey through the Territory, analysing the policy blows Country Liberal Party (CLP) and Labor governments have delivered to Aboriginal people, focusing particularly on how successive CLP governments, aided at times by Canberra Coalition administrations, have tried to erode federal NT Aboriginal land rights laws.

The book claims successive governments from both major parties have failed Aboriginal people in the NT. (Torsten Blackwood, AFP)

He writes the Territory's first CLP chief minister Paul Everingham's 1978 administration opposed Aboriginal land rights and "ruthlessly" challenged almost every land claim.

This continued through to the 2013 CLP Adam Giles administration, McLaughlin writes, as they tried to persuade the Commonwealth to hand control of the land rights law to them.

McLaughlin documents how "Aboriginal incarceration rates have grown exponentially", starting with 1995 CLP chief minister Shane Stone's administration introducing mandatory sentencing for a range of offences.

"The law, predictably, had a disproportionate impact on Aboriginal people, and its impact had been cynically calculated," he writes.

The book also chronicles a series of Labor government policies during the early 2000s that harmed Aboriginal interests, including the 2001 Clare Martin administration's approval for Xstrata to dig through a sacred site to expand its McArthur River Mine in 2006.

The book uses the approval to destroy a sacred site at the McArthur River Mine as an example of how governments have ignored Aboriginal interests. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

McLaughlin labels this as "a conspicuous example of how governments have brutally brushed aside Aboriginal interests when development proposals take priority".

He writes how the following 2007 Paul Henderson Labor administration wound back bilingual education in Aboriginal community schools, concentrated government funding into larger Indigenous communities and amalgamated 53 remote local government councils into eight "super shires".

"Worse, the resultant changes coincided with the Howard government's Intervention, with communities never recovering from that double calamity," he writes.

McLaughlin analyses how both a "flawed" ABC Lateline story about an alleged paedophile ring in Central Australia and Clare Martin's "failure to respond with boldness and urgency to the Little Children Are Sacred report" resulted in the NT National Emergency Response — the Intervention.

John Howard and his Indigenous affairs minister Mal Brough launched the Intervention, with Mr Brough visiting Mutujulu in 2007. (Ian Waldie, file photo: Getty Images)

Seventy-three communities were identified as primary sites for intervention and the army and police were brought in from other jurisdictions.

"The scope of the Intervention was extraordinary and its impact on Aboriginal people cataclysmic," he writes. "Although Aboriginal men were offended because the Intervention had branded them child molesters and, as traditional owners, they felt threatened about the Commonwealth's compulsory leasing of community lands, the most troubling policy … was compulsory income management, facilitated by the suspension of the Racial Discrimination Act 1975. "Federal Labor, not wanting to be wedged, embraced the Intervention."

Treatment of youth detainees scrutinised

The 2013 Adam Giles government's treatment of youth prisoners, including the use of tear gas, mechanical restraints, spit hoods and indefinite detention isolation, that was exposed by the ABC is scrutinised in the book.

Youth detainees were shackled and hooded the day after tear gas was used on them at Don Dale. (Supplied)

"The brutalisation of children and their bastardisation in detention were painfully illustrated by the treatment of a 14-year-old Aboriginal boy, whose explosive behaviour on 21 August 2014 precipitated the tear-gassing of him and other detainees," McLaughlin writes.

McLaughlin analyses how the 2016 administration of Labor's Michael Gunner — summed up as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister who promised plenty but delivered little" — "slithered and dithered" over recommendations of the royal commission into youth justice abuse.

He writes that Mr Gunner toughened bail laws "in the full knowledge that incarceration rates, especially of Aboriginal people, would blow out beyond already record-breaking numbers, and his commitment to a treaty began to fade".

Murray McLaughlin describes Michael Gunner as "an uninspiring and shallow chief minister". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McLaughlin also accuses the Gunner government of attacking Aboriginal land rights by passing laws making it easier for pastoralists to develop cattle stations for other uses without native title holders having to be consulted or compensated.

"Gunner's government would soon resort to drawing from the same well of prejudice against Aboriginal land claims as had nourished the Country Liberal Party," he writes.

The veteran journalist follows the NT right up to the current CLP government, documenting how Indigenous incarceration continued to dramatically increase with tightened bail laws following the 2023 murder of a bottle shop worker, Declan Laverty.

"By August 2025, the government was boasting that more than 3,300 people had been refused bail, a 44 per cent increase over the same period in 2024," the books reads.

'Things are deadly serious'

McLaughlin's chronicle finishes with current Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro's appointment of former NT Cattlemen's Association President David Connolly earlier this year, and her determined defence of that after racist social media posts he had previously made were exposed.

Territorians protested David Connolly's appointment as administrator earlier this year. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"Obduracy and disdain for proper process marked Finocchiaro's announcement," he writes. "Albanese's refusal … to reject the Territory government's egregious recommendation of a man with a record of racist commentary to be the Territory's Administrator … spoke of a deliberate avoidance of responsibility."

McLaughlin told the ABC he hoped the federal government was starting to understand that the Territory's Aboriginal people were facing a crisis so severe that it must now intervene.

Despite its 'litany of failure', Murray McLaughlin is hopeful the federal government will intervene.

"The Commonwealth has got to recognise that it's got responsibilities here," he said.

"It's going to take something like a Marshall Plan to just catch up.

"Something has to happen — these remote communities are on their knees.

"[Independent NT politician] Yingiya Guyula said it when he resigned, that Aboriginal culture is being destroyed in front of our eyes.

"Things are deadly serious."

World.title: Swimming stars tipped for big 2027 despite illness, injury hiccups
World.content:
Battered by illness and injury, a trio of Australian Olympic swimming stars are being backed to be ready for Los Angeles Games.

Between them, Kaylee McKeown, Mollie O'Callaghan and Kyle Chalmers have won 11 Olympic gold medals.

McKeown returned to competition over the weekend at the inaugural Swim GP in Melbourne, having not raced since last year because of glandular fever.

Chalmers was poolside at the event, in the midst of a six-week break from swimming as he manages long-term back problems.

O'Callaghan, who nursed back and shoulder injuries through the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, was a late withdrawal from the Swim GP because of a skin infection.

McKeown said the one positive of her illness was that it had happened this year, not next.

Australian swimming head coach Rohan Taylor echoed that sentiment about the three stars in the context of the four-year Olympic cycle.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed competing at Swim GP due to an infection. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"No-one will remember what happens in 2026 [in terms of injury or illness]. You can't worry about that now," Taylor told AAP.

"You have to get them right, you have to remember their talent won't go anywhere.

"It's about getting them healthy and then letting the fitness build. We know they can race and we just have to get ourselves to the arena fit and healthy, then we will be right."

McKeown made a successful return to racing at the Swim GP and Taylor was pleased with the backstroke queen's progress after the illness knocked her flat.

"I live on the Sunshine Coast, so I get to see it up close and see the progression," Taylor said.

"It's really good to see her back racing. She's such a competitor.

"She just looked back to her normal self, competitive, focused when the race was on, but enjoying herself.

"She just has to build momentum back."

McKeown gave a glimpse of her blistering backstroke speed on Saturday night, storming home after the staggered start to beat Ella Ramsay's breaststroke in the 50m skins champions race.

It was her first racing since the world championships in July last year.

Kaylee McKeown is one of Australian swimming's biggest stars. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"I've been doing some pretty solid sessions, but it's hard to come into these races — not racing all year — and then my body just hasn't recovered as quickly as it would," McKeown said.

"It's good, nice practice and gives a bit of confidence that I'm still swimming well.

"It's great there are no times, which takes the pressure off. It's just about racing."

As McKeown notes, glandular fever affects people differently and in her case, "it just really knocked me flat".

So competing for the Tsunami team at the Swim GP, with nothing riding on the results, was an ideal stepping stone as McKeown looks to next year's world championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

"It's really good fun and I'm glad we can race in this format," she said.

"It's taken a long time to build back and then I have to build to where I was, which is even more of a gap.

"I'm lucky it was this year and not next year, when it counts, so it's a blessing in disguise. I've had some nice time at home."

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The Wahoo team, lead by Meg Harris and Sam Short, dominated the two-night Swim GP and comfortably won on 222 points.

McKeown's Tsunami were next on 173, ahead of Kraken (170) and KingTide (149).

AAP

World.title: The parade of high-profile men doing wrong is getting exhausting
World.content:
This coming Thursday is International Men's Day. Unaware of it? So are most carbon-based life forms, even though it's been around for about three decades now.

Google Trends advises that the term "International Men's Day" bumps along at low rates of interest most of the year, with two identifiable annual spikes; one smaller, one larger.

The smaller occurs around now, in the lead-up to the day itself — November 19.

The larger spike occurs in early March, around International Women's Day. It doesn't take an expert to decode the March spike; men who've just seen a poster for International Women's Day (IWD) and want to know why there isn't a day for them, or women juggling a tray of IWD-themed cupcakes who've just been asked that question by a male colleague and are googling it with the other hand to confirm their vague recollection that it's not that there isn't one, it's just that nobody organised a brunch and a speaker for it.

It's coming along, though, and there are events planned for Thursday, a day on which we are encouraged to reflect on the broad patterns of male experience that are visible from space: higher suicide rates, shorter life span, higher likelihood of violent death, lower performance at all levels of education.

This year's theme? "The Future is Everyone."

How awkward, then, that the November pre-sizzle to International Men's Day has so far consisted of a daily, multi-nation parade of high-profile men for whom the future — and indeed the present, and the past too — are mainly organised around a far more specific and compelling figure: ME ME ME.

Russell Brand's path to prison The disgraced British entertainer-turned-conspiracy theorist charted a course towards fame and notoriety before a criminal trial in London found him to be a sexual predator.

In the United States, there's a president for whom even a crushing performance review from 125 million constituents cannot dislodge his conviction that what struggling Americans really want is more detail about the chandelier count in his billion-dollar ballroom.

Or Jensen Huang, the "godfather of AI" who over three decades single-handedly built a company silicon-paving humanity's path to a future in which we either lounge about doing craft projects on a living wage or are torn apart by robot dogs (nobody's quite sure which), only to undo it all using only his penis.

In the UK, formerly beloved TV stars and writers Russell Brand and David Walliams are confronted with the carefully catalogued consequences of their actions and conclude that the real victims are … themselves.

And in Australia this very week, we find ourselves once more ensnared in an intense argument among Australia's best-known cricketing men about exactly who knew what, and when, about whether sandpaper was going to be secreted in the jocks of a bowler in Cape Town eight years ago.

What purpose does this new outbreak of finger-pointing, flounce-outs, self-justification and mic-drop moments serve? Apart from ensuring that a fresh new generation of junior cricketers can be as confused and disappointed as their predecessors were back in 2018?

You can dress it up as the pursuit of justice, or the righting of wrongs, or the promotion of a book, but let's call it what it is: a handful of guys who feel they were personally wronged by the way the last village-burning went, and are now torching the joint again to correct the record.

This whole month feels like one of those old choose-your-own-adventure novels, where every single storyline leads to a dude who has let everyone down but still wants to go for a coffee about it.

Main character energy goes into overdrive

So, what is it about this parade that has caused anyone with an internet connection and two X chromosomes to want more than usual to go for a lovely lie down in the snow and never get up?

I think it's the shamelessness. The relentless, insistent, main-character energy that leads some humans — having done a wrong or been proved wrong — to argue the toss or return to the scene in the garb of a victim, rather than do the normal human thing, which is to go to bed indefinitely in a soup of self-loathing and hope that someone else will soon take the heat off you by doing something exponentially worse.

In a way, it's transfixing. Also, to a bone-deep level, exhausting.

Let's go to the details, starting with Russell Brand, whose conviction and 10-year sentence for rape rather crystallises the speculation that has mounted around him over the course of this century. This may or may not have inspired him to move to America, convert to Christianity, be baptised by Bear Grylls and engineer an entrée into the kind of conspiracy theorist circles where a sexual assault allegation is a fungible token of victimhood.

The re-Branding exercise allows this story to continue to be — for Russell Brand and his remaining fans — about Russell Brand, rather than the young women he groped, raped or abused.

Asked if he had anything to say to the women his son was convicted of assaulting, Brand's dad Ronald snapped at reporters outside court this week:

"The victim? What, Russell? The girls, you mean, who chased him and harassed him? Is that what you mean?"

Multiple people have now alleged David Walliams groomed teenage fans and harassed women. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Or David Walliams, another British TV star and writer long reputed to have used his celebrity as a pretext for approaching young women. Confronted with allegations of this behaviour after several journalists worked for years with multiple women, Walliams demanded their stories be suppressed, as their publication would — given his fame — cause him distress to the point at which he was likely to kill himself.

Fame, in other words — having for years delivered this guy just about whatever and whomever he wanted — could now be repurposed as victimhood.

In Walliams's public statement, the key paragraph ran to 36 words, five of which were "I" or "me":

"I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Spare a thought for the other victims, though. Like fellow celebrity Jonathan Ross.

Jonathan Ross said he was "as horrified by the revelations … as the rest of the nation". (Supplied: ITV News)

As MC of the 15th British Comedy Awards in 2004, Ross got a big laugh by likening the comedy gong to any other 15-year-old: "It's drunk, it's unpredictable and it's probably going home with David Walliams."

Four years later, co-hosting a BBC Radio show with Russell Brand, Ross was recorded shrieking "He f***ed your granddaughter!" as Brand left voicemail after voicemail for actor Andrew Sachs (famous for playing Manuel in Fawlty Towers). In one of the messages, Brand croons: "It was consensual … and she wasn't menstrual …"

Ross would now like everyone to know that he didn't know anything about any of it, and someone else wrote the joke for him, and had he known his pals were actual creeps, he absolutely would have done something about it.

This is part of the exhaustion, for any normal member of the public who's bought the tickets, bought the T-shirts, bought the books, taken their kids along to the live events or the games or in any way boarded the bus, liked and subscribed, only to discover there's a whole VIP lounge up the back where everyone's necking champagne and braying at a joke from which cattle class have been excluded.

Finding this out is bad enough. But when the charlatans involved still think they can talk you back onto the bus? And would like you to consider just how rough this has all been for them? My God. Where does this level of shamelessness come from?

UK comedy confronts 'lad' culture Britain's culture secretary describes the reported allegations against David Walliams as "the latest in a long line of reported abuses of power" in the entertainment industry.

Not to dwell too grimly on the misdeeds of chaps we've actively invited into the lives of our children, but this Big Me Energy was unmistakeable in Australian writer Craig Silvey's 9,000-word apologia, published on Substack this month as he trudged off to prison convicted of possessing and distributing child exploitation material.

I haven't counted how many times the words "I" and "me" were deployed in this screed, mainly because doing so would involve Nvidia chips and I don't want to get pregnant, but they certainly appeared a lot.

Silvey devoted the bulk of his unsolicited essay to a discussion of his own trauma: sexual and physical abuse in his childhood; a brother who defrauded him; a lifetime of never feeling enough; a father whose transgressions are rather exhaustively listed, ranging from violence, to betrayal, to the lesser offences of coldness and being nicer to other kids at footy training.

These are deployed as "context" for Silvey's own transgression, which warrants one clipped and euphemistic sentence: "In January this year, while participating in an awful and inappropriate online conversation with another adult, I downloaded and sent an image of CEM."

Craig Silvey was found guilty of possessing and distributing child exploitation material. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

A reader would have to cross-research quite doggedly through the court records to find that Silvey's online activity was not restricted to one conversation. That his lengthy consideration of paternal failing excluded, for instance, the court's chat room transcripts of Silvey confiding he was aroused by the idea of mothers having sex with their boy children, or that a child of eight was "the perfect age".

The essay rounds off with an assurance that Silvey has done the work in therapy and now is prepared to love himself again. All of which is welcome news. But there is no doubt who continues to be the main character of this story, and it's certainly not the children harmed by the material Silvey sought out and/or shared.

Nor is it Silvey's own wife and three children, from whose silkily present-tense mention in the essay ("people I love and care about devotedly") it might be inferred that the family unit remained supportively intact.

It fell to Silvey's wife to take a minute or two out of sole-parenting a toddler and twin babies to pen a rather more economical note, clarifying that "we separated as soon as I learned of his crimes".

Loading

Everything is not, in fact, about you

Enough of all this! Humans are poor, sometimes damaged creatures, and we all fail in some way. Usually every day. And for powerful men who are accustomed to being the main character in their own lives, it's very hard to relinquish that role, even when they screw up incredibly badly.

To hedge against this terrible possibility, they are prepared to do extraordinary things. Brand changes his entire persona. Walliams threatens to kill himself. Silvey unveils a lifetime of suffering sufficiently grim to rival that of the children affected by his online activities.

It's too early to say how Jensen Huang, Destroyer of Worlds, will jump. Will we never see him again? Or will he be on the cover of next month's GQ, "speaking out" about his pain from the depths of a billionaire python-skin jacket (RRP $20,000)?

Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after 33 years. (Reuters)

(Honestly, one hates to pre-empt the inquiry into how elite Chinese spycraft came to identify Huang as a promising target for a honey trap, but his practice of wearing a leather jacket every single day, at 63, cannot have been immaterial.)

Is there a more biblical parable than Huang's? He builds a company with the express aim of immortalising and super-proliferating human intelligence, only to knock about a trillion dollars off its value with the most conventional bit of human stupidity imaginable.

It kind of makes you proud in a weird way, doesn't it? That artificial intelligence can scrape the entire universe of human wisdom but still get caught out by the undigitised impulses of man's least governable muscles — the heart and the one to the south of the heart? Bless us all, in our fleshy imperfection.

International Men's Day could not come at a better time, with its quiet reminder that men in general are not reducible to the antics of an ego-obsessed few.

In Becoming a Man, a thoughtful new collection of essays by men published this month by HarperCollins and edited by writer Julia Baird with her teenage son Sam Baird Sparks, several contributors deal specifically with the phenomenon of men who place themselves at the centre of everything.

British-born WA creative director Sam Harris describes this creature as "spotlight man".

Becoming a Man is edited by Julia Baird and her son. (Supplied: HarperCollins)

"A spotlight man will blind others with his talent, fame, wealth and success," Harris writes.

"He feels most alive when he's the centre of attention, with crowds cheering his name. But you'll see the real shape of spotlight man when the light's not on him, leaving him in a black hole of shadows. His dreams are more important than anyone else's — if you take his spotlight, he'll pull you into his black hole too."

Arne Rubinstein, founder of Rites of Passage, defines the transition from boyhood to manhood specifically around the changing sense of self. While boys might believe "I am the centre of the universe … I am always right and I will lie rather than admit I am wrong", manhood is about realising that everything is not, in fact, all about you.

"A problem arises when we end up with leaders and people in power who still have boy behaviours running their lives," Dr Rubinstein writes.

"Unfortunately, I believe a lot of our global leaders are boys, and that is a massive problem that puts the future of the world at risk."

So. This International Men's Day, let's understand properly that the victims of toxic masculinity are not just women.

Let's recognise the men who have completed the journey from boyhood to manhood and as a result are tough enough to confront the harshness of life — even its unfairness, even its humiliations, even their own inevitable mistakes — without requiring the world to drop everything to pity or exonerate them.

Men who have evolved past the childish notion that winning at life means having all the toys, all the praise, all the power. Who care for the people around them at work and at home, through good times and bad, not so they can be named Man of the Year, but because they're smart enough to work out that this is the most durable path to happiness.

World.title: Author Tim Winton says Exmouth wrong place for a port
World.content:
A proposed deepwater industrial port in northern Western Australia has been described as unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable by locals and conservationists worried about the impact on marine animals.

The Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex is proposed to be built just outside of Exmouth, 1,230km north of Perth, where it will feature a single jetty wharf, bulk fuel storage, a solar farm, and a seawater desalination plant.

The port is proposed to be built 10km south of the township. (Supplied: Gascoyne Gateway Ltd.)

The port will be designed to service cruise liners, defence and commercial supply vessels.

The proposal has caught the attention of conservationist and famous author Tim Winton who has opposed the project.

Locals voice concern

Exmouth local Brinkley Davies also said she was concerned about the port's location so close to town and World Heritage Ningaloo.

"It is worrying because it is my front yard, but also the marine ecosystem that is at risk is a major factor," Ms Davies said.

" It should be a place that's federally protected and not at risk of something that's going to be so damaging to the local ecosystem. "

Having worked in marine conservation herself, Ms Davies has been involved in the campaign against the port since its initial proposal in 2020.

Brinkley Davies believes more people are now aware of the issues with the port. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

"It was not widely spoken about then and in the last five or six years, the town has really boomed and there is a lot more people living here and more people standing up for the place," she said.

"There are a few key species that really have an importance in this area, one of them is dugongs.

"There is a very important seagrass meadows where they are feeding and they also come in here to nurse their calves and rest, and that area is at direct risk of being covered in silt if they are going to dredge."

Signs with messages opposing the port have been placed around town. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Fellow Exmouth local Violeta Brosig said she was concerned the port could impact the humpback whales that rely on the Gulf.

"My main concern is it is going to be right in the middle of the parts of the humpback highway in Exmouth Gulf," she said.

"It needs to be preserved and protected instead of destroyed."

'Loud minority' opposition

However, the Exmouth Chamber of Commerce president David Gillespie said it was an opportunity of a lifetime for locals and there would be flow-on benefits for the community.

"There will be upgrades and roads, jobs, " he said.

"There's for and against on both sides with businesses that agree to disagree, but I just get back to what the positives are from an economic perspective and what that will do for the town, for increased housing and population."

Exmouth Gulf is now the chosen site for the Gascoyne Gateway Marine Complex. (ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel)

Gascoyne Gateway CEO Daniel Jackson said there had been extensive community consultation and believed the majority of locals and businesses were in favour of the port.

"There is those that have opposed the project, but I would put them in the loud minority," he said.

"We certainly acknowledge that there's seasonal windows, we're talking a few months of the year in which higher degree of risk mitigation is required to manage interaction between vessels and fauna, as it does now.

"There's commercial vessels operating there today that are moving in and out and around fauna in the Gulf."

The project is still undergoing approvals, with the WA Environmental Protection Authority currently undertaking public consultation.

Conservationist leads the charge

World renowned author, conservationist and patron of Protect Ningaloo, Tim Winton, said the Exmouth Gulf was the wrong place for a port.

"It is one of the world's most important humpback whale nurseries and the idea of building a wharf a kilometre long into the whale refuge and to bring up to 600 vessels a year into the whale nursery just seems fundamentally wrong," Mr Winton said.

"We're of the view that this is unnecessary, unjustified and unacceptable in its impacts to the Ningaloo estate."

While this proposal could be approved by and started by 2029, the Exmouth Gulf is also being considered for National Heritage Listing, with that decision not expected until 2030.

The WA government is also looking to establish a new marine park covering the entire Exmouth Gulf.

Exmouth Gulf is also currently undergoing an assessment to be added to National Heritage List. (Supplied: Australian Marine Conservation Society)

"Exmouth Gulf, is about to become a marine park, it is currently being assessed for national heritage status, which is obviously a pathway to world heritage protection," Mr Winton said.

Protect Ningaloo has so far gathered over 74,000 signatures for their submission to the EPA.

Mr Jackson said a large portion of the environmental review submission focused on dredging during the construction phase and it would be done in a controlled manner to ensure the seabed was not overly disturbed.

If approved, construction on the port is expected to begin in 2029 and be operational by end of that year.

World.title: Construction of $1.4b Brisbane Arena to begin within weeks. Take a look around
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Construction of $1.4b Brisbane Arena to begin within weeks. Take a look around Cloe Read November 15, 2026 — 12:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Construction of the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena is set to begin within weeks, after it was announced on Sunday that the Gather Brisbane consortium would deliver the entertainment precinct, with its opening expected by 2031. The 17,000-seat arena will host various events, such as concerts, family shows, and sports, and will have access to Woolloongabba’s underground Cross River Rail station, alongside a new pedestrian bridge connecting to Stanley Street and the South East Busway. The Gabba Entertainment Precinct, which comprises two pieces of land totalling nine hectares, will replace the Brisbane Entertainment Centre at Boondall in the city’s north. Loading The nearby Gabba Stadium will be demolished following the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games as part of a state government plan for almost 4000 homes.



Earlier this year, Gather Brisbane was shortlisted alongside Ignite, formerly Brisbane Entertainment Alliance, for the build. On Sunday, the government announced Gather Brisbane, which brings together Plenary, Live Nation, Oak View Group and Webuild, would be responsible for the arena’s design, build, financing, maintenance and operation. Gather Brisbane has been selected to deliver the Gabba Entertainment and Housing Precinct. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the consortium’s selection marked a major milestone, with work expected to start in January. “The stage is now set for something special at Woolloongabba. This will be transformational for the area, and generational for millions of people who will come to live, visit and enjoy this new precinct,” he said.



Taking aim at Labor over “taxpayers forking out billions for a new arena”, Bleijie said the government had instead gathered a group of powerhouses in their fields to deliver an incredible legacy for Queensland that would also “respect taxpayers’ money”. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Ekka upgrade’s quarter-billion-plus price tag revealed “We knew that this was a site that had so much potential, but we saw the chaos and confusion before the October 2024 election, where the Gabba was either going to be knocked down, rebuilt, refurbished, painted, and we had a different vision for this area,” he said. Once the arena is completed, the state government will make a one-off $600 million capital investment in the project, which is not part of the $7.1 billion venue infrastructure budget for the 2032 Olympics. “You will recall the previous government had a plan for an arena at a cost of $2.4 billion that had to be changed three locations because it was over the old Roma Street railyards … we said we’d partner with the private sector, and we’ve gone through a competitive process,” Bleijie said.



“This is a $1.4 billion arena, a $600 million capital contribution from the state government, but we don’t pay that until 2031.” Related Article Exclusive

Jobs Queensland leads nation for civil engineering jobs amid Olympic build Bleijie said the contribution would be offset by the sale and staged release of the Gabba stadium land to the consortium, to make way for about 4000 new homes. Under the deal, the government will continue to own the Brisbane Arena land until at least 2071, and will enter into a long-term commercial arrangement with the operator. The build was also backed by Brisbane singers The Veronicas, who said the arena would give the next generation of artists a bigger stage.



“We were saying we are definitely down to christen the arena once it’s fully up and running,” Jess Origliasso said. Plenary Group head of development Sergio Calcarao said the project would redefine the way city precincts in Australia and abroad are designed, developed and delivered. “With a diverse range of housing and community infrastructure being integrated into this master planned precinct, this project is arguably the most significant urban renewal legacy opportunity stemming from this Games infrastructure program.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Commercial childcare is hitting a brick wall. Who will pick up the pieces?
World.content:
Analysis BusinessCompaniesChildcare Commercial childcare is hitting a brick wall. Who will pick up the pieces? Colin Kruger November 15, 2026 — 12:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

At first blush it looked like great news for investors in Australia’s largest listed childcare provider. G8 Education shares more than doubled within hours on Thursday after the group revealed its warm welcome of a potential private equity offer at a 260 per cent premium to its record-low share price. G8 Education’s board have warmed to a takeover offer valuing the group at less than $200 million. G8 chief executive Pejman Okhovat (centre) and board directors: (from top left down) Debra Singh, Margaret Zabel and Toni Thornton; (from top right down) Julie Cogin, Stephen Heath and Peter Trimble. Like most of the kids in G8’s care, the suitor – Majority Capital Partners – is a newborn with little experience of the sector. It was set up just this year by Vidhur Rangaswamy, a veteran of John Wylie, and backed by rock-star investors like Will Vicars. The 26¢ a share indicative cash offer, subject to further due diligence, contrasts with shares that had dropped from 70¢ at the start of the year to a low of 10¢ before the offer was revealed. Last year the stock was worth as much as $1.40.



That was before G8 revealed the scale of the challenges it faces with occupancy levels plunging, leading to the suspension of 40 underperforming centres that are not expected to reopen. Related Article Analysis

Billionaires There has never been another scandal like this G8’s fortunes reflect a market landscape rocked by falling fertility rates, rising costs, and rising standards of care demanded by customers following the sex abuse scandals, which have hit commercial operators particularly hard. As you would expect, G8 is not the only one to have suffered. Just weeks ago, Shared Beginnings childcare collapsed after its owners, ASX-listed private lender Finexia, called in administrators.



Finexia got lumbered with the centres last year, thanks to its role as a lender to Genius childcare when it collapsed. Genius and its boss, Gold Coast entrepreneur Darren Misquitta, got lumbered with many of these centres in 2023, when G8 Education paid it $26.5 million to take 31 struggling centres off its hands. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese wants universal early education and care to be part of his legacy but experts say a different model might be needed. Outside of this G8 loop we have private-equity-owned Edge Early Learning, which went into voluntary administration in August with 70 centres. Just last week, six centres were closed in South Australia and Victoria. Not-for-profit Goodstart had agreed to acquire them last month but these centres failed to pass due diligence.



It’s not a good sign when an operator built from the ashes of Australia’s largest for-profit childcare failure, ABC Learning, could not make these centres sustainable. “As a not-for-profit we must make careful decisions about where we invest,” a spokesperson said. “While Goodstart stands ready to make investments in extra staff, capital upgrades, and more professional development in those centres we are purchasing, some centres come with major difficulties which even extra investment will struggle to fix.” ‘The risk of viability doesn’t sit with the people making the decisions when the property is built. It ends up with providers, families and governments. A handful of unviable leases can drag down a whole provider.’ Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow, childcare think tank The Front Project The collapse of commercial operators is a growing trend.



Data extracted from the corporate regulator by not-for-profit social impact investment fund manager For Purpose Investment Partners (FPIP) shows 58 childcare centres collapsed between July 1 and October 11 this year. This compares with 35 failures in the whole of the 2025/26 financial year, which was marred by the sex abuse scandals. In less than four months we had more failures than any full year since ASIC started collecting information in 2021. Of the 210 childcare companies that have failed since 2021, only four were not privately owned. Perversely, this is where most of the new supply is coming from. Since 2022, more than 90 per cent of new centre approvals were privately owned.



But as a recent report from childcare think tank The Front Project (TFP) shows, it is the landlords who have been dictating terms. This has created oversupply and cannibalisation in lucrative areas, and childcare deserts in others. Related Article Opinion

Cost of living We’re supposed to be struggling, yet we’re spending more. Why? Millie Muroi Economics Writer “Right now, how big a centre is – and where it’s located – comes down to what it costs to build. Children’s needs barely come into it. That’s why some communities have no access to childcare and others have too much,” TFP chief executive Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow says. The specialised needs of childcare centres – and the limit on competition due to the fact that markets are hyper-localised, restricting parent choices to a narrow geographic radius – have given developers the upper hand, while operators wear all the business risk. “The risk of viability doesn’t sit with the people making the decisions when the property is built. It ends up with providers, families and governments. A handful of unviable leases can drag down a whole provider, and because the lease follows the business when it’s sold to the next provider, the impact can last for years,” Croser-Barlow says.



TFP is among those calling for an independent commission to oversee a sector that is failing to match services with demand, thanks to a model where the government hands billions to private operators and leaves the result to market forces. Georgie Dent, head of advocacy group The Parenthood, says a clear picture is emerging of a funding model that has driven significant investment from listed companies, private equity and investors but with no management or oversight of where services are actually needed. G8 faces challenges with occupancy levels plunging, leading to the suspension of 40 underperforming centres that are not expected to reopen. Paul Jeffers “[It] has really led us to the position where we are today, where we are seeing really significant closures,” Dent says. The Parenthood says childcare provision needs to be put through the same lens as school provision and based on community needs, not market forces.



“We are not leaving it up to the market to determine which suburbs have got greater capacity to pay higher fees for school … We provide it because we recognise that public education is essential infrastructure.” Former Macquarie executive Michael Traill, who is chair of FPIP, says the ownership model is also an important factor for sustainable quality care. Traill, who helped set up Macquarie’s private equity business, understands the outsized returns demanded by PE and listed company owners that drive up costs and affordability issues. His answer? Long-term ownership, ethically focused and capable of driving long-term ethical returns. His “patient capital” model calls for super funds to play a bigger role, like Australian Ethical Super is in the aged care sector.



“They’re very long-term investors, so the objective is of owning these assets, running them with an emphasis on quality and inclusion, but driving a long long-term ethical return,” he says. Related Article Media & marketing It’s a vertical world in Hollywood’s new gold rush Traill says this funding model doesn’t just apply to childcare and should be welcomed by governments spending billions on these services. “If you look at the sectors we’re talking about – aged care, early learning, social and affordable housing, social disability support for housing – they’re all areas where governments are very, very significant players in terms of the policy and funding it provides,” he says. But Traill, who was instrumental in setting up Goodstart from the ABC Learning failure, also pointed to the split between ownership and operation of childcare centres as another issue to address.



Traill calls it a “natural tension” between the objectives of a landlord to maximise development profits and rent, and an operator for whom rents are such a significant component of costs. “There’s a different skill set in developing and building childcare centres but, certainly, our view would be it’s easy to have alignment where you’ve got ownership of that under one entity.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
