World.title: Secret report finds 2000-tonne ship poses severe environmental threat
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWWater Secret report finds 2000-tonne ship poses severe environmental threat Harriet Alexander and Carrie Fellner Updated November 15, 2026 — 12:32pm ,first published November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A 2000-tonne ship seized by NSW Maritime near the busiest shipping zone in Sydney Harbour has holes in its hull so gaping that a passing wave could sink the vessel and cause an environmental catastrophe. An independent surveyor’s report on the condition of the MV Cape Don warned early last year that the vessel was “severely deteriorated” and the bilge pumping arrangements were grossly inadequate to manage flooding or water ingress. NSW Maritime took possession of the MV Cape Don last month. Sam Mooy “The risk of catastrophic failure of the port side hull plate is extremely high, which would pose an immediate and severe environmental threat,” the confidential report by AMSA Accredited Marine Surveyors reported. But the hazard is unlikely to be removed from its mooring at Balls Head in Waverton until next year, due to the logistical challenges of dismantling a ship in such frail condition.



NSW Maritime executive director Nicole Watts said the agency was exploring options, including dismantling the vessel in place or scooping it out of the water from underneath in a “bath tub scenario” to ensure it did not crumble during disassembly. This may require specialist equipment to be brought in from overseas. One such option is operating in Darwin and that facility may be available to NSW Maritime after its current job is complete. Depending on which option NSW Maritime pursues, the salvage is likely to cost $15 to $20 million and will be borne by the taxpayers because the vessel is uninsured. “We’ve obviously got to go through our procurement process, but we’re aware of the emergency,” Watts said, recalling the 2022 sinking of the former Manly ferry MV Baragoola. The MV Baragoola was moored beside the Cape Don on the Coal Loader at Waverton when it sank. Edwina Pickles



“It needs to be done very urgently because things can change imminently. We don’t want a repeat of the Baragoola.” NSW Premier Chris Minns on Sunday said the government had to step in because of the serious implications for the environment, Sydney Harbour and the reputation of the state. “I’d expect anyone who owns or operates a boat in the maritime sector to follow the rules,” he said. “We have to make sure that there are appropriate regulations and penalties in place if there is a breach because it can’t just be shovelled over to the taxpayer when things go wrong.” MV Cape Don, a former lighthouse supply tender, was bought by the charitable Sea Heritage Foundation in 2004, since which time volunteers have been painstakingly repairing it with plans to open it up as a museum. In recent years, it has been used for university research and as a classroom for cub scouts, who drew on the expertise of the marine engineers and shipwrights working on its restoration to design a water surface cleaning robot.





The private surveyors noted the presence of environmental hazards, including asbestos, zinc chromate paint and the previous use of tributyltin (TBT) antifouling paint, a chemical that changes the genders of marine snails. Related Article Water The 2000-tonne ship at risk of sinking and causing chaos on harbour and across the city Other concerns included corroded guardrails, water ingress, missing and rotten timber planks, large areas of flaking paint, a crane that was not stowed correctly, a stairway at high risk of failure and holes large enough to see daylight. Heavy rust wastage at the stern left it “extremely vulnerable” to flooding, and its positioning near the waterline on the exposed side of the ship meant such flooding was highly likely, the report found. The hull plate in the main hold was also pocked with large holes that were likely to get bigger if disturbed.



“It could be as simple as the wake from a passing vessel and wave pressure breaching the hull further, and due to the size of this void space it could potentially be catastrophic,” the report said. Sea Heritage Foundation did not directly answer questions about the condition of the ship, but disputed through its legal adviser any suggestion that it was incompetent or indifferent to safety or environmental protection, and said it was exploring legal action against the Herald. “It would be seriously misleading to present historical observations as current findings without assessing subsequent repairs, mitigation measures and technical evidence,” legal counsel George Caramanlis said. He did not address questions about the foundation’s lack of insurance on the vessel. Watt said many insurers were unwilling to take on ageing vessels and Maritime NSW planned to crack down on unsafe vessels, removing them when necessary.



“When you go out on Sydney Harbour, you can see this is not the only vessel in disrepair. I can tell you it will not be the only one,” she said. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: ‘Heartbreaking milestone’: WA’s road toll overtakes 2025 figure in horror 48 hours
World.content:
NationalWARoad safety ‘Heartbreaking milestone’: WA’s road toll overtakes 2025 figure in horror 48 hours Holly Thompson November 15, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Five people have died on West Australian roads over the past two days, bringing the state’s road toll to 186 for the year – surpassing the 184 people who lost their lives in 2025. Three people – a 23-year-old man, a 22-year-old woman and a 21-year-old man – all lost their lives on Friday morning, after the car they were driving, along Yilliminning Road towards Narrogin, left the road and collided with trees. Tailgating was the third most common broken road rule seen on WA roads, according to a survey last year. Paul Rovere On Friday evening, a 35-year-old man died when his Kawasaki motorcycle collided with a Triumph motorcycle along Mandurah Road in Dudley Park. The rider of the Triumph motorcycle sustained non-life-threatening injuries.



And a 41-year-old man died on Saturday night in Mumballup, south-east of Bunbury, after his car left the road and struck a tree. All five were declared deceased at the scene of the crashes. The majority were in regional areas. Shadow Minister for Road Safety Julie Freeman said it was a “heartbreaking milestone that no Western Australian wanted to see”. “My thoughts are with the families, friends and communities grieving these devastating losses, particularly in Narrogin where three young lives were taken far too soon,” she said. “Every road death is one too many, but the fact we’ve already surpassed last year’s toll with weeks still to come should be setting off alarm bells.”



Back in July, head of communications at insurer RAC Rhys Heron warned that “if we keep going the way we’re going, we will likely see more than 200 people killed on our roads for the first time in 18 years.” And a WA Road Safety Commission spokesperson said the issue was complex, challenging, constantly changing, “and it requires a unified community-driven approach to reduce fatalities”. Freeman said regional communities continue to carry a disproportionate share of the road toll, highlighting the urgent need for greater investment in practical road safety improvements. “For years we’ve seen the same tragic patterns repeated on regional roads, yet too many high-risk stretches remain without the safety upgrades proven to save lives,” she said. “Money collected through the Road Trauma Trust Account should be directed towards delivering safer regional roads through shoulder sealing, audible edge lines, overtaking lanes and other evidence-based improvements, not diverted into government administration.



“We cannot accept rising road deaths as inevitable.” The government has previously stated it is tipping millions of dollars into regional point-to-point speed cameras over the coming years, alongside an investment in school zone speed enforcement and a plan to double the number of safety camera trailers on WA roads. Freeman urged motorists travelling in the lead-up to Christmas to drive to the conditions, avoid fatigue and make safety their priority. If you or anyone you know has been affected by a road crash, contact Road Trauma Support WA on 1300 004 814.

World.title: ‘Baby, she’s back!’ SpaceX’s Starship is caught midair in a dramatic first
World.content:
Perspective WorldNorth AmericaElon Musk ‘Baby, she’s back!’ SpaceX’s Starship is caught midair in a dramatic first Marcia Dunn November 15, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Canaveral: SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday (US time), caught by giant mechanical arms on its launchpad. It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for – the first-ever capture of a Starship returning from space. As the first-stage booster exploded shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas 22 hours earlier, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel. Booster wreckage was still cordoned off in the Gulf of Mexico, as the sleek stainless-steel spacecraft lowered itself upright onto the pad, sci-fi style. Loading The capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned up and down the spacecraft, supported by the arms of the launch tower.



“Look at her! Baby, she’s back!” shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot, then Musk congratulated his “incredible team”. SpaceX officials said the catch demonstrated Starship’s capacity for full re-use, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling, while three previous booster catches validated the technique. SpaceX’s mega rocket Starship lifts off for a test flight from Texas on November 13. AP Photo/Eric Gay NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: he wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars. “It was almost magic,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer.” He added emojis of the moon and the US flag.



The world’s largest and most powerful rocket – a 124-metre behemoth – blasted off from the Starship base near the US-Mexican border, separating neatly from its booster before things went awry. Related Article Space Lasers and a table-sized spider: What the next lunar landing could look like The upper stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites. From 265 kilometres up, Starship streamed down live views of itself and Earth via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 orbits, outshining the previous mission. It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and only its second trip to orbit. SpaceX reported that all equipment, including the craft’s vital heat shield, appeared to work well. As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down – its guidance system sensed it was out of position and automatically initiated the watery detour and destruction. Engineers are investigating.



The booster for Starship on its ill-fated return over the Gulf of Mexico. AP Photo/Eric Gay SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy centre within months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice. Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with both Starship and Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will alternate delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago. World.title: Enough with all the ‘learnings’. It’s time for the Wallabies to pass a big test
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Enough with all the ‘learnings’. It’s time for the Wallabies to pass a big test Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter November 15, 2026 — 11:30am

November 15, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The internet attributes the quote to Nelson Mandela, but it may as well have come from Ted Lasso: “You either win or you learn.” Whoever coined it, modern athletes have wholeheartedly embraced the cliché and its derivations. Listen to any post-match media comments of a losing team, and you will hear endless chat about taking “learnings” from the defeat. Loading There’ve been countless learnings for the Wallabies in recent times, we are told. And no wonder, given the last three games for Australia have all been monster losses that have exposed a litany of problems. But just as we came to ruefully understand at school, there comes a point where the learning stops and exams have to be passed.



For the Wallabies, that moment arrives in Edinburgh. Up against a skilful Scotland side that sits one place above them in the world rankings, and are captained by the pugnacious ex-Australian Sione Tuipulotu, the visiting Wallabies will be given another stern test in all the areas they’ve been painfully learning from in recent outings. They have come in a number of places, but it’s hard to not start with the defence. The Wallabies have leaked 138 points in three Tests, and while that’s an obviously ugly headline figure, other stats are insightful. The Wallabies observed a minute’s silence ahead of training on Remembrance Day. Getty Images The Wallabies have missed an average of 31 tackles per game, and conceded an average of 12 line breaks, in the two losses to New Zealand and against England. In July, however, against Ireland, France and Italy, they only missed 20 tackles per game and gave up an average of six line breaks. The fact the Wallabies had one centre pairing throughout July – Ikitau and Suaalii – but had a new midfield combination for each of the past three, points to a contributing cause: constant change brings a lack of connection and understanding, under pressure.



Whatever system the Wallabies are trying to use – and it has felt confusing – almost doesn’t matter when individuals make a rash decision to shoot up solo or bite in, and then everything rapidly unfolds. “Once you lose one connection piece, you get on the back foot, and then you’re not getting into a set piece or a set position where you can get off the line hard as you’d like to,” Kiss said on Friday about the “learnings” in defence. “That’s been — it sort of dominoes on us a bit. That’s obvious, I think we can all see that once a little bit of a chink happens, that domino effect on you happens quickly.” Harry Wilson training in Edinburgh. Getty Images The return of Ikitau and Suaalii, and the instinctive trust earned in 19 Tests together, will help shore up the Wallabies defence. Some old-fashioned dominant tackling is needed, too, however. England crossed the gainline with 56 per cent of their carries, and averaged almost five metres per carry. Any defence, when back-peddling, will find it tough to maintain shape.



Indeed, that’s the basis of the Wallabies’ attack plans: punch through the line and then use momentum, pace and skill to play on top of a rival. But the Wallabies haven’t recently won the physical battle when they have the ball, either, and have this week been working on those “learnings”. Josh Moorby of the All Blacks cuts through the Wallabies defence. Getty Images Some of that will be more variety in ball-carrying to be less predictable with one-out running, more ball-playing from Ryan Lonergan near the ruck, more deception at the line, and more smart kicking against rush defences. But it will also be a healthy dose of “just give the ball to Bobby V”, given Rob Valetini’s reputation of carrying like a concrete truck. But the biggest “learning” the Wallabies will need is a reminder that winning can often come down to who wants it more.



Former All Blacks coach Steve Hansen said on a podcast last week he was stunned by the Wallabies’ “lack of urgency” against England. Harry Wilson conceded post-game that, for some reason, they didn’t arrive with the right mindset. England were hungrier. Ensuring this doesn’t happen again in Edinburgh must be the Wallabies’ biggest “learning”. Henry Pollock of England celebrates with his teammates after scoring his second try. Getty Images Mindset and hunger levels will be the decisive battleground at Murrayfield. Scotland are, lest we forget, also coming off a humbling loss to the All Blacks. They have had a similar week of “hurting” and “soul-searching” and will be just as fired-up as the Wallabies, and they’ll have a buzzing Murrayfield at their backs.



There is yet another layer of pressure to ensure they get mindset right, and be dominant early. Related Article Analysis

Australian rugby It won’t be the last time the French raid Australia’s top rugby talent Given what they’ve recently been through, it’s easy to imagine the team that doesn’t start well quickly loses confidence and gets the dreaded “here we go again” feel. The side that rediscovers their mojo will, by contrast, likely keep it, and use it to push it away. Less than one year out from the World Cup, Monday brings a test the Wallabies must pass, if they are to prove to the world – and, more importantly, to themselves – that they are contenders. World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics Construction of $1.4b Brisbane Arena to begin within weeks. Take a look around Cloe Read November 15, 2026 — 12:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Construction of the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena is set to begin within weeks, after it was announced on Sunday that the Gather Brisbane consortium would deliver the entertainment precinct, with its opening expected by 2031. The 17,000-seat arena will host various events, such as concerts, family shows, and sports, and will have access to Woolloongabba’s underground Cross River Rail station, alongside a new pedestrian bridge connecting to Stanley Street and the South East Busway. The Gabba Entertainment Precinct, which comprises two pieces of land totalling nine hectares, will replace the Brisbane Entertainment Centre at Boondall in the city’s north. Loading The nearby Gabba Stadium will be demolished following the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games as part of a state government plan for almost 4000 homes.



Earlier this year, Gather Brisbane was shortlisted alongside Ignite, formerly Brisbane Entertainment Alliance, for the build. On Sunday, the government announced Gather Brisbane, which brings together Plenary, Live Nation, Oak View Group and Webuild, would be responsible for the arena’s design, build, financing, maintenance and operation. Gather Brisbane has been selected to deliver the Gabba Entertainment and Housing Precinct. Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the consortium’s selection marked a major milestone, with work expected to start in January. “The stage is now set for something special at Woolloongabba. This will be transformational for the area, and generational for millions of people who will come to live, visit and enjoy this new precinct,” he said.



Taking aim at Labor over “taxpayers forking out billions for a new arena”, Bleijie said the government had instead gathered a group of powerhouses in their fields to deliver an incredible legacy for Queensland that would also “respect taxpayers’ money”. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Ekka upgrade’s quarter-billion-plus price tag revealed “We knew that this was a site that had so much potential, but we saw the chaos and confusion before the October 2024 election, where the Gabba was either going to be knocked down, rebuilt, refurbished, painted, and we had a different vision for this area,” he said. Once the arena is completed, the state government will make a one-off $600 million capital investment in the project, which is not part of the $7.1 billion venue infrastructure budget for the 2032 Olympics. “You will recall the previous government had a plan for an arena at a cost of $2.4 billion that had to be changed three locations because it was over the old Roma Street railyards … we said we’d partner with the private sector, and we’ve gone through a competitive process,” Bleijie said.



“This is a $1.4 billion arena, a $600 million capital contribution from the state government, but we don’t pay that until 2031.” Related Article Exclusive

Jobs Queensland leads nation for civil engineering jobs amid Olympic build Bleijie said the contribution would be offset by the sale and staged release of the Gabba stadium land to the consortium, to make way for about 4000 new homes. Under the deal, the government will continue to own the Brisbane Arena land until at least 2071, and will enter into a long-term commercial arrangement with the operator. The build was also backed by Brisbane singers The Veronicas, who said the arena would give the next generation of artists a bigger stage.



“We were saying we are definitely down to christen the arena once it’s fully up and running,” Jess Origliasso said. Plenary Group head of development Sergio Calcarao said the project would redefine the way city precincts in Australia and abroad are designed, developed and delivered. “With a diverse range of housing and community infrastructure being integrated into this master planned precinct, this project is arguably the most significant urban renewal legacy opportunity stemming from this Games infrastructure program.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Commercial childcare is hitting a brick wall. Who will pick up the pieces?
World.content:
Analysis BusinessCompaniesChildcare Commercial childcare is hitting a brick wall. Who will pick up the pieces? Colin Kruger November 15, 2026 — 12:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

At first blush it looked like great news for investors in Australia’s largest listed childcare provider. G8 Education shares more than doubled within hours on Thursday after the group revealed its warm welcome of a potential private equity offer at a 260 per cent premium to its record-low share price. G8 Education’s board have warmed to a takeover offer valuing the group at less than $200 million. G8 chief executive Pejman Okhovat (centre) and board directors: (from top left down) Debra Singh, Margaret Zabel and Toni Thornton; (from top right down) Julie Cogin, Stephen Heath and Peter Trimble. Like most of the kids in G8’s care, the suitor – Majority Capital Partners – is a newborn with little experience of the sector. It was set up just this year by Vidhur Rangaswamy, a veteran of John Wylie, and backed by rock-star investors like Will Vicars. The 26¢ a share indicative cash offer, subject to further due diligence, contrasts with shares that had dropped from 70¢ at the start of the year to a low of 10¢ before the offer was revealed. Last year the stock was worth as much as $1.40.



That was before G8 revealed the scale of the challenges it faces with occupancy levels plunging, leading to the suspension of 40 underperforming centres that are not expected to reopen. Related Article Analysis

Billionaires There has never been another scandal like this G8’s fortunes reflect a market landscape rocked by falling fertility rates, rising costs, and rising standards of care demanded by customers following the sex abuse scandals, which have hit commercial operators particularly hard. As you would expect, G8 is not the only one to have suffered. Just weeks ago, Shared Beginnings childcare collapsed after its owners, ASX-listed private lender Finexia, called in administrators.



Finexia got lumbered with the centres last year, thanks to its role as a lender to Genius childcare when it collapsed. Genius and its boss, Gold Coast entrepreneur Darren Misquitta, got lumbered with many of these centres in 2023, when G8 Education paid it $26.5 million to take 31 struggling centres off its hands. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese wants universal early education and care to be part of his legacy but experts say a different model might be needed. Outside of this G8 loop we have private-equity-owned Edge Early Learning, which went into voluntary administration in August with 70 centres. Just last week, six centres were closed in South Australia and Victoria. Not-for-profit Goodstart had agreed to acquire them last month but these centres failed to pass due diligence.



It’s not a good sign when an operator built from the ashes of Australia’s largest for-profit childcare failure, ABC Learning, could not make these centres sustainable. “As a not-for-profit we must make careful decisions about where we invest,” a spokesperson said. “While Goodstart stands ready to make investments in extra staff, capital upgrades, and more professional development in those centres we are purchasing, some centres come with major difficulties which even extra investment will struggle to fix.” ‘The risk of viability doesn’t sit with the people making the decisions when the property is built. It ends up with providers, families and governments. A handful of unviable leases can drag down a whole provider.’ Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow, childcare think tank The Front Project The collapse of commercial operators is a growing trend.



Data extracted from the corporate regulator by not-for-profit social impact investment fund manager For Purpose Investment Partners (FPIP) shows 58 childcare centres collapsed between July 1 and October 11 this year. This compares with 35 failures in the whole of the 2025/26 financial year, which was marred by the sex abuse scandals. In less than four months we had more failures than any full year since ASIC started collecting information in 2021. Of the 210 childcare companies that have failed since 2021, only four were not privately owned. Perversely, this is where most of the new supply is coming from. Since 2022, more than 90 per cent of new centre approvals were privately owned.



But as a recent report from childcare think tank The Front Project (TFP) shows, it is the landlords who have been dictating terms. This has created oversupply and cannibalisation in lucrative areas, and childcare deserts in others. Related Article Opinion

Cost of living We’re supposed to be struggling, yet we’re spending more. Why? Millie Muroi Economics Writer “Right now, how big a centre is – and where it’s located – comes down to what it costs to build. Children’s needs barely come into it. That’s why some communities have no access to childcare and others have too much,” TFP chief executive Dr Caroline Croser-Barlow says. The specialised needs of childcare centres – and the limit on competition due to the fact that markets are hyper-localised, restricting parent choices to a narrow geographic radius – have given developers the upper hand, while operators wear all the business risk. “The risk of viability doesn’t sit with the people making the decisions when the property is built. It ends up with providers, families and governments. A handful of unviable leases can drag down a whole provider, and because the lease follows the business when it’s sold to the next provider, the impact can last for years,” Croser-Barlow says.



TFP is among those calling for an independent commission to oversee a sector that is failing to match services with demand, thanks to a model where the government hands billions to private operators and leaves the result to market forces. Georgie Dent, head of advocacy group The Parenthood, says a clear picture is emerging of a funding model that has driven significant investment from listed companies, private equity and investors but with no management or oversight of where services are actually needed. G8 faces challenges with occupancy levels plunging, leading to the suspension of 40 underperforming centres that are not expected to reopen. Paul Jeffers “[It] has really led us to the position where we are today, where we are seeing really significant closures,” Dent says. The Parenthood says childcare provision needs to be put through the same lens as school provision and based on community needs, not market forces.



“We are not leaving it up to the market to determine which suburbs have got greater capacity to pay higher fees for school … We provide it because we recognise that public education is essential infrastructure.” Former Macquarie executive Michael Traill, who is chair of FPIP, says the ownership model is also an important factor for sustainable quality care. Traill, who helped set up Macquarie’s private equity business, understands the outsized returns demanded by PE and listed company owners that drive up costs and affordability issues. His answer? Long-term ownership, ethically focused and capable of driving long-term ethical returns. His “patient capital” model calls for super funds to play a bigger role, like Australian Ethical Super is in the aged care sector.



“They’re very long-term investors, so the objective is of owning these assets, running them with an emphasis on quality and inclusion, but driving a long long-term ethical return,” he says. Related Article Media & marketing It’s a vertical world in Hollywood’s new gold rush Traill says this funding model doesn’t just apply to childcare and should be welcomed by governments spending billions on these services. “If you look at the sectors we’re talking about – aged care, early learning, social and affordable housing, social disability support for housing – they’re all areas where governments are very, very significant players in terms of the policy and funding it provides,” he says. But Traill, who was instrumental in setting up Goodstart from the ABC Learning failure, also pointed to the split between ownership and operation of childcare centres as another issue to address.



Traill calls it a “natural tension” between the objectives of a landlord to maximise development profits and rent, and an operator for whom rents are such a significant component of costs. “There’s a different skill set in developing and building childcare centres but, certainly, our view would be it’s easy to have alignment where you’ve got ownership of that under one entity.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Secret report finds 2000-tonne ship poses severe environmental threat
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWWater Secret report finds 2000-tonne ship poses severe environmental threat Harriet Alexander and Carrie Fellner Updated November 15, 2026 — 12:32pm ,first published November 15, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A 2000-tonne ship seized by NSW Maritime near the busiest shipping zone in Sydney Harbour has holes in its hull so gaping that a passing wave could sink the vessel and cause an environmental catastrophe. An independent surveyor’s report on the condition of the MV Cape Don warned early last year that the vessel was “severely deteriorated” and the bilge pumping arrangements were grossly inadequate to manage flooding or water ingress. NSW Maritime took possession of the MV Cape Don last month. Sam Mooy “The risk of catastrophic failure of the port side hull plate is extremely high, which would pose an immediate and severe environmental threat,” the confidential report by AMSA Accredited Marine Surveyors reported. But the hazard is unlikely to be removed from its mooring at Balls Head in Waverton until next year, due to the logistical challenges of dismantling a ship in such frail condition.



NSW Maritime executive director Nicole Watts said the agency was exploring options, including dismantling the vessel in place or scooping it out of the water from underneath in a “bath tub scenario” to ensure it did not crumble during disassembly. This may require specialist equipment to be brought in from overseas. One such option is operating in Darwin and that facility may be available to NSW Maritime after its current job is complete. Depending on which option NSW Maritime pursues, the salvage is likely to cost $15 to $20 million and will be borne by the taxpayers because the vessel is uninsured. “We’ve obviously got to go through our procurement process, but we’re aware of the emergency,” Watts said, recalling the 2022 sinking of the former Manly ferry MV Baragoola. The MV Baragoola was moored beside the Cape Don on the Coal Loader at Waverton when it sank. Edwina Pickles



“It needs to be done very urgently because things can change imminently. We don’t want a repeat of the Baragoola.” NSW Premier Chris Minns on Sunday said the government had to step in because of the serious implications for the environment, Sydney Harbour and the reputation of the state. “I’d expect anyone who owns or operates a boat in the maritime sector to follow the rules,” he said. “We have to make sure that there are appropriate regulations and penalties in place if there is a breach because it can’t just be shovelled over to the taxpayer when things go wrong.” MV Cape Don, a former lighthouse supply tender, was bought by the charitable Sea Heritage Foundation in 2004, since which time volunteers have been painstakingly repairing it with plans to open it up as a museum. In recent years, it has been used for university research and as a classroom for cub scouts, who drew on the expertise of the marine engineers and shipwrights working on its restoration to design a water surface cleaning robot.





The private surveyors noted the presence of environmental hazards, including asbestos, zinc chromate paint and the previous use of tributyltin (TBT) antifouling paint, a chemical that changes the genders of marine snails. Related Article Water The 2000-tonne ship at risk of sinking and causing chaos on harbour and across the city Other concerns included corroded guardrails, water ingress, missing and rotten timber planks, large areas of flaking paint, a crane that was not stowed correctly, a stairway at high risk of failure and holes large enough to see daylight. Heavy rust wastage at the stern left it “extremely vulnerable” to flooding, and its positioning near the waterline on the exposed side of the ship meant such flooding was highly likely, the report found. The hull plate in the main hold was also pocked with large holes that were likely to get bigger if disturbed.



“It could be as simple as the wake from a passing vessel and wave pressure breaching the hull further, and due to the size of this void space it could potentially be catastrophic,” the report said. Sea Heritage Foundation did not directly answer questions about the condition of the ship, but disputed through its legal adviser any suggestion that it was incompetent or indifferent to safety or environmental protection, and said it was exploring legal action against the Herald. “It would be seriously misleading to present historical observations as current findings without assessing subsequent repairs, mitigation measures and technical evidence,” legal counsel George Caramanlis said. He did not address questions about the foundation’s lack of insurance on the vessel. Watt said many insurers were unwilling to take on ageing vessels and Maritime NSW planned to crack down on unsafe vessels, removing them when necessary.



“When you go out on Sydney Harbour, you can see this is not the only vessel in disrepair. I can tell you it will not be the only one,” she said. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: ‘Heartbreaking milestone’: WA’s road toll overtakes 2025 figure in horror 48 hours
World.content:
NationalWARoad safety ‘Heartbreaking milestone’: WA’s road toll overtakes 2025 figure in horror 48 hours Holly Thompson November 15, 2026 — 11:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Five people have died on West Australian roads over the past two days, bringing the state’s road toll to 186 for the year – surpassing the 184 people who lost their lives in 2025. Three people – a 23-year-old man, a 22-year-old woman and a 21-year-old man – all lost their lives on Friday morning, after the car they were driving, along Yilliminning Road towards Narrogin, left the road and collided with trees. Tailgating was the third most common broken road rule seen on WA roads, according to a survey last year. Paul Rovere On Friday evening, a 35-year-old man died when his Kawasaki motorcycle collided with a Triumph motorcycle along Mandurah Road in Dudley Park. The rider of the Triumph motorcycle sustained non-life-threatening injuries.



And a 41-year-old man died on Saturday night in Mumballup, south-east of Bunbury, after his car left the road and struck a tree. All five were declared deceased at the scene of the crashes. The majority were in regional areas. Shadow Minister for Road Safety Julie Freeman said it was a “heartbreaking milestone that no Western Australian wanted to see”. “My thoughts are with the families, friends and communities grieving these devastating losses, particularly in Narrogin where three young lives were taken far too soon,” she said. “Every road death is one too many, but the fact we’ve already surpassed last year’s toll with weeks still to come should be setting off alarm bells.”



Back in July, head of communications at insurer RAC Rhys Heron warned that “if we keep going the way we’re going, we will likely see more than 200 people killed on our roads for the first time in 18 years.” And a WA Road Safety Commission spokesperson said the issue was complex, challenging, constantly changing, “and it requires a unified community-driven approach to reduce fatalities”. Freeman said regional communities continue to carry a disproportionate share of the road toll, highlighting the urgent need for greater investment in practical road safety improvements. “For years we’ve seen the same tragic patterns repeated on regional roads, yet too many high-risk stretches remain without the safety upgrades proven to save lives,” she said. “Money collected through the Road Trauma Trust Account should be directed towards delivering safer regional roads through shoulder sealing, audible edge lines, overtaking lanes and other evidence-based improvements, not diverted into government administration.



“We cannot accept rising road deaths as inevitable.” The government has previously stated it is tipping millions of dollars into regional point-to-point speed cameras over the coming years, alongside an investment in school zone speed enforcement and a plan to double the number of safety camera trailers on WA roads. Freeman urged motorists travelling in the lead-up to Christmas to drive to the conditions, avoid fatigue and make safety their priority. If you or anyone you know has been affected by a road crash, contact Road Trauma Support WA on 1300 004 814.

World.title: ‘Baby, she’s back!’ SpaceX’s Starship is caught midair in a dramatic first
World.content:
Perspective WorldNorth AmericaElon Musk ‘Baby, she’s back!’ SpaceX’s Starship is caught midair in a dramatic first Marcia Dunn November 15, 2026 — 11:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Cape Canaveral: SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday (US time), caught by giant mechanical arms on its launchpad. It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for – the first-ever capture of a Starship returning from space. As the first-stage booster exploded shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas 22 hours earlier, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel. Booster wreckage was still cordoned off in the Gulf of Mexico, as the sleek stainless-steel spacecraft lowered itself upright onto the pad, sci-fi style. Loading The capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned up and down the spacecraft, supported by the arms of the launch tower.



“Look at her! Baby, she’s back!” shouted SpaceX commentator Dan Huot, then Musk congratulated his “incredible team”. SpaceX officials said the catch demonstrated Starship’s capacity for full re-use, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling, while three previous booster catches validated the technique. SpaceX’s mega rocket Starship lifts off for a test flight from Texas on November 13. AP Photo/Eric Gay NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: he wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars. “It was almost magic,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer.” He added emojis of the moon and the US flag.



The world’s largest and most powerful rocket – a 124-metre behemoth – blasted off from the Starship base near the US-Mexican border, separating neatly from its booster before things went awry. Related Article Space Lasers and a table-sized spider: What the next lunar landing could look like The upper stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites. From 265 kilometres up, Starship streamed down live views of itself and Earth via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 orbits, outshining the previous mission. It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and only its second trip to orbit. SpaceX reported that all equipment, including the craft’s vital heat shield, appeared to work well. As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down – its guidance system sensed it was out of position and automatically initiated the watery detour and destruction. Engineers are investigating.



The booster for Starship on its ill-fated return over the Gulf of Mexico. AP Photo/Eric Gay SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy centre within months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice. Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with both Starship and Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will alternate delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago. World.title: Enough with all the ‘learnings’. It’s time for the Wallabies to pass a big test
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion Enough with all the ‘learnings’. It’s time for the Wallabies to pass a big test Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter November 15, 2026 — 11:30am

November 15, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The internet attributes the quote to Nelson Mandela, but it may as well have come from Ted Lasso: “You either win or you learn.” Whoever coined it, modern athletes have wholeheartedly embraced the cliché and its derivations. Listen to any post-match media comments of a losing team, and you will hear endless chat about taking “learnings” from the defeat. Loading There’ve been countless learnings for the Wallabies in recent times, we are told. And no wonder, given the last three games for Australia have all been monster losses that have exposed a litany of problems. But just as we came to ruefully understand at school, there comes a point where the learning stops and exams have to be passed.



For the Wallabies, that moment arrives in Edinburgh. Up against a skilful Scotland side that sits one place above them in the world rankings, and are captained by the pugnacious ex-Australian Sione Tuipulotu, the visiting Wallabies will be given another stern test in all the areas they’ve been painfully learning from in recent outings. They have come in a number of places, but it’s hard to not start with the defence. The Wallabies have leaked 138 points in three Tests, and while that’s an obviously ugly headline figure, other stats are insightful. The Wallabies observed a minute’s silence ahead of training on Remembrance Day. Getty Images The Wallabies have missed an average of 31 tackles per game, and conceded an average of 12 line breaks, in the two losses to New Zealand and against England. In July, however, against Ireland, France and Italy, they only missed 20 tackles per game and gave up an average of six line breaks. The fact the Wallabies had one centre pairing throughout July – Ikitau and Suaalii – but had a new midfield combination for each of the past three, points to a contributing cause: constant change brings a lack of connection and understanding, under pressure.



Whatever system the Wallabies are trying to use – and it has felt confusing – almost doesn’t matter when individuals make a rash decision to shoot up solo or bite in, and then everything rapidly unfolds. “Once you lose one connection piece, you get on the back foot, and then you’re not getting into a set piece or a set position where you can get off the line hard as you’d like to,” Kiss said on Friday about the “learnings” in defence. “That’s been — it sort of dominoes on us a bit. That’s obvious, I think we can all see that once a little bit of a chink happens, that domino effect on you happens quickly.” Harry Wilson training in Edinburgh. Getty Images The return of Ikitau and Suaalii, and the instinctive trust earned in 19 Tests together, will help shore up the Wallabies defence. Some old-fashioned dominant tackling is needed, too, however. England crossed the gainline with 56 per cent of their carries, and averaged almost five metres per carry. Any defence, when back-peddling, will find it tough to maintain shape.



Indeed, that’s the basis of the Wallabies’ attack plans: punch through the line and then use momentum, pace and skill to play on top of a rival. But the Wallabies haven’t recently won the physical battle when they have the ball, either, and have this week been working on those “learnings”. Josh Moorby of the All Blacks cuts through the Wallabies defence. Getty Images Some of that will be more variety in ball-carrying to be less predictable with one-out running, more ball-playing from Ryan Lonergan near the ruck, more deception at the line, and more smart kicking against rush defences. But it will also be a healthy dose of “just give the ball to Bobby V”, given Rob Valetini’s reputation of carrying like a concrete truck. But the biggest “learning” the Wallabies will need is a reminder that winning can often come down to who wants it more.



Former All Blacks coach Steve Hansen said on a podcast last week he was stunned by the Wallabies’ “lack of urgency” against England. Harry Wilson conceded post-game that, for some reason, they didn’t arrive with the right mindset. England were hungrier. Ensuring this doesn’t happen again in Edinburgh must be the Wallabies’ biggest “learning”. Henry Pollock of England celebrates with his teammates after scoring his second try. Getty Images Mindset and hunger levels will be the decisive battleground at Murrayfield. Scotland are, lest we forget, also coming off a humbling loss to the All Blacks. They have had a similar week of “hurting” and “soul-searching” and will be just as fired-up as the Wallabies, and they’ll have a buzzing Murrayfield at their backs.



There is yet another layer of pressure to ensure they get mindset right, and be dominant early. Related Article Analysis

Australian rugby It won’t be the last time the French raid Australia’s top rugby talent Given what they’ve recently been through, it’s easy to imagine the team that doesn’t start well quickly loses confidence and gets the dreaded “here we go again” feel. The side that rediscovers their mojo will, by contrast, likely keep it, and use it to push it away. Less than one year out from the World Cup, Monday brings a test the Wallabies must pass, if they are to prove to the world – and, more importantly, to themselves – that they are contenders. A failed federal Liberal candidate and anti-trans campaigner from Sydney’s Northern Beaches, a forklift driver, and a South Coast surf lifesaver are among One Nation candidates contesting the NSW state election in March.

One Nation NSW leader Mike Newman on Sunday announced four new upper house candidates for the state poll as he emphasised their “real-world experience” and said the group was “not a team of career politicians”.

One Nation’s latest upper house candidate Katherine Deves speaks to the media on Sunday. George Chan

“This is a team that reflects our membership ... They are not taxpayer-funded political careerists or cookie-cutter candidates,” Newman said.

The candidates are Sydney lawyer Katherine Deves, who is the former Liberal Party candidate for the federal seat of Warringah; Arnon Wither from the Hunter region, who has worked in manufacturing, construction; educator and mother-of-eight Manti Steele from western NSW; and teacher and surf lifesaver Daniel Hill from the NSW South Coast.

A person died at Te Mata Peak in Havelock North on Saturday afternoon, with the park now closed under a rāhui.

Local mana whenua had blessed the area and placed a rāhui over the park, she said.

World.title: All Blacks coach Dave Rennie promises tough review after shock Wales loss
World.content:
The All Blacks will look at all aspects of their preparation and performance after their historic 35-28 defeat to Wales in Cardiff.

Head coach Dave Rennie admitted to being "hurt" by the setback, stating, "We expect a lot more of ourselves".

Wales outscored the All Blacks five converted tries to four on Sunday morning NZT, but their defensive intensity in the final 25 minutes was the most notable aspect of the nation's first win against New Zealand since 1953.

The All Blacks were missing several key players, with the selectors opted to make eight changes to the starting line-up, following their excellent win over Scotland last week. They were held up over the tryline three times and, despite a wealth of possession and territory in the final quarter, they could not break what skipper Beauden Barrett described as a defensive "brick wall".

It was easily New Zealand's worst test performance since their defeat to England at Twickenham under former coach Scott Robertson 12 months ago.

"We'll look at everything, because when you lose, it's not just on the players," Rennie said afterwards. "It's everything around how did we prepare the team this week, selections and our decision-making around substitutions coming on."

The players' own decision-making during the 80 minutes will also come into focus, because there was a huge step backwards in this area, after keeping Scotland scoreless in the second half in Edinburgh seven days earlier.

Their commitment to an offloading game at inappropriate times hurt them in the first half, and after the break, their determination to charge straight at a set Welsh defence time and again was a big failure in terms of strategy, if not common sense.

"I think we turned the ball over nine times in the first half and four of them were offloads," Rennie said. "It's a point of difference for us, but it's about the quality of decision - sighting the target and using the appropriate pass.

"The quality of our decision-making wasn't sharp enough.

Wales celebrate their historic victory over the All Blacks in Cardiff. Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

"Credit to Wales, they were really clinical when they got their chances and then they defended for massive amounts of periods. They were the better side tonight.

"We created opportunities, but I thought we got a bit one-dimensional. There were times when I thought we could have stayed on one side of the field and played through them when we had good numbers.

"We'd play away from that... and try to carry through them, when we had actually squeezed them up. That's decision-making under pressure and they provided a lot of pressure tonight."

For skipper Barrett, the test - his first as captain and 149th in total - was meant to be a celebration of a hugely successful 14-year career, but instead became mired in misery.

"It's a tough one to take, particularly when we were building a lot of pressure and we couldn't convert that into points," he said. "Numerous times, we were held up and it just felt like we needed one of those [to be successful] to get back in the game and level the scoreboard.

"The whole game would have changed. Frustrated - it felt like a brick wall at times."

Wales made more than 300 tackles during the match and, critically, did not concede a penalty in the final 15 minutes.

The All Blacks badly missed the quality of halfback Cam Roigard, and solidity of second-five Jordie Barrett and wing Will Jordan, the latter two recovering from injury.

The combination of Cortez Ratima in the No.9 jersey and No.10 Richie Mo'unga, back from a calf injury for his second test of the year, did not gel, and while Quinn Tupaea was busy and brave, midfield partner Anton Lienert-Brown struggled for influence.

Asked about Mo'unga, Rennie was not glowing in his praise.

"We were under a fair bit of pressure and he was forced to run a fair bit. It was a tough day for a lot of people today."

Wing Fehi Fineanganofo scored a try in his first test - an important one just before halftime, thanks to assistance from No.8 Wallace Sititi and Tupaea - but he struggled defensively, with Wales too easily finding space down his sideline.

For all of Barrett's experience at fullback, his occasional indecision was costly.

Quizzed on whether he was "out-coached" by Wales rival Steve Tandy, Rennie said: "We certainly got out-passioned - you can put it how you like."

Wales coach Steve Tandy celebrates the win with player Dafydd Jenkins. Gareth Everett / Photosport

Asked about the wholesale changes to his team during the week, he replied: "We had a good enough side on the field to win tonight.

"If you look at the stats, we had enough opportunities. We created enough chances, we just weren't clinical enough and Wales were very good defensively.

"I have no regrets about the side we put out. It hurts, but you've got to take it on the chin.

"Wales were passionate and every time they kept us out, I reckon they grew and became harder to break down.

"We've got to be better - we expect a lot more of ourselves and we need to see a response at Twickenham next week."

Wales coach Tandy and captain Dewi Lake received a standing ovation, as they entered the post-test press conference.

"It's probably nice to sit in this room and not be disappointed for once," Lake said.

Tandy said: "You see what it means to the nation and the players. We've been wanting some positivity and I think the players did that today.

"The overriding emotion is pride for the playing group and staff."

A day after France's remarkable 21-19 victory over South Africa in Paris, the result has blown the Nations Championship wide open again.

A victory for the All Blacks before next weekend's England clash would have put them in the boxseat for the top playoff fixture against the No.1-ranked northern hemisphere side.

Instead, Rennie's men hold only a one-point advantage over the Springboks, thanks to their two losing bonus points.

World.title: 'Flood' of weka sightings in Dunedin becomes a trickle
World.content:
Weka look likely to disappear from Dunedin again, despite a breeding pair making their home in a northern suburb last year.

They used to live in the area - Otago Peninsula's iconic Hereweka translates to 'catch the weka' - but they were wiped out along the east coast of the South Island and now the nearest populations live a few hundred kilometres away.

Retired ornithologist Bruce McKinlay started to record weka sightings in the city over the last five years, after receiving credible reports.

"In February, March 2025, there was a real flood of them," he said.

McKinlay recorded about 76 sightings by September last year.

Audio player for " Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2607793%2Fflood-of-weka-sightings-in-dunedin-becomes-a-trickle

Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return Morning Report Download MP3 3m

There were three clearly different groups of weka - a breeding pair in Normanby that had three broods of chicks, one at Seconds Beach at St Clair and one on the Otago Peninsula, he said.

Then the reporting unexpectedly stopped.

The last sighting of the St Clair weka was in October last year and reports of the Normanby weka stopped from about March, he said.

Only the weka on the peninsula remained.

"Weka, no matter how confident or bolshy you think they look, are susceptible to predation," he said.

Stories from iwi suggested weka were an important seasonal food in the area before European settlement and hapū would travel to harvest weka at the right time, he said.

A trail camera photo of a weka on the Otago Peninsula. Supplied/Supplied/Fiona Morrison, Otago Peninsula Biodiversity Group

They were vulnerable to environmental changes, and the introduction of mustelids, cats and dogs.

McKinlay said people had to be involved in the return of weka to Dunedin, as it was too far for weka to walk.

He urged people not to bring weka into the area, although acknowledged the curious birds [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regions_west-coast/559994/weka-hitches-a-300-kilometre-ride-to-christchurch

could have become stowaways].

"If you're going to think it's fun to bring a weka home, you are condemning it to eventually die," he said. "If we wanted weka back in Dunedin, it will take quite a lot of effort and co-ordination."

McKinlay believed the decision should be taken lightly, and was not risk free to weka or other native species.

Weka were a known predator of sooty shearwater and the one on the peninsula lived near the colony at Sandfly Bay.

"If you've got one precious taonga like the sooty shearwater and you've got another one that eats it, which one do you actually want?

"How do you actually make these choices to actually accommodate a predator within your landscape?"

Weka are slowly disappearing from Dunedin. Tess Brunton/RNZ

McKinlay encouraged anyone who spotted a weka in Dunedin to log it with the DOC Hotline 0800 362 468.

He has reached out to previous weka spotters, but none of them reported further sightings.

McKinlay recorded their absences, saying it was part of their story in the city and painted a picture of how vulnerable weka were, if their arrival was not managed properly.

"One of the problems with this sort of work is the absence of records really doesn't attract people's attentions as much as the positive," he said.

World.title: Diabetes patients battle blame, shame and judgment over medical condition
World.content:
For people with diabetes, everyday language can carry a weight of judgment and stigma.

Lifestyle choices. Sufferer. Burden.

Those words, among others, have come up again and again during Dr Liz Holmes-Truscott's 16 years of diabetes study.

As the deputy director of the Australian Centre for Behaviour Research in Diabetes, she told RNZ they were used by the media, by the public, by people's families, even by doctors.

"Diabetes stigma occurs when people with diabetes - those at risk of the condition or even those connected to it in different ways, such as health professionals or those caring for people with diabetes - when they're negatively labelled, stereotyped and separated, due to diabetes," she explained.

Of more than 365,000 New Zealanders living with diabetes, 80 percent report facing blame, shame or judgment, according to Diabetes New Zealand.

Holmes-Truscott explained stigma could look like overt discrimination, but was often much more subtle - everyday assumptions, comments, interactions.

At a family barbecue, it might look like this: "You don't look like a person with diabetes" or "Should you be eating that?"

At a doctor's appointment, it could look like this: "Have you been taking your medication correctly?"

Research had shown some patients were even reluctant to share their glucose levels with their doctor for fear of being judged, blamed or shamed, Holmes-Truscott said, which could get in the way of effective care.

A 2024 study in The Lancet, which Holmes-Truscott co-authored, found four in five adults reported experiencing diabetes stigma.

A separate 2026 research review found people reported delaying appointments, disengaging from care, withholding information from doctors and changing self-care behaviour to hide their condition or avoid questions.

"This isn't about policing every word people use," Holmes-Truscott explained. "Our understanding evolves over time and so does our language.

"What's important is being willing to listen, learn and use language that respects people's experiences."

What's her beef with the word 'lifestyle'?

One risk factor for type 2 diabetes is high body weight, but risk is also influenced by factors outside a person's control, including genetics, age, ethnicity and socio-economic circumstances.

Still, diabetes carries the label of 'lifestyle' disease.

"I think it's well long past the time to reconsider this term," Holmes-Truscott said.

As well as implying someone was entirely at fault for their diagnosis, it was also unclear.

"It's not a scientific term and yet it's a term that researchers, that healthcare professionals, that the media really latch onto as a bit of a coverall.

"If we're talking about physical activity, let's talk about physical activity. If we're talking about food intake, let's talk about that.

"If we're talking about food access, let's talk about food access. For me, this isn't just about political correctness, it's about communication."

When stigma affects care

Pregnancy brings its own risk of diabetes.

During pregnancy, the body needs significantly more insulin and gestational diabetes develops, when it cannot produce enough to keep blood glucose within the recommended range.

Health data shows it will affect up to one in six women, with some evidence showing it could be even higher, particularly for Māori and Pacific people.

During her own pregnancy eight years ago, Holmes-Truscott experienced firsthand how quickly judgment could land.

"I received my diagnosis [of gestational diabetes] over the phone from a healthcare professional, who had never met me, who didn't know anything about my circumstances, my situation, and I was told to cut the junk."

She said her immediate reaction was one of shock and concern, quickly followed by a feeling she'd done something wrong.

"There's an immediate judgment around what I'm eating and a suggestion that I need to do better," she said.

Her own research on women with gestational diabetes showed her that was not an isolated experience - in fact, it was very common.

"We know some women with gestational diabetes report a lack of interest in going for follow-up screening," she said.

Despite her many years of work with diabetes, Holmes-Truscott said her response to that doctor eight years ago was defensive.

She remembered telling them she barely ate junk food as it was.

World.title: New study shows what does and doesn't work for ADHD kids
World.content:
A new study says giving kids with ADHD extra time for tasks and more frequent breaks while in class may not affect their behaviour.

Researchers from Florida International University got more than 200 primary school children at summer camps in the US to switch between taking and not taking medication and different classroom environments.

The study, published in the Jama Pediatrics medical journal found medication improved the kids' rule-following and test results but the adaptations in the classroom, including extended time for tasks, frequent breaks, using a standing desk and having a low distraction space, didn't affect their behaviour or achievement.

University of Auckland development neuropsychology expert Professor Karen Waldie said the study came as no surprise to those who work with children with ADHD and do research in the area.

"Procrastination and time blindness are one of the key symptoms of ADHD. The main reason for the benefits of medication and behavioural therapy comes down to the brain chemical dopamine and the reward system of the brain.

"Stimulant medication such as Ritalin works to increase dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and this helps those with ADHD focus on the task at hand: right now."

Waldie said the study found that medication and behaviour therapy improved academic productivity and rule-following behaviour in the classroom, but accommodations such as extended time on tasks had no effect.

"Another thing that works in a similar way as stimulant meds is a hard deadline and quick consequences of actions - so basically people with ADHD work very well under pressure, which gives them a dopamine reward hit, and do less well when there is time available to perform a task like a test or when there is a distant or inconsequential reward."

Consultant clinical psychologist and honorary senior lecturer at University of Auckland's Te Ara Hāro Centre for Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Dr Melanie Woodfield, said the study is an important signal from a carefully designed experiment, but needs testing in the real world.

"Positive behaviour supports, medication, or both, are known to improve academic performance and decrease challenging behaviour for many children with ADHD."

Woodfield said the study leaned towards strict control, excluding children with low IQ or autism alongside ADHD, and taking place in a specialist American summer camp treatment classroom, where staff even counted the ratio of teacher praise to commands, to ensure it was 3:1.

"That's quite far removed from a messy, complex, real world classroom with fewer resources, stretched teachers, and children with higher needs. The authors themselves recommend the study now needs to be repeated in real- world classrooms, where they expect the effects would be weaker.

"Ideally, we should also acknowledge that some accommodations do work for some children, some of the time," Woodfield said.

"However, this research suggests that a blanket, Oprah-style giveaway 'You get extra time! And you get extra time' may not return reliable dividends, compared to behavioural approaches and/or medication."

Clinical psychologist Giselle Bahr said there's been no specific research about what happens when children with ADHD are offered structured classroom changes, and while the study showed they did not make a difference to behaviour in this instance, it was food for thought.

"It's like, of course it would make sense to give a child more time if they're struggling, but it looks like it's not as simple as that," she said.

"What we already know is that behavioural strategies help children and they don't have any adverse effects, there's no risks associated with them. We already know that methylphenidate changes children's behaviour in the short term, but over the long term it leads to worse outcomes."

However, Waldie did not agree and said she had not seen that supported in scientific literature.

Bahr said the study had not been done in a normal classroom setting, but at a summer camp during one-hour class periods, and the adjustments were randomised.

"The rest of the hours of the day they were doing fun activities and the classes were small. They only had 15 to 18 students in them and there were two adults in each of those classrooms. It's not an exact match with how a classroom generally run, so we have to be careful about what we extrapolate from that.

"It doesn't look like they matched a child's kind of need for what's going to help them learn better in a classroom, they just kind of trailed these adaptations."

She said the researchers, Fabiano and Pelham, had authored papers about children and ADHD for decades and said behavioural interventions remained an important, low-risk strategy for supporting children with ADHD.

"Some of their previous work looked at the best order for interventions. They found that starting with behavioural strategies was more effective than starting with medication. Also, that ADHD medication made things worse for children in the long term, even if it produced improvements in the short-term."

Bahr said ADHD medication came with serious risks, including reduced growth, a risk of psychotic symptoms, and cardiovascular problems.

Waldie said the only well-established effect would potentially be with appetite, however research on that aspect was conducted with fast-acting mythylphenidate before the slow-release medication was available.

Waldie said methylphenidate was the most-studied pediatric medication, with evidence showing it reduced rates of mortality, accidents, and self-medication.

Waldie was interested in understanding the study's findings in relation to the dopamine system in a person with ADHD, procrastination and the need to go down to the wire before panic set in.

"That's when the ADHD person tends to excel, it's like a light flipping, that's when things get done," Waldie said.

World.title: Cyber protection of critical infrastructure is 'priority work' but taking at least a year
World.content:
Government officials are working on policies to strengthen cyber protection of critical infrastructure more than seven months after consultations closed.

"This remains priority work," they told RNZ this week.

They are working through submissions to refine policy options, after the February-April public consultation.

"Our intention is to provide advice to ministers early in the next term of government."

Friday's Microsoft Outlook outage has sparked fresh questions about New Zealand's vulnerability to global technology glitches and whether government was doing enough.

"From a cyber security perspective, the government needs to be much more engaged," said frequent critic Don Christie of Catalyst IT.

Other countries move

In early 2026, the officials laid out two new proposed categories of infrastructure that could be subject to mandatory minimum requirements to enhance cyber security and resilience.

Official documents said critical national infrastructure was "increasingly vulnerable to cyber attack".

"Current regulatory settings are not designed to drive a consistent uplift in cyber security across the critical infrastructure system".

It was acknowledged New Zealand's approach was not keeping pace with other countries.

This week, Australia flagged changes to criminal law to crack down on future breaches by artificial intelligence companies, after a frontier artificial intelligence agent hacked government systems for sensitive information in OpenAI tests.

The European Union has mandated stringent cyber security measures for operators of critical infrastructure since 2024.

The EU has also moved to boost the ways consumers and businesses determine which products are cybersecure, with more measures coming in two months ago.

'Priority work'

The government's 'Enhancing the cyber security of critical infrastructure' work revolves around a public consultation that ran from February to April.

"Submissions have since been worked through to refine policy options," the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet said.

It said the 2026 submissions from the public would be shared in due course. However, the website carries submissions from three years ago.

"Our intention is that submissions would be published on the DPMC website around the same time in 2027."

Big new threats in months

Since the consultation in early 2026, the threats globally and here have escalated rapidly, and morphed greatly, with the advent of frontier AI models that have launched unauthorised, autonomous swarm attacks on government and commercial targets in testing.

In June, Five Eyes cyber agencies warned that frontier models would fundamentally alter offensive and defensive capabilities.

"The timeline is not years, it is months."

In New Zealand, the National Cyber Security Centre said that, by early 2027, "malicious actors may have access to advanced AI capabilities currently available only through leading frontier AI models".

Attacks could occur with little warning and organisations should prepare now, it said in September.

Early 2027 co-incides with when some policy on enhancing cyber security for critical infrastructure might emerge.

Concrete achievements

The proposals have envisaged "a minimum level of cyber risk management by all critical infrastructure entities" and effective management of cyber threats affecting national security.

In addition, a category of critical infrastructure of national significance (CINS) could have additional obligations beyond the minimum requirements.

As of early 2026, the documents said, "Cyber risks are generally not well understood or collectively managed to a consistent level across New Zealand's critical infrastructure system".

The critical infrastructure work was signed off by Christopher Luxon as national security and intelligence minister. It is part of a cyber security strategy 2026-2030 the government put out in February.

RNZ asked officials what concrete achievements there had been.

World.title: MetService warns of heavy rain, severe gales across South Island
World.content:
MetService has issued warnings for four areas in the South Island, with up to 400mm of rain forecast over the next two days.

Orange heavy rain warnings are in place for Westland, the Canterbury headwaters, Grey and Buller districts.

The warning for Westland runs from noon Sunday to 1pm Monday, while the Canterbury headwaters warning runs from 2pm Sunday to 2pm Monday.

The ranges of the Grey District could receive 100 to 130mm, while 100 to 150mm is forecast for the Buller ranges.

Peak rainfall rates of up to 40mm an hour are expected about the Westland ranges and Canterbury main divide on Monday morning.

A front moving slowly northwards is the cause, bringing heavy north-westerly rain to the western South Island and the Tararua Range.

Severe northwest gales are also possible about the Canterbury High Country, Wellington and Wairarapa.

The rain may cause streams and rivers to rise rapidly, MetService warns. Surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions are also possible.

The strong wind watch for Wellington and Wairarapa runs from noon until 8pm Monday; the Canterbury watch runs from 10pm Sunday to 10am Monday.
