Tech.title: Tesla is inviting some people to buy a Cybercab ‘for personal use’ — but read the fine print
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to “select customers” to purchase a Cybercab for “personal use.” But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will “only be available in supported service areas” — meaning you’ll only be able to buy one if you live in one of the cities where Tesla currently operates its Robotaxi service.

The price of a Cybercab is listed at $29,990, plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription.” Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X announced the new offer, including screenshots of the order page and the invite email. But don’t expect a fleet of personally owned Cybercabs to suddenly materialize on public roads: “Initial availability is limited,” the invitation email warns.

Previous Next



1 / 3 Image: Tesla

Tesla began offering rides in the Cybercab as part of its Model Y-powered Robotaxi service in Austin in September. The company now has 278 Cybercabs in operation, representing approximately 40 percent of its fleet, according to the crowd-sourced Robotaxi Tracker.

The inclusion of a mandatory $299/month subscription is sure to rankle some fans who may have dreamed of cruising around in a $30,000 driverless Tesla, as originally promised by Tesla CEO Elon Musk when he first introduced the Cybercab in 2024. Musk made no mention of the Autonomy Subscription at that event, though it shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise given the $99/month fee Tesla currently charges for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature.

Still, that money adds up over time. Over a standard 5-year ownership period, the mandatory $299/month fee adds $17,940 to the sticker price (even with the first month included), bringing the real baseline cost to roughly $47,600 before taxes, charging, and insurance — more than a brand-new Model 3 or Model Y that you can actually drive anywhere in the country.

Unlike a standard Tesla where canceling FSD just reverts the car to manual driving, canceling the $299/month Autonomy Subscription renders the Cybercab completely unusable on public roads because there is no manual fallback. In effect, the car becomes a brick. Additionally, Tesla says that buyers will have to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit just to get in line for a December delivery window that isn’t guaranteed.

One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car.

Moreover, Tesla only has to give you 30 days’ warning before raising the price. If they update the rules and you keep using the service, you automatically agree to the new terms. Also, if you cancel — or if Tesla suspends your access — you won’t get a partial refund for the rest of the month you already paid for.

Of course, that’s just the fine print. On X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk was promising a much wider rollout, subject — of course — to “regulatory approval.” Musk frequently frames regulatory approval as the primary external bottleneck holding back his robotaxi timelines as a way to shift focus away from Tesla’s technological shortcomings.

(For what it’s worth, he also called his own company’s $299/month Autonomy Subscription “too high,” arguing that it should actually be $115/month or closer to Tesla’s $99/month Full Self-Driving subscription.)

But Musk seemed more focused on taunting YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027, than answering any of the litany of safety and liability questions raised by this offer. (For his part, Brownlee says he thinks his hair is safe.)

For starters, how does Tesla plan on selling a vehicle that doesn’t comply with current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards that require traditional controls like steering wheels and pedals? Tesla says the Autonomy Subscription covers autonomous driving, maintenance, and towing, but explicitly excludes auto insurance. The company hasn’t explained how personal auto insurers will underwrite a car with no human driver, or how liability is split between the owner and Tesla if the vehicle causes an accident while operating autonomously. Nor has Tesla disclosed how it selects invited buyers or how many units are earmarked for private sale versus its internal fleet.

Then there is the small matter of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration already opening a formal audit into how Tesla self-certified a vehicle without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla submitted its legal justification to NHTSA in October, requested that the entire response be kept confidential, and is now taking customer deposits while NHTSA’s ruling is still pending.

Which means early buyers aren’t just paying $47,600 for a geofenced car they aren’t allowed to drive — they’re putting down non-refundable cash on a vehicle the federal government hasn’t even decided is street-legal.

Tech.title: This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle.

Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app.

The 8BitDo Zero 2 gamepad (bottom) is still much smaller than the Atom Plus (top) but lacks triggers and thumbsticks.

Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.)

The thumbsticks on the Atom Plus (center) are nearly identical in size to those on the original Switch’s Joy-Con (right) but smaller than the thumbsticks on the Switch 2 (left).

I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.

At times, the Atom Plus’ layout can feel a little too crowded. I often found my thumb bumping other controls and buttons when playing with the D-pad.

While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.

The shoulder buttons and digital triggers sit at different heights, but I still found myself accidentally pressing both at times.

The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.

Connecting the Atom Plus to CRKD’s mobile app lets you remap its controls, turn certain features on or off, and update its firmware.

I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.

The Atom Plus (top) is excellent for travel but not nearly as comfortable as a full-size controller.

Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.

If you aren’t sold on using the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con as standalone gamepads, the Atom Plus is an excellent travel accessory.

I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

Photos by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

Screen share

A lot of you out there in the Installerverse have become iPhone Duo users over the last few weeks, and I’ve heard a lot about how you’re all using Apple’s new foldable phone. (I’d say the sentiment in my inbox is roughly 80 percent positive, 5 percent negative, 15 percent deeply confused about interface choices.) I’ve also gotten some questions about which Duo apps are great, and how best to set yours up.

Alas, I do not have a Duo. So I turned to The Verge’s Allison Johnson, who coauthored our review of the device and has used it as aggressively as anyone I know. I asked her to share how she’s wielding the Duo, and she sent over a truly unhinged color scheme and otherwise a bunch of very good ideas. Her’s her homescreen, plus some info on the apps she uses and why:

The phone: iPhone Duo.

The wallpaper: It’s one of those color gradient options you can pick in iOS. I was trying to go for a minimalist thing.

The apps: NYT Games, Kindle, Headspace, Spotify, Google Maps, Safari, Messages, Mail.

So I tried the whole aspirational “dress for the homescreen you want” thing for a few days, with just a few apps like Headspace and NYT Games, and it was a miserable failure. It just made me mad every time I had to search for Messages. I added a row of essential apps to the bottom of the screen and a big calendar widget, and things have been much better.

There’s a big widget / shortcut to TypeDraw, which is a fantastic app on the Duo that makes the whole phone behave like a physical notebook. It’s great with the Apple Pencil. I also realized I need weather close by, so I added a giant widget to the left panel of the homescreen.

I also have a shortcut for the built-in lo-fi playlists on iOS, which is handy if I need to pop in earbuds and play something instrumental so I can focus real quick. Highly recommended to anyone who hasn’t discovered these yet and also gets overstimulated! They’re already on your phone!

I did nuke the dock entirely in my minimalist experiment and I’m actually fine with it. Maybe I’ll never go back to the dock again.

I also asked Allison to share a few things she’s into right now. Here’s what she sent back:

I don’t have a Switch 2 so I’m having extreme Zelda FOMO right now. I WISH I was playing Ocarina of Time but I’m just playing through every last bit of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on my PS5 to distract myself.

I’m like 20 minutes away from finishing Widow’s Bay and that has been a really fun watch.

I just finished reading the Planet Money book , which is like, The Economy For Dummies. It’s pretty entertaining and was very helpful for an economy dummy like me.

I also got a book called Coffee, For Here by an award-winning barista and creator named Morgan Eckroth. They have lots of specialty drink recipes you can make with a home espresso setup. I made one over the weekend and I’m still thinking about how good it was. The photos are beautiful too.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week.

“Search, a browser developed by a small Parisian design studio of all things. I’d say they have created the classy European cousin of Arc, based on Webkit so it’s super light & responsive on Mac while also having the flexibility of Chrome extensions.” — Elliot

“Trying out Monarch to potentially break my years-long Quicken habit. So far I’m about 90% sure I’m switching.” — Bruce

“Dungeon Crawler Carl. I recently started listening to the audiobook. It has consumed my life. I listen to it on my drive to work, I take breaks at work to listen to it, I play it throughout my day, and eventually fall asleep listening to it. It’s almost 200 hours of content and Jeff Hays does an amazing job voicing all the characters. I’m currently on book seven of eight, and not looking forward to the withdrawals as we wait for book 9. Seriously, check it out.” — William

“Brenpoly on YouTube has open-sourced his “I built an Apple Vision Pro for $5” project. It’s a great watch even if you don’t dabble in 3D printing. It also shows how much potential there is for affordable VR with just the phones in our pockets and some very clever people and communities.” — Owen

“For anyone with an iPhone Duo. On the outer display, Safari keeps a column down the side for its buttons, and web pages stop short of it. I’m a Duo owner, and am now using a great Safari extension called Widen that runs pages underneath that column: ~25% more page, with text kept clear of the buttons.” — Marcus

“I took my kid to see Wildwood, the new Laika movie, this past weekend and left the theater with my jaw on the floor and dragging a few feet behind me. It is extraordinary. For me, put it up there with the all time Studio Ghibli greats. (I know, I know, but I’m serious.) In a way that no Marvel movie special effects have done, I sat at multiple times in the movie thinking, ‘I just can’t believe humans made this.’” — Stephen

“I am a browser snob, constantly flitting back and forth trying to find the one that combines speed with features with proper UX with privacy. I had begrudgingly settled on Safari for Apple and Chrome for everything else when I stumbled upon Brave Origin. It’s a little steep at a one-time purchase of $59, but it’s completely cross platform, syncs, and gets rid of all the Brave cruft. It’s just a good, minimal, fast Chromium-based browser.” — Kait

“Queen’s Domain, a wonderful King’s Field-like game, was released this past weekend and it conjures up all those familiar FromSoftware feelings of combat and exploration! Highly recommended, it’s quite the experience.” — Kyle

“I finished Jet Lag: The Game’s Japanorama, and it is the absolute best tourism video series for Japan without trying at all to be one. It is part scavenger hunt, part race across Japan, and shows off the wonderful scenery and the beautiful public transit of the country. I learnt that Japan loves making lists (OCD folks rejoice!) and has lists of Three Views, Three Great Gardens, 100 Best Sunsets, 100 Remarkable Waters and many more.” — Utkarsh

Signing off

I’m working on a story about the new era of hardware hacking, in which people are suddenly discovering they can vibe-code their way to a better TV, the e-reader of their dreams, and a million other things besides. In almost all my conversations, one thing keeps coming up: the M5Stack developer kits. This company will send you an ESP32-based device you can hack to bits, whether you’re looking for something with an E Ink display or something with a round touchscreen. I’m about to spend an alarming amount of money buying these things, and an equally alarming amount of time making Claude Code do weird stuff with them. I’m already stealing ideas from the fabulous M5Stack subreddit. If you get up to something fun while hardware hacking this weekend, tell me all about it.

See you next week!

Tech.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
Tech.content:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Not all of those relationships are the business of the security team. Relationships with subordinates typically fall to HR, legal, and the board. But an affair with an executive at a company under federal investigation is a different animal. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Security specialists say affairs can create vulnerabilities that foreign intelligence services look to exploit.

Catching that kind of exposure isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security very narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”

Still, some of it is beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers are one example. These devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if these were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But either way, what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, should become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

Tech.title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
In Brief

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

Tech.title: Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee
Tech.content:
In Brief

Tesla said on Friday evening that “select customers” now have the opportunity to pre-order the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.”

More details became clear as those select customers looked at the order page. Tech reviewer Marques Brownlee posted that buyers “must accept delivery” in one of a handful of Texas cities and that the Cybercab will only operate in certain geofenced areas. The estimated delivery date is December 2026.

In addition to the $29,990 price tag, Cybercab owners will need to pay $299 per month to operate their vehicle.

In response to Brownlee’s post, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the Cybercab “will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval.” He added that the monthly fee is “too high”: “Should match the cost of Tesla [Full Self-Driving] and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

Tesla’s Ashok Elluswamy offered more information about the geofencing, saying that Cybercab will work “unsupervised inside all the same geo locations as @robotaxi, just serving the owners’ needs.”

After falling far short of projected sales, Tesla recently announced it will cease Cybertruck production next year and use the additional factory capacity to build more Cybercabs.

Tech.title: Got an iPhone Duo? These 9 settings make it easier to use
Tech.content:
Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has proven popular enough that the company can’t keep the device in stock. While the Duo introduces a new way to use an iPhone, getting the most out of this initial version may require adjusting a few settings to make it work better when it comes to everyday tasks, like unlocking the device with Touch ID, navigating the interface, and taking photos.

After spending some time with the Duo, we’d recommend making the following adjustments to make the new iPhone a bit easier to use, most notably when it comes to the use of Touch ID.

Settings to make it easier to live with Touch ID

Unlike modern iPhones, the Duo doesn’t support Face ID. That means you have to adjust to pressing a finger on the side of the device once again to authenticate with apps, unlock the device, and use Apple Pay. But there are a few things you can do to make the switch back to the older technology a bit less painful.

Register extra fingerprints: This may seem like an obvious suggestion, but if you’re used to just registering a fingerprint or two with Touch ID, prepare to rethink that strategy with the Duo. Because the device can be held in multiple orientations, flipped both horizontally and vertically, and because of the small size of the Duo’s screen, you may find that a lot of your fingers (and thumbs!) can now reach the Touch ID button. We’d recommend holding the device in your hand and turning it in different ways, then register the fingerprints where you end up holding the device the most — on both hands. Yes, setting up Touch ID can be a bit tedious compared with Face ID, as there are multiple prints to register. Still, it’s a one-time setup, and later on you’ll be glad that you took the time to make more of your fingerprints work. To register a fingerprint, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Add a Fingerprint. Unlock with Apple Watch: If you’re in the market for the iPhone Duo, there’s a good likelihood that you own other Apple devices, like the Apple Watch. If that’s the case, you’re in luck because you can use your Watch to unlock the Duo without having to bother with Touch ID. This will save you time and frustration in the long run, so get used to wearing your Apple Watch more often, especially when you’re out and about and don’t want to fiddle as much with finger placement. To use the Apple Watch unlock, your watch will need to be passcode-protected and worn near your phone. To turn this feature on, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Unlock with Apple Watch. Rest finger to Open: This is an optional setting, not necessarily a “must” like the above, but we’ve found it useful. The “rest finger” setting is actually an accessibility feature, but it can double as a usability feature, too. When enabled, you only have to rest your finger lightly on the Touch ID sensor to unlock the device, instead of having to press down. Those who prefer this setting find it can make unlocking the phone faster and more convenient, but others may disagree, as they like the more tactile sensation of a button press. Try it both ways and see which one fits you best. To enable this one, go to Settings > Touch ID & Passcode > Rest Finger to Open.

Usability Improvements

Image Credits:Apple

There are a few settings that could also improve your experience with the iPhone Duo, as they may make it easier to perform certain everyday tasks, like taking screenshots or reaching different parts of the screen, among other things.

Turn off Fixed Volume Controls: This is a favorite hack for new Duo owners, as it makes using the device in any orientation much easier. By default, the iPhone Duo’s volume buttons are “fixed,” which means that no matter how you rotate the device, the Volume Up button remains the button that increases the volume and the Volume Down button decreases it. But many people find it’s easier if the buttons’ functionality rotates with the device. That is, the buttons re-orient themselves based on how you are holding the phone, making the “up” option always on the top or right. As you fold, unfold, and flip the phone, having buttons that flip with you actually makes more sense. To turn off the fixed volume controls, go to Settings > Sounds & Haptics > Fixed Position Volume Controls. Back Tap for Screenshots: The Duo tries to make it easier to take a screenshot by pressing the side button and either the Volume Up or Volume Down button at the same time. However, you still might find the process a two-handed affair (unless you just ask Siri to do it for you). That’s why many Duo owners are turning to a buried Accessibility feature to make taking screenshots a bit less complicated. In the phone’s accessibility settings, you can configure whether a double tap or triple tap on the back of the device triggers a particular action — which you can set to ‘take a screenshot.’ (Some people prefer the triple tap so they don’t accidentally trigger the feature.) Once enabled, you could hold your Duo in one hand, then use a finger to tap on the back of the phone to take the screenshot, saving you a bit of the hassle that comes with managing the button combinations. To configure this, go to Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Back Tap > then choose a double or triple tap and your action. (Screenshot is under the “Device” menu.) Reachability: This is another accessibility feature that some Duo owners like to configure, but others like to have off. The option was originally designed to make larger-screened devices easier to use with one hand, which makes it sometimes hard to reach, depending on your hand size. Typically, when Reachability is turned on, the iPhone will lower the top half of the screen to make it easier to reach with your thumb. The Duo does things a little differently, though. Because the phone is wide — it’s shaped like a passport — it’s the far side of the screen that’s harder to reach than the top. So when you turn on Reachability, you will instead be able to swipe the left or right edge of the screen to bring a side into reach. We should note that this feature is enabled by default, but if you find yourself accidentally triggering it and want to turn it off, you can under Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability. Lock when folded: This one is more of a personal preference, we’ll admit. But if you tend to unfold the device when you’re working with it, then snap it closed when you’re done, you might like to configure a setting that will automatically lock the screen for you when the device is folded shut. However, doing so requires you to create a new shortcut, as there isn’t a setting for this — at least, not yet. To make the shortcut, you’ll open the Shortcuts app, tap the plus (+) sign, then the Edit button in the upper-right. You then tap into the search bar, and tap on the word “automation” that appears in blue under the search bar that appears at the top of the screen. Next, you’ll scroll down until you find the option “Opened or Closed” under the Display section. Tap that, tap on the word “Opened” to change it to “Closed,” then tap in the search bar at the bottom again and type in “Lock Screen.” Tap on the option

“Lock Screen” when it appears in the search results, and you’re done — the shortcut has been made. You can tap on the play button here to test it, if you’d like. And if you ever change your mind, just delete the shortcut!

Special Camera Tricks

Tech.title: Transportation secretary blames ‘routine’ equipment upgrade for grounding flights nationwide
Tech.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop halting flights across the United States was caused by seemingly routine maintenance work.

Duffy said that during “routine maintenance,” copper wire at a remote location was upgraded to fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration. After the upgrade, a router overloaded a critical communication system, leading to the ground stop.

“It’s pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location,” Duffy said during a Saturday press conference that appeared to have technical issues of its own. “What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning, was it user error or [installer] error from L3Harris? Or did they install a faulty router?”

The FAA’s acting CTO Rebecca Guy added, “When we started to see the occurrence where our network was having instability, we started to look at what was the cause. And as such, we saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds.”

Guy said the FAA disabled “both of those, right away and were able to stabilize our network,” and is now performing a root cause analysis.

Duffy has repeatedly insisted, at multiple press conferences, that Congress needs to provide more funding for aviation equipment upgrades. Asked why the upgrades were made at 3pm on a Friday afternoon — rather than, say, at midnight on a Saturday — he responded that while “switchovers” at bigger airports will take place late at night, remote switchovers happen during the day.

“There will be reevaluation of when we do this work,” he said.

This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century. More than 8,200 flights were canceled on Friday evening, according to aviation data firm Cirium. And the effects continued after the ground stop was lifted, with at least another 3,000 flights canceled on Saturday.

The ground stop came just a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers; the air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted in designing the system. However, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees “zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related.”

“We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue, and we’re working through what this defective piece of equipment was,” Bedford said.

When Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was asked earlier if the ground stop was caused by AI, he replied, “We call it SI [super intelligence] around here, remember? SI.”

Tech.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
Tech.content:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

OpenAI has taken several stumbles

Image Credits:SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg / Getty Images

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

Apple’s Siri AI

Image Credits:Artur Widak/NurPhoto / Getty Images

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs. This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Character.ai

Image Credits:Character.AI

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie

Image Credits:Ollie

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Microsoft’s Recall

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail

Image Credits:Notion

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22.

Humane AI Pin

Image Credits:Brian Heater

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

Rabbit R1

Image Credits:Rabbit

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe

Image Credits:Huxe

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp

Image Credits:Yupp

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down.

Tech.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
Tech.content:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.

China

China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.

Singapore

In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.

In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.

South Korea

South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.

Taiwan

Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.

Japan

In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

Tech.title: Amazon’s new Kindle Colorsoft is a premium e-reader with a premium price
Tech.content:
Amazon recently unveiled its refreshed Kindle lineup, introducing a new basic Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new Kindle Colorsoft starts at $290, while the Signature Edition, which I’ve spent the past few weeks testing, costs $320.

The base model comes with 16GB of storage, while the Signature Edition doubles that to 32GB and is available in graphite or a maroon-like Fig finish with an aluminum back.

Amazon first brought color to its Kindle lineup in 2024 with the launch of the original Colorsoft. The latest model is lighter and thinner than its predecessor and features an edge-to-edge display. If you already own the first-generation Colorsoft, there’s little reason to upgrade.

The core reading experience remains largely the same. Both models have a 7-inch color E-Ink display, 300ppi resolution for black-and-white content and 150ppi for color.

However, if you’ve been eyeing a color e-reader, the new Colorsoft is worth considering if you can get past the hefty price tag.

Unlike standard Kindles, which display everything in black and white, the Colorsoft brings your digital bookshelf to life with their original colors. This makes it a particularly appealing option for readers who enjoy comics, graphic novels, or cookbooks, where color makes a big difference. It’s also great for readers who like highlighting passages in different colors.

Image Credits:Aisha Malik / TechCrunch

It’s worth noting that colors on the Colorsoft are still relatively muted and not as vibrant as what you’d see on an iPad. Still, they add a welcome splash of color and make a noticeable difference compared to the black-and-white displays of standard Kindles.

The Colorsoft lets you adjust the screen’s color temperature, so you can switch to a warmer, more yellow-toned display that’s easier on the eyes when reading at night. There’s also an auto-adjusting brightness option that comes in handy.

When it comes to battery life, Amazon says that the Colorsoft can last up to eight weeks on a single charge, compared to up to 12 weeks for the Paperwhite. During my testing, I didn’t have to stress about charging the Colorsoft because like other Kindles, its battery lasts a relatively long time compared to other everyday electronics.

One small but welcome improvement on the new Colorsoft is the repositioned power button. On the previous generation, it was on the bottom of the device next to the charging port, making it easy to accidentally press it when handling the Kindle. On the new model, Amazon has moved it to the top-right edge, where it’s less likely to get in the way. I quite like this change, and found the new location more intuitive when powering the device on and off.

Image Credits:Aisha Malik / TechCrunch

I enjoyed the premium feel of the aluminum back on the Signature Edition. Although Amazon provided a case with my review unit, I rarely used it, and the finish held up well. While the slimmer design isn’t a major change, I found the new Colorsoft quite comfortable to hold compared to older Kindle devices.

For those who enjoy reading in the bath or by the pool, the Colorsoft is waterproof, so you don’t have to worry about accidental splashes or spills damaging the e-reader.

One thing I appreciated about the Colorsoft was how infrequently the screen needed to refresh, which was something I noticed more often with the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. I also didn’t experience any noticeable ghosting, where text from previous pages lingers on the screen, which is common on some e-readers.

The Signature Edition supports a magnetic cover with built-in page-turn buttons that connects to the pogo pins on the back of the device, but I can’t speak to this experience because I didn’t have access to the case.

The biggest drawback of the Colorsoft is its price. It’s a steep investment for a device that’s just used for reading. That said, if you really want a color display, the Colorsoft is definitely worth considering. For everyone else, it’s a nice upgrade, but far from a must-have. Many readers would be better off with the basic Kindle or Paperwhite, which start at $169.99 and $199.99, respectively.

Tech.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
Tech.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.

It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Tech.title: I Put the Best Digital Notebooks to the Test. Here Are My Favorites (2026)
Tech.content:
Comparing Our Favorite Digital Notebooks

Model Display Resolution Color? Storage Weight Battery life ReMarkable Paper Pro 11.8 inches, adjustable front light 229 pixels per inch Yes 64 GB 1.16 pounds Up to 2 weeks Supernote Manta 10.7 inches 300 pixels per inch No 32 GB, and can expand storage with a microSD card 0.83 pounds Under a week Supernote Nomad 7.8 inches 300 pixels per inch No 32 GB, and can expand storage with a microSD card 0.59 pounds Under a week Kobo Libra Colour 7 inches, adjustable front light 300 ppi for black-and-white, 150 ppi for color Yes 32 GB 0.44 pounds About a month Kindle Scribe 10.2 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 pixels per inch No 16, 32, or 64 GB 0.96 pounds Up to 12 weeks TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper 11.5 inches 2200 x 1440 Yes 8GB RAM and 256 GB ROM 1.1 pounds Unspecified

Our Favorite Smart Pens

Neo Smartpen M1+ for $129: If you don't want an entire tablet to write your digitized notes on, you can get a smart pen to use on regular paper that will log your notes into its companion app. The Neo Smartpen M1+ was the thinnest and lightest smart pen former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordiano tried, and she easily used it with notebooks and planners alike. You'll pair it with the Neo Studio app, which has a notebook system that's easy to navigate and organize your notes.

Neo Smartpen Dimo for $59: This is the cheapest smart pen option and uses replaceable batteries. It isn't compatible with Google Calendar, iCal, or Outlook like our other picks.

Honorable Mentions

Boox Note Air4 C for $470: If you're looking for something a little more powerful than just taking notes and annotating, but still want the E Ink screen experience, then a Boox device is what you need. The Boox Note Air4 C has an e-paper screen and is primarily described as an “e-paper notebook,” but runs on Android 13 and has access to the Google Play Store, giving it more of a tablet feel that happens to have a colorful e-paper screen instead of your usual brightly lit iPad or Android tablet. You're able to easily access the web (called NeoBrowser) right from the Boox homepage, which usually takes several steps and is incredibly slow on a true digital notebook. You'll also access apps that look like a tablet, including an image gallery, calendar, music player, and tools like a clock, recorder, and calculator. It was a pick in this guide, but it's now out of stock for US warehouses (you can still order from the Hong Kong warehouse, but you might have to pay extra tariffs and fees), and there's a new version out, the Note Air5 ($530).

The 3rd Gen Kindle Scribe (left) and the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. Photograph: Nena Farrell

Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630 and Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: The new versions of the Kindle Scribe are still solid all-around devices that have a good mix of e-reader and digital notebook features, but I still prefer the older model's price point. While the new Scribe Colorsoft is a nice option if you want color, I think these are too expensive for what they are. The price comes from all the AI features packed into the device, plus connectivity to services like Google and Microsoft, but it still isn't as powerful as a ReMarkable or Supernote if you want better tools. My picks above are a better price for similar features, though the Scribe does have the most impressive battery life of any digital notebook device I've tried (and that's still true for the older model that I recommend above, too, so you don't need the newest model for the best battery life).

Moleskine Smart Writing Set for $225: Moleskine is already known for its notebooks, and the brand has a smart version now, too. Our team previously tested a version in 2018 that only cost $149, but the current version that's $224 is next on my list to test. The set comes with a notebook and pen that will pair with the Moleskine Notes app to show you your notes.

Montblanc Digital Paper for $950: Yes, that Montblanc, the one with the famous pens, now has a digital notebook of its own. It's no surprise that I'd call its digital pen one of the best. It's got a super-lightweight feel while sporting three different buttons, two of which you can customize. (There's no eraser, but I'll give it up for that end of the pen to instead be a home button). I really like this device overall, but it's pricey for what you get—aside from the customizable pen buttons, there's not much to differentiate it from my top picks.

ReMarkable Paper Pro Move for $449: The ReMarkable Paper Pro Move is similar in size to a reporter's notebook, which turns out to be a pretty great size for daily task and to-do lists. There's room for a multilevel to-do list and brainstorming, and it's a nice, small size with just a 7.3-inch screen. There are other small options on the market, but this is the only one designed like a long notebook rather than a square, e-reader-like design. I like this size to layer on top of a paper planner or slip into a bag. It can do everything the larger Paper Pro can, including packing a color screen, and honestly feels like you sliced off a bottom third of the device and kept using it.

The ReMarkable Paper Pure. Photograph: Nena Farrell

ReMarkable Paper Pure for $399: This is another good budget option if you want something larger than the Supernote Nomad. It has the same price as the second-generation Kindle Scribe I adore, but with more powerful digital notebook tools instead of a focus on reading. If you're looking for a great digital notebook without spending the better part of a grand, ReMarkable's new Paper Pure is its new basic digital notebook with a black-and-white screen, a lightweight feel, and a great writing experience that is one of the closest things you'll get to writing on actual paper. It doesn't have a front light, though, so you need to use it in lit rooms only.

ReMarkable 2 for $419 (Refurbished): This is the older ReMarkable digital notebook from 2020, and it's still a great device with a great range of accessories—while they're still available, that is. This device is only available refurbished or secondhand after getting essentially replaced earlier this year with the ReMarkable Paper Pure.

Rocketbook Fusion Plus for $30: If you really prefer the paper experience and don't want something you need to charge, then Rocketbook is for you. Rocketbook makes several reusable notebooks, planners, and accessories like index cards and sticky notes. I like the Rocketbook Fusion Plus since it comes with a ton of different template styles, from your classic monthly and weekly pages to project management layouts and meeting notes, making it feel closer to the variety a digital notebook can offer you. Take notes with an erasable Pilot Frixion Pen (one comes with whichever item you buy), scan photos of the pages into the Rocketbook app, and erase the whole thing with the damp microfiber cloth (also included). The app is designed to keep everything organized and easily send things off to Google Drive, Slack, Trello, OneNote, and a handful of other options.

FAQs Do You Need a Digital Note-Taking Device? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The short answer is no. These devices are expensive, usually costing several hundred dollars when a simple notebook and pen costs a few bucks. But if you like the physical act of writing but need to have digital copies, they're worth considering. Pros: Digital notebooks are thin and light but hold hundreds of notes.

You can transcribe your notes into text files, making them easier to read and manipulate.

Depending on the device, you can export files as PDFs, Google Docs, Evernote files, and more.

Instantly digitizes your art, too. Cons: Expensive.

Need to be charged.

Have a learning curve.

Most smart pens need to be paired with an accompanying notebook. The upcoming Nuwa Pen promises smart notes on any paper. What About an iPad? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron E Ink notebooks are easier on the eyes and feel closer to paper than a glass-screened tablet. But in some cases, you might spend less getting an iPad and an Apple Pencil (and a keyboard if you also want to type sometimes). You can also do more on them thanks to the thousands of apps in the App Store. An iPad is pretty intuitive if you're familiar with the Apple ecosystem (though both ReMarkable and Supernote's ecosystems are also very intuitive). Past WIRED reviewers liked using an iPad with the GoodNotes and Notability apps; check out our guide to the Best iPads for more advice on which to buy. I also have an iPad, and I'll say the upside of a digital notebook is that the battery tends to last longer, especially if you're the type to use it for a day or two and then forget about it for a few days. My trusty Kindle Scribe usually manages to have plenty of battery available for whenever I feel the note-taking itch, even if it's been a week or two since I last touched it. Why Are Digital Notebooks So Expensive? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Just because these devices look like paper doesn't mean they're as cheap to make as a sheet of paper. Like any tablet or smartphone, these devices are packed with features, a special ecosystem, and the E Ink technology is no small feat to perfect, along with a sensation similar to writing on paper. It's an impressive piece of technology. Prices haven't gotten cheaper for this category in the wake of tariffs' causing technology prices to rise. ReMarkable recently raised the price of our top pick, the ReMarkable Paper Pro. Another favorite of ours from Supernote has gone up a little less than $50, and Kobo also slightly raised its prices, though the $10 increase is pretty minor compared to other increases we’ve seen. We'll continue to monitor prices and flag if more price changes are to come.

Tech.title: How to Run SteamOS on Your Mac
Tech.content:
Most of my Steam collection won't run on my Mac. It's not (entirely) my fault.

I will be the first to admit that my collection is mostly old indie games, all of which work fine on Windows. Less so on the Mac. Apple stopped supporting 32-bit games back in 2019 when it released macOS Catalina. A good chunk of my Steam library has a "No" symbol next to it because of that restriction. And next year it will get even worse: macOS will drop support for running Intel Mac applications, which could leave even more games unplayable (though Apple claims that certain older games will keep working).

But there's another way. A free, open source app called FX Steam Launcher boots the ARM version of SteamOS—the operating system that powers Valve's Steam Deck gaming handheld—right on your Mac, using a combination of a virtual machine and compatibility layers. You will need a Mac with an Apple Silicon processor, as Intel Macs aren't supported, running macOS 15 or later. I set this up recently, connected a controller, and I've been playing all kinds of games that are otherwise unplayable on my MacBook Air.

It wasn't even hard to set up. To get started, download the application, mount the DMG file, and drag the app to your Applications folder. The first time you launch the application, a pop-up will offer to download and install SteamOS for you in a virtual machine.
